### [1] [Explaining GAND: A Resource on Gender-Ambiguous Natural Data & Contrastive Attribution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22546)
*Janiça Hackenbuchner,Jasper Degraeuwe,Arda Tezcan,Joke Daems*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces GAND, a natural-data benchmark to study how machine translation systems handle gender when the source text is ambiguous, and uses it to analyze which contextual cues drive gender choices in translations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Machine translation systems often default to gender stereotypes or biased defaults when translating sentences without explicit gender cues, potentially harming users and misrepresenting their identities. Existing benchmarks do not sufficiently capture naturally occurring, gender-ambiguous contexts needed to diagnose this behavior. The authors aim to provide a resource and analysis framework to understand how contextual information in source sentences affects gender realization in target languages with grammatical gender.

Method: The authors construct GAND, a benchmark of English sentences that are naturally gender-ambiguous but contain varied contextual cues relevant to gender realization in translation. They then select a subset of these sentences and translate them into two target languages that mark grammatical gender. For each translation, they manually create contrastive variants that differ in the gender realization of the referent. Using these original and contrastive translations, they perform a feature attribution analysis to identify which specific source words and contextual elements most influence the model’s gender choice for ambiguous referents.

Result: GAND enables a systematic interpretability study showing that MT systems rely on particular lexical and contextual cues in the source language when assigning gender in the target. The feature attribution analysis highlights which words in the English input steer the translation toward one gender or another in the grammatically gendered target languages. This reveals how and when gender stereotypes or default behaviors arise in practice.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that benchmarking on natural, gender-ambiguous data is crucial for diagnosing gender bias in machine translation. GAND provides such a benchmark and, combined with contrastive translations and feature attribution methods, offers a way to interpret and quantify how contextual cues influence gendered outcomes. This approach can guide future debiasing and evaluation efforts for MT systems to better respect user identity and reduce harm from stereotyped translations.

Abstract: Machine translation (MT) systems continue to produce gender-biased translations. In a time where self-expression is paramount, mistranslations based on default behaviour and stereotyping can lead to harm for users of these systems. To better understand how these systems translate gender in the absence of clear gender cues, we need benchmarking resources that reflect gender-ambiguous scenarios in a natural way. To this end, we present GAND, a gender-ambiguous natural data benchmarking resource for MT consisting of English source sentences, specifically designed to analyse the influence of contextual cues on gender in translation. We leverage GAND to conduct an interpretability analysis: we translate a subset of GAND into two grammatical gender languages and extend these with manually crafted contrastive translations. A following feature attribution analysis reveals source words in context that inform the gender translation of an ambiguous referent entity in the target translation.

</details>


### [2] [MioFFAn: an Annotation Software for Formula Formalization with LLM Automation Capabilities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22552)
*Nicolas Sibuet,Horacio Saggion,Riccardo Rossi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces MioFFAn, a framework to accelerate the creation of datasets for translating mathematical expressions in scientific papers into executable symbolic code.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Formula Formalization—translating mathematical notation in scientific texts into executable symbolic code—lacks sufficient, high-quality ground-truth datasets, especially in technical domains. This data scarcity blocks progress in automation and evaluation of methods for this task.

Method: The authors build MioFFAn on top of the existing MioGatto architecture, extending it with features tailored to Formula Formalization: selecting relevant equations, assisting users in specifying symbolic code, allowing configurable taxonomies and properties for symbols and operators, and integrating partial automation via Large Language Models. They define modular automated sub-tasks with strict output formats so that automation can be iteratively refined and quantitatively evaluated with NLP metrics.

Result: They provide an open-source, document-centric, customizable annotation framework that supports human-in-the-loop creation of Formula Formalization datasets. They also describe a current automation pipeline based on LLMs and conduct a preliminary evaluation showing that the framework and automation approach are effective in supporting the annotation process.

Conclusion: MioFFAn makes it easier to build high-quality datasets for translating mathematical formulas into symbolic code across specialized scientific domains. Its configurable annotation tools and modular, LLM-assisted automation create a flexible, extensible, and evaluable human-in-the-loop workflow for Formula Formalization.

Abstract: The automatic translation of mathematical expressions in scientific literature into executable symbolic code (a process we refer to as Formula Formalization) is hindered by a severe scarcity of high-quality, ground-truth datasets specialized for technical scientific domains. In this paper, we present MioFFAn, an open-source, document-centric, and customizable framework designed to facilitate rapid annotation for this task. Building upon the MioGatto architecture, we extend existing features to overcome structural limitations and pivot its scope by introducing specific functionalities for Formula Formalization, such as selection of equations of interest and aided symbolic code specification. By allowing users to configure custom taxonomies and properties for identified symbols, and compatible symbolic operators, we ensure the framework is adaptable to diverse specialized scientific fields. Furthermore, MioFFAn is designed to incorporate partial automation via Large Language Models. By defining a modular set of automated sub-tasks with strict output formats, we enable researchers to iteratively refine automation capabilities and evaluate competing strategies using standard NLP metrics. We specify the current automation methodology and perform a preliminary evaluation that demonstrates to efficacy of this human-in-the-loop approach.

</details>


### [3] [Evaluating the Impact of Reviewer Guideline Design on LLM-Based Automated Peer Review](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22553)
*Haowen Li,Yoichi Ishibashi,Masafumi Oyamada*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how different types of reviewer guidelines influence the quality of automated peer review and finds that official conference guidelines work best, while rigid rubrics and LLM-generated reviewer-style guidelines perform worse.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Peer review workloads are increasing, making automation desirable, but it is unclear what kind of guidelines best steer automated reviewing systems toward human-like, high-quality judgments.

Method: The authors compare multiple guideline types for automated peer review: (1) official conference reviewer guidelines and (2) reviewer-imitating guidelines generated by LLMs from high-quality human reviews, and they also study the effect of imposing strict rubric-style scoring versus allowing more subjective, holistic scoring. They then empirically evaluate how well the resulting automated reviews align with human judgments.

Result: Official conference guidelines lead to automated review outputs that are most consistent with human evaluators. Reviewer-imitating, LLM-generated guidelines generally perform worse than official guidelines, and strict rubric-style scoring systematically reduces performance compared to more flexible, subjective scoring schemes.

Conclusion: Refined, practice-tested conference guidelines are highly effective for steering automated peer review systems, while trying to imitate human reviewers via LLM-generated guidelines or enforcing rigid rubric scores can hurt performance. Successful automated reviewing should preserve some subjectivity and holistic assessment rather than relying on overly strict rubrics.

Abstract: Peer review is an essential process in scientific research, yet the growing workload has made its automation increasingly necessary. In this study, we analyze how different types of reviewer guidelines, such as official conference guidelines and reviewer-imitating ones generated from high-quality human reviews using LLMs, affect automated peer review. Our experiments show that official conference guidelines produce review results most consistent with human judgments, suggesting that evaluation criteria refined through conference practice serve as effective guidance for automated reviewing as well. In contrast, reviewer-imitating guidelines were generally less effective than official conference guidelines. Furthermore, enforcing strict rubric-style scoring consistently degraded performance, highlighting the importance of allowing subjective and holistic scoring.

</details>


### [4] [Learning When to Reason for Text-to-SQL via SFT and DPO](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22622)
*Soohyuk Jang,Jiheum Yeom,Nohil Park,Sang Hun Kim,Yoonyoung Choi,Kiwook Bae,Sungroh Yoon*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: AutoThinkSQL dynamically decides when to use step-by-step reasoning in Text-to-SQL, improving accuracy on complex benchmarks while cutting tokens and latency versus always using Chain-of-Thought.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recent Text-to-SQL systems lean heavily on Chain-of-Thought reasoning to handle complex queries, which boosts performance but significantly increases inference cost. In practice, many real-world SQL queries are simple and do not require multi-step reasoning, so forcing CoT on all inputs wastes computation and time. There is a need for a mechanism that selectively applies deep reasoning only when necessary, balancing accuracy and efficiency.

Method: The authors introduce AutoThinkSQL, a framework that embeds an "auto-thinking" mechanism into both Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) for Text-to-SQL models. The model is trained to conditionally decide whether to bypass explicit reasoning for simple queries or to generate full Chain-of-Thought style reasoning for more complex ones. This decision process is learned from data rather than fixed by heuristics, and is applied during decoding so the model can adapt its reasoning depth per query.

Result: Using Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B as the base model, AutoThinkSQL outperforms strong baselines on the Spider and BIRD Text-to-SQL benchmarks. Compared to a CoT-only generation strategy, it reduces average output tokens by 24.6% on Spider and 18.3% on BIRD, and cuts average latency by 17.1% and 11.5%, respectively, while still improving accuracy. Analysis shows that the learned mechanism tends to invoke more reasoning on genuinely difficult queries and skip it on easier ones.

Conclusion: AutoThinkSQL demonstrates that reasoning in Text-to-SQL can be made adaptive rather than uniform: models can learn when to think step-by-step and when to respond directly. This leads to better accuracy–efficiency trade-offs, with less token generation and lower latency without sacrificing (and even improving) performance. The alignment between the model’s reasoning decisions and query difficulty suggests that selective reasoning is a promising direction for cost-effective deployment of reasoning-augmented LLM systems.

Abstract: Recent Text-to-SQL methods rely heavily on reasoning-centric paradigms such as Chain-of-Thought (CoT), achieving substantial gains on complex benchmarks at the cost of high inference-time overhead. However, a large fraction of real-world queries are simple lookups or aggregations that can be resolved without multi-step deduction, making forced reasoning wasteful. Thus, we propose AutoThinkSQL, a framework that integrates an auto-thinking mechanism into both Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) on Text-to-SQL. Our approach enables the model to dynamically bypass reasoning for simple queries while invoking deep CoT for complex queries. On Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, our method achieves consistent gains compared to the best counterpart baseline on both Spider and BIRD benchmarks while simultaneously reducing average output tokens by 24.6% and 18.3%, and average latency by 17.1% and 11.5% compared to CoT-only generation. Further analysis indicates that the model learns to align its reasoning decisions with query difficulty.

</details>


### [5] [Between Suppression and Collapse: Evaluating Narrative Unlearning with LENS](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22657)
*Viktoriia Makovska,George Fletcher*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes LENS, a framework to evaluate how well machine-unlearning methods suppress specific geopolitical disinformation narratives in LLMs, introduces a new efficiency metric (SCE), and shows that unlearning can reduce narrative reproduction but may still allow recovery of real-world actors in abstract prompts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large language models can generate plausible explanations that align with known disinformation narratives. Existing machine-unlearning methods aim to "forget" specific data or behaviors, but there has been no systematic way to evaluate whether they truly suppress targeted narratives across different kinds of prompts and contexts, or whether they cause harmful side effects like general capability collapse. The authors aim to fill this evaluation gap.

Method: The authors introduce LENS (Level-based Evaluation of Narrative Suppression), a contextual evaluation protocol that tests whether models reproduce target narratives under four resistance levels: direct prompts about the narrative, attributed prompts (e.g., citing a source), contrastive prompts (e.g., asking to compare or critique), and abstract prompts (more oblique A/B/C style descriptions). They apply LENS to two geopolitical narratives linked to disinformation and evaluate four ~12B-parameter multilingual instruction-tuned models. They further define the Suppression-Collapse Efficiency (SCE) score, which aggregates how much a checkpoint reduces target narrative reproduction while measuring and penalizing general output degradation, and they analyze behavior before and after unlearning interventions.

Result: Using LENS, the authors find that certain model checkpoints after unlearning interventions successfully reduce reproduction of the targeted narratives, and that this suppression can generalize beyond the exact "forget" prompts used during unlearning. However, they also observe a side effect they call entity recovery: even when direct narrative reproduction is suppressed, abstract prompts can still elicit mention of the real-world actors involved in the targeted frames. The SCE metric allows them to identify checkpoints that balance effective suppression with minimal collapse in overall response quality.

Conclusion: LENS provides a practical and nuanced diagnostic protocol for evaluating and guiding narrative unlearning in LLMs, showing that unlearning can reduce disinformation-aligned narrative reproduction across multiple prompt types, but that deeper narrative structure and actor associations may persist in more abstract settings. The work suggests that future research on unlearning must consider multiple contextual levels and subtle forms of narrative recovery, and that metrics like SCE are useful tools for selecting and comparing unlearning strategies and checkpoints.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can reproduce disinformation-aligned narrative frames as plausible explanations, raising the question of whether existing machine-unlearning algorithms can suppress this behavior. We introduce Level-based Evaluation of Narrative Suppression (LENS), a contextualization based evaluation protocol for testing target narrative reproduction across direct, attributed, contrastive, and abstract resistance levels. We evaluate two source-grounded narratives: one framing Russia's war against Ukraine as forced by NATO expansion, and one framing the United States as exploiting or abandoning Taiwan. The experiments cover four near-12B multilingual instruction models: Lapa LLM, Gemma-12B, Qwen-14B, and TAIDE-Gemma.
  We introduce the Suppression-Collapse Efficiency (SCE) score as a checkpoint selection summary that rewards target-narrative suppression while penalizing degraded outputs. Our results shows that selected checkpoints can reduce narrative reproduction and suppression may transfer beyond direct forget prompts. We also report entity recovery as a separate side effect: abstract A/B/C prompts can cause models to recover the real-world actors associated with the target frame after unlearning. These findings demonstrate that LENS is a successful diagnostic protocol for both reporting and guiding the further study of the deeper structure of narrative unlearning.

</details>


### [6] [PatiGonit22K: A Comprehensive Dataset for Solving Complex Bengali MWPs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22859)
*Swastika Kundu,Azizul Hakim Fayaz,Tashreef Muhammad*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces PatiGonit22K, a large-scale Bengali mathematical word problem dataset of 22,441 problems to advance research on mathematical reasoning in a low-resource language.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mathematical word problems are key for testing language understanding and quantitative reasoning, but Bengali lacks large, annotated datasets compared to high-resource languages, hindering progress in this area.

Method: The authors extend the original PatiGonit dataset by adding a large set of more complex problems. They translate, annotate, culturally adapt, and carefully verify each problem to maintain both linguistic consistency and mathematical correctness, and include a mix of simple and multi-operation equations to balance difficulty.

Result: They create PatiGonit22K, a dataset with 22,441 Bengali mathematical word problems covering a range of difficulty levels, with ensured quality through translation, annotation, adaptation, and verification steps.

Conclusion: PatiGonit22K substantially increases the scale and complexity of available Bengali MWPs, offering a comprehensive benchmark and resource for future work in mathematical reasoning and educational NLP for low-resource languages like Bengali.

Abstract: Mathematical Word Problems (MWPs) are an important benchmark for evaluating natural language understanding and quantitative reasoning. Despite recent progress in high resource languages, Bengali remains underexplored due to the limited availability of large scale annotated datasets. In this work, we introduce PatiGonit22K, an expanded Bengali MWP dataset containing 22,441 problems, developed by extending the original PatiGonit dataset with a substantially larger collection of complex mathematical problems. The dataset includes both simple and multi operation equations, providing a balanced benchmark for evaluating mathematical reasoning across different difficulty levels. Each problem is carefully translated, annotated, culturally adapted, and verified to ensure linguistic consistency and mathematical correctness. By increasing both the scale and complexity of Bengali MWPs, PatiGonit22K provides a more comprehensive resource for future research on mathematical reasoning and educational NLP applications in low resource languages.

</details>


### [7] [CHiPS: Character Histograms and Positional Signals for Lightweight Authorship Attribution in Romanian Texts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22884)
*Sanda-Maria Avram,George C. Ţurcaş*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: CHiPS is a lightweight, transparent, character-level method for Romanian authorship attribution that avoids complex NLP pipelines and higher-order n-grams, yet still achieves high accuracy under strict leakage control.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Authorship attribution systems often rely on complex pipelines (tokenization, syntax, large language models) and high-order character n-grams, which can be opaque, resource-intensive, and vulnerable to data leakage, especially when texts from the same source group appear in both train and test. The authors want to understand how far one can go using only simple, transparent, and tightly controlled character-level evidence for Romanian texts, under rigorous experimental protocols that prevent leakage.

Method: They design CHiPS, which combines two complementary character-level style fingerprints. (1) CH-SVM: a character-histogram SVM classifier using only one-character marginal distributions (no n-grams with n ≥ 2). (2) FFT12-LR: a positional-signal classifier that turns selected characters and punctuation classes into impulse trains over character positions and extracts spectral descriptors via Fourier/Welch methods, classified with logistic regression. They also build CHiPS-F, a leakage-safe fusion of these two classifiers at decision level, plus an optional top-5 reranker trained exclusively on out-of-fold predictions to avoid leakage. They evaluate on Romanian corpora with grouped, locked train/test splits and grouped five-fold model selection to ensure source-text-level separation and strict leakage control.

Result: On a locked grouped ROST split (400 files from 392 source-text groups, 10 authors), CHiPS-F achieves 0.9310 accuracy and 0.9341 macro-F1, with evaluation at the source-text level and grouped five-fold model selection. A stronger but less constrained baseline—character 2–5-gram TF–IDF with SVM—achieves perfect performance (1.0000 accuracy and macro-F1) on the same held-out groups. On a secondary corpus, ROSTories-cleaned (1,248 files from 1,240 groups, 19 authors), CHiPS-R under the same protocol obtains 0.8919 accuracy and 0.8708 macro-F1.

Conclusion: The study shows that even heavily constrained, interpretable character-level features—single-character histograms and positional spectral signals—can support strong authorship attribution performance in Romanian under strict leakage control, though they do not match the ceiling performance of unrestricted character n-gram TF–IDF SVMs. The contribution lies not in state-of-the-art accuracy but in demonstrating how much can be achieved with transparent, low-complexity models and rigorously leakage-safe evaluation protocols.

Abstract: We propose CHiPS, a lightweight character-level authorship attribution method for Romanian texts. All reported experiments are closed-set: the true author is one of the candidate authors in the training data. CHiPS studies two complementary fingerprints of writing style: CH-SVM, a character-histogram classifier based on one-character marginal distributions, and FFT12-LR, a positional-signal classifier that represents selected characters and punctuation classes as impulse trains (binary indicator sequences over character positions) and extracts Fourier/Welch spectral descriptors. We also report CHiPS-F, a leakage-safe decision-level fusion variant, and an optional top-5 listwise reranker trained only on out-of-fold predictions. The method requires no tokenization, syntactic analysis, pretrained language model, or transformer fine-tuning, and it avoids character $n$-gram features with $n \geq 2$ in the histogram component. On a locked grouped ROST split comprising 400 files from 392 source-text groups, written by 10 authors, with source-text-level evaluation and grouped five-fold model selection, CHiPS-F reaches 0.9310 accuracy and 0.9341 macro-F1. A matched but unrestricted character 2--5-gram TF--IDF SVM comparator reaches 1.0000 accuracy and macro-F1 on the same held-out groups, so the contribution is not a claim of best possible classification accuracy. Instead, the experiments ask how far restricted, transparent character evidence can go under strict leakage control. On ROSTories-cleaned, a secondary ROST-overlapping corpus comprising 1,248 files from 1,240 source-text groups, written by 19 authors, the same protocol gives 0.8919 accuracy and 0.8708 macro-F1 for CHiPS-R.

</details>


### [8] [Simple Language Normalization Wins: Cross-Lingual Speaker Verification for the TidyVoice 2026 Challenge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22923)
*Nina Hosseini-Kivanani*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper tackles cross-lingual speaker verification by applying a simple back-end language-normalization method (NAP) on top of a strong ResNet34 baseline, significantly improving error rates and matching more complex systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern speaker verification systems degrade notably when enrollment and test utterances are in different languages, especially in text-independent scenarios without language labels. Existing high-performing approaches can be complex and resource-intensive. The authors aim to explore whether a simple, classical technique—Nuisance Attribute Projection—can effectively mitigate language mismatch in a large, multilingual challenge setting (TidyVoice2026) with many training, development, and unseen evaluation languages.

Method: They start from the official SimAM-ResNet34 embedding model, pretrained on VoxBlink2 and VoxCeleb2 and fine-tuned on the TidyVoice2026 data. In the embedding space, they estimate a low-dimensional language subspace using cross-language same-speaker embedding differences. They then apply Nuisance Attribute Projection to remove (project out) this language subspace, effectively normalizing language information. After this projection, they perform cosine similarity scoring between enrollment and test embeddings, followed by Adaptive Symmetric score normalization (AS-Norm) as a back-end scoring enhancement.

Result: On the development set, the baseline cosine scoring has an EER of 2.97%, and AS-Norm reduces it to 2.70%. With the proposed NAP-based language-normalization, EER further drops to 2.18%. On the Codabench evaluation for TidyVoice2026, the system achieves a score of 8.40, which is competitive with much more complex approaches in the challenge.

Conclusion: A straightforward application of Nuisance Attribute Projection as a language-normalization step in the embedding space can substantially reduce cross-lingual mismatch in text-independent speaker verification. When combined with a strong SimAM-ResNet34 baseline and AS-Norm scoring, this simple back-end technique attains performance comparable to more elaborate systems, suggesting that careful handling of language variation at the embedding level is highly effective and should be considered before resorting to complex architectures.

Abstract: Cross-lingual mismatch remains a key source of overall degradation in modern speaker verification. The TidyVoice2026 Challenge targets this setting with text-independent verification, comprising 3,666 training and 808 development speakers in 40 languages and 2,200 evaluation speakers in 38 unseen languages, without language labels at test time. Starting from the official SimAM-ResNet34 baseline pretrained on VoxBlink2 and VoxCeleb2 and fine-tuned on TidyVoice, we revisit Nuisance Attribute Projection (NAP) as a simple language-normalization step in the embedding space. We estimate a compact language subspace from cross-language same-speaker differences and project embeddings onto its orthogonal complement before cosine scoring with Adaptive Symmetric score normalization. This reduces development EER from 2.97\% with cosine and 2.70\% with AS-Norm to 2.18\% and yields a Codabench evaluation score of 8.40, showing that simple back-end language normalization can rival more complex systems.

</details>


### [9] [Not All LLM Reasoning is Visible in the Chain-of-Thought](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22925)
*Vatsal Baherwani,Tom Goldstein,Ashwinee Panda*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Paper shows that large language models can do hidden reasoning using semantically irrelevant filler tokens, improving performance without visible reasoning traces.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate whether language models reveal all their reasoning in their output tokens, a core concern for AI safety and interpretability. The authors want to find concrete evidence of 'invisible reasoning' where models perform meaningful internal computation that is not explicitly expressed in natural language reasoning steps.

Method: They design synthetic reasoning tasks and introduce semantically irrelevant filler tokens into the prompts. They then systematically evaluate 13 frontier language models on three such tasks, varying the filler tokens and measuring changes in accuracy. They also construct a hidden modular arithmetic constraint task for Claude Opus 4.5 to test if the model can satisfy a secondary objective encoded via filler tokens without affecting primary task performance. Finally, they study the effect of reinforcement learning and supervised fine-tuning on models’ use and preference for filler tokens, focusing on Qwen3-235B.

Result: Many evaluated models show significant accuracy gains—up to 13 percentage points—when specific filler tokens are included, even though these tokens are semantically irrelevant to the nominal task. The effect depends on the choice of filler tokens and differs by model. Claude Opus 4.5 is able to use filler tokens to satisfy a hidden modular arithmetic constraint while still solving the main task correctly, meaning the extra reasoning is invisible to chain-of-thought monitoring. Qwen3-235B develops strong preferences over the content of filler tokens under reinforcement learning, but neither RL nor supervised fine-tuning leads to a filler-token-induced performance benefit that generalizes to test time.

Conclusion: Frontier language models can already perform important internal computations that are not reflected in their output tokens, enabling hidden objectives and constraints that escape chain-of-thought or output-based monitoring. This challenges assumptions in AI safety and interpretability that reasoning is fully externalized in model outputs, suggesting the need for new methods to detect and govern invisible reasoning and hidden objectives.

Abstract: A key question for AI safety is whether a language model expresses all of its reasoning in its output tokens. We demonstrate a concrete failure mode where frontier models exhibit invisible reasoning by leveraging semantically irrelevant filler tokens to improve performance on synthetic reasoning tasks. We evaluate 13 frontier language models across three tasks and find that many models benefit significantly from filler tokens, with accuracy improvements of up to 13 percentage points. The benefit depends on which tokens are used and differs across models. We further show that filler tokens enable Claude Opus 4.5 to satisfy a hidden modular arithmetic constraint without sacrificing accuracy on its primary task, demonstrating that invisible reasoning can serve objectives entirely invisible to CoT monitoring. Reinforcement learning gives Qwen3-235B strong preferences over filler token content, but neither RL nor supervised fine-tuning produces a filler token benefit that persists at test time. Our results indicate that frontier models already perform consequential computation with no interpretable trace in their output tokens.

</details>


### [10] [Toward Automated Detection of Documentation Inconsistencies in Electronic Health Records](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22954)
*Jian Lu,Panyu Chen,Miriam Treggiari,Robert Blessing,Danyang Zhuo,Chunhua Weng,William W. Stead,Anru R. Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper evaluates whether a general-purpose LLM can detect internal inconsistencies in real-world hospital discharge summaries and analyzes both the types of inconsistencies found and the LLM’s failure modes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Electronic health record (EHR) discharge summaries often contain internal contradictions or inconsistencies (e.g., in demographics, meds, or diagnoses) that can undermine clinical reasoning and patient safety. Manual auditing is infeasible at scale, and it is unclear how reliably general-domain LLMs can identify such inconsistencies in noisy, real-world notes. The authors aim to systematically characterize the strengths and weaknesses of using an LLM-based pipeline for this task, to inform future large-scale, validated approaches.

Method: The authors built a two-stage LLM pipeline and applied it to 3,000 randomly sampled discharge summaries from the MIMIC-IV-Note corpus. Stage 1 used Gemini 2.5 Pro to perform open-ended detection of potential internal inconsistencies within each note. Stage 2 used Gemini 2.5 Flash to re-check each candidate in a more constrained, context-grounded fashion. Clinical experts then manually reviewed a subset of the pipeline’s outputs to categorize the inconsistency types and to identify where and why the LLMs failed.

Result: The pipeline identified 3,460 potential inconsistencies across the 3,000 notes, impacting roughly 70% of admissions. The inconsistencies covered multiple domains, including demographics, allergies, procedures, diagnoses, labs, medications, and care planning, and many had direct relevance to reasoning about the case or to patient safety. Expert review also highlighted systematic failure modes, such as difficulty with temporal reasoning (e.g., changes over time in the note), understanding evolving diagnoses, and lacking specific knowledge about outpatient prescribing conventions, all of which limited verification reliability.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates that a general-domain LLM can surface a wide range of clinically meaningful documentation inconsistencies in discharge summaries, but also exhibits systematic limitations that must be addressed before deployment at scale. The authors offer a graded ontology and schema to classify inconsistencies by contradiction severity, note section, domain, and inconsistency axis, providing a conceptual and methodological basis for future, validated large-scale analyses of EHR documentation quality.

Abstract: Objective: To characterize the kinds of internal documentation inconsistencies a general-domain large language model (LLM) can surface from real-world discharge summaries, and to identify recurring failure modes that limit reliability at scale.
  Materials and Methods: We applied a two-stage LLM pipeline---open-ended candidate identification (Gemini 2.5 Pro) followed by context-grounded verification (Gemini 2.5 Flash)---to 3,000 randomly sampled MIMIC-IV-Note discharge summaries. A subset of the pipeline output was then reviewed manually by clinical experts.
  Results: Our pipeline surfaced 3,460 candidate inconsistencies, affecting 69.7% of admissions. Representative examples spanned demographics, allergies, procedures, diagnoses, laboratory, medications, and care-planning domains, with direct implications for clinical reasoning or patient safety. Expert review also revealed recurring failure modes that arise when verification requires temporal reasoning, evolving-diagnosis context, or knowledge of outpatient-prescribing conventions the model does not natively possess.
  Discussion: Detection is highly context-dependent: many flagged pairs require anchoring each statement to its source section and clinical domain, then assessing whether the conflict reflects a true contradiction or missing context. We propose a graded ontology spanning strict contradiction and ambiguity, with a schema characterizing each flagged case by category, section, domain, and inconsistency axis.
  Conclusion: This formative study establishes a methodological foundation and conceptual framework to guide subsequent validated, large-scale EHR-inconsistency analysis.

</details>


### [11] [Beyond Direct Answering: Aligning Educational LLMs as Socratic Guides via Heuristic Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22996)
*Xiaokun Wang,Siyu Song,Wentao Liu,Xiaodong Zou*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They align a 7B LLM to behave like a Socratic tutor rather than a direct answerer using a two-stage training pipeline with heuristic rewards and show big gains in scaffolding quality and reduced answer leakage, while a much larger unaligned model fails.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs in education tend to give away answers immediately, which conflicts with Socratic, inquiry-based pedagogy that aims to scaffold students’ thinking. Existing large models don’t naturally show this behavior, so there is a need for explicit alignment methods and better evaluation metrics for educational dialogue quality beyond fluency.

Method: They propose HeuristicEdu, a two-phase alignment pipeline for Qwen2.5-7B: (1) supervised warm-up on SocraticEdu, a dataset of 797 reconstructed multi-turn Chinese science tutoring dialogs, and (2) GRPO-based reinforcement learning using heuristic rewards that promote cognitive depth (Rcog), curiosity engagement (Reng), and discourage direct answer leakage (Rdir), plus a K_query correction to handle student-introduced terms. They also define new evaluation metrics, Scaffolding Effectiveness (SE) and Conversation Depth (CD), to assess Socratic quality.

Result: On 30 held-out children’s science questions, their best GRPO variant nearly doubles Scaffolding Effectiveness (SE) from 30.0% to 63.3% and cuts keyword leakage from 30.0% to 13.3%. Interestingly, the best-performing setup does not include the explicit directness penalty during optimization, implying that such anti-leakage heuristics may interfere with gradient-based alignment. A much larger, unaligned Qwen-72B performs poorly on Socratic behavior (0% SE and 96.7% leakage), indicating that scaling alone does not yield good tutoring conduct.

Conclusion: HeuristicEdu effectively steers a mid-sized LLM toward Socratic tutoring behavior using a combination of supervised learning, heuristic-reward reinforcement learning, and specialized evaluation metrics. Performance gains over both the supervised-only and much larger unaligned model show that targeted alignment, not just scale, is key to eliciting high-quality, inquiry-based educational dialogues. The surprising benefit of dropping the explicit directness penalty highlights the subtlety of designing reward functions for pedagogical alignment.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) deployed in educational settings often behave as direct answerers: they disclose target concepts in the opening turn instead of guiding students through progressive inquiry, as Socratic pedagogy prescribes. We present HeuristicEdu, a two-phase pipeline that aligns Qwen2.5-7B toward Socratic tutoring via supervised warm-up and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Training uses SocraticEdu, 797 multi-turn Chinese children's science dialogues reconstructed from a live platform, with a heuristic reward over cognitive depth (R_cog), curiosity engagement (R_eng), and directness (R_dir), together with a K_query correction for student-introduced terms. We introduce Scaffolding Effectiveness (SE) and Conversation Depth (CD) to evaluate outcomes beyond surface fluency. On 30 held-out questions, the best GRPO variant improves SE from 30.0% to 63.3% and lowers keyword leakage from 30.0% to 13.3%. Notably, this best variant omits the directness penalty during optimization, suggesting that explicit anti-leakage terms can conflict with gradient-based behavioral alignment. An unaligned Qwen-72B baseline reaches 0% SE and 96.7% leakage, showing that scale alone does not induce Socratic behavior.

</details>


### [12] [Speech Signals Complement LLMs for Predicting Interpersonal Attraction in Speed Dating](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23037)
*Yuriko Kikuchi,Takato Hayashi,Ryusei Kimura,Naoya Inoue,Ryo Ishii,Shogo Okada*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies whether adding speech-based features improves prediction of interpersonal attraction beyond what large language models can infer from text transcripts alone, using Japanese speed-dating conversations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Previous work shows that large language models can predict how much people like each other from conversation transcripts, but it is unclear whether acoustic/prosodic information in speech still adds anything once text-based LLM predictions are available. Understanding this matters for building better social interaction predictors and for clarifying when multimodal signals are complementary.

Method: Using recordings of Japanese speed-dating conversations, the authors: (1) obtain transcript-only LLM predictions of each participant’s reported liking of their partner; (2) train a supervised speech-based predictor on acoustic features; (3) combine the two predictors and evaluate performance on two tasks: pairwise ranking accuracy of attraction and per-participant Pearson correlation between predicted and self-reported liking; (4) analyze how much and under what conditions the speech predictor adds value beyond the LLM.

Result: Combining speech-based predictions with transcript-only LLM predictions improves pairwise ranking accuracy in all tested conditions compared with using the transcript-only LLM alone. However, improvements in per-participant Pearson correlation are inconsistent across conversation rounds and rating directions and do not remain statistically significant after multiple-comparisons correction. Post-hoc analysis shows that the correlation gains are mostly found among participants for whom the speech predictor by itself is relatively accurate.

Conclusion: Speech carries complementary information about interpersonal attraction that can enhance transcript-based LLM predictions, but this benefit is conditional rather than universal. The added value of speech appears concentrated in subsets of participants where the speech model performs well. Therefore, the key question is not just whether speech helps prediction overall, but in which contexts and for which individuals its complementarity with text-based LLMs emerges.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can predict interpersonal attraction from conversation transcripts, but it remains unclear what a speech predictor can add beyond transcript-only LLM prediction. Using Japanese speed-dating conversations, we combine predictions from a transcript-only LLM and a supervised speech predictor to estimate participants' reported liking of their partners. We show that speech can complement transcript-only LLM prediction, but that this complementarity is conditional rather than universal. Combining the two predictions significantly improves pairwise ranking accuracy over the transcript-only LLM alone in all evaluated conditions. By contrast, gains in per-participant Pearson $r$ vary across conversation rounds and rating directions, with none significant after correction. Retrospectively, these $r$ gains are concentrated among participants for whom the speech predictor is more accurate. Speech can therefore retain predictive value even when an LLM predicts attraction from transcripts. The relevant question is not simply whether speech helps, but where its complementarity emerges.

</details>


### [13] [ADAGE: A Language-Agnostic Pipeline for Analogical Reasoning Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23058)
*Ahmed Haj Ahmed,Alvin Grissom*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They build a new, translation-free multilingual benchmark (ADAGE) for testing culturally grounded analogical reasoning, showing big performance drops for current models outside English.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current multilingual reasoning evaluation mostly translates English benchmarks, which (1) introduces translation artifacts, (2) fails to capture culture-specific, native-language reasoning like proverbs and analogies, and (3) can overestimate models’ real-world multilingual reasoning abilities. The authors want a way to rigorously test abstract, culturally grounded reasoning directly in different languages without relying on English as the source.

Method: They propose ADAGE, a language-agnostic pipeline. It combines curation by native speakers with LLM-assisted generation to design hard, translation-free benchmarks targeting abstract analogical reasoning (e.g., proverb-like analogies). They apply this pipeline to create new datasets in three typologically and culturally distinct languages: Arabic, Amharic, and Japanese. Then they evaluate 14 open-weight language models on these benchmarks and compare performance to English proverb reasoning benchmarks.

Result: Using the ADAGE-created benchmarks, they observe a clear “cultural reasoning gap”: models that perform strongly on English proverb reasoning perform much worse on the new Arabic, Amharic, and Japanese benchmarks. The accuracy drops by around 12–52 percentage points when moving from English to these native-language, culturally grounded tasks, even though the models are presumably multilingual.

Conclusion: Translation-based multilingual benchmarks are insufficient for testing culturally grounded reasoning. The ADAGE pipeline effectively constructs hard, native-language analogical reasoning benchmarks and reveals substantial gaps in current models’ cultural reasoning abilities across languages. The released pipeline, datasets, and evaluation suite enable more realistic and rigorous assessment and future improvement of multilingual reasoning models.

Abstract: Multilingual reasoning evaluation overwhelmingly relies on translating English benchmarks, a practice that introduces linguistic artifacts and fails to test culturally-grounded reasoning. We introduce ADAGE (Analogical Difficulty-by-design Assessment for Grounded Evaluation), a language-agnostic pipeline that combines native-speaker curation with LLM-assisted generation to construct challenging, translation-free benchmarks for abstract analogical reasoning. We validate ADAGE by constructing benchmarks for Arabic, Amharic, and Japanese. Evaluating 14 open-weight models, we find a consistent cultural reasoning gap: models that perform well on English proverb reasoning struggle substantially on all three native benchmarks, with accuracy dropping by 12--52 percentage points relative to English. We release the pipeline, all three benchmarks, and the full evaluation suite.

</details>


### [14] [Attention-Guided Layer Selection for Contrastive Decoding in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23067)
*Yusuke Sakai,Natthawut Kertkeidkachorn,Kiyoaki Shirai*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They improve contrastive decoding for LLMs by using attention-based signals to choose which layers to contrast, yielding better factuality than DoLa on TruthfulQA.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing contrastive decoding like DoLa improves factuality by contrasting mature vs. premature layers, but it picks layers only by looking at divergences in output token distributions. This may miss richer internal signals about what the model is attending to, potentially limiting factuality gains.

Method: They introduce three attention-guided layer selection strategies—Attention-JSD, Attention-Entropy-Max, and Attention-Entropy-Min—that use statistics of self-attention patterns (e.g., divergence between attention distributions and entropy of attention) as the signal for choosing which layer pairs to contrast during decoding instead of relying purely on output logits.

Result: On the TruthfulQA benchmark, especially for the multi-answer settings (MC2 and MC3), their attention-guided variants, notably Attention-JSD and Attention-Entropy-Min, consistently beat the original DoLa in factuality metrics.

Conclusion: Internal attention distributions carry useful structural information about factual reasoning that is more sensitive than output-token distributions alone. Using attention-based signals for dynamic layer selection in contrastive decoding can yield more truthful LLM outputs than the original DoLa approach.

Abstract: Contrastive decoding methods such as DoLa improve the factuality of Large Language Models (LLMs) by contrasting the output distributions of mature and premature layers. However, DoLa's dynamic layer selection relies solely on divergences in output vocabulary distributions. In this work, we propose three attention-guided strategies: Attention-JSD, Attention-Entropy-Max, and Attention-Entropy-Min, which leverage structural information carried by internal self-attention mechanisms as a signal for layer selection. Experimental results on TruthfulQA demonstrate that our strategies, particularly Attention-JSD and Attention-Entropy-Min, consistently outperform the original DoLa. We observe significant gains on multi-answer metrics (MC2 and MC3), suggesting that attention distributions can provide a more sensitive signal for resolving factual knowledge than output vocabulary distributions.

</details>


### [15] [LoRA for Gender-Inclusive Rewriting and Activation Steering for Counter-Narrative Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23083)
*Akhil Rajeev P,Manoj Balaji J*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces IHLC, a system for gender-inclusive language rewriting and counter-narrative generation that combines LoRA fine-tuning with an activation-steering method based on PCA-derived directions in hidden states.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current language models often produce gender-biased or non-inclusive text and can struggle to generate effective, polite counter-narratives. Existing mitigation methods usually require costly parameter updates or full fine-tuning, limiting practicality for deployment and rapid adaptation. The authors aim to create a more compute-efficient, controllable approach that encourages inclusive, socially aligned outputs without heavy retraining.

Method: For gender-inclusive rewriting, the authors use parameter-efficient LoRA fine-tuning to adapt a base model to rewrite biased text into inclusive alternatives while preserving meaning and coherence. For counter-narrative generation, they propose an inference-time representation engineering technique: they collect contrastive hidden-state activations from inclusive vs. non-inclusive outputs, apply PCA to extract a main “steering direction,” and then inject this direction into intermediate hidden layers of Gemma-3-4B-it during inference. This is combined with constrained prompting to guide the model toward polite, contextually grounded counter-narratives, all without updating model weights.

Result: The LoRA-based gender-inclusive rewriting system achieves an official score of 80.00% on the LT-EDI 2026 Shared Task. The activation-steering-based counter-narrative system, combined with constrained prompting, achieves an official score of 78.12%. Manual analysis reveals both successful steering toward inclusivity and a set of systematic failure modes, such as semantic drift, residual bias, layer-specific sensitivity, over-steering, and text degeneration.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates that activation steering via PCA-derived directions in hidden states is a promising, lightweight alternative to parameter updates for controlling and aligning language model behavior, particularly for gender-inclusive and counter-narrative tasks. However, observed failure modes indicate that the approach is not yet robust: steering intensity, layer choice, and safeguards against semantic drift and degeneration need further refinement before such methods can reliably replace fine-tuning for socially aligned text generation.

Abstract: Gender-inclusive language generation seeks to transform biased text into inclusive alternatives while preserving semantic meaning and contextual coherence. This paper presents the IHLC system for the LT-EDI 2026 Shared Task, addressing both gender-inclusive rewriting and counter-narrative generation. For gender-inclusive rewriting, we employ parameter-efficient Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning, achieving an official score of 80.00%. Our primary contribution is a compute-efficient inference-time representation engineering approach for counter-narrative generation. We derive a principal steering direction from contrastive hidden-state activations using principal component analysis (PCA) and inject it into the intermediate representations of Gemma-3-4B-it during inference, enabling behavioral steering toward inclusive responses without modifying model weights. Combined with constrained prompting, this approach produces polite and contextually appropriate counter-narratives, achieving an official score of 78.12%. We further present a manual analysis of steering behavior, identifying key failure modes including semantic drift, residual bias leakage, layer sensitivity, over-steering, and text degeneration. Our findings highlight both the practical potential and current limitations of activation steering as a lightweight alternative to parameter updates for controllable and socially aligned language generation.

</details>


### [16] [Interview with Kalle Lyytinen on "Implications of Theories of Language for Information Systems"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23142)
*Kalle J. Lyytinen,Pierre Maier,Paul Ackah Toffey*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Reflective interview with Lyytinen on his seminal 1980s paper about language theories in Information Systems, updated with implications of modern large language models and generative AI, and proposing future linguistics‑oriented IS research directions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To revisit and reinterpret the foundational ideas from Lyytinen's classic paper on language theories in information systems in light of dramatic technological and conceptual advances, especially large language models and generative AI, and to assess their continued relevance and evolution.

Method: A reflective, retrospective interview with Lyytinen that combines historical reconstruction of the original paper’s context and intentions, conceptual discussion of the linguistic nature of information systems, and interpretive analysis of how contemporary developments in AI and language technologies relate to those earlier ideas.

Result: The interview surfaces how the original linguistic framing of information systems anticipated later concerns about meaning, communication, and representation in digital systems. It connects these ideas to current developments in large language models and generative AI, clarifying both continuities (IS as fundamentally linguistic) and disruptions (new forms of automation of language use). It also articulates several concrete themes and questions for future IS research from a linguistic perspective.

Conclusion: The linguistic perspective on information systems remains highly relevant and has gained new significance with the rise of generative AI and large language models. Revisiting Lyytinen’s early work helps frame current challenges about meaning, interpretation, and responsibility in AI‑mediated information systems, and suggests a research agenda that integrates linguistic theory, IS design, and emerging AI technologies.

Abstract: Over fourty years after the initial publication of "Implications of Theories of Language for Information Systems" in MIS Quaterly, Lyytinen reflects about the origins of his publication and the developments in this area of research over the past decades. In the here presented interview, Lyytinen discusses the linguistic core of information systems also in light of recent trends and developments in the field, especially with regards to large language models and generative AI. Future research directions following a linguistic perspective on Information Systems (IS) research are outlined.

</details>


### [17] [Beyond a Global Norm: Personalizing Toxicity Sensitivity in Language Models Without Retraining](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23175)
*Rares A. C. Diaconescu,Iulia Slanina,Alina Florea,Andrei B. Trache,Miruna E. Coroi,Anne Arzberger,Jie Yang,Enrico Liscio*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Evaluation of training-free, user-specific toxicity alignment methods across different inference-time stages, showing effectiveness and trade-offs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Global toxicity reduction ignores that harm perceptions are subjective and context-dependent. There is a need to adapt language generation to individual users' toxicity sensitivities without expensive retraining, and to understand which inference-time strategies work best.

Method: Comparative evaluation of multiple training-free alignment methods applied at three inference-time stages: pre-decoding (prompt conditioning and rewriting), in-decoding (token/logit/representation steering), and post-decoding (candidate re-ranking). These methods are tested against user-specific toxicity sensitivity targets derived from the PRISM dataset, and performance is measured in terms of alignment error, personalization, and general language quality.

Result: All evaluated methods reduce alignment error relative to an unaligned baseline by 28–47%. The comparison exposes different performance profiles across methods and stages in terms of how well they match user-specific toxicity thresholds versus how much they degrade general language quality.

Conclusion: Inference-time, training-free methods can substantially improve alignment of text generation to user-specific toxicity sensitivities, but no single method optimizes all goals. Toxicity sensitivity alignment is inherently a multi-objective problem, forcing trade-offs between alignment strength, personalization fidelity, and overall language quality.

Abstract: Reducing toxicity is often framed as a global alignment problem, yet perceptions of harmful language are subjective and context-dependent. We present the first comparative evaluation of training-free methods for aligning language generation to user-specific toxicity sensitivities across three inference-time intervention stages: pre-decoding (prompt conditioning and rewriting), in-decoding (token, logit, and representation steering), and post-decoding (candidate re-ranking). Evaluated against toxicity sensitivity targets derived from the PRISM dataset, all methods reduce alignment error by 28-47%. However, the results reveal a fundamental trade-off between alignment effectiveness, personalization, and general language quality, showing how toxicity sensitivity alignment is an inherently multi-objective problem.

</details>


### [18] [IndicTalk: A Large-Scale Persona-Based Multilingual Conversational Corpus for Indic Languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23242)
*Sahil Deepak Gawande,Mayank Singh*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: IndicTalk is a large, automatically generated, multilingual Indic code-mixed dialogue corpus grounded in news events, designed to improve conversational AI for underrepresented Indic languages.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: High-quality multilingual code-mixed conversational resources, especially for Indic languages, are scarce, limiting the development and evaluation of realistic dialogue systems that reflect speakers’ natural alternation between English and native Indic languages in both native and Romanized scripts.

Method: The authors build a fully automated pipeline that: (1) collects real-world news to ground conversations in concrete events; (2) uses multilingual LLMs with persona conditioning to generate multi-turn dialogues in code-mixed Indic–English, across native and Romanized scripts; and (3) performs automatic quality validation. They then conduct linguistic analysis, automatic metrics, and human evaluations to assess fluency, coherence, and naturalness of code-mixing.

Result: The outcome is IndicTalk: over 1.3 million (1,328,604+) event-grounded, multi-turn conversations spanning 18 language varieties and 9 Indic languages, in both native and Romanized scripts. Evaluations show the generated dialogues are generally fluent, coherent, and exhibit realistic code-mixing patterns.

Conclusion: IndicTalk is one of the largest Indic code-mixed conversational corpora, demonstrating that an LLM-based, fully automated pipeline can produce high-quality, news-grounded, persona-rich dialogues in multiple code-mixed Indic languages. The released dataset can serve as a key resource for training and evaluating multilingual conversational AI systems for underrepresented Indic languages.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have transformed conversational AI, yet high-quality multilingual code-mixed dialogue resources remain scarce, particularly for Indic languages where speakers naturally alternate between English and their native language in both native-script and Romanized forms. We present IndicTalk, one of the largest multilingual Indic code-mixed conversational corpora, comprising over 13,28,604 event-grounded multi-turn conversations across 18 language varieties covering 9 Indic languages. The corpus is generated through a fully automated pipeline that combines real-world news grounding, persona-conditioned dialogue generation using multilingual LLMs, and automatic quality validation. Extensive linguistic, automatic, and human evaluations demonstrate that IndicTalk produces fluent, coherent, and naturally code-mixed conversations across both script variants. We will release IndicTalk to support the development and evaluation of multilingual conversational AI for underrepresented Indic languages. The dataset is available at: https://huggingface.co/datasets/LingoIITGN/IndicTalk .

</details>


### [19] [Co-Evolving Graph and Text Memory for Training-Free Multi-Hop Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23278)
*Hieu Man,Thien Huu Nguyen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper presents Co-E, a training-free system that synchronizes a graph and textual working memory to improve multi-hop question answering.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multi-hop QA methods tend to focus on either text retrieval or knowledge graphs, or on memory mechanisms that are not tightly integrated, leaving a gap in effectively coordinating relational and textual evidence over multiple reasoning steps. There is a need for a system that can leverage both textual context and structured relational knowledge in a unified, dynamically updated way, without requiring heavy training.

Method: The authors introduce Co-E, a training-free framework with synchronized bidirectional graph-text working memory. The system runs a repeated synchronization cycle: it consolidates and updates the textual working memory, extracts relational triples from the text to update a graph memory, and then injects the graph-derived facts back into the language model’s generation context. Both the text memory and the graph memory are maintained and updated across reasoning steps, influencing future retrieval and generation in a closed-loop fashion.

Result: On six multi-hop QA benchmarks, Co-E yields better performance than comparable training-free baselines that use open LLM backbones, and its performance is competitive with larger or specifically trained systems, indicating that the synchronized graph-text memory design is effective even without additional training.

Conclusion: Maintaining and synchronizing both textual and graph working memories in a training-free framework enables more effective multi-hop reasoning than approaches that treat text and structure in isolation. Co-E demonstrates that careful coordination of graph and text evidence can close much of the gap with larger or fine-tuned multi-hop QA systems.

Abstract: Multi-hop question answering requires coordinating relational and textual evidence across reasoning steps, a combination neither a text corpus nor a knowledge graph can supply alone. Prior work often emphasizes only part of this loop: graph-augmented RAG retrieves from a pre-built or query-updated graph, KGQA systems search within topic-centered subgraphs, and memory-augmented agents maintain evolving memories without continuously reconciling graph memory with textual context. We propose Co-E, a training-free system built around synchronized bidirectional graph-text working memory. A synchronization cycle consolidates textual memory, extracts relational triples into graph memory, and injects graph facts back into the generation context. Because both memories are maintained, they shape subsequent retrieval and generation. Evaluated on six multi-hop QA benchmarks, Co-E improves over comparable training-free open-backbone baselines and is competitive with larger or trained systems.

</details>


### [20] [BHARATI: Morphology-Aware Tokenizers for Classical Indian Languages with Subword Fertility Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23319)
*Poornima Kumaresan,Pavithra Muruganantham,Lakshmi Rajendran,Santhosh Sivasubramani*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces BHARATI, a family of multilingual SentencePiece/BPE tokenizers optimized for classical and modern Indic languages, significantly reducing token counts and sequence lengths for Indian Knowledge Systems (IKS) text compared to common baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing subword tokenizers like BPE and SentencePiece are trained mostly on modern, general-purpose text and on non-Indic scripts. They perform poorly on classical Indic languages such as Sanskrit and Tamil, which have agglutinative morphology, sandhi, and specialized IKS vocabularies not present in standard corpora. This leads to inefficient segmentations, longer sequences, and reduced effective context for LMs. The paper aims to build tokenizers that better respect Indic scripts and IKS terminology, improving efficiency and coverage.

Method: The authors construct a 781 MB balanced multilingual corpus covering seven languages (English, Hindi, Sanskrit, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam) and train SentencePiece BPE tokenizers with a 32k vocabulary. They release three successive versions: v1 supporting English and Sanskrit (with limited Tamil via broken byte-fallback), v2 adding four-language support with byte-level fallback for southern languages, and v3 with full seven-language native script subword coverage. They evaluate via subword fertility (tokens per IKS term) and sequence length on a held-out IKS-domain sentence set, comparing against GPT-2, generic multilingual SentencePiece, byte-level encoders, and mBART-50.

Result: The final tokenizer version v3 achieves an average of 2.6 tokens per IKS technical term versus 5.25 for GPT-2 and 3.75 for a multilingual SentencePiece baseline, with especially strong gains on reserved IKS terms that are enforced to be single tokens. On a 490-sentence IKS-domain test set (70 per language across seven languages), v3 reduces average sequence length by ~90% relative to GPT-2 and byte-level encodings, and by ~25% relative to mBART-50, averaged over the six Indic languages. These reductions imply a substantial increase in effective context window for downstream language models.

Conclusion: BHARATI tokenizers substantially improve subword segmentation and sequence length efficiency for classical and modern Indic languages, especially in IKS domains, compared with widely used GPT-2, generic SentencePiece, and mBART-50 tokenizers. The work demonstrates the importance of language- and domain-specific tokenizer training on balanced multilingual corpora with native script support. The authors provide open-source tokenizers, training code, and evaluation benchmarks to facilitate better Indic NLP and future LM development.

Abstract: Standard subword tokenization algorithms such as Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) and SentencePiece are trained predominantly on modern language corpora and produce inefficient segmentations when applied to classical Indian languages. Sanskrit, Tamil, and other classical Indic languages exhibit agglutinative morphology, productive sandhi (phonological fusion at word boundaries), and domain-specific vocabularies absent from general-purpose training data. This paper presents BHARATI, a set of SentencePiece BPE tokenizers trained on a balanced 781 MB corpus spanning seven languages (English, Hindi, Sanskrit, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, and Malayalam) with native script support for all languages. We describe three successive tokenizer versions: v1 (English and Sanskrit only, with broken byte-fallback for Tamil), v2 (four-language support with byte-level fallback for southern languages), and v3 (full seven-language native subword coverage). Subword fertility analysis demonstrates that v3 averages 2.6 tokens per Indian Knowledge System (IKS) technical term, compared to 5.25 tokens per term with GPT-2's tokenizer and 3.75 tokens with the multilingual SentencePiece baseline, with the largest gains on a set of reserved IKS terms that are represented as single tokens by construction. On a held-out test set of 490 IKS-domain sentences (70 per language across seven languages, released with the measurement script), v3 reduces sequence length by roughly 90% relative to GPT-2 and byte-level encoding (which lack native Indic subwords) and by approximately 25% relative to the mBART-50 multilingual baseline, averaged across the six Indic languages, directly translating to increased effective context length for downstream language models. The tokenizer models (32,000 vocabulary), training scripts, and evaluation benchmarks are released under open licenses.

</details>


### [21] [IKS-Instruct: A 24,000-Example Multilingual Dataset for Teaching Language Models Indian Knowledge Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23322)
*Shwetha Singaravelu,Gayathri Muruganantham,Lakshmi Rajendran,Santhosh Sivasubramani*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces IKS-Instruct, a multilingual instruction-tuning dataset focused on Indian Knowledge Systems for educational use, and shows it enables a compact 7B model to approach the performance of a stronger general-purpose model on IKS-specific tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most instruction-tuning datasets are English-centric and general-purpose, with poor coverage of specialized educational domains like Indian Knowledge Systems. The authors aim to create a pedagogically rich, curriculum-aligned dataset to teach models to deliver high-quality educational content grounded in IKS across multiple Indian languages.

Method: The authors construct a dataset of 24,795 instruction-response pairs spanning seven languages, 41 pedagogical techniques, and CBSE classes 6–12. Data is sourced from classical text corpora, curriculum-aligned templates, Vedic math demonstrations, bilingual pairs, multi-turn dialogues, and comparative analyses. They train compact 7B models with this dataset and evaluate quality using a multi-judge LLM-based framework scoring 12 dimensions, plus a five-judge external panel over a stratified sample, using median aggregation.

Result: The best IKS-Instruct fine-tuned 7B model achieves a median external-judge score of 6.39, very close to a much stronger general-purpose reference model (Nemotron-Nano at 6.54), while being much cheaper to deploy. The base 7B model without IKS-specific fine-tuning performs near zero on IKS-specific criteria. They also find that more aggressive data curation does not always yield monotonic gains in model quality, even when measured data quality improves.

Conclusion: A targeted, curriculum-aligned instruction dataset like IKS-Instruct can effectively specialize relatively small models for rich, domain-specific educational tasks in Indian Knowledge Systems, achieving near state-of-the-art performance at lower cost. However, the relationship between data curation and downstream model quality is non-monotonic, highlighting the need for nuanced data engineering strategies.

Abstract: Instruction tuning has become the standard method for adapting large language models to follow human intent, yet existing instruction datasets are dominated by English-language general-knowledge tasks and lack coverage of specialized pedagogical domains. This paper presents IKS-Instruct, a dataset of 24,795 instruction-response pairs for teaching language models to deliver educational content grounded in Indian Knowledge Systems (IKS). The dataset spans seven languages (English, Hindi, Sanskrit, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, and Malayalam), covers 41 pedagogical techniques from the Vedic oral and mathematical traditions, and is aligned with the Central Board of Secondary Education (CBSE) curriculum for classes 6 through 12. The pairs are derived from six source types: classical text corpora (Bhagavad Gita, Thirukkural, Sangam literature, Vedic texts), curriculum-aligned pedagogical templates, Vedic mathematical sutra demonstrations, bilingual instruction pairs, technique-grounded multi-turn dialogues, and cross-tradition comparative analyses. Quality is assessed through a multi-judge evaluation framework in which independent language models score responses on 12 dimensions including technique fidelity, pedagogical quality, factual accuracy, and IKS cultural depth. Under a uniform five-judge external panel (median aggregation over 1,201 stratified items), the strongest IKS-Instruct fine-tune of a compact 7B model reaches a median judge score of 6.39, within 0.15 of a strong general-purpose reference model (Nemotron-Nano at 6.54) at a fraction of its deployment cost, while the base model without IKS fine-tuning scores near zero on the IKS-specific dimensions. Model quality does not increase monotonically with data curation, a result we report together with the corresponding data-quality gains.

</details>


### [22] [BERT-based Models vs. Large Language Models for Low-Resource Named Entity Recognition: A Comparative Study on Marathi](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23344)
*Hariom Ingle,Ronit Ghode,Ishwari Gondkar,Jidnyasa Harad,Raviraj Joshi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper compares fine-tuned, Marathi-specific MahaBERT models against general-purpose LLMs for Marathi NER and shows that specialized, task-focused models clearly outperform large, generic LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Low-resource languages like Marathi lack large annotated NER datasets, making it unclear whether recent general-purpose LLMs can replace or outperform smaller, language-specific models. The authors want to verify if fine-tuning a Marathi-focused model (MahaBERT-v2) is still superior to using off-the-shelf large LLMs for NER in this setting.

Method: Fine-tune MahaBERT-v2 on multiple variants of the MahaNER dataset. Evaluate these fine-tuned models, the existing MahaNER baseline model, and several strong general-purpose LLMs (Gemini, LLaMA-3.3-70B, Gemma) on a Marathi NER test set. Use standard sequence labeling metrics: precision, recall, and F1-score, and perform a systematic comparison across all systems.

Result: Fine-tuned MahaBERT-based models achieve F1-scores between 0.88 and 0.91, slightly improving over the existing MahaNER model (0.8843) and clearly outperforming all tested general-purpose LLMs, whose F1-scores lie between 0.57 and 0.69.

Conclusion: For Marathi NER, specialized, task-specific models like fine-tuned MahaBERT remain more effective than large, general-purpose LLMs, especially in low-resource scenarios. This underscores the ongoing need for language- and domain-focused architectures and datasets instead of relying solely on generic LLMs for low-resource language processing tasks.

Abstract: Named Entity Recognition (NER) for low-resource languages such as Marathi remains a challenging task due to limited annotated resources and linguistic complexity. Although recent Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance across a wide range of natural language processing tasks, their effectiveness for language-specific NER in low-resource settings remains uncertain. In this study, we fine-tune MahaBERT-v2 on different variants of the MahaNER dataset and systematically compare the performance of these models with an existing MahaNER baseline and prominent general-purpose LLMs, including Gemini, LLaMA-3.3-70B, and Gemma models. All models are evaluated on a Marathi NER test dataset using standard metrics of precision, recall, and F1-score. The experimental results show that the fine-tuned MahaBERT-based models consistently outperform both the baseline and all evaluated LLMs, with the fine-tuned models achieving F1-scores ranging from 0.88 to 0.91, surpassing the existing MahaNER model (0.8843) and significantly exceeding the performance of LLM-based approaches, whose F1-scores range from 0.57 to 0.69. These findings demonstrate that task-specific, language-focused models trained on domain-relevant data remain more effective than general-purpose LLMs for Marathi NER, highlighting the continued importance of specialized architectures for low-resource language processing.

</details>


### [23] [Joint Optimization for Greedy Longest-match Tokenization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23362)
*Adhiraj Singh,Deepanshu Mody,Ghina Al Shdaifat,Hamza Alshamy,Adam Wiemerslage,Varshini Reddy,Craig W. Schmidt*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes JOLT, a method to learn subword vocabularies that are directly optimized for greedy longest-match tokenization (like WordPiece), achieving near-optimal compression and outperforming BPE by a small but consistent margin.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard subword vocabularies (e.g., BPE, WordPiece) are built with greedy heuristics that do not exactly match the behavior of the decoding rule used at inference, potentially wasting compression efficiency. Prior work optimized vocabularies for a different inference rule; this paper extends optimization to the widely used greedy left-to-right longest-match rule to better align training-time vocabulary construction with deployment-time tokenization and quantify how much improvement over BPE is still possible.

Method: Formulate vocabulary learning as an integer program (JOLT) with variables representing which subwords are in the vocabulary and how sequences are segmented. Add greedy-consistency constraints so that the optimization’s segmentations must coincide with those produced by greedy longest-match decoding under the chosen vocabulary. To make this scalable, relax the integer program to a linear program, solve it, and then iteratively refine it by adding higher-order segmentations only for ambiguous or unresolved pretokens. Finally, round the nearly integral LP solution to obtain a concrete vocabulary and segmentation scheme.

Result: The LP relaxation is almost integral, and the rounded solutions are within 0.008–0.176% of the LP lower bound on the training data, giving a tight near-optimality certificate. The analysis shows that standard BPE is already within 1–2% of the best possible compression achievable under greedy longest-match decoding. JOLT closes 89.6–99.4% of the remaining improvement margin.
