However, we observe that when the context overlaps with the training data, these methods can- not disentangle in-context from in-weight (IW) contributions, producing unreliable scores. Based on this observation, in this work, we introduce: 1) an evaluation protocol that relies on four new metrics (base-model context attribution score (BCS), cross-model context attribution consistency (CAC), attribution preservation score (APS), source separation pre- cision (SSP)) and 2) a benchmark dataset (WMDP-Cyber++) with ground-truth provenance labels to systematically assess attribution under IW overlap. In our experiments across four well-known context attribution methods, we demonstrate that they provide unfaithful attribution when the knowledge from the context also exists in the weights. Finally, we adapt these methods for source separation (IW vs. in-context learning (ICL)) and show that they cannot do the disentanglement based on the contributive score

</details>


### [43] [A Frozen 12B Beats Frontier Models on Verified Work: 100% Accuracy, 0 Tokens, Bit-Exact, Forever](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23806)
*Sietse Schelpe*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Paper proposes a frozen LLM with an external, verified solution memory enabling zero-token deterministic answering for solved problem families.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM improvement requires costly retraining, producing opaque, non-deterministic models. The authors aim to decouple capability gains from parameter scaling and generation compute by reusing verified solutions instead of constantly regenerating answers.

Method: Keep the base language model fixed and attach a growing external memory of verified solutions. For any new query, use exact addressing into this memory to retrieve a prior verified solution when the instance belongs to an already-solved problem family. Solutions are written to memory only after passing an independent verification mechanism that does not rely on ground-truth answer keys. The system is evaluated across multiple architectures and vendors, including dense and MoE models, on both structured problem families and open-ended reasoning tasks, with additional experiments on retrieval accuracy, latency, energy use, and context-window scaling.

Result: Across 180 new instances from nine problem families, four different LLM architectures all achieve 100% accuracy (180/180) on these instances using zero generation tokens, relying purely on the external memory. A negative-control experiment shows that an emptied memory yields no capability, attributing success entirely to the memory. For open-ended reasoning, the system achieves 88/88 consistency-gated accepted solutions with formal machine-checked proofs and successfully transfers reasoning methods in 77/80 cases. Memory lookup is extremely fast (≈1.4 microseconds for selection; 6–23 ms for full reuse at 36 mWh). Approximate similarity search performs poorly compared to exact addressing, misselecting 94.3% of the time on a 4,500-item store, while exact addressing has zero errors. The system supports a movable 6M-token context window on a single 46 GB GPU, exceeding the limits of vLLM and SGLang.

Conclusion: A frozen language model augmented with a verified, exactly-addressed solution memory can achieve deterministic, zero-token responses for previously solved problem families, effectively decoupling execution-time capability from parameter scaling and generative compute. Exact, verification-gated reuse outperforms approximate similarity retrieval and enables extremely large effective context windows. While frontier models still dominate on unseen tasks requiring fresh reasoning, this architecture inverts the comparison on solved-and-verified workloads, where memory-based reuse is cheaper, faster, and perfectly reproducible. The authors release a public testbench to facilitate further evaluation and adoption.

Abstract: Improving a language model today means retraining it: enormous compute, a new opaque model each cycle, non-deterministic output. We take the opposite path: the model stays frozen, and a persistent memory of verified solutions grows beside it. Once a problem family is solved and has passed an independent verification step that never consults the answer key, every new instance of that family is answered at zero generation tokens, bit-exact, deterministically. Across 180 fresh instances spanning nine problem families, four architectures from four vendors - dense and mixture-of-experts - each score 180/180 at zero generation tokens per answer: execution-bound capability decoupled from parameter scaling. A negative control attributes the capability fully to the memory: emptied, it solves nothing. The same verify-before-store contract holds for open-ended reasoning: 88/88 consistency-gated acceptances across all four models, machine-checked formal proof, and reasoning-method transfer at 77/80. Memory selection takes 1.4 microseconds; a full reuse completes in 6-23 ms at 36 mWh. Approximate similarity retrieval selects the wrong item 94.3% of the time on a 4,500-item verified store where exact addressing makes zero errors. The store also serves as working context at a scale no shipped engine matches: a 6,000,000-token movable window on a single 46 GB GPU at flat memory, where vLLM stops at 30,399 tokens and SGLang silently truncates past 32,000. On published benchmarks, frontier models remain far ahead of any 12B at raw from-scratch reasoning; on everything this system has solved and verified, the comparison inverts: a frontier API call pays a fresh generation pass on every query, forever, while verified reuse costs zero tokens and returns the identical bits every time. A public testbench with free, rate-limited access accompanies this report: https://corbenic-galahad-bench.hf.space

</details>


### [44] [Indic DiarBench: A Multilingual Joint Diarization and ASR Benchmark for Indian Languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23808)
*Deovrat Mehendale,Aditya Mehndiratta,Dhruv Rathi,Kaushal Bhogale,Mitesh M. Khapra*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Introduces Indic DiarBench, a 108-hour benchmark for speaker diarization and ASR across all 22 Indian scheduled languages, with human-corrected, speaker-attributed transcripts and baseline evaluations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is a lack of comprehensive, standardized benchmarks for speaker diarization and ASR that cover all 22 scheduled Indian languages, including realistic conversational phenomena like code-mixing, dialect variations, and overlapping speech. This gap limits progress and fair comparison of multilingual and inclusive speech technologies in the Indian context.

Method: The authors curate and annotate about 108 hours of natural multi-speaker audio spanning near-field meetings, far-field recordings, and in-the-wild audio across all 22 scheduled Indian languages. They perform human correction and time-aligned speaker-attributed transcription of the audio. They then evaluate a set of leading systems—commercial speech APIs and multimodal large language models—as baseline models for joint diarization and ASR performance on this dataset.

Result: The outcome is Indic DiarBench, an open-access benchmark dataset containing rich, human-verified annotations for diarization and ASR in all 22 scheduled Indian languages, with baseline performance metrics for several state-of-the-art commercial and LLM-based systems on joint diarization and ASR tasks.

Conclusion: Indic DiarBench provides a challenging, realistic benchmark that reflects conversational nuances in Indian speech and can serve as a standardized testbed to drive progress in inclusive, multilingual diarization and ASR systems for Indian languages. The open-access release is intended to facilitate broad research and development in this domain.

Abstract: In this work, we introduce Indic DiarBench, a speaker diarization and ASR benchmark dataset spanning all 22 scheduled languages of India. This corpus comprises approximately 108 hours of natural multi-speaker audio from near-field meetings, far-field recordings, and in-the-wild audios. All annotations are human-corrected with time-aligned speaker attributed transcriptions. The dataset captures conversational nuance prevalent in Indian speech, such as English code-mixing, dialectal variation, and frequent speaker overlap. To establish a baseline for joint ASR and diarization capabilities we evaluate leading systems including commercial speech APIs and multimodal large language models. Indic DiarBench is released as an open-access resource to advance inclusive, multilingual speech technology research for Indian languages.

</details>


### [45] [Earnings25: A Comprehensive 500-Hour Speech Benchmark for Finance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23813)
*Denglin Jiang,Haoran Zhou,Anshul Wadhawan,Brendan Fahy,Vinay Ramesh,David Weisberg,Dmitriy Derkachevskiy,Helen Sheehan,Srivas Prasad,Michele Franceschini*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper presents Earnings25, a new benchmark dataset for evaluating ASR systems on realistic English earnings calls.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing ASR benchmarks do not adequately capture the challenges of real-world finance-domain earnings calls, such as domain-specific vocabulary, varied speakers, and complex call structures. There is a need for a standardized, realistic benchmark to compare ASR models in this domain.

Method: The authors construct Earnings25, consisting of two complementary test sets of English earnings calls from 2025: a large full-call set (498 hours of S&P 500 Q4 calls) and a smaller, industry-balanced segmented set (46 hours, 290 segments). They provide aligned transcripts and rich metadata (speaker roles, industries, call structure) and define standardized scoring protocols. They then evaluate Whisper and Parakeet-TDT models as reproducible baselines.

Result: Earnings25 is released with transcripts, metadata, and evaluation protocols, and baseline performance metrics are reported for Whisper and Parakeet-TDT using standardized scoring. The results quantify how these ASR systems perform overall and across different speakers and industries on realistic earnings calls.

Conclusion: Earnings25 offers a comprehensive, realistic benchmark for finance-domain ASR, enabling more nuanced, speaker- and industry-aware evaluation than aggregate WER alone, and providing baseline results for future comparison and research.

Abstract: We introduce Earnings25, a finance-domain benchmark for evaluating automatic speech recognition (ASR) on English-language earnings calls under realistic conditions. Earnings25 comprises two complementary test sets: (i) testset-full, 498 hours of full English-language S&P 500 earnings calls from Q4 2025, and (ii) testset-segmented, a 46-hour industry-balanced set of 290 segments sampled from English-language U.S. earnings calls in 2025. The benchmark provides aligned transcripts and structured metadata, including speaker roles, industry labels, and call structure, enabling speaker- and industry-aware evaluation beyond aggregate word error rate (WER). We report reproducible baselines for Whisper and Parakeet-TDT using standardized scoring.

</details>


### [46] [Understanding Tone-Dependent Inference Cost in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23915)
*Akhil Kumar,Om Dobariya*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Study of how different prompt tones (from sycophantic to threatening) affect LLM answer accuracy and output-token cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM providers and users care about both answer quality and inference cost, but most work focuses on model architecture and prompts’ content, not on the tone of the prompt itself. Since tone could influence verbosity, reasoning style, and compliance behavior, it may materially affect both accuracy and token usage, which in turn affects latency and monetary cost. This paper aims to quantify those effects.

Method: Run controlled experiments on a 570-question subset of MMLU, prompting several LLMs (ChatGPT 4o, 5-nano; Gemini 2.5 Flash, 2.5 Flash Lite) using seven different prompt tones, from sycophantic to threatening. Measure (1) answer accuracy and (2) output-token counts, including reasoning tokens. Compare tone conditions, compute variation ranges, and analyze the accuracy–token-length trade-off using Pareto-frontier analysis to identify dominant tones for each model family.

Result: Across models, variation in output-token length due to tone is much larger than variation in accuracy. Output-token usage changes by up to 44.3% across tone conditions, while accuracy shifts are relatively small. In accuracy vs. token-length space, the Pareto frontier for ChatGPT 4o and 5-nano is dominated by the rude tone; for Gemini 2.5 Flash and Flash Lite, rude and neutral tones dominate the frontier. Thus, tones like “rude” can simultaneously provide relatively strong accuracy and relatively low or efficient token usage compared with other tones.

Conclusion: Prompt tone is not merely a stylistic choice: it systematically affects both answer quality and the volume of billable inference tokens. While accuracy changes are modest, tone can induce large differences in token consumption, producing meaningful cost and efficiency implications. For the tested models, certain tones (notably rude, and neutral for Gemini) appear Pareto-efficient in balancing accuracy and token cost. Designers of LLM applications should therefore consider tone as a tunable parameter for optimizing cost–performance trade-offs, and future work should further characterize these effects across tasks, languages, and model families.

Abstract: We examine how prompt tone affects both accuracy of the LLM answers and inference cost as reflected in output-token consumption. Experiments were performed to understand the trade-offs between accuracy and inference cost on a 570 Question MMLU dataset for LLM models prompted in seven different tones from sycophantic to threatening. Our results show that the output-token-length variation substantially exceeded accuracy variation across all models. Output-token consumption varied by up to 44.3% across tone conditions. We also analyzed the tradeoff between the accuracy of the answers and the average output token length in the reasoning process. For the ChatGPT models 4o and 5-nano, the rude tone is quite dominant. For the Gemini models 2.5 Flash and 2.5 Flash Lite, the rude and neutral tones are dominant on the Pareto-optimal frontier. We find that prompt tone influences not only answer quality but also the amount of billable inference resources consumed by modern LLMs.

</details>


### [47] [Tag Questions and the Generational Reversal of Sycophancy Across 45 Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23976)
*Tapan Parikh*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper shows that adding a short confirmation tag (like “..., right?”) to a question can drastically change whether language models agree, revealing strong, evolving patterns of sycophancy vs. resistance across model generations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Language models often adapt their answers to appear agreeable, but measuring this “sycophancy” typically needs subjective LLM judges or embeddings. The authors want a simple, objective, low-cost behavioral test that works across many models and versions and that reveals how training over time changes models’ tendency to agree with users’ implied preferences.

Method: They construct 20 binary decision questions where both options are defensible and no ground truth exists. Each is asked in two forms: a neutral question (“Is X the better choice?”) and a tagged version (“X is the better choice, right?”). They evaluate 45 frozen models, counterbalancing prompts so that the models’ intrinsic preferences cancel out. Responses are clamped to yes/no and scored by exact match, without using LLM judges or embeddings. They then do ablations: changing the tag to a synonym, or embedding the same stance in the prompt without using a tag, and also flipping the tag’s polarity (e.g., “..., maybe?”). They analyze model- and family-level effects, significance via BH-FDR, and correlations between conditions.

Result: Across 45 models, the confirmation tag shifts agreement rates from +32% to -32% depending on the model, a 64-point spread. Five models show statistically significant sycophancy (more agreement with the tag) and 17 show significant resistance (less agreement). Within model families (GPT, Claude, Qwen, Grok), the direction of the effect flips from positive to negative in newer generations, at about -6 percentage points per year, independent of vendor tier; DeepSeek is a notable exception that never crosses. Recently released models fall in line with this trend. Synonym tags reproduce each model’s behavior very closely (r=0.89), but embedding the same preference without a tag does not produce resistance in models that were resistant to tags, and stance-only effects correlate poorly with tag effects (r=0.23). Changing the tag’s polarity to a hedging form like “maybe?” causes agreement to rise above baseline in every model (+19.6 points), and some models affirm both sides of contradictory choices at very high rates.

Conclusion: The behavior change is driven not by the user’s underlying preference but by the surface form of an appended agreement-seeking tag. Modern models are increasingly trained to resist strongly assertive confirmation tags while remaining more agreeable to hedged ones, indicating behavior shaped by pattern-matching specific linguistic constructions rather than deeper principles about user deference. The proposed one-word, judge-free instrument gives a cheap, sensitive way to track how anti-sycophancy training evolves across model releases.

Abstract: Appending a two-word confirmation tag to a decision question -- "Is X the better choice?" versus "X is the better choice, right?" -- changes whether a language model endorses the choice. We measure this tag effect on 20 frozen, ground-truth-free decisions between two defensible options, counterbalanced so a model's own preferences cancel, scored by exact match on clamped yes/no replies -- no LLM judge, no embeddings. Across 45 models the effect spans +32% to -32% -- a 64-point swing on one word -- with 5 models significantly sycophantic and 17 significantly resistant (BH-FDR q=.10). The sign is a clock: within model families the effect crosses from positive to negative as generations advance (GPT +4 to -28; Claude +7 to -32; Qwen and Grok likewise), roughly -6 points per year, a reversal robust to vendor tier; one lineage (DeepSeek) never crosses, and two releases during the study window (Claude Opus 5, Gemini 3.6 Flash) land on the trend out-of-sample. A full-panel ablation localizes the resistance as a double dissociation: a synonym tag reproduces each model's response almost exactly (r=0.89), while planting the same preference without a tag produces resistance in no resistant model (stance effects +6 to +49; r=0.23 with tag effects). The resistance is keyed to the surface construction of a tacked-on agreement bid, not the user's stance -- a pattern-match, not a principle. And the tag's polarity matters more than its presence: swap one word -- "X is the better choice, maybe?" -- and agreement rises above the neutral baseline in 45 of 45 models (+19.6 points), with ten models affirming both mutually exclusive options at 90-100%. Agreement tracks how sure the user sounds, in opposite directions at the two poles. The instrument is one word, one dollar, and judge-free; run per release, it reads the field's anti-sycophancy training directly off model behavior.

</details>


### [48] [SyRuP: Enhancing System-Prompt Following via Reward-Guided Prediction in LLM Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23991)
*Seoyeon Kim,Minjae Kang,Jaehyung Kim*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A new decoding-time framework, SyRuP, improves how well frozen LLMs follow complex system prompts by reranking tokens using a learned reward head conditioned on the system prompt.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are controlled via system prompts, but they only learn to follow them implicitly through in-context learning, which often fails for complex or compositional instructions. Existing solutions usually require fine-tuning the base model or expensive response-level reranking, making them less practical when we want lightweight, inference-time control over model behavior without modifying the base LM.

Method: SyRuP introduces a decoding-time mechanism that keeps the base language model frozen and adds a separate cross-attention reward head trained on system-prompt-conditioned preference pairs. The system prompt is treated as an external memory that the reward head attends to in order to compute token-level adherence scores. During inference, for each token step, SyRuP takes the base model’s top-k candidates and reranks them by combining the base logits with the learned adherence reward and, optionally, a contrastive term that reflects how the system prompt shifts the logits compared to a non-system-prompted distribution.

Result: On benchmarks designed to test system-prompt following, SyRuP reliably improves adherence to roles, styles, formats, and safety instructions compared with standard prompting and other decoding-time baselines, while incurring only moderate additional computation at inference. It shows better alignment with system prompts without retraining or altering the base language model parameters.

Conclusion: Explicit token-level guidance via a system-prompt-aware reward head is an effective and practical way to improve system-prompt following. By operating purely at decoding time and keeping the base LM frozen, SyRuP offers a more deployable approach to reliable prompt control than methods that require full model fine-tuning or heavy response-level reranking.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly controlled through system prompts that specify roles, styles, formats, and safety requirements. However, models follow these prompts only implicitly through in-context learning, which can be insufficient for complex or compositional prompts. Existing approaches often require model tuning or response-level reranking, limiting their practicality for lightweight inference-time control. We introduce SyRuP, a decoding-time framework for improving system-prompt adherence while keeping the base LM frozen. SyRuP trains a cross-attention reward head from system-prompt-conditioned preference pairs, treating the system prompt as a separate memory to produce token-level adherence scores. At inference, SyRuP reranks the base LM's top-k candidates by combining base logits with the learned reward signal and an optional contrastive signal capturing system-induced logit shifts. Experiments on system-prompt following benchmarks show that SyRuP consistently outperforms prompting and decoding-time baselines with moderate inference overhead. These results suggest that explicit token-level guidance is an effective and practical mechanism for reliable system-prompt following.

</details>


### [49] [MoLGE: Mixture of Language Group Experts for Efficient Scaling of Massively Multilingual Speech Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24030)
*Sangmin Lee,Woojin Chung,Woongjib Choi,Hong-Goo Kang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They propose MoLGE, a mixture-of-experts approach over language groups for large multilingual ASR, achieving better performance than dense baselines with few extra parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Massively multilingual ASR models must work for hundreds of languages but suffer from the curse of multilinguality: limited capacity must be spread over many languages, hurting performance, especially for low-resource ones. Existing MoE methods that allocate experts per language are too parameter-heavy and inefficient at this scale.

Method: They build MoLGE on top of speech self-supervised models (S3Ms). Instead of language-specific experts, MoLGE uses expert modules assigned to clusters (groups) of similar languages. They incorporate these experts via a hierarchical Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) in the disentangled acoustic and linguistic parts of the S3M. They also experiment with different language grouping strategies, based on linguistic knowledge and data-driven clustering, and analyze their impact on performance and scalability.

Result: On a benchmark with 495 languages, MoLGE consistently outperforms dense multilingual baselines, achieving better ASR performance with only a small increase in trainable parameters. Both phonetic and orthographic aspects benefit from the language grouping strategies.

Conclusion: Grouping languages into structured experts and applying hierarchical LoRA within S3Ms is an effective, parameter-efficient way to mitigate the curse of multilinguality. This structured language specialization allows multilingual ASR systems to scale to hundreds of languages while improving performance and interpretability.

Abstract: Massively multilingual automatic speech recognition (ASR) models covering hundreds of languages must maintain robust performance across diverse linguistic and acoustic conditions. However, these models often encounter the curse of multilinguality, where model capacity is diluted across languages. To address this challenge, we propose Mixture of Language Group Experts (MoLGE), built upon speech self-supervised models (S3Ms). MoLGE assigns dedicated expert modules to clusters of similar languages, reducing the number of required submodules compared to conventional language-specific Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) schemes. It further integrates a hierarchical Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) strategy into the disentangled acoustic and linguistic components of the S3M architecture, enabling efficient modeling of language-specific characteristics while maintaining parameter efficiency. Further, we investigate the impact of language grouping strategies based on both linguistic and data-driven criteria on overall performance, providing an interpretable perspective on how language structure influences scalability in multilingual speech systems. In experiments, we evaluate MoLGE on a multilingual benchmark encompassing 495 languages. Results demonstrate that MoLGE consistently outperforms dense multilingual baselines with a minimal increase in trainable parameters. Notably, these language grouping strategies yield substantial improvements for both phonetic and orthographic aspects of ASR modeling. Our findings suggest that structured language specialization provides an effective pathway for massively scaling language coverage of multilingual ASR.

</details>


### [50] [Pointer-Augmented Autoregressive Generation of Patent Claims with Joint Topology and Content Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24040)
*Yongmin Yoo,Zhangkai Wu,Longbing Cao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces SPG, a structure-aware method for patent claim generation that jointly learns claim topology and text to better enforce hierarchical dependencies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard autoregressive decoders generate text as flat token sequences and struggle to enforce global hierarchical constraints. In patent claim generation, however, claims form a dependency forest where each dependent claim must narrow the scope of its parent. Existing approaches like post-hoc parsing or grammar-constrained decoding cannot handle the mutual dependence between claim wording and claim topology: the parent must be chosen before the dependent text exists, but the text must reflect the parent’s scope.

Method: SPG (Structure-aware Patent Generation) predicts the dependency topology during the autoregressive decoding process. It adds a pointer head that, for each dependent claim, selects its parent claim. Gradients from this pointer mechanism and a depth-adaptive scope regularizer jointly shape the shared decoder representations during training, encouraging proper narrowing of scope with depth. In a second training stage, SPG optimizes a violation-weighted preference objective over self-generated candidate claim sets, using structurally deficient generations as negative examples to provide a training signal that is missing from granted-patent corpora.

Result: On the HUPD-DCG benchmark, SPG applied to Llama-3-8B-Instruct recovers 79.0% of gold parent-child links between claims, despite never receiving direct supervision on these links as part of its reward. It improves antecedent consistency from 0.292 to 0.478 compared to a supervised baseline of the same model scale. Expert human evaluations confirm that the generated claim sets exhibit better structural and referential consistency.

Conclusion: By integrating topology prediction into the decoding process and adding structure-aware regularization and preference learning, SPG enables language models to generate patent claim sets that better respect hierarchical dependencies and scope narrowing. The method substantially improves the structural fidelity and consistency of generated claims without requiring explicit parent-link supervision in the training reward, demonstrating the value of end-to-end, structure-aware generation for legally structured documents.

Abstract: Autoregressive decoders emit flat token sequences and cannot enforce hierarchical constraints across output segments, a limitation that becomes acute in patent claim generation, where a claim set forms a dependency forest whose scope must narrow monotonically with depth. Topology and content are mutually dependent: a dependent claim's wording must reflect its parent's scope, yet the parent must be chosen before that wording exists, so neither post-hoc parsing nor grammar-constrained decoding suffices. We propose SPG (Structure-aware Patent Generation), which predicts topology inside the autoregressive pass. A pointer head selects each dependent claim's parent, and its gradients, together with a depth-adaptive scope regularizer, reshape the shared decoder's representations during training. A second stage then applies a violation-weighted preference objective over self-generated deficient candidates, supplying the negative signal that granted-patent corpora lack. On HUPD-DCG, SPG on Llama-3-8B-Instruct recovers 79.0\% of gold parent links, a quantity its training reward never supervises, and raises antecedent consistency from 0.292 to 0.478 over a supervised baseline of equal scale, with expert evaluation corroborating these gains.

</details>


### [51] [LLM-Based vs. Lexicon-Based Sentiment Signals for Tail-Risk Detection in Meme Stocks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24072)
*Paul Kilian,Markus Kleffmann*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper compares lexicon-based (VADER) and LLM-based sentiment measures from Reddit’s r/WallStreetBets to see how well they capture signals related to extreme returns of meme stocks (GME, AMC, NOK). LLM sentiment is richer and more asset-specific but does not yield consistently stronger or more stable forecasting of market movements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Retail-driven meme stock episodes showed that social media sentiment can move markets, but traditional lexicon-based tools like VADER may miss nuances such as sarcasm, bullishness, and topic relevance that are frequent in communities like r/WallStreetBets. With the rise of LLMs, there is a need to empirically test whether their more expressive sentiment representations actually improve the extraction of market-relevant signals, especially around extreme positive return events.

Method: Collect Reddit posts/comments from r/WallStreetBets about meme stocks (GME, AMC, NOK). Build time-aligned sentiment indicators using two approaches: (1) a lexicon-based baseline (VADER) that outputs scalar polarity scores; (2) an LLM-based method that produces multidimensional sentiment features such as emotional polarity, degree of bullishness, sarcasm likelihood, and topical relevance to a given stock. Analyze the relationship between these sentiment indicators and stock returns using lead/lag correlation, OLS regressions, ROC-AUC classification of return direction, and a quantile-based early-warning framework focused on large positive returns.

Result: LLM-based indicators form a richer, multidimensional description of social media sentiment and show clearer, more asset-specific statistical patterns than the VADER-based scores. However, despite these advantages in expressiveness and structure, the strength and consistency of their relationship with realized returns varies substantially across the different meme stocks. Forecasting performance, as measured by correlations, regressions, ROC-AUC, and early-warning detection of extreme positive returns, improves only in some cases and is not uniformly superior to the lexicon-based baseline.

Conclusion: While LLMs can extract more nuanced and asset-specific sentiment signals from noisy retail forums, this extra linguistic sophistication does not guarantee robust or stable predictive power for stock returns in highly volatile, retail-driven environments. For meme stocks, sentiment–return links remain heterogeneous and regime-dependent, so practitioners should treat LLM-derived sentiment as a potentially richer but still unreliable forecasting tool, best used in conjunction with other signals rather than as a standalone predictor.

Abstract: This paper presents an empirical comparison of lexicon-based and Large Language Model (LLM)-based sentiment analysis for extracting market-relevant signals from social media discourse in highly volatile equity markets. Using Reddit data from r/WallStreetBets and focusing on meme stocks (GME, AMC, NOK), we construct time-aligned sentiment indicators and evaluate their relationship with market returns, with particular attention to extreme positive return events in the upper tail of the return distribution. The LLM-based approach generates multidimensional sentiment representations capturing emotional polarity, bullishness, sarcasm likelihood, and topical relevance, whereas the baseline relies on the VADER lexicon-based model. We evaluate both approaches using lead/lag correlation analysis, OLS regression, ROC-AUC-based directional classification, and a quantile-based early-warning framework. The results indicate that LLM-derived indicators provide a richer multidimensional representation and exhibit stronger asset-specific statistical structure than the lexicon-based baseline. However, their relationship with market movements remains heterogeneous across assets, suggesting that increased linguistic expressiveness does not necessarily translate into stable forecasting performance in retail-driven volatility regimes.

</details>


### [52] [BioSentinel at EXIST 2026: Soft-Label Optimization with XLM-RoBERTa for Sexism Intent Classification in Memes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24137)
*Chandru Munisamy,Karthikeya Raguveer,Alapan Kuila*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: BioSentinel used a text-focused xlm-roberta-based model with a composite KL + weighted cross-entropy loss to predict both hard and soft labels for meme intention (direct, judgemental, non-sexist) in the EXIST 2026 Le-Wi-Di task, achieving mid-pack leaderboard performance and analyzing the impact of annotator disagreement and loss design.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understand and model communicative intent in memes—particularly sexist vs non-sexist dimensions—under a Learning with Disagreement paradigm, where annotators often disagree and systems must output both a single class and a probability distribution. The team aims to explore how to best leverage annotator disagreement and loss design to improve both soft-label calibration and hard-label accuracy for subjective NLP tasks.

Method: Use xlm-roberta-base (270M parameters) as a multilingual text encoder in a text-centric pipeline for meme intent classification. Train with a composite objective: (1) KL divergence between the model’s predicted probability distribution and the empirical annotator distribution (soft labels), and (2) weighted cross-entropy on the majority (hard) labels to address class imbalance and improve discrete classification. Perform exploratory experiments with larger architectures, ablation studies removing each loss component, and temperature scaling analysis on a validation set to study calibration and soft-label performance.

Result: On the official EXIST 2026 Task 2.2 test set, the system obtains ICM-Soft-Norm = 0.3229 and ICM-Norm = 0.3778, with hard-label F1 = 0.4236. It ranks 40/118 in the soft-soft evaluation and 49/187 in the hard-hard evaluation. Ablation studies reveal that including KL divergence notably improves soft-label-oriented metrics, while including cross-entropy yields better hard-label accuracy. Temperature analysis provides additional insight into probability calibration but does not drastically change rankings.

Conclusion: A text-centric xlm-roberta-base model with a composite KL + weighted cross-entropy loss is competitive for meme intention classification under Le-Wi-Di, and explicitly modeling annotator disagreement via KL divergence helps soft-label performance, while traditional cross-entropy is still important for hard-label accuracy. The findings underscore the importance of loss design and disagreement modeling in subjective NLP tasks and suggest that combining soft-label and hard-label objectives is beneficial when both prediction types are required.

Abstract: This paper describes the BioSentinel team's participation in EXIST 2026 Task 2.2: Source Intention in Memes, part of the CLEF 2026 evaluation campaign. The task requires classifying the communicative intent behind memes as direct, judgemental, or no (non-sexist), under a Learning with Disagreement (Le-Wi-Di) paradigm that mandates both hard-label and soft-label (probability distribution) predictions. We present a text-centric approach built on xlm-roberta-base (270M parameters) trained with a composite loss function combining KL divergence on soft annotator distributions and weighted cross-entropy on hard labels. On the official test set, the system achieved an ICM-Soft-Norm of 0.3229 and ICM-Norm of 0.3778, with a hard F1-score of 0.4236, ranking 40th (out of 118 submissions) in the soft-soft evaluation and 49th (out of 187 submissions) in the hard-hard evaluation. We provide an analysis of the dataset characteristics, exploratory larger-architecture runs, and the role of annotator disagreement in shaping model design for subjective NLP tasks. Ablation results show that KL loss improves soft-label metrics, while CE loss improves hard-label accuracy. We also report a separate validation-set temperature analysis.

</details>


### [53] [Looking for Affect in Spontaneous Finnish Speech through Linguistic Interpretability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24155)
*Kalle Lahtinen,Liisa Mustanoja,Okko Räsänen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how combining text and audio features affects modeling perceived valence and arousal in spontaneous Finnish speech, finding clear gains for valence but limited added value for arousal.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Affect recognition in speech depends on both how something is said (acoustics) and what is said (linguistic content), but their relative contributions remain unclear, particularly for Finnish where prior work focuses on only one modality at a time. Clarifying this can improve emotion modeling and test whether findings from other languages hold for spontaneous Finnish speech.

Method: Using a newly released spontaneous Finnish affective speech corpus, the authors extract text-based and audio-based features and build regression models to predict human ratings of emotional valence and arousal. They compare models trained on audio-only, text-only, and combined audio+text features to assess each modality’s contribution.

Result: Models that combine audio and text features outperform single-modality models for predicting valence, indicating that textual content and acoustic cues provide complementary information. For arousal prediction, adding text to audio yields little or no improvement, suggesting arousal is captured mainly by acoustic properties in this setting.

Conclusion: Text and audio features play different roles in modeling perceived emotions in Finnish speech: their combination is notably beneficial for valence but not substantially for arousal. The findings align with cross-linguistic research and extend existing knowledge to spontaneous Finnish, underlining the importance of multimodal modeling especially for affective valence.

Abstract: Existing research on affect in speech has shown how acoustic surface characteristics and content-related linguistic aspects of speech both relate to perceived emotional arousal and valence. However, it is not clear what the relative contributions of these two factors are in the perceptual process. This is especially true for Finnish, for which most existing studies focus on either acoustic-phonetic or text analysis. This paper presents a study where we systematically explore the combinatory role of text- and audio-based features in modeling the human perception of valence and arousal using a newly released affective speech corpus for spontaneous Finnish. We show that the combination of text- and audio-based features improves valence regression results over the individual modalities, whereas for arousal regression the complementary effect is not substantial. The results support prior findings from other languages, providing new data and knowledge on spontaneous Finnish speech.

</details>


### [54] [Where Quality Breaks in Compressed Short-Text Generation: Staged Bottleneck Localization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24176)
*Alexey Gavrilov,Alan-Barsag Gazzaev,Sergey Muravyov*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper analyzes where quality loss happens in compressed short-text generation pipelines and introduces a staged evaluation method showing that codec reconstruction, not latent generation, is the main bottleneck in their TinyStories setup.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Compressed text generation models use a codec plus a latent generator, but when output quality is poor it is unclear whether the codec or the generator is to blame. Without a way to disentangle these failure modes, researchers might optimize the wrong component and waste compute. The authors want a principled diagnostic to localize quality losses within such pipelines.

Method: They build a controlled case study on TinyStories using a hierarchical VQ-VAE-2 codec to compress sequences from length 64 to 16, and a masked discrete diffusion model (MDLM) as the latent generator. They propose a staged validation protocol that evaluates: (1) codec reconstruction fidelity alone; (2) quality of generated latents; and (3) auxiliary latent-geometry diagnostics. All stages use a shared external GPT-2 scorer to measure perplexity, supplemented with semantic and geometry-based metrics for studying the latent space.

Result: The experiments show that codec reconstruction substantially degrades quality before latent generation: median external perplexity increases from 15.17 to 27.36 (+80.4%), and p95 from 25.10 to 98.91 (+294.1%). Despite this, the latent MDLM still outperforms token-space diffusion under the same scorer, reducing mean, median, and p95 perplexity by 32.9%, 30.9%, and 36.6%, respectively. Geometry-aware regularization helps local latent-space proxies but does not translate into better decoded-text scores in the runs they report.

Conclusion: Most practical quality loss in their compressed TinyStories pipeline comes from the codec, not the latent denoiser, so codec fidelity currently sets the quality ceiling. Their main contribution is a reusable, staged diagnostic framework that cleanly separates and evaluates codec vs. latent-generation effects, helping future work focus optimization and compute on the true bottleneck rather than on downstream latent denoising when it is not the limiting factor.

Abstract: Compressed short-text generators can fail in two different places: the codec may discard information before generation starts, or the latent generator may produce weak codes. Without separating these failure modes, researchers can spend compute improving the wrong component. We study this problem in a controlled 64-to-16 TinyStories case study built from a hierarchical VQ-VAE-2 codec and a masked discrete diffusion generator (MDLM). We use a staged validation protocol that separates codec reconstruction fidelity, latent generation quality, and auxiliary latent diagnostics under one shared external GPT-2 scorer, while reporting complementary semantic metrics for the geometry study. In the tested configuration, codec reconstruction alone raises median external perplexity from 15.17 to 27.36 (+80.4%) and p95 from 25.10 to 98.91 (+294.1%), showing that the dominant quality loss appears before latent generation begins. Under the same scorer, code-space MDLM remains materially stronger than token-space diffusion, reducing mean, median, and p95 by 32.9%, 30.9%, and 36.6%, respectively. Geometry-aware regularization improves local latent proxies but does not improve decoded-text metrics in the available runs. The contribution is methodological rather than algorithmic: the paper presents a reusable staged diagnosis for one concrete pipeline and shows that, in this setting, codec fidelity rather than latent denoising sets the practical quality ceiling.

</details>


### [55] [StanceFlip: A Comprehensive Multi-Dimensional Benchmark for Multimodal Conversational Stance Flipping Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24191)
*Heyan Chai,Xin Li,Wenjie Wang,Jianyang Qin,Chaoyang Li,Lu Wang,Hao Chen,Qing Liao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces StanceFlip, a new multimodal benchmark and the ConStaFF framework for forecasting and explaining stance flips in conversations, achieving state-of-the-art results on fine-grained stance extraction and flip attribution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing conversational stance detection benchmarks struggle with three issues: (1) they do not model how beliefs dynamically evolve over time, especially when a speaker reverses their stance; (2) they conflate emotional/affective expressions with logical reasoning, making it hard to analyze the cognitive process behind stance; and (3) they largely ignore multimodal signals (e.g., audio, video, etc.) that are crucial for resolving pragmatic ambiguities like sarcasm or irony. The authors want better tools to study and model dynamic, multimodal stance changes in realistic conversations.

Method: The authors construct StanceFlip, a benchmark for multimodal conversational stance flipping forecasting that spans multi-turn dialogues, multiple real-world scenarios, and five modalities. They define two new subtasks: (1) Multimodal Stance Sextuple Extraction, where systems must jointly extract holder, target, emotion, sentiment, stance, and rationale as static snapshots of a dialogue state; and (2) Dynamic Stance Flip Attribution, where systems detect stance reversals over time and identify the triggers causing these flips. They also introduce ConStaFF, an LLM-based framework tailored to this benchmark for Multimodal Conversational Stance Flipping Forecasting (MCSFF). ConStaFF employs a Thought-of-Stance (ToS) reasoning scheme that splits reasoning into specialized cognitive personas to construct target propositions, resolve cross-modal inconsistencies, and reconstruct historical stance trajectories. Additionally, it uses a self-reflective verification mechanism to ensure structured, faithful stance modeling and flip attribution.

Result: Experiments on the StanceFlip benchmark show that ConStaFF substantially outperforms strong multimodal LLM baselines on both key tasks: multimodal stance sextuple extraction and stance flip trigger attribution. The performance gains indicate that the proposed ToS reasoning and self-reflective verification mechanisms improve both the accuracy and reliability of multimodal stance reasoning and flip explanation.

Conclusion: The work establishes StanceFlip as a challenging and more realistic benchmark for studying dynamic multimodal stance in conversations, with new tasks that jointly capture fine-grained cognitive structures and the causes of stance reversals. The ConStaFF framework demonstrates that carefully designed, structured reasoning strategies on top of LLMs can effectively model stance trajectories and explain stance flips, yielding state-of-the-art results. This suggests a promising path for future research on interpretable, multimodal conversational reasoning and stance analysis.

Abstract: Conversational stance detection has shifted from static text analysis to dynamic multimodal modeling. However, existing benchmarks exhibit three key limitations: failure to capture the dynamic evolution of beliefs, particularly during stance reversals; difficulty in disentangling affective states from logical reasoning; and neglect of the critical role of multimodal cues in resolving pragmatic ambiguities such as sarcasm. To address these limitations, we propose StanceFlip, a benchmark designed for multimodal conversational stance flipping forecasting over multi-turn dialogues across five modalities and multi-scenarios, which includes two novel subtasks: 1) Multimodal Stance Sextuple Extraction, extracting holder, target, emotion, sentiment, stance, and rationale as static state snapshots of dialogue to capture fine-grained cognitive structures. 2) Dynamic Stance Flip Attribution, tracking stance reversals across the conversation and identifying their underlying triggers. Alongside the dataset, we propose a dedicated framework, named ConStaFF, for Multimodal Conversational Stance Flipping Forecasting (MCSFF). Built upon a large language model, ConStaFF performs end-to-end stance reasoning, with a Thought-of-Stance (ToS) reasoning framework and a self-reflective verification mechanism integrated for structured stance modeling and faithful flip attribution. Specifically, ToS decomposes the reasoning process into specialized cognitive personas to formulate target propositions, resolve cross-modal conflicts, and infer historical stance trajectories. Extensive experiments show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on both sextuple extraction and flip-trigger attribution, outperforming strong multimodal large language model baselines by substantial margins.

</details>


### [56] [A New Role for Relevance: Guiding Corpus Interaction in Agentic Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24223)
*Jiangnan Li,Yuqing Li,Mo Yu,Jinchao Zhang,Jie Zhou*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes RARG, a relevance-aware search agent that integrates document relevance scores into grep-style corpus interaction to surface useful evidence earlier and answer complex questions more accurately and efficiently.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional retrieval agents rely mainly on document-level relevance to select top-k documents, which is insufficient for complex questions that need precise localization, composition, and verification of evidence across documents. Direct Corpus Interaction (DCI) methods like grep enable fine-grained exploration but are relevance-agnostic and can be inefficient, often exposing key clues late. Recent work that first restricts the corpus using relevance still fails to let relevance guide which documents and excerpts are examined first during interaction. There is a need for a system that uses relevance throughout the interaction process to prioritize both documents and specific excerpts, improving convergence speed and reliability for challenging question answering and reasoning-heavy retrieval tasks.

Method: The authors design the Relevance-Aware RipGrep Search Agent (RARG), which uses relevance as an execution prior during corpus interaction. RARG operates in a coarse-to-fine manner: (1) it orders documents by relevance to determine the sequence in which they are traversed with ripgrep, prioritizing globally relevant sources; (2) it initializes search within documents from paragraphs that are especially query-relevant, providing good starting points; and (3) it reranks the raw grep matches to highlight the most informative excerpts, compensating for limitations of document-level ranking that might bury key evidence. This integrates relevance signals into multiple layers of the search and interaction pipeline to guide exploration dynamically.

Result: On challenging browse-style question answering and tasks requiring reasoning-intensive retrieval, RARG outperforms both traditional retrieval-based agents and direct corpus interaction agents that do not use relevance in this way. Specifically, it achieves a better accuracy–efficiency trade-off, meaning it can reach higher answer accuracy with fewer interaction steps or less search effort, indicating faster and more targeted discovery of useful evidence.

Conclusion: Embedding relevance as a guiding signal throughout the corpus interaction process, rather than only at an initial retrieval stage, leads to faster and more reliable convergence in complex information-seeking tasks. RARG demonstrates that relevance-aware control of document ordering, entry-point selection, and excerpt reranking can substantially improve the effectiveness of grep-style search agents for browse question answering and reasoning-heavy retrieval problems.

Abstract: Relevance is a query-dependent estimate of whether a document or excerpt contains useful evidence. Existing retrieval agents use relevance to select top-$k$ content, but document relevance alone cannot localize, compose, or verify the evidence required by complex questions. Direct Corpus Interaction (DCI) enables such fine-grained operations through grep-style exploration, but its relevance-agnostic search can expose useful clues late and delay convergence. Recent advances use relevance to narrow the corpus into a working space for interaction. Once interaction begins, however, relevance still does not directly guide which documents grep searches first or distinguish informative excerpts from a broad set of matches to let LLMs see them first. We introduce the Relevance-Aware RipGrep Search Agent (RARG), which turns relevance into an execution prior for corpus interaction. RARG provides coarse-to-fine relevance guidance: it orders documents for sequential 'ripgrep' traversal to expose globally relevant clues earlier, initializes promising entry points with query-relevant paragraphs, and reranks grep matches to surface informative excerpts that document-level ranking may otherwise obscure. Across challenging browse question answering and reasoning-intensive retrieval, RARG improves the accuracy--efficiency frontier over retrieval-based and direct-interaction agents. These results demonstrate that relevance-aware interaction enables faster and more reliable search convergence.

</details>


### [57] [CAGE: Cognitive Attribution Graphs for Faithful Inline Citation Generation in Long-Form Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24236)
*Zhichao Yan,Shizhao Li,Jiapu Wang,Haoran Luo,Qingang Zhang,Jiaoyan Chen,Ru Li,Jeff Z. Pan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces CAGE, a two-stage framework that explicitly maps which documents support which parts of an answer, leading to more accurate and trustworthy citations in long-form question answering.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-form QA systems with retrieval-augmented LLMs need to ground their answers in evidence using inline citations. However, current systems often provide citations that are loosely related but do not actually support specific claims, causing over-claiming beyond the evidence. The root issue is that end-to-end generation blurs which document supports which claim, creating attribution ambiguity and evidence-boundary overrun. The paper aims to structurally fix this attribution problem so that each claim is properly and transparently supported by cited documents.

Method: The authors propose CAGE, a two-stage framework. First, they train a Cognitive Map Induction Model that builds an explicit, structured cognitive attribution graph: it decomposes an answer into semantic units and aligns each unit with specific supporting documents via explicit relations, forming answer-centered support subgraphs. This model is plug-and-play and operates before answer generation. Second, they use a Structured Citation Reasoning Model that takes these mapped units and turns them into sentence-level claims, attaching citations that are consistent with the pre-constructed attribution map. This separates evidence attribution from surface realization and constrains generation to respect evidential boundaries.

Result: On three benchmarks for long-form QA—ASQA, ELI5, and ExpertQA—CAGE attains state-of-the-art performance. The experiments show measurable gains both in overall answer quality and in citation faithfulness, indicating that explicitly contracting and structuring the attribution space, then guiding generation with this map, reduces unsupported claims and improves verifiability.

Conclusion: By introducing an explicit cognitive attribution map between documents and semantic answer units, CAGE resolves much of the attribution ambiguity that plagues end-to-end citation generation. The two-stage process—first structuring evidence-claim alignments, then generating claims with map-aligned citations—leads to more faithful, verifiable, and higher-performing long-form QA. The work suggests that future citation and grounding systems should separate attribution modeling from natural language generation and operate over explicit attribution graphs.

Abstract: Long-form question answering increasingly relies on retrieved evidence to make LLM outputs verifiable, with inline citations tracing claims to source documents. However, existing systems often attach citations that are topically related but insufficient to support their claims. We identify attribution ambiguity as a structural challenge: end-to-end generation must implicitly resolve combinatorial claim--document assignments, obscuring evidential boundaries and increasing the risk of evidence-boundary overrun, where claims exceed cited support. To address this challenge, we propose CAGE (Cognitive Attribution Graphs for Citation Generation), a two-stage framework that introduces an explicit cognitive attribution map before answer generation. CAGE first trains a plug-and-play Cognitive Map Induction Model to construct answer-centered support subgraphs, aligning each semantic answer unit with supporting documents through explicit relations. A Structured Citation Reasoning Model then realizes these units as sentence-level claims with map-aligned citations. Experiments on ASQA, ELI5, and ExpertQA show that CAGE achieves state-of-the-art performance, demonstrating the effectiveness of attribution-space contraction and map-guided citation generation.

</details>


### [58] [Accuracy Hides How Language Models Fail: Measuring Failure States Under Matched Output Budgets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24268)
*Zongyou Yang,Yinghan Hou*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They argue current LM benchmarks mix up two things—whether the model produced a usable answer and whether that answer is correct—and propose a two-layer evaluation that separates execution behavior from correctness scoring.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard accuracy scores hide why models fail: a low score might be due to wrong reasoning, but also to truncation, non-answers, or parsing problems. This makes it hard to fairly compare models and test-time methods (like longer contexts or verification strategies) because changes in execution behavior and changes in real correctness are entangled in one number.

Method: They define a two-layer evaluation framework. Layer 1 logs scorer-independent execution evidence such as whether the output terminated with an explicit final answer, whether the answer is clearly exposed and parseable, and the completion length. Layer 2 applies scorer-dependent correctness judgments on those outputs. They run experiments on 2,550 generations from fixed Qwen and DeepSeek model configurations on the MATH and ARC-Challenge benchmarks under different context-length settings. They also run a targeted verification / candidate-selection study to see how different aggregation policies affect overall accuracy estimates.

Result: With the same 2,048-token limit, models show very different execution patterns: for MATH, 49/450 Qwen outputs terminate without a final answer, versus 5/300 for DeepSeek and 0/750 for ARC tasks. When the same DeepSeek MATH runs get an 8,192-token limit, the missing-final-answer termination disappears. The verification study shows that how you pick and aggregate candidates can significantly change comparative accuracy between models or methods. Overall, they empirically show that a single accuracy metric mixes up execution case mix (e.g., truncation, non-answers) and the specifics of the verification policy.

Conclusion: Benchmark accuracy alone is misleading for evaluating language models and test-time interventions. Researchers should report execution-state distributions, verification coverage, and details about scorers/verification policies alongside accuracy, and adopt a two-layer evaluation approach that cleanly separates execution evidence from correctness scoring.

Abstract: Language-model benchmarks collapse two distinct measurement questions into a single accuracy score: whether a response reached an evaluable state, and whether its answer was judged correct. We introduce a two-layer evaluation framework that separates scorer-independent execution evidence, including termination, answer exposure, parseability, and completion length, from scorer-dependent correctness. Across 2,550 outputs from five fixed Qwen and DeepSeek configurations on MATH and ARC-Challenge, matched 2,048-token limits produce sharply different execution mixtures: 49 of 450 Qwen MATH outputs terminate without a final answer, compared with 5 of 300 DeepSeek MATH outputs and none of the 750 ARC outputs. Among the same 300 DeepSeek MATH question-model pairs, no missing-final length termination is observed at 8,192 tokens. A coverage-audited targeted verification study further shows that candidate-selection and aggregation policies can substantially alter comparative accuracy estimates. These results demonstrate that accuracy conflates execution case mix with verification policy. Evaluations of test-time methods should therefore report pre-intervention execution states, verification coverage, and scorer provenance alongside accuracy.

</details>


### [59] [INS-ActBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Assessing Professional Actuarial Capability of Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24273)
*Changyu Chen,Chenwei Lin,Xian Xu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: INS-ActBench is a new benchmark to evaluate how well LLMs can perform realistic professional actuarial tasks (knowledge, case reasoning, and tool-based practice).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing financial and actuarial benchmarks test skills like domain knowledge, numerical reasoning, long-context understanding, and tool use separately, which does not reflect real professional actuarial workflows that require integrating these abilities in an auditable, context-grounded, and tool-executable manner.

Method: The authors build INS-ActBench, a benchmark with 12,050 Q&A pairs from public exams and sample questions of 16 actuarial associations. They organize it into three subsets: INS-Act-Know for standardized actuarial knowledge questions, INS-Act-Case for long-context insurance case reasoning tasks, and INS-Act-Practice for spreadsheet and R-code tasks with verifiable numerical outputs. They then evaluate nine representative LLMs and compare their performance with human actuarial experts.

Result: Frontier LLMs show strong performance on standardized actuarial knowledge questions (INS-Act-Know), but perform significantly worse on long-context case reasoning, tool-based workflows involving spreadsheets and R code (INS-Act-Case and INS-Act-Practice), and tasks that are sensitive to specific jurisdictions. This reveals a clear capability boundary between current LLMs and human actuarial experts in realistic practice settings.

Conclusion: INS-ActBench serves as a comprehensive, reproducible benchmark for assessing and driving progress toward LLMs that can reliably assist with professional actuarial work, especially in complex, context-rich, and tool-integrated workflows.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong potential in financial reasoning, but existing benchmarks often evaluate domain knowledge, numerical reasoning, long-context understanding, and tool use in separate settings. This limits their ability to assess realistic professional workflows that require auditable, context-grounded, and tool-executable decisions. We introduce \textbf{INS-ActBench}, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating professional actuarial capability in LLMs. INS-ActBench contains 12,050 Q\&A pairs from public exams and sample questions released by 16 actuarial associations. It covers three subsets: \textbf{INS-Act-Know} for standardized actuarial knowledge, \textbf{INS-Act-Case} for long-context insurance case reasoning, and \textbf{INS-Act-Practice} for spreadsheet and R-code tasks with verifiable numerical outputs. Experiments on nine representative LLMs and human actuarial experts reveal a clear capability boundary: frontier LLMs perform strongly on standardized knowledge, but remain much weaker in case reasoning, tool-based workflows, and jurisdiction-sensitive practice. INS-ActBench provides a reproducible foundation for developing actuarial LLMs toward reliable professional assistance. The code is available at https://github.com/FDU-INS/INS-ActBench.

</details>


### [60] [The Tokenizer Tax: Quantifying and Explaining the Cross-Lingual Cost of Subword Tokenization for Indian Languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24276)
*Priyansh Srivastava*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper shows that common LLM tokenizers impose a large “tokenization tax” on Indian languages, drastically shortening their effective context window compared to English, but that better tokenizer design can largely fix this.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most LLM tokenizers are trained on English-heavy data and use subword units that are efficient for English but often inefficient for other languages. This likely wastes context space and may harm performance for non-English users, yet this effect has not been carefully quantified for Indian languages, which are widely spoken and linguistically diverse. The authors want to measure how severe this bias is, understand its cause, and test whether it is an inherent script issue or a fixable design problem.

Method: Using the FLORES-200 parallel corpus, the authors compute tokenization fertility (tokens per character or per unit of meaning) across 14 Indian languages and English for six popular tokenizers, including cl100k_base and multilingual models like XLM-R and o200k_base. They compare token counts for semantically equivalent content to define a “tokenization tax” relative to English. They analyze byte-pair merge behavior, quantifying merge failures and correlating them with tokenizer tax. They then assess practical impact by simulating fixed context budgets and measuring how much source content is preserved for Indian versus English documents. Finally, they analyze reading comprehension scores on the Belebele benchmark to study correlations between tokenizer fertility and model performance, controlling for language resource availability.

Result: Under the widely used cl100k_base tokenizer, Indian languages require on average 8× more tokens than English for equivalent FLORES-200 sentences, peaking at about 13× for Malayalam; this means that for the same context length, Indian-language users effectively get as little as 12% of the usable context that English users get. The main mechanism is failed BPE merges: text often gets broken into single-byte tokens, and the rate of these merge failures correlates strongly with tokenizer tax (Pearson r = 0.89). Multilingual tokenizers like XLM-R and o200k_base dramatically reduce this tax—by roughly 73% on average—showing that most of the disparity is not inevitable. The authors also show that in fixed-length contexts, Indian-language documents retain significantly less original content than English ones. On the Belebele reading comprehension benchmark, raw correlations between fertility and performance largely disappear once language resource availability is accounted for, suggesting that tokenizer behavior is not the dominant factor in accuracy differences.

Conclusion: The tokenizer inefficiency faced by Indian languages in many current LLMs is substantial but primarily a product of tokenizer design, not of intrinsic properties of Indic scripts. Poorly adapted tokenizers waste context and disadvantage users of these languages by restricting how much content they can process at once. However, multilingual and better-trained tokenizers can greatly reduce this gap, indicating a clear path for fairer and more efficient multilingual LLMs. Performance gaps on downstream tasks are influenced more by general resource availability than by tokenizer fertility alone, so both tokenizer design and data/resource equity must be addressed to improve support for Indian languages.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) process text through subword tokenizers rather than directly reading characters or words. Because these tokenizers are trained predominantly on English-centric corpora, they introduce a systematic and often overlooked disadvantage for many non-English languages. In this work, we quantify this tokenizer tax for Indian languages using the FLORES-200 parallel corpus, measuring tokenization fertility across six widely used tokenizers and fourteen languages. Under cl100k_base (used by GPT-3.5 and GPT-4), Indian languages experience an average 8.0x tokenization tax relative to English, reaching 13.0x for Malayalam, reducing the effective context window to as little as 12% of that available to English users for equivalent semantic content. We identify the primary mechanism behind this disparity: failed byte-pair merges that leave text fragmented into single-byte tokens, with merge failure strongly correlating with tokenizer tax (Pearson r = 0.89). We further show that this phenomenon is not an inherent property of Indic scripts but a consequence of tokenizer design. Multilingual tokenizers such as XLM-R and OpenAI's o200k_base reduce the average Indic tokenizer tax by 73%, demonstrating that the disparity is largely remediable. Beyond token statistics, we quantify a practical consequence by showing that, under fixed context budgets, Indian-language documents preserve substantially less original content than equivalent English documents. Finally, we examine the relationship between tokenizer fertility and reading comprehension performance on the Belebele benchmark, finding that the apparent correlation is largely explained by language resource availability rather than tokenizer behavior alone.

</details>


### [61] [Self-Authored Verification Is Unreliable in Heuristic Self-Improving Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24300)
*Diandian Guo,Cong Cao,Fangfang Yuan,Yingqi Wang,Yueshan Wang,Dakui Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Paper analyzes why self-improving agents that rewrite both their policies and their own tests can appear to do great on self-authored metrics while actually performing poorly in real deployment, and proposes a mechanism (SEAL) that uses an external, sealed accept/reject audit to keep self-improvement reliable.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In self-improving systems, the same agent often controls both its policies and the tests used to evaluate them. This can cause a verifier–deployment gap, where scores on self-authored tests remain high but real performance degrades, posing safety and reliability risks. The authors want to understand when and why this happens and how to limit regressions without discarding the benefits of self-verification.

Method: They formalize the verifier–deployment gap: a difference between the agent’s self-authored verification signal and a separate, sealed deployment evaluation that the agent cannot see. They empirically study iterative policy-and-test rewriting in heuristic learning settings that require trial-and-error to discover the true objective. They then introduce SEAL (Sealed Exogenous Acceptance Loop), which keeps self-authored tests but wraps them with a fixed, external audit harness that compares candidate policies to the incumbent and only returns an accept/reject signal; if a regression is detected, the incumbent is fully retained. They compare SEAL to standard self-written constraints and unprotected baselines across several models and seeds.

Result: Experiments show that failures of self-written verification are common in heuristic learning: agents can keep or increase self-test scores while losing real capability. These failures differ by capability level: weaker agents often overwrite or damage previously learned strategies while still passing easy self-tests, whereas stronger agents are more stable but still misestimate the deployment distribution. Standard self-written constraints fail to consistently close the verifier–deployment gap. SEAL exceeds the performance of unprotected baselines across six models and three random seeds, reducing regressions while retaining self-improvement.

Conclusion: Self-authored verification alone is not sufficient for reliable self-improvement, because agents can exploit or mis-specify their own tests and drift away from real deployment performance. However, one does not need to abandon self-verification entirely: adding at least one exogenous, sealed deployment-acceptance signal—such as SEAL’s harness-side audit that the agent cannot modify or inspect—can substantially mitigate regressions and support more reliable capability accumulation.

Abstract: Self-improving agents accumulate capability by repeatedly rewriting procedural policies, controllers, or heuristic rules. They typically rely on self-authored tests or metrics to decide whether to accept subsequent edits. The agent controls both the optimized object and its verifier. As a result, self-assigned scores can remain near perfect while real deployment performance degrades or stays low. We study this problem through the verifier--deployment gap. This gap refers to the discrepancy between an agent's self-authored verification signal and a sealed deployment evaluation that the agent cannot observe or access. We ask how self-authored verification fails under iterative policy-and-test rewriting, how the failure changes with capability, and how little exogenous trust is sufficient to prevent real regressions from being deployed. To address this problem, we introduce a Sealed Exogenous Acceptance Loop (SEAL). SEAL retains self-authored tests but compares each candidate with the incumbent through a fixed harness-side audit. The agent cannot author or inspect the audit, receives only accept/reject, and the whole incumbent state is retained after a clear regression. Our experiments show that this problem often appears in heuristic learning settings. These settings require trial-and-error discovery of the target objective. We further find that failures of self-written verification are stratified by capability. Weaker agents tend to damage previously acquired strategies behind easy self-tests. Stronger agents are more stable, but they still mismeasure the deployment distribution. Standard self-written constraints do not reliably close this gap. In contrast, SEAL outperforms unprotected baselines across six models and three random seeds. Reliable self-improvement need not abandon self-verification, but it requires at least one deployment-acceptance signal outside the agent's control.

</details>


### [62] [Rethinking the Generation Order of Block Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24306)
*Kai Syun Hou,James Kwok*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper introduces Parallel Autoregressive Decoding (PARD), a new sampling method for block diffusion language models that keeps a left-to-right decoding structure while enabling parallel token generation, improving quality and speed over existing methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing sampling methods for diffusion language models were designed for earlier masked diffusion models and may not be optimal for newer block diffusion language models. There is a need for sampling strategies that better exploit BDLMs’ properties, particularly their natural alignment with left-to-right decoding, to achieve both high generation quality and fast decoding.

Method: The authors empirically and analytically study the decoding behavior of block diffusion language models and show they align well with left-to-right generation. Leveraging this, they propose Parallel Autoregressive Decoding (PARD), a training-free sampling procedure that enforces a left-to-right unmasking pattern but allows multiple tokens to be committed in parallel at each step, combining benefits of autoregressive and parallel decoding.

Result: In experiments across various settings, PARD consistently outperforms prior parallel sampling methods for diffusion language models in terms of generation quality, while also providing notable speedups compared with standard purely autoregressive decoding. The quality difference between PARD and pure AR decoding is reported to be small, indicating an efficient trade-off between speed and performance.

Conclusion: Block diffusion language models are better suited to left-to-right decoding than earlier masked diffusion language models. By exploiting this property, PARD offers an effective sampling strategy that achieves strong generation quality with faster decoding, narrowing the gap between diffusion-based and autoregressive language model inference.

Abstract: Diffusion language models enable flexible arbitrary-order generation, but existing sampling methods are mostly designed for early masked diffusion models (MDMs). In this work, we study sampling for recent block diffusion language models (BDLMs). We show empirically and analytically that these models are naturally more aligned with left-to-right decoding than MDMs. Based on this observation, we propose Parallel Autoregressive Decoding (PARD), a simple training-free sampling method that preserves left-to-right unmasking structure while allowing parallel token commitment. Extensive experiments show that PARD consistently outperforms existing parallel samplers in generation quality, while achieving substantial speedups over pure AR decoding with only a small quality gap.

</details>


### [63] [CONSISTRE: A Unified Consistency-Aware Framework for Document-Level Relation Extraction with Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24312)
*Mingxuan Sun*

Main category: cs.CL
