TL;DR: CONSISTRE is a framework to make document-level relation extraction with LLMs logically consistent by enforcing relational constraints during inference for black-box models and during training for open-source models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Document-level relation extraction needs to handle multiple entities and long contexts while keeping all predicted relations logically consistent (e.g., respecting transitivity, symmetry, and functional uniqueness). Standard LLM-based approaches treat each candidate triple independently, which often produces contradictory relations and undermines reliability. There is a need for methods that explicitly model and enforce such consistency for both API-based and locally deployed LLMs.

Method: CONSISTRE has two complementary tracks built on a unified consistency formulation. (1) Inference-time track for black-box LLMs: uses constraint-aware prompting, constraint-based verification, and iterative self-reflection so the model revises outputs that violate relational constraints, without fine-tuning. (2) Training-time track for smaller open-source models: first distills reasoning traces from a strong teacher into a student with supervised fine-tuning, then applies GRPO-based reinforcement learning with a composite reward that balances extraction quality and relational consistency, injecting constraint knowledge directly into the model.

Result: On the DocRED benchmark, both tracks outperform their respective baselines. The inference-time track, using off-the-shelf proprietary LLMs via API, reaches competitive F1 scores while improving consistency. The training-time track significantly reduces the performance gap between 7–8B open-source models and state-of-the-art proprietary LLMs, doing so with much lower inference cost. Ablations show that removing explicit consistency components increases contradictions and reduces reliability.

Conclusion: Explicitly modeling and enforcing relational consistency substantially improves document-level relation extraction with LLMs. CONSISTRE provides a unified framework that works both at inference time for black-box APIs and at training time for open-source models, yielding more reliable, contradiction-free relational predictions across deployment settings and demonstrating that consistency constraints are a valuable inductive bias for DocRE.

Abstract: Document-level relation extraction (DocRE) aims to extract relations among multiple entities across extended contexts while maintaining consistency across predicted triples. Although large language models (LLMs) show remarkable reasoning capabilities in information extraction, their predictions are typically generated independently for each candidate triple and may violate fundamental relational constraints such as transitivity, symmetry, and functional uniqueness, leading to contradictory and unreliable outputs. We propose CONSISTRE, a unified consistency-aware framework for DocRE that addresses this limitation through two complementary tracks. The first operates at inference time for black-box LLMs, combining constraint-aware prompting, constraint-based verification, and iterative self-reflection to refine predictions without task-specific fine-tuning. The second injects consistency knowledge into smaller open-source models via a knowledge distillation and reinforcement learning pipeline: reasoning traces from a powerful teacher are distilled into a student via supervised fine-tuning, followed by GRPO alignment using a composite reward that jointly optimizes extraction performance and relational consistency. Together, the two tracks cover both API-accessible and locally deployable scenarios under a unified consistency formulation. Experiments on DocRED show that both tracks outperform their baselines, with the inference-time track achieving competitive F1 using off-the-shelf black-box LLMs and the training-time track substantially narrowing the gap between 7--8B open-source models and state-of-the-art proprietary LLMs at a fraction of their inference cost. Ablation studies confirm that explicit consistency modeling mitigates relational contradictions and enhances the reliability of LLM-based DocRE across both deployment paradigms.

</details>


### [64] [Cross-Attention Calibrated Deduplication for Retrieval-Augmented Generation System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24332)
*Phuong Le Huy,Nam H. Nguyen,Quan V. Dang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes CACD, a cross-attention-based deduplication method that removes redundant chunks in RAG systems more accurately and faster than strong baselines, without relying on lossy single-vector representations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RAG chunking strategies create many redundant chunks, inflating vector databases and slowing retrieval. Current deduplication via cosine similarity over single pooled vectors loses token-level information, making it hard to distinguish true duplicates from merely topically similar chunks. Exact-match filters, on the other hand, remove almost nothing. The authors aim to design a deduplication method that preserves fine-grained information while remaining efficient and effective at removing semantically redundant chunks.

Method: They introduce Cross-Attention Calibrated Deduplication (CACD). For each new chunk, CACD compares it against an in-memory pool of already-kept chunks using a cross-encoder to maintain token-level detail. It computes a New Information Score (NIS) from the attention entropy of the cross-encoder to quantify how much of the new chunk is not explained by candidate chunks. Instead of relying on the single best match, CACD aggregates a majority vote across several candidate matches. They benchmark CACD against five existing filtering methods across nine chunking strategies and 18 total configurations using the full SQuAD 1.1 validation set.

Result: Across all tested configurations, CACD removes on average 9.75% of chunks, comparable to other semantic-level filters and much higher than exact-match-based methods, which remove almost nothing. In terms of processing speed, CACD averages 51.0 seconds per configuration, which is about 27% faster than the strongest baseline NERExact (69.6s) and roughly seven times faster than cosine-similarity-based filtering (356.7s).

Conclusion: CACD is an effective and efficient semantic deduplication approach for RAG chunk stores, achieving substantial chunk reduction while outperforming strong baselines in speed. By using cross-attention, attention-entropy-based New Information Scores, and multi-candidate voting, it avoids the limitations of single-vector cosine similarity approaches. However, the findings are based on SQuAD 1.1 only, so the authors position the work as an early comparison and encourage further validation on more datasets.

Abstract: Common chunking strategies in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems often create redundant chunks. These redundant chunks make the vector database bigger and slow down retrieval. A common fix is cosine-similarity thresholding. This method reduces each chunk to a single vector, then compares vectors using a similarity score. But a single vector can lose the fine-grained, token-level detail needed to tell a true duplicate apart from a chunk that just shares the same topic. We propose Cross-Attention Calibrated Deduplication (CACD). CACD checks each new chunk against an in-memory pool of chunks already kept, using a cross-encoder instead of a single pooled vector. This keeps token-level detail all the way to the final comparison. CACD combines three parts: the cross-encoder comparison itself, a New Information Score (NIS) that measures how much of a chunk is not explained by a candidate already kept, and a majority vote across several candidates rather than a single best match. NIS is calculated from the attention entropy of the cross-encoder. We tested CACD against five existing filtering methods, nine chunking strategies, and 18 configurations, all on the full SQuAD 1.1 validation set. In our experiments, CACD removes 9.75% of chunks on average. This drop rate is close to other semantic-level methods, and much higher than exact-match filters, which barely remove anything. In these experiments, CACD also processes each configuration in 51.0 seconds on average, about 27% faster than the strongest baseline, NERExact (69.6s), and about 7x faster than cosine-similarity filtering (356.7s). These results come from a single dataset, so we present them as an early comparison, not a general claim. Code for the baseline evaluation and for CACD is available at https://github.com/lehuyphuong/rag_bench and https://github.com/lehuyphuong/cacd_dedup.

</details>


### [65] [Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models as Components of Cognitive Computing architecture for Regulatory Knowledge Management](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24352)
*Dariusz Nowak-Nova*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper tests whether combining locally deployed LLMs with a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) layer can turn them into reliable, auditable components of a cognitive system for legal and regulatory tasks, even on consumer hardware.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standalone LLMs hallucinate, lack traceability of sources, and are hard to update for fast-changing legal domains. Many organizations also cannot or do not want to use cloud-based, GPU-heavy solutions for sensitive regulatory workloads. The authors want a way to use smaller, local LLMs as trustworthy tools for regulatory analysis and compliance support, with better factual reliability and auditability.

Method: They design a hybrid architecture where locally hosted LLMs (Polish models Bielik and PLLuM) run in Ollama and LM Studio on consumer hardware. These LLMs are coupled with a RAG layer connected to external knowledge bases of legal acts. In this setup, the LLM focuses on semantic understanding and formulation, while RAG handles controlled retrieval, contextualization, and citation of legal sources. They then validate this setup in regulatory management scenarios, comparing behavior with and without RAG.

Result: The RAG-enhanced setup substantially improves factual correctness, domain relevance, and normative precision of generated legal texts, while reducing hallucinations and unsupported claims. It also enables clear traceability of which legal sources were used, plus easier and safer updating of regulatory knowledge without retraining the LLM. The system runs effectively on consumer-level hardware in on-prem environments.

Conclusion: LLMs combined with RAG can act as semantic processing modules inside a broader cognitive computing infrastructure, especially for regulatory and compliance work. When deployed locally and augmented with external knowledge repositories, they become more reliable, auditable, and maintainable than standalone text generators, making them suitable for decision support in legally and informationally volatile environments.

Abstract: The aim of this article is to verify whether integrating large language models (LLMs) with the Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture enables their transformation from standalone generative models into components of cognitive computing infrastructure with enhanced epistemic reliability. The study proposes an architectural approach based on locally deployed LLMs operating in on-premises environments without high-end GPU accelerators and examines their applicability in supporting regulatory management processes requiring continuous analysis and interpretation of legal acts. The proposed solution combines local LLMs with external knowledge repositories, creating a hybrid cognitive architecture in which the language model performs semantic interpretation while the RAG layer provides controlled knowledge retrieval, contextualization, and traceability of information sources. The implementation was validated using the Ollama and LM Studio execution environments together with the Polish language models Bielik and PLLuM running on consumer-class hardware. The results demonstrate that augmenting LLMs with RAG significantly improves the factual consistency, domain specificity and normative precision of generated texts while reducing the risk of unsupported content generation. Furthermore, the study shows that integrating RAG introduces auditability, controlled knowledge management and dynamic updating of regulatory information without retraining the language model. The findings indicate that locally deployed LLMs enhanced with RAG should be regarded not merely as text generation tools but as semantic processing modules within cognitive computing infrastructures supporting regulatory compliance and organizational decision-making in environments characterized by high legal and informational volatility.

</details>


### [66] [Keep It InMind: Benchmarking the Implicit-Association Blind Spot in Agent Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24368)
*Ruizhe Li,Mingxuan Du,Benfeng Xu,Zhendong Mao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces InMind, a benchmark to study how long-term memory systems fail on queries that require implicit associations not textually similar to stored facts, showing that current retrieval systems are the main bottleneck and that better routing of which facts remain visible is the key open problem.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing long-term memory systems assume that relevant memories will be textually or semantically similar to incoming queries. However, real-world knowledge often requires implicit associations where the needed fact and the query share no obvious lexical or embedding cue (e.g., a tree‑nut allergy affecting macaron recommendations because of almond flour). Current benchmarks do not clearly distinguish whether failures come from missing knowledge, missing bridging reasoning, or failure of retrieval interfaces. The authors want to isolate and quantify this specific failure mode to better understand and improve memory-augmented models.

Method: The authors define the 'implicit-association blind spot' where a system must use a stored fact that is not explicitly similar to the query. They construct InMind, a 125-task benchmark across ten life domains, with 113 tasks grounded in publicly citable sources. Each task has paired controls that allow separating three causes of error: (1) fact not stored, (2) model lacks bridging world knowledge, (3) fact stored but not surfaced by retrieval. They evaluate a backbone model under two conditions: (a) the decisive memory is directly placed in the context, and (b) the same memory must be retrieved from an external store using six different memory systems (vector, graph, and agentic memory). They also test higher-dimensional embeddings and a minimal diagnostic probe that keeps memory visible before the query to locate where the failure occurs.

Result: When the decisive memory is directly provided in the prompt, the backbone model correctly answers 84.0% of indirect, implicit-association queries, showing it can use the knowledge once it is surfaced. However, when the same facts must be retrieved by long-term memory systems, six different retrieval approaches achieve at most 14.4% accuracy on these queries, even though they can recall the facts on explicit prompts with up to 100% success. Increasing embedding dimensionality by 8x improves recall of answer-relevant targets but does not materially close the performance gap on implicit queries. A minimal diagnostic probe that keeps candidate memories visible before seeing the query recovers most of the lost performance, pinpointing the main failure to the query-conditioned retrieval/routing interface rather than pure storage or knowledge limitations.

Conclusion: The core limitation in current long-term memory systems is not storing facts or the model’s ability to reason with them once seen, but the query-conditioned retrieval interface: systems fail to surface the right memories when the query and the necessary fact are only implicitly related. InMind provides a targeted benchmark to measure and analyze this 'implicit-association blind spot.' The findings suggest that simply improving embeddings or memory structures is insufficient; the key open problem is designing better routing and visibility mechanisms that decide which facts must remain accessible across time, especially when future queries will be indirectly related to stored information.

Abstract: Long-term memory systems store what a user says in an external store and retrieve it when a related query arrives. This interface rests on an assumption so natural that it is rarely stated: a memory that is needed will resemble the query that needs it. World knowledge breaks the assumption. A tree-nut allergy should change the answer to a macaron request through their almond-flour ingredient, yet the two texts share no cue a retriever can see. We call this failure mode the implicit-association blind spot and introduce InMind, a 125-task, expert-verified benchmark spanning ten life domains, with 113 tasks grounded in citable public sources. Its paired controls separate three explanations that existing evaluations conflate: the fact was never stored, the model lacks the bridging knowledge, or the fact was stored and never surfaced. The verdict is clean. With the decisive memory placed in context, the backbone answers 84.0 percent of indirect queries; when the same memory must be retrieved, six vector, graph, and agentic memory systems reach at most 14.4 percent, even though they recall the same facts on demand at up to 100 percent. An embedding with eight times the dimensionality raises answer-blind target recall for every system yet leaves the gap essentially intact. A minimal diagnostic probe that keeps memory visible before the query arrives recovers most of the gap, locating the failure in the query-conditioned interface itself and pointing to routing, deciding which facts must stay visible, as the open problem InMind is built to score.

</details>


### [67] [Closed-Loop Validation-Repair for Healthcare Interoperability: A Multi-Model Study of Schema Compliance in Clinical LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24371)
*Jianru Shen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies how well open-source medical LLMs comply with healthcare data schemas and shows that a validation-repair loop greatly boosts schema compliance for interoperability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Although LLMs can perform clinical reasoning, they often fail to output data in strict standardized formats (ICD-10, CPT, HL7 FHIR) required by EHRs and billing systems. This schema noncompliance blocks real-world integration of LLMs into healthcare workflows. The authors aim to quantify this problem across models and test whether a system-level validation-repair pipeline can reliably fix schema issues and make models practically usable for interoperability.

Method: The authors locally deploy three open-source LLMs—Qwen2.5 7B, Llama 3.1 8B, and Gemma2 9B—on 320 curated clinical scenarios from 10 medical specialties. For each scenario and model (960 pairs), they generate structured outputs under two conditions: (1) baseline generation and (2) a closed-loop validation-repair framework where a validator checks schema conformity and feeds back corrections for iterative regeneration. They categorize failures into representation-level (format/notation issues) versus deeper content/schema errors, and compute compliance rates, iteration counts to repair, and McNemar tests to assess statistical significance of improvements between baseline and repaired outputs.

Result: Baseline schema compliance is similar across the three model families, around 85.9–91.6%, implying that noncompliance is a general issue not tied to a specific architecture. The vast majority (96%) of validator-flagged failures are representation-level issues such as using non-standard abbreviations or incorrect code prefixes, meaning that models generally understand the clinical content but violate IT formatting conventions. With the validation-repair loop, overall schema compliance rises to 99.0% (98.4–99.4% by model), with most errors corrected within one or two iterations. Improvements of 7.8–12.5 percentage points are statistically significant with exact McNemar p-values < 0.001.

Conclusion: LLMs’ main barrier to healthcare interoperability is not clinical reasoning but lack of strict adherence to standardized schema formats. Since most noncompliance is representational and easily corrected, a closed-loop validation-repair framework provides an effective, statistically validated safeguard, elevating open-source medical LLMs to near-perfect schema compliance and making them more viable for integration into EHRs and other clinical IT systems.

Abstract: Healthcare interoperability requires AI systems to produce structured outputs conforming to standardized schemas including ICD-10 for diagnostic coding, CPT for procedure billing, and HL7 FHIR for data exchange. While large language models demonstrate clinical reasoning capabilities, their integration into electronic health record systems faces a critical barrier: schema noncompliance. We evaluate three open-source models, Qwen2.5 7B, Llama 3.1 8B, and Gemma2 9B, via local deployment across 320 clinical scenarios spanning ten medical specialties, yielding 960 model-scenario pairs assessed under paired baseline and validation-repair conditions. First, schema noncompliance is consistent across the three model families, with baseline compliance rates ranging from 85.9 to 91.6 percent despite varying architectures and training data, suggesting shared gaps in medical training corpora rather than model-specific limitations. Second, 96 percent of validator-detected failures are representation-level format violations such as alternative medical abbreviations and code prefixes, indicating models follow clinical writing conventions but lack awareness of healthcare IT standards. Third, the validation-repair framework achieves 99.0 percent overall compliance, ranging from 98.4 to 99.4 percent across models, with most errors resolving within one or two iterations. Exact McNemar p-values below 0.001 and absolute improvements of 7.8 to 12.5 percentage points across model sizes confirm statistical significance. These results support closed-loop validation-repair as an effective system-level safeguard for healthcare interoperability, improving schema-level readiness for downstream clinical system integration.

</details>


### [68] [LEX-EC: A Lexical Evidence-Channel Audit Framework for Zero-Shot LLM Personality Classification in Black-Box Settings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24435)
*Brittany Harbison,Ashok K. Goel*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Introduces LEX-EC, a black-box audit framework that uses lexical ablation and multiple diagnostics to interpret how language models infer personality traits from text.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While large language models can assign personality labels from text, it is unclear what lexical evidence they rely on, how robust these inferences are across genres, and to what extent results reflect real trait signals versus dataset artifacts. There is a need for an interpretable, reusable framework to audit personality classification behavior in black-box models.

Method: The authors design LEX-EC, a black-box interpretability framework that combines several components: (1) prevalence analysis of trait predictions, (2) item-level association and chance-corrected agreement diagnostics, (3) controlled lexical ablation and masking of different word classes (topical, demographic, function words, affective and cognitive-style terms), and (4) prompt-based probing of model self-explanations. They apply this pipeline to multiple text genres (free-form essays, graduate student introductions, and single Facebook statuses) and to multiple models and prompts, measuring how trait associations change as lexical evidence is systematically restricted.

Result: Applying LEX-EC reveals that: (a) free-form essays show the broadest, yet still weak, personality signal; (b) in graduate student introductions, an initially observable association with Extraversion weakens substantially after lexical masking; (c) single Facebook status updates provide little stable evidence for personality traits, even when the sample is balanced by trait labels, suggesting a minimum content/length requirement; and (d) masking topical and demographic content reduces some trait associations but leaves others detectable via function words, affect-related vocabulary, and cognitive-style terms. Linguistic prompting changes the form of model self-explanations but fails to fully remove topical content from them.

Conclusion: LEX-EC provides a systematic way to audit and interpret how black-box language models infer personality traits from text, disentangling marginal-distribution artifacts from recoverable trait signals under constrained lexical evidence. The framework shows that personality signal strength and stability vary strongly by genre and available lexical content, and that models can still exploit non-topical linguistic cues even after masking. This establishes lexical ablation–based auditing as a useful tool for understanding and stress-testing personality labeling behavior in large language models.

Abstract: Large language models may easily assign personality labels from text, but model interpretability remains an open problem. To address this gap, we introduce LEX-EC, a reusable black-box audit framework combining prevalence and agreement diagnostics with controlled lexical ablation to distinguish marginal-distribution effects from trait-associated signal recoverable under restricted evidence. Using this framework, we illustrate how various text genres may exhibit sharply different profiles: free-form essay text contains the broadest, but still weak, signal; in graduate student introductions, an observable Extraversion association weakened after masking; and single Facebook statuses yield little stable evidence even in a trait-balanced sample, indicating a possible lower bound of content or length. Masking topical and demographic content weakened some associations while leaving others detectable from function words, affective terms, and cognitive-style vocabulary. Linguistic prompting shifted model self-explanations but did not eliminate topical content. LEX-EC jointly evaluates classification prevalence, item-level association, chance-corrected agreement, persistence under lexical restriction, and prompt sensitivity in model-generated explanations. Across datasets, models, and prompts, LEX-EC characterizes how trait associations may vary with available lexical evidence, introducing a novel application of lexical methods to black-box interpretability in personality labeling.

</details>


### [69] [Grounding latent algorithm routing in transformer reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24471)
*Xiangbo Zhang,Xiaoxu Ma*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper investigates whether transformers can internally route between different algorithmic solution families depending on the data regime, using a new controlled benchmark (ROUTEBENCH) that pits several inductive-bias families against each other.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In-context learning appears to let transformers adapt their behavior to different tasks without parameter updates, but it is unclear whether this adaptation corresponds to systematically choosing among different solution algorithms depending on the underlying data regime. The authors want a controlled setting to test if transformers can internally learn such routing behavior, beyond surface-level prompt changes, and whether the responsible internal variables are stable, decodable, and causally linked to behavior.

Method: They design ROUTEBENCH, a diagnostic benchmark with several data-generating regimes that differentially favor four inductive-bias families: global shrinkage (ridge-like), sparsity (lasso-like), robustness (Huber-like), and locality (kNN-like). They train dense decoder-only transformers from scratch across a range of sizes (44M–612M) on this benchmark and measure how well models route between solver families given fixed prompt forms. They evaluate route quality (route F1), how closely models approach an oracle router, robustness under various perturbations (natural-language renderings, shuffling, paraphrases, unified four-way routing), and compare against explicit routing baselines (input-conditioned soft mixture, unsupervised Gumbel router). They also run probe-based analyses and activation-patching controls to test whether route-relevant internal directions are decodable and causally affect solver-family-consistent outputs.

Result: A 306M-parameter transformer closes 80.9% of the gap to an oracle router and achieves a route F1 of 84.1, indicating strong latent routing across solver families. This routing behavior persists under multiple perturbations (natural-language variants, shuffled supports, paraphrases, four-way routing). Explicit routing alternatives such as a soft mixture and a Gumbel router improve over simpler baselines but still underperform the larger transformers on route F1 and out-of-distribution performance. Probing and activation-patching show that specific internal directions encode routing information and that intervening on them selectively affects which solver-family behavior the model exhibits, without large performance degradation.

Conclusion: Dense decoder-only transformers trained on the ROUTEBENCH benchmark can develop stable, decodable, and causally influential internal variables that implement route-like selection among different inductive-bias families, supporting a structured form of episode-level adaptation in in-context learning. However, these findings are limited to this controlled synthetic setting and do not imply that general-purpose pretrained language models possess universal routing abilities for arbitrary natural-language reasoning tasks.

Abstract: A central question in the in-context learning literature is whether transformers can organize episode-level adaptation around different inductive-bias families. We study this question in a controlled setting through latent algorithm routing: route-like behavior in which the solver-family preference changes with the latent data-generating regime while prompt form is held fixed, remains stable under nuisance perturbations, and is selectively influenced by targeted activation interventions without large losses in answer quality. We introduce ROUTEBENCH, a diagnostic benchmark whose regimes differentially favor global shrinkage, sparsity, robustness, and locality, operationalized by ridge-like, lasso-like, Huber-like, and kNN-like family representatives. Across dense decoder-only transformers trained from scratch at 44M-612M parameters, a 306M model closes 80.9 percent of the oracle-routing gap and achieves route F1 of 84.1. The effect remains substantial under natural-language renderings, shuffled supports, lexical paraphrases, and a unified four-way routing setting. Stronger adaptive alternatives, including an input-conditioned soft mixture and an unsupervised Gumbel router, narrow the gap but remain below the 306M and 612M models on route F1 and OOD performance. Probe controls and matched activation-patching controls further show that route-relevant internal directions are decodable and functionally involved in solver-family-consistent output behavior. These results provide controlled evidence that dense transformers trained on ROUTEBENCH can develop route-like internal variables, but they do not establish universal routing in pretrained language models or unrestricted natural-language reasoning.

</details>


### [70] [SINT-Flow: Schema Integration using Large Language Model Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24492)
*Keti Korini,Christian Bizer*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They propose SINT-Flow, an LLM-based, fully automated framework for integrating multiple database schemata, including messy denormalized tables, and show it works very accurately on a new benchmark they introduce.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Schema integration is essential for combining data from multiple sources into a unified view, but existing solutions struggle with denormalized tables that mix multiple entity types in a single table and often require manual effort. With the rise of powerful large language models, there is an opportunity to automate schema integration more flexibly and handle complex, real-world tables while maintaining high accuracy.

Method: The authors design SINT-Flow, a framework built from five modular LLM-based operators that can be assembled into workflows to carry out end-to-end schema integration. A key capability is to first analyze and decompose denormalized input tables into separate relations for distinct entity types, and then detect entities, attributes, and mappings with self-consistency strategies and a review loop for schema matching. They instantiate SINT-Flow using LLM backbones (GPT-5.2 and Qwen-3.6-27B) and design prompts and operator logic to perform each step automatically.

Result: They introduce SINT-Bench, a benchmark of 10 schema integration tasks over 93 relational tables, including multi-entity denormalized tables, and evaluate SINT-Flow on it. Using GPT-5.2 and Qwen-3.6-27B as backbones, SINT-Flow obtains at least 96% F1 for entity-type detection, 85% for attribute detection, and 83% for schema mapping. An ablation study shows that self-consistency and the review loop significantly contribute to these performance levels.

Conclusion: SINT-Flow demonstrates that LLM-based operators can enable fully automated, end-to-end schema integration, including challenging denormalized tables, while achieving high accuracy on a dedicated benchmark. The framework and SINT-Bench together provide a foundation for future research on LLM-driven data integration, and the study shows that design choices such as self-consistency and review loops are important for robust schema matching performance.

Abstract: The goal of schema integration is, given a set of input schemata or tables, to derive a global, unified schema that is able to represent the concepts, attributes, and relationships of all input tables in a coherent fashion. This paper presents SINT-Flow, a schema integration framework composed of five LLM-based operators that can be combined into workflows to perform fully automated, end-to-end schema integration. In contrast to existing approaches, SINT-Flow can process denormalized source tables that contain attributes describing multiple entity types. During the schema integration process, these tables are decomposed into separate entity-specific relations. To evaluate SINT-Flow, we introduce SINT-Bench, a schema integration benchmark comprising 10 schema integration tasks consisting of altogether 93 relational tables, including tables that describe multiple types of entities. We evaluate SINT-Flow using GPT-5.2 as well as the open-weight model Qwen-3.6-27B as alternative backbone models. Using these models, SINT-Flow achieves F1 scores of at least 96% for entity-type detection, 85% for attribute detection, and 83% for schema mapping. Furthermore, we perform an ablation study to prove the utility of the applied self-consistency strategy as well as the inclusion of a review loop into the schema matching operator.

</details>


### [71] [Systematic Analysis of Large Language Models and Transformer-Based Machine Translation for English-Tamil and Tamil-English Across Diverse Datasets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24515)
*Sriharshaa S,Sangeetha Sivanesan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper evaluates multilingual machine translation models and a Tamil-specific LLM for English↔Tamil, showing that domain-matched, high-quality data and attention analysis improve performance and interpretability, while few-shot prompting with a Tamil LLM can yield coherent translations even with limited parallel data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Low-resource languages like Tamil suffer from limited parallel corpora, domain mismatch, and high morphological complexity, which degrade machine translation quality. The authors want to systematically assess how current multilingual NMT models and a Tamil-focused LLM handle English↔Tamil translation across datasets of varying domain and quality, and to understand model behavior rather than just raw scores.

Method: They evaluate supervised multilingual NMT systems (NLLB and mBART) on multiple English–Tamil/Tamil–English datasets (NTREX, EnTamV2, WikiMatrix, PMIndia) using BLEU and chrF. They analyze performance differences across domains and data quality levels. They also conduct attention-based alignment visualizations to interpret how models map source to target tokens. In parallel, they use in-context prompting with a Tamil-capable TamilLaMA model to perform few-shot translation, then qualitatively compare its translations with those of supervised NMT systems.

Result: Supervised models’ performance varies significantly with dataset quality and domain alignment; better curated, domain-matched data yields higher BLEU/chrF scores. Attention visualizations reveal meaningful source–target token alignments, indicating that attention helps explain translation decisions. The TamilLaMA model, when prompted in-context with a few examples, can produce structurally coherent English↔Tamil translations despite limited supervision, though its quality is compared mainly qualitatively rather than via full metric-based evaluation.

Conclusion: Translation quality in low-resource settings like Tamil is highly dependent on dataset quality and domain match, even for strong multilingual NMT models. Attention mechanisms are useful for interpretability, offering insights into how models align and translate tokens. Additionally, few-shot prompting of a Tamil-capable LLM such as TamilLaMA is a promising alternative or complement to supervised systems, as it can generate structurally coherent Tamil translations despite limited parallel data.

Abstract: The challenge of Machine Translation for low resource languages such as Tamil is primarily caused by the restricted amount of parallel data for these languages, as well as their substantial amount of domain variation and morphological complexity. This research presents the comprehensive evaluation of the performance of several multilingual translation models on English-Tamil and Tamil-English translations across multiple datasets: NTREX, EnTamV2, WikiMatrix and PMIndia. This study evaluates supervised NMT systems, NLLB and mBART, using both the BLEU and chrF metric, and examines how these systems perform on data of different quality levels and domains. This performs an attention-based analysis to increase model interpretability by visualising the alignments of tokens in an English source text and their Tamil translations and vice-versa to provide insight into how they make translations. This study also demonstrates that using in-context prompting can provide an excellent way to perform a few-shot translation of English to Tamil and Tamil-English using a Tamil capable TamilLaMA model, and compare this to supervised approaches qualitatively. These findings show that the quality of the datasets and their alignment with the domain will greatly affect the performance of the model, that attention-based mechanisms can aid in explain ability, and that few-shot large language models can still produce structurally coherent translations of Tamil.

</details>


### [72] [From transcription to semantic corpus analysis: unsupervised learning of sentence representations for ancient languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24542)
*Th{é}otime de la Selle*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They adapt existing language models into sentence encoders for ancient languages using only raw text and show these unsupervised methods work better than many strong baselines for detecting and retrieving biblical text reuse in patristic literature, even on noisy OCR-like data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Digital humanities now have lots of noisy machine-recognized text in ancient languages, but downstream tasks like text reuse detection and semantic search need high-quality sentence embeddings. Existing multilingual or specialized models do not work well: multilingual models underperform on ancient languages, specialized models produce poorly structured (anisotropic) embedding spaces, and there is no labeled similarity data to do supervised fine-tuning. The authors want a way to get strong sentence embeddings for ancient languages without labeled data, usable for philological research.

Method: Starting from a specialized token-level language model for the target ancient languages, they investigate two fully unsupervised adaptation strategies that require only raw sentences: (1) TSDAE (Text-Style Denoising AutoEncoder), where the model learns to reconstruct original sentences from noised inputs to obtain robust sentence embeddings; and (2) contrastive sentence embedding (CSE), where the model pulls semantically similar sentences together and pushes dissimilar ones apart using self-supervised signals. They test these adapted encoders on a benchmark of biblical reuse in patristic literature (Latin and Ancient Greek from Augustine, Jerome, and Athanasius), splitting the problem into binary detection of reuse vs. non-reuse and fine-grained correspondence retrieval. They compare against multilingual encoders, specialized and distilled models, and supervised fine-tuned baselines, and also evaluate robustness on artificially noised data mimicking ATR/HTR errors and scribal abbreviations. They visualize embedding spaces with UMAP to interpret geometric changes.

Result: Both unsupervised adaptation methods produce sentence encoders that outperform all baseline systems on binary detection and correspondence retrieval for biblical reuse. TSDAE performs best on detection when there is a large in-domain corpus available, while CSE performs best on retrieval and achieves near-optimal performance with only 4–8k in-domain sentences and very short training times on modest hardware. The adapted models generalize across different authors and works and remain effective on noisy, post-ATR text if they are retrained directly on that noisy data. UMAP visualizations reveal that each strategy reshapes the embedding space in ways that align with the observed performance improvements.

Conclusion: Unsupervised adaptation of specialized token-level language models into sentence encoders using TSDAE and contrastive sentence embedding is an effective solution for ancient-language semantic tasks when labeled data is absent. These methods yield robust, corpus-specific sentence embeddings that improve text reuse detection and correspondence retrieval, transfer across corpora and authors, and can handle ATR-induced noise. TSDAE is preferable for detection with ample data, whereas CSE is more data-efficient and better for retrieval, making them complementary tools. The authors package the full workflow, including segmentation, fine-tuning, and cross-corpus semantic search, into an accessible online tool (Paraphrasis) for scholars without technical expertise.

Abstract: Automatic Text Recognition (ATR) now supplies digital humanities with large volumes of unstructured, heterogeneous, and often noisy text in ancient languages. Downstream semantic analysestext reuse identification, alignment, and semantic search-rely on sentence embeddings, yet existing methods transfer poorly to ancient languages: generic multilingual encoders underperform, specialized language models yield anisotropic representation spaces, and labeled similarity data is unavailable. We study two fully unsupervised strategies - TSDAE and contrastive sentence embedding (CSE) - that adapt a specialized token-level language model into a corpus-specific sentence encoder using only raw sentences. On the philologically central case of biblical reuse in patristic literature (2,935 expert-verified parallels in Latin and Ancient Greek, from Augustine, Jerome, and Athanasius), we decompose reuse identification into two separately evaluated tasks-binary detection and correspondence retrieval-and benchmark the adapted encoders against multilingual, specialized, distilled, and supervised fine-tuned baselines, as well as on artificially noised data simulating HTR artifacts and scribal abbreviations. The adapted encoders outperform all baselines on both tasks, with complementary profiles: TSDAE leads detection given a large in-domain corpus, while CSE leads retrieval, reaches its optimum with as few as 4-8k raw in-domain sentences-a few tens of seconds of training on a laptop GPU-and transfers across works and authors, including to noisy post-ATR text when retrained directly on it. UMAP atlases relate the geometric effect of each strategy to the measured gains, and the full pipeline-segmentation, fine-tuning, cross-corpus semantic search-is made available to non-specialists through the online tool Paraphrasis.

</details>


### [73] [From Data to Device: ELMOD An Efficient German-First 2.7B Language Model for Mobile Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24585)
*Darina Gold,Alexander Schwirjow,Viktor Haag,Viktor Hangya,Joel Schlotthauer,Fabian Küch,Luzian Hahn*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ELMOD is a compact 2.7B-parameter German language model optimized for on-device deployment that achieves performance comparable to 7B models by using German-specific preprocessing and quality-filtered, rephrased training data on a modest compute budget.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To build a strong German language model that can run efficiently on resource-constrained, on-device hardware, using only public data and limited compute, while closing the performance gap to much larger 7B models.

Method: Train a 2.7B-parameter German LLM on exclusively public data with about 55k H100 GPU hours, using a German-tailored preprocessing pipeline that accounts for morphology, compounding, and orthography; apply quality filtering and rephrasing of the instruction data to increase educational and instructional quality, which improves training efficiency and performance, especially during the annealing phase.

Result: The resulting model, ELMOD, is the strongest known German language model under 3B parameters and achieves performance comparable to 7B-parameter models on German tasks, while being suitable for efficient on-device inference.

Conclusion: Careful architectural choices plus language-specific preprocessing, aggressive quality filtering, and instructional rephrasing enable a relatively small 2.7B German model, trained with moderate compute and public data, to match the performance of much larger 7B models and be deployable on constrained devices.

Abstract: We present ELMOD - Efficient Language Model for On-Device Deployment - a compact (2.7B) German language model designed for efficient inference on resource-constrained hardware. ELMOD was trained on a limited computational budget (55k H100 GPU hours) using exclusively publicly available data. We developed a suite of German-specific data pre-processing, which differ from English-oriented counterparts in their handling of morphological variation, compounding, and orthographic conventions. Furthermore, we introduced a quality filtering and rephrasing step, which increased the instructional quality of the data, improved performance during the annealing phase, and reduced overall compute requirements. Thanks to our architectural model and data choices, including prefiltering, our educational-quality filtering and rephrasal to raise the educational-quality, ELMOD is the strongest performer in its size class (<3B), matching the performance of 7B-parameter models in German.

</details>


### [74] [D-Score: A Spectral Hidden-State Signal for Hallucination Detection in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24586)
*Bianca Raimondi,Davide Evangelista,Maurizio Gabbrielli,Elena Loli Piccolomini*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: They propose a simple, single-pass, geometry-based score (D-Score) from hidden activations of an LLM to detect hallucinations, showing it works well without external tools or multiple generations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs often generate fluent but false or unsupported content (hallucinations), and most existing detectors need external verifiers, retrieval, or multiple model calls. The authors want an internal, cheap, and model-intrinsic hallucination signal derived directly from the model’s own hidden states.

Method: They examine the singular value spectrum of the hidden activation matrix at a chosen layer when processing an input text. For a given tolerance, they count how many singular values remain close to the largest one; this count is the D-Score. The hypothesis is that conflicting or unsupported content causes the model’s representation to spread over more singular directions. They provide a spectral argument to justify this and then use the D-Score as a hallucination detector by thresholding it, evaluating on benchmarks such as FAVA-Annotation and RAGTruth.

Result: The D-Score strongly correlates with hallucination: hallucinated texts tend to have higher D-Scores. Across the evaluated benchmarks, this simple hidden-state statistic performs competitively as a hallucination detector, despite requiring only a single forward pass and no external verification or retrieval.

Conclusion: A basic spectral property of hidden activations—how many directions have strength comparable to the leading one—can serve as a strong, cheap signal for hallucination detection in LLMs. This allows effective detection using only the model’s internal geometry, without auxiliary systems or extra generations.

Abstract: Large Language Models can produce fluent text that is false, unsupported by the available evidence, or inconsistent with information that appears to be internally represented by the model. We study hallucination detection from the geometry of hidden activations and introduce the D-Score, a simple spectral statistic computed from a single forward pass. For a fixed model, layer, and tolerance parameter, the D-Score counts how many singular directions of the hidden activation matrix have singular values that remain close to the leading one. We use this quantity as a hallucination score, classifying an input text as hallucinated when its D-Score is larger than a pre-defined quantity. The motivation is that, when a model processes a text that conflicts with information available in its own internal state, the hidden representation may encode both the asserted content and some form of counter-evidence, uncertainty, correction, or lack of support; this can make the hidden trajectory spread across additional singular directions. We formalize this intuition through a lightweight spectral argument and evaluate the resulting detector on FAVA-Annotation and RAGTruth. The experiments indicate that the D-Score is a strong hidden-state signal for hallucination detection, while requiring no external verifier, no retrieval step, and no multiple generations.

</details>


### [75] [PIVOT: Efficient Query-Group Indexing for Token-Level Sparse Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24593)
*Hong Liu,Yuan Cheng,Lin Niu,Yi Su,Yufei Xue,Anmin Liu,Guanghua Yu,Jianchen Zhu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: PIVOT is a training-free, drop-in replacement indexer for token-level sparse attention that shares one prefix scan across nearby queries to cut indexer cost while preserving accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Token-level sparse attention (e.g., DSA) speeds up attention computation but leaves the indexer as a new bottleneck, since it still must score all previous tokens per query, costing O(L^2). The authors notice redundancy in this per-query scanning because neighboring queries tend to pick similar top-k tokens and indexer scores are long-tailed. They want a method that removes this redundancy, reduces the indexer cost, and accelerates long-context inference without retraining or hurting accuracy.

Method: They introduce PIVOT (Proxy Indexing Via One full-prefix Traversal), a training-free drop-in replacement for the DSA indexer. PIVOT groups nearby queries and builds a single proxy query for each group. It runs one full-prefix scan with this proxy to get a candidate key set, then derives each query’s final top-k from that smaller set. Two variants balance speed and fidelity: PIVOT-Reuse simply reuses the proxy’s top-k for all queries in the group; PIVOT-Refine re-scores the candidate set per query using the original indexer and then selects an individual top-k, closely mimicking dense indexing with much lower cost. The same core algorithm handles both prefill (using fixed-size groups of consecutive queries) and decode (using all queries decoded together in a multi-token prediction step as a group).

Result: On DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5.1 models evaluated on LongBench and RULER long-context benchmarks, PIVOT achieves accuracy essentially matching that of the dense DSA indexer while accelerating the indexer by up to 4x and reducing end-to-end latency by up to 1.6x for long contexts.

Conclusion: By exploiting overlap in top-k selections across nearby queries and the long-tailed nature of indexer scores, PIVOT eliminates most redundant per-query scanning in token-level sparse attention. It provides a practical, training-free, drop-in indexer that significantly accelerates long-context inference with negligible accuracy loss and works uniformly across prefill and decode phases.

Abstract: Token-level sparse attention, as implemented by DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) in production systems, makes the downstream attention efficient but shifts the bottleneck to the indexer that feeds it. To select the top-k tokens for each query, the indexer must still score every preceding token, incurring a cost of O(L^2) per layer for a sequence of length L. We observe that this per-query scan is largely redundant: nearby queries select highly overlapping top-k tokens, and the indexer scores are long-tailed along the key axis. We exploit these properties in PIVOT, Proxy Indexing Via One full-prefix Traversal, a training-free, drop-in replacement for the DSA indexer that shares one prefix scan across a group of nearby queries. PIVOT aggregates a group into a single proxy query, performs one shared full-prefix scan to obtain a candidate set, and then selects a top-k for each query from that set. Two variants trade speed for fidelity: PIVOT-Reuse shares the proxy top-k across the group for maximum speed, whereas PIVOT-Refine re-scores the candidate set with the indexer of each query and then selects an individual top-k, matching the dense indexer at a small additional cost. A single algorithm covers both inference phases, differing only in how groups are formed: fixed-size groups of consecutive queries in prefill, and the queries decoded together in one multi-token prediction (MTP) step in decode. On DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5.1 across LongBench and RULER, PIVOT matches the accuracy of the dense DSA indexer while accelerating it by up to 4x and reducing end-to-end latency by up to 1.6x at long context.

</details>


### [76] [Looping Is Not Reliability: State-Bound Evidence and Typed Revision Contracts for Agentic Code Repair](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24604)
*Xueping Gao,Jianwei Yang,Qiang Yang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper studies why code-repair agents that use generate–test–revise loops can lose correct fixes during later revisions, and proposes a formal loop contract and implementation that preserves verified correct states instead of repeatedly overwriting them.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Many coding agents iteratively generate and revise code patches using tests or verifiers, but even when a correct patch is found, later revisions can accidentally discard it, and current frameworks lack reliability guarantees about retaining and certifying correct fixes. The authors want to quantify how often this happens, understand the mechanisms (like stale traces), and design a principled structure that separates concerns such as finding fixes, preserving them, and certifying them against evidence.

Method: They run controlled empirical studies on code-repair tasks (e.g., HumanEval repairs and repository bugs) using sealed multi-seed experiments and branching trajectories from common initial states to avoid bias. They compare the impact of using stale versus current verification traces, analyze correctness across multiple forced revisions, and test a prospective policy intended to avoid harming already-correct starts. They also examine different coder stacks for heterogeneity and floor effects. Based on these findings, they develop a conceptual decomposition of the repair loop (admission, preservation, grounded certification, competence, liveness) and derive an evidence-bound typed loop contract, then implement a reference system that ties verifier evidence to exact code states, preserves verified checkpoints, and issues auditable receipts.

Result: Empirically, they find that forcing additional revisions often reduces current correctness, even though the probability of ever having been correct increases. Stale verification traces significantly harm runs that start from correct patches compared with using current traces. A policy meant to prevent harming correct starts succeeds at that narrow goal but worsens repairs from incorrect starts and fails the overall joint performance criterion. Repository-level experiments reveal no statistically significant improvements and show floor effects and variation across components. Conceptually, they identify distinct roles in the repair loop and design a contract that formally binds verifier evidence to specific code states and ensures preservation and auditability of verified checkpoints.

Conclusion: Iterative generate–test–revise coding loops, as commonly implemented, offer no guarantee that discovered correct patches will be preserved, and naive improvements (e.g., more revisions or certain safety policies) can degrade reliability. The authors argue for a structured separation of loop responsibilities and introduce an evidence-bound typed loop contract with a reference implementation that mechanically enforces state–evidence binding and checkpoint preservation. This serves as a specification and conformance baseline rather than proof of better repair ability, clarifying what reliability properties can and should be guaranteed independently of the underlying model’s competence.

Abstract: Generate--test--revise loops are common in coding agents, but repetition alone provides no reliability guarantee. We study the gap between finding a correct patch and retaining, verifying, and submitting it. A sealed five-seed study over 30 HumanEval repairs produces 900 three-revision trajectories. Under forced revision, current correctness with current traces falls from 0.820 after one revision to 0.673 after two, although ever-correct rises to 0.847. Two common-state studies use 2,430 branches from identical frozen programs to remove post-treatment risk-set bias. In a prespecified 14B replication, stale traces harm 34/135 correct starts versus 4/135 with current traces, a 22.2-point increase (task-cluster 95\% CI $[8.9,37.0]$, exact Holm $p=0.0337$). A prospective 540-rollout policy eliminates observed correct-start harm but reduces wrong-start repair and fails its joint criterion. Repository experiments over 24 bugs and four coder stacks expose floor effects and component heterogeneity without Holm-significant effects. We therefore separate admission, preservation, grounded certification, competence, and liveness. We derive an evidence-bound typed loop contract and instantiate its mechanically enforceable subset in a reference implementation that binds verifier evidence to exact code states, preserves verified checkpoints, and emits auditable admission receipts. The implementation is an executable specification and conformance artifact, not evidence of improved repair competence or calibrated verifier dependence.

</details>


### [77] [Kimi K3: Open Frontier Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24653)
*Kimi Team,Tongtong Bai,Yifan Bai,Yiping Bao,M. C.,Jianfeng Cai,Xinyuan Cai,Peizhou Cao,Yuxuan Cao,Ziwei Chai,Y. Charles,H. S. Zhou,Qiankang Zhou,Runjie Zhou,Ruozhang Zhou,Xinyu Zhou,Yiqiao Zhou,Zaida Zhou,Jinguo Zhu,Liya Zhu,Xinhao Zhu,Yangjunfeng Zhu,Yuxuan Zhu,Zhen Zhu,Chen Zhuang,Weiyu Zhuang,Xinxing Zu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Kimi K3 is a 2.8T-parameter Mixture-of-Experts multimodal model with a 1M-token context window that, through architectural and training innovations, achieves frontier-level performance and ~2.5x better scaling efficiency than its predecessor, and is fully open-weight released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Push open models closer to frontier proprietary systems by improving scaling efficiency, long-context reasoning, multimodal capabilities, and agentic behavior, while also making such a powerful model openly available to accelerate research and deployment.

Method: Design a 2.8T-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model (104B active parameters) with native vision and 1M-token context, built on Kimi Delta Attention and Attention Residuals to enhance information flow, plus Stable LatentMoE that routes each token to 16 of 896 experts. Combine these with refined data and training recipes, large-scale reinforcement learning across general, agentic, and coding tasks (with multiple reasoning-effort levels), and large-scale infrastructure optimizations including algorithm-system co-design, expert-parallel training, persistent-state long-context RL, and deployment innovations.

Result: Kimi K3 achieves approximately 2.5x improved scaling efficiency over Kimi K2 and reaches frontier-level performance across long-horizon coding, agentic tasks, knowledge, reasoning, and vision benchmarks. It still lags the very strongest proprietary models (Claude Fable 5, GPT-5.6 Sol) but surpasses all other evaluated open and proprietary alternatives in the authors' benchmark suite.

Conclusion: Architectural innovations in attention and MoE routing, combined with targeted RL post-training and substantial systems engineering, can significantly improve the efficiency and capability of very large multimodal MoE models. Kimi K3 demonstrates that open-weight models can approach the performance of the strongest proprietary systems on challenging long-context, coding, and agentic tasks, and its release is intended to catalyze further research and broader adoption of high-capability AI models.

Abstract: We introduce Kimi K3, a 2.8T parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with 104 billion activated parameters, native vision capabilities, and a 1-million-token context window. Kimi K3 is built on Kimi Delta Attention and Attention Residuals, which improve information flow across sequence length and model depth. Together with Stable LatentMoE, which effectively activates 16 of 896 routed experts per token, and refined training and data recipes, these advances yield an approximately 2.5x improvement in overall scaling efficiency over Kimi K2. Post-training highlights reinforcement learning across general, agentic, and coding domains and multiple reasoning-effort levels, enabling compositional generalization and robust long-horizon execution. At 2.8T scale, Kimi K3 is supported by infrastructure advances in multiple areas: algorithm-system co-design for KDA, perfectly balanced expert-parallel training with efficient memory management, million-token agentic RL with persistent rollout and sandbox states, and deployment innovations. Extensive evaluations show that Kimi K3 achieves frontier-level performance across long-horizon coding, agentic, knowledge, reasoning, and vision tasks. While its overall performance still trails the most powerful proprietary models, namely Claude Fable 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol, Kimi K3 consistently outperforms other open and proprietary models evaluated in our suite. We release the full Kimi K3 model weights to facilitate future research and accelerate the broader deployment and adoption of frontier intelligence.

</details>


### [78] [DataOrchestra: Learning to Orchestrate Per-Example Curation of Pretraining Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24717)
*Zhen Huang,Yikun Wang,Shijie Xia,Pengfei Liu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: DataOrchestra is a framework that adaptively decides, for each pretraining data chunk, whether to drop it, keep it, or clean/rewite it (using programmatic or LLM-based tools), yielding better LLM performance than fixed data-processing pipelines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM pretraining data pipelines usually apply a single, fixed processing strategy at the corpus or domain level, ignoring that different examples may need different treatments (e.g., some should be dropped, some lightly cleaned, some heavily rewritten). This rigidity can hurt downstream model quality and wastes compute on unnecessary processing. The paper aims to build a more flexible, example-specific orchestration of data processing steps that can improve pretraining quality and efficiency.

Method: They introduce DataOrchestra, which: (1) takes each chunk of web pretraining data; (2) an orchestrator model decides to drop, leave unchanged, or clean the chunk; (3) if cleaning is chosen, it selects one or more downstream operations (programmatic editing or various LLM-based rewriting tools); (4) for each chosen rewriting tool, the orchestrator generates a concrete instruction to guide the transformation; (5) the cleaned data is then used for pretraining. The framework unifies these heterogeneous operations in a single, example-specific pipeline.

Result: Models from 0.5B to 7B parameters, pretrained from scratch on web data processed by DataOrchestra, show consistent average improvements over any single, fixed data-processing method on 11 evaluation benchmarks. In math continued pretraining, DataOrchestra also surpasses stronger baseline processing pipelines, while cutting processing computation by skipping unnecessary operations.

Conclusion: Adaptive, example-specific orchestration of data processing operations leads to better and more compute-efficient pretraining datasets for LLMs than uniform, corpus-level strategies. DataOrchestra demonstrates that learning when and how to transform each example, and when to skip processing, yields stable performance gains across model sizes and tasks.

Abstract: Pretraining data processing is critical to the downstream performance of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, many existing approaches define a fixed processing strategy at the corpus or domain level and apply it uniformly to many examples, without adapting to the needs of each example. We propose DataOrchestra, a framework that unifies different processing operations and orchestrates an example-specific pipeline for each example. Given a chunk of pretraining data, an orchestrator decides whether to drop, untouch, or clean it. For a chunk to be cleaned, it selects one or more downstream operations, ranging from programmatic editing to different forms of LLM-based rewriting. For each rewriting step, it further generates a concrete instruction, which is executed by the corresponding downstream tool model. We pretrain models from 0.5B to 7B from scratch on web data processed by DataOrchestra and observe stable average gains over individual data-processing methods across 11 benchmarks. DataOrchestra is also effective for math continued pretraining and outperforms stronger processing baselines, while reducing processing compute by skipping unnecessary downstream operations.

</details>


### [79] [The Physics of Multi-Turn Long-Horizon Planning: From Pre-training to Post-training via Single- and Multi-Teacher On-Policy Agentic Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24720)
*Tianyi Men,Zhuoran Jin,Kang Liu,Jun Zhao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper builds a controlled benchmark and methodology to dissect how multi-turn, long-horizon planning emerges, is shaped, and is combined in foundation model agents across pre-training and post-training stages.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon, multi-step planning is essential for foundation model agents but current models are trained on uncontrolled web data, making it opaque how planning capabilities arise and how to systematically improve them. There is a need for a controlled environment to study data, training methods, and their effects on planning acquisition, refinement, and integration.

Method: The authors create a unified, controllable multi-turn environment for studying planning. They analyze three stages: (1) pre-training, varying data format (e.g., CoT state transitions), distribution, horizon length, and optimality to see how planning emerges; (2) post-training with GRPO and OPD, using mutual information to separate general planning patterns from task-specific knowledge and mapping where each method is helpful; (3) a new multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) scheme to integrate capabilities learned from different teachers, examining pattern compatibility across environments.

Result: (1) Explicit CoT world modeling improves long-horizon generalization; a small amount of long-horizon trajectory data helps, but suboptimal trajectories greatly degrade performance due to error amplification. Atomic skills without longer-horizon experience do not yield strong compositional generalization. (2) OPD outperforms GRPO especially with low-quality or very long-horizon data by providing more stable updates; post-training has distinct regimes where it is unnecessary, beneficial, or not supported. Distillation of unseen procedures from differently knowledgeable teachers can harm the student’s pre-existing world model. (3) MOPD allows integrating planning skills from multiple teachers by converging to shared planning patterns, enabling cross-environment generalization when patterns are compatible, partial continual learning when partially shared, and revealing strong interference when patterns conflict.

Conclusion: Careful control over training data and post-training strategies is crucial to develop robust long-horizon planning in foundation model agents. Explicit world-model-style CoT, some high-quality long-horizon data, and appropriate post-training (particularly OPD and MOPD) can significantly enhance planning, but suboptimal data, mismatched teacher knowledge, and conflicting planning patterns can damage or limit capabilities. The proposed environment and analysis framework offer a principled way to understand and systematically improve planning across stages.

Abstract: Multi-turn long-horizon planning is critical for foundation model agents, yet how to fundamentally improve it remains unclear. Existing models are trained on uncontrollable and opaque Internet data, making it difficult to identify how planning ability is acquired, shaped, and integrated. To address this challenge, we introduce a unified and controlled multi-turn environment that enables precise control. It allows systematically study long-horizon planning across three stages. (1) Planning ability acquisition during pre-training. We study data format, distribution, and quality. Explicit world model construction through CoT state transition modeling yields stronger long-horizon generalization. Atomic skills alone are insufficient for compositional generalization, whereas a litte long-horizon data works. Moreover, suboptimal trajectories severely impair performance because errors amplify over long horizons. (2) Planning ability shaping via GRPO and OPD post-training. Through mutual information, we distinguish general planning patterns from task-specific planning knowledge. For planning patterns, we identify three application regions of post-training: unnecessary, effective, and unsupported. OPD has a broader effective region than GRPO under low-quality and long-horizon settings, as it provides more consistent update directions. For planning knowledge, distilling unseen procedures from a teacher with different knowledge may impair student's prior world modeling without fully establishing new knowledge. (3) Planning ability integration through MOPD post-training. We show that multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) integrates capabilities by converging to shared planning-pattern across environments. Compatible patterns enable cross-environment generalization, partially shared patterns support continual learning, while completely conflicting patterns cause severe interference.

</details>


### [80] [Creative Integration: A Decidable Criterion of Creativity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.13977)
*Yoshinori Nomura*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper defines a precise, testable criterion for when a supposed “integrative” or creative solution really integrates conflicting ideas, using information-compression as the yardstick.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: People frequently praise “integrative” or “both-and” solutions, but there is no clear operational test to distinguish truly integrative, creative resolutions from mere clever re-descriptions or compromises. Existing views that link creativity and intelligence to compression lack a concrete, decidable way to apply this idea to real cases of conflict resolution. The authors aim to fill this gap with a rigorous criterion and validation framework.

Method: The authors model creative integration (CI) as information compression in the resolution of a genuine conflict between two elements, A and B. Using a fixed description language, they define a compression ratio C = L_pre / L_post, where L_pre is the description length of the conflict before resolution and L_post after; CI occurs iff C > 1 and the compression is located specifically in the conflicting parts. They operationalize this with four binary conjunctive decision gates that make the judgment decidable, and construct a taxonomy of pseudo-integrations (look-alikes) that must be excluded. They then evaluate the criterion with a curated multi-domain corpus and four falsifiable tests: (1) an independent computational compression check, (2) discrimination against hard negative examples, (3) out-of-sample predictive performance, and (4) robustness to changes in the description language.

Result: The proposed criterion for creative integration successfully passes all four validation tests with margin. It aligns with an independent computational compression check, reliably distinguishes genuine integrations from hard negative pseudo-integrations, predicts outcomes on new, unseen cases, and remains stable under reasonable variations in the description language. The authors also provide a taxonomy and corpus that clarify and delimit which kinds of conflict resolutions count as genuinely integrative.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that what makes a move genuinely creative—beyond mere novelty—is its ability to compress a real conflict between A and B, measurable as a strict reduction in description length localized to the conflict. Novelty and value then appear as downstream consequences, not defining features. The key contribution is not the general slogan that “creativity is compression,” but a concrete, decidable, and discriminating test plus a supporting corpus. The authors explicitly conjecture, without fully proving, that all creativity may be constituted in this way, and position their criterion as a foundational primitive for broader research programs in creativity and integration.

Abstract: "Integrative" solutions are widely praised but rarely defined: we lack an operational way to tell a genuine integration -- one that makes the world cheaper to describe -- from a tidy re-description. Building on the lineage that
  treats creativity and intelligence as compression, we give such a criterion for creative integration (CI): the resolution of a real conflict between A and B is CI if and only if, under a fixed description language, the description
  length strictly shrinks (C = L_pre/L_post > 1), with the reduction located in the conflict itself. We make the judgment decidable through four binary, conjunctive gates, and we fix its extension through a taxonomy of
  pseudo-integration that names and rejects the look-alikes. We back the criterion with a curated, multi-domain corpus and -- crucially -- validate it not by human inter-rater agreement but by four falsifiable tests it could fail: an
  independent computational check, discrimination against hard negatives, out-of-sample prediction, and description-language robustness; all pass with margin. The contribution is not "creativity is compression" but its decidability,
  discrimination, and corpus: on this account, what makes a move genuinely creative -- rather than merely novel -- is that it compresses a conflict, with novelty and value as downstream symptoms; whether all creativity is so
  constituted we state as an explicit conjecture. We claim only the sign of C-1; we judge, not generate. The result is a citable primitive for a broader program.

</details>

### [81] [Concept-based Visual Counterfactual Explanations with Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22544)
*Yassine Oueslati,Daniil Kirilenko,Martin Gjoreski,Marc Langheinrich*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose C-VCE, a diffusion-based visual counterfactual framework with a built-in concept bottleneck classifier, producing realistic, minimal, and interpretable image edits without relying on an external noise-robust classifier.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing diffusion-based visual counterfactual methods depend on external classifiers that must operate reliably on noisy images, making them fragile and hard to trust in safety-critical applications. There is a need for counterfactual generation that is both realistic and tightly coupled to human-interpretable concepts, without separate noise-robust classifiers.

Method: C-VCE incorporates a classifier directly into a diffusion model via a concept bottleneck layer. Users can toggle high-level semantic concepts during sampling, and the model minimally modifies only the relevant image regions while preserving others and respecting feature correlations. The method adds (1) a probabilistic regularizer that trades off prediction change vs. proximity to the original image, and (2) a gradient-based spatial mask that confines edits to the most relevant regions.

Result: On datasets like CelebA, C-VCE achieves equal or higher flip rates than baselines while generating counterfactual images that are visually closer to the original, less distorted, and do not require an external noisy-image classifier for guidance.

Conclusion: Embedding a concept bottleneck classifier directly inside a diffusion model enables practical, interpretable, and localized visual counterfactual explanations. This architecture reduces reliance on fragile external classifiers and suggests that exposing and controlling internal concept layers is a promising direction for making powerful generative models more understandable and safer for deployment.
