Abstract: Visual counterfactual explanations aim to answer "what minimal change to this image would flip the model's prediction?", and are increasingly important as vision models are deployed in safety-critical domains (e.g., medicine). Existing diffusion-based methods can produce realistic edits, but they rely on external classifiers that must work reliably on noisy images, which makes them fragile and hard to deploy for robust explanations. We introduce C-VCE, a new diffusion framework that builds the classifier directly into the generative model via a concept bottleneck layer, so that counterfactuals are guided by human-interpretable features (concepts) instead of a separate noise robust classifier that works with pixel-level edits. Our model lets users to toggle on/off semantic concepts during sampling, then minimally adjusts relevant image regions, while preserving the rest of the image, respecting feature correlations. To keep edits small and controlled, we add a simple probabilistic regularizer that balances "change the prediction" against "stay close to the original", plus a gradient-based mask that confines modifications to the most relevant regions. On benchmarks such as CelebA, C-VCE matches or improves flip rates while producing counterfactuals that are visually closer to the input and less distorted than baselines that depend on separate noisy-image classifiers. These properties make C-VCE a practical tool for vision systems where users need concrete "what-if" images without having to trust an additional, noise-robust classifier. More broadly, our results suggest that exposing and controlling an internal concept layer is a promising way to make powerful generative models easier to understand and safer to use.

</details>


### [82] [SeT-Diff: Towards Semantic Foundation Models for HPC Telemetry and Time-Series](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22548)
*Giovanni B. Esposito,Francesco Antici,Daniele Cesarini,Andrea Bartolini*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces SeT-Diff, a diffusion-based foundational model for flexible, sensor-description–conditioned modeling of compute node telemetry, enabling robust digital twins for HPC systems across multiple tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing ML models for HPC telemetry rely on fixed, anonymous sensor sets and are trained per-task, making them fragile: when sensors change, are reordered, added/removed, or when tasks shift (e.g., from forecasting to imputation), the models break or must be retrained. Data centers need a single, adaptable model that can capture system dynamics independent of specific sensor layouts, to support digital twins for monitoring, optimization, and prediction.

Method: They design SeT-Diff, a diffusion-based generative model for time-series telemetry that conditions on each sensor’s semantic description (e.g., type, location, meaning) rather than on fixed sensor indices. This conditioning lets the model learn underlying system dynamics while remaining invariant to sensor permutations or changes. The single trained model is then used for multiple downstream tasks—reconstruction, imputation, forecasting, and virtual sensing—by appropriate conditioning and sampling strategies.

Result: On a real supercomputer telemetry dataset, SeT-Diff achieves a Mean Absolute Error of 0.0470 for reconstruction tasks. It shows zero-shot permutation stability: shuffling sensor positions causes negligible performance loss. The same pre-trained model successfully handles data imputation, forecasting, and virtual sensing, with a reported MAE of 0.033 for thermal inference (predicting temperature-related metrics).

Conclusion: SeT-Diff serves as a foundational, task-agnostic digital twin model for HPC compute nodes, robust to changes in sensor layout and applicable to multiple telemetry tasks without retraining. Conditioning on sensor semantics via a diffusion architecture decouples system dynamics from dataset structure, enabling flexible, accurate, and reusable modeling of complex data center environments.

Abstract: Data centers and their compute nodes require accurate and flexible digital twins capable of modeling the complex interplay of workloads, environmental parameters, and physical metrics. Current machine learning approaches for HPC and its telemetry typically rely on a static subset of anonymous, fixed-position sensor variables tailored to single tasks. Consequently, these models become obsolete when target tasks change or sensor metrics vary. We propose SeT-Diff, the first foundational model for compute node telemetry and time-series. Unlike rigid architectures, our diffusion-based approach conditions the generative process on each sensor's semantic description, decoupling the system dynamics from the structure of the dataset. Experiments on a real-world supercomputer dataset demonstrate a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 0.0470 on reconstruction tasks. SeT-Diff exhibits zero-shot permutation stability, maintaining accuracy with negligible degradation even when sensors are shuffled. A single pre-trained model effectively performs data imputation, forecasting, and virtual sensing - achieving a 0.033 MAE in thermal inference - making SeT-Diff an effective data-driven digital twin for HPC systems.

</details>


### [83] [QFoldAgent: An Autonomous Quantum Optimization Multi-Agent System for Protein Structure Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22549)
*Winson Chen,Yuqi Zhang,Sixu Chen,Nuo Xu,Qiang Guan,Caiwen Ding*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A multi-agent, closed-loop system (QFoldAgent) learns to tune Hamiltonian penalty weights for quantum-classical protein fragment folding, improving structure quality without using ground-truth RMSD in the loop.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing hybrid quantum-classical protein structure prediction workflows rely on hand-tuned Hamiltonian penalty coefficients and are usually tested only on very short fragments in simulation. This manual tuning is suboptimal, does not generalize across sequences or noise conditions, and leads to unstable optimization and failure cases. There is a need for an automated, data-driven controller that can adapt penalty weights per sequence and across optimization cycles, using only physically grounded feedback signals and working under realistic quantum noise.

Method: The authors propose QFoldAgent, a closed-loop multi-agent framework for folding 5-residue fragments on a tetrahedral lattice. A design agent proposes sequence-dependent Hamiltonian penalty weights. A VQE-based quantum-classical optimization pipeline, simulated with Qiskit Aer noise, optimizes the folding Hamiltonian to obtain low-energy structures. A feedback agent analyzes the resulting energy landscape plus structure-quality metrics (e.g., MolProbity, Ramachandran statistics) and then updates the penalty proposals over multiple cycles. Ground-truth metrics like RMSD to native are withheld from the agents and used only for external evaluation on two datasets.

Result: On a 55-fragment QDockBank-derived benchmark with known structures, QFoldAgent lowers the median backbone RMSD from 3.64 Å with static penalties to 3.20 Å with learned penalties, with the largest improvements on the most difficult fragments. On 100 coverage-optimized unseen sequences without native structures, the closed-loop controller increases the fraction of structurally valid solutions from 87.5% to 98.7% and successfully repairs 87% of initially invalid cases. The strongest agent configuration improves the cycle-3 energy for 87% of sequences while preserving high backbone geometry quality, with 96% of residues in favored Ramachandran regions.

Conclusion: Iterative multi-agent control of Hamiltonian penalty weights can systematically improve the behavior of hybrid quantum-classical protein folding workflows, even in very small (5-residue) lattice settings. By using only physical and geometric diagnostics as feedback, QFoldAgent reduces structural errors and failure modes compared to fixed-penalty baselines, suggesting that intelligent penalty tuning is a promising direction for scaling quantum-assisted protein structure prediction under realistic noise.

Abstract: Hybrid quantum-classical protein structure prediction depends strongly on Hamiltonian penalty weights, yet existing lattice-based workflows typically fix these coefficients by hand and evaluate only very short fragments in simulation. We present QFoldAgent, a closed-loop multi-agent framework for 5-residue tetrahedral-lattice folding in which a design agent proposes sequence-conditioned penalties, a VQE-based quantum-classical pipeline optimizes the resulting Hamiltonian under Qiskit Aer noise, and a feedback agent uses energy-landscape diagnostics and MolProbity validation signals to refine penalties across cycles. Ground-truth metrics such as RMSD are never exposed to the agents and are used only for evaluation. We study the framework on two complementary datasets: 55 QDockBank-derived fragments with known structures and 100 coverage-optimized unseen sequences. On the QDockBank benchmark, QFoldAgent reduces median RMSD from 3.64 Å to 3.20 Å, with the largest gains on the hardest targets. On unseen sequences, the closed loop raises structural validity from 87.5% to 98.7%, recovers 87% of initially invalid cases, and the strongest controller improves cycle-3 energy on 87% of sequences while maintaining 96% Ramachandran-favored geometry. These results show that iterative agent control can systematically improve optimization behavior and reduce failure cases in a 5-residue quantum setting.

</details>


### [84] [Same Question, Different Answers: Evaluating LLM Reliability Beyond Accuracy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22554)
*Kazem Faghih,Yize Cheng,Shoumik Saha,Mobina Pournemat,Armin Gerami,Soheil Feizi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper shows that large language models often change their answers when equivalent questions are paraphrased, revealing instability hidden by standard accuracy metrics, and proposes using self-paraphrasing at inference time to better retrieve latent knowledge and improve reliability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Although LLMs achieve high benchmark accuracy, it is unclear whether they answer consistently when the same question is phrased differently. Single-prompt accuracy may overestimate reliability if models are sensitive to wording. The authors want to rigorously measure this instability and explore whether the underlying knowledge is present but inconsistently accessed.

Method: The authors evaluate 13 LLMs on four benchmarks covering factual QA and mathematical reasoning. They generate meaning-preserving paraphrases of questions and compare model outputs across paraphrased variants. They compute metrics like overall accuracy, instance-level mismatch rates (how often answers differ across paraphrases), and answer flip rates conditioned on originally correct responses. They then design and test a simple self-paraphrasing inference strategy where the model is prompted to paraphrase a question multiple times and aggregate answers to see if performance improves.

Result: They find that models’ answers depend strongly on the exact wording of prompts. While aggregate accuracy across paraphrases changes only modestly, instance-level stability is poor, with mismatch rates above 23% on some settings. Even when a question is answered correctly in its original form, paraphrases often induce incorrect answers, producing high flip rates and revealing that single-prompt success does not imply robust knowledge use. However, models usually answer at least one paraphrase correctly for many questions, indicating that the knowledge exists but is inconsistently retrieved. The proposed self-paraphrasing strategy partially recovers this latent knowledge and improves inference-time performance.

Conclusion: Standard accuracy metrics on a fixed set of prompts underestimate the instability of LLM behavior. Evaluating consistency across meaning-equivalent paraphrases provides a more realistic view of reliability. LLMs often know the correct answer but fail to access it consistently, and simple self-paraphrasing techniques can exploit this by surfacing correct answers more often. Future evaluation and deployment of LLMs should consider paraphrase robustness as a key dimension of model reliability.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often achieve strong accuracy on benchmarks, yet it remains unclear how reliably they apply this knowledge when the same question is phrased in different but equivalent ways. In this work, we study how model answers change under meaning-preserving paraphrases across factual question answering and mathematical reasoning tasks. Across four benchmarks and 13 models, we find that model outputs frequently depend on the exact wording of the prompt. While overall accuracy typically changes only modestly across paraphrases, instance-level behavior is far less stable: for many questions, models alternate between correct and incorrect answers depending on phrasing, with mismatch rates reaching more than 23%. Conditioning on questions that are answered correctly in their original form reveals even larger failures measured by answer flip rates, showing that single-prompt correctness is often a poor indicator of reliability. At the same time, we find that models often produce a correct answer for at least one paraphrase of a question, suggesting that the underlying knowledge is present but inconsistently retrieved. Building on this observation, we show that a simple self-paraphrasing strategy can partially recover this latent knowledge and improve performance at inference time. Together, these findings suggest that standard accuracy metrics can mask substantial instability, and that evaluating consistency across equivalent inputs provides a clearer picture of LLM reliability.

</details>


### [85] [DeepLens Diagnosis Agent: Agentic Workflow Design Lets a Small Reasoning Model Compete with Frontier LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22555)
*Mahmood Bayeshi,Veysel Kocaman,Muhammed Ali Naqvi,Yigit Gul,David Talby*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces DeepLens Diagnosis Agent, a structured, multi-stage workflow around a small medical LLM plus RAG that dramatically improves diagnostic accuracy and cost-efficiency over single-shot use and some larger frontier models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Frontier LLMs, while strong generalists, show brittle and unreliable diagnostic reasoning when used with single-shot prompts, especially under uncertainty. There is a gap between high scores on standard medical QA benchmarks and actual end-to-end diagnostic performance on realistic multi-stage clinical tasks. The authors aim to design a workflow that better matches the real clinical reasoning process and extracts more robust diagnostic performance from smaller, cheaper models.

Method: They design a five-stage diagnosis pipeline around a 7B-parameter medical model (JSL Medical Small 7B v2) with retrieval-augmented generation. The stages enforce: (1) structured extraction of clinical facts from the case, (2) disciplined, targeted retrieval of external knowledge, (3) constrained generation of a limited set of diagnostic candidates, (4) explicit triangulation of evidence across patient facts, knowledge, and candidates, and (5) a final, auditable diagnostic decision with explanations. The workflow is implemented as an “agent” that orchestrates the model and RAG under explicit process constraints, producing structured intermediate artifacts at each step.

Result: On the 915-case DiagnosisArena benchmark, the agent achieves 60.14% top-1 diagnostic accuracy—state-of-the-art among small/medium models. The same base model used without the workflow scores only 23.99%, implying roughly a 36-point gain from workflow design alone despite the model’s strong 88.2% performance on standard medical benchmarks. The system runs at about USD 0.0072 per case with 24-second latency (24K tokens on A100), making it 35–45% cheaper than Claude Sonnet 4.5 and Gemini 3.1 Pro, while beating their accuracy by 9.70 and 9.17 percentage points, respectively.

Conclusion: Structured “harnessing” of LLMs via a multi-stage, constraint-driven workflow can be more important than model size for difficult diagnostic reasoning tasks. DeepLens Diagnosis Agent demonstrates that explicit process control, RAG, and intermediate structured artifacts can substantially improve accuracy, reduce cost, and provide traceability and error localization. In high-stakes domains like medicine, such auditable, reproducible workflows may outperform naive, single-shot prompting of even larger frontier models, suggesting that workflow design is a critical lever for safe and effective AI deployment.

Abstract: Medical diagnosis is a multi-stage process: extract facts, consult knowledge, generate a differential analysis, and select the best diagnosis with explanations. Frontier LLMs are strong generalists, but single-shot prompting often yields brittle diagnostic reasoning. We present the DeepLens Diagnosis Agent, a five-stage harnessing pipeline (combining model capabilities with disciplined process constraints) centered on a small medical reasoning model (JSL Medical Small 7B v2) and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). The pipeline enforces structured clinical extraction, disciplined retrieval, constrained candidate generation, explicit evidence triangulation, and an auditable final decision. On the 915-case DiagnosisArena benchmark, the agent achieved 60.14% top-1 diagnostic accuracy, the highest among small and medium-sized models. The same model without the agent workflow achieved 23.99%, a +36-point gain from workflow design alone, despite 88.2% on standard medical benchmarks, showing that diagnostic reasoning under uncertainty requires more than knowledge recall. The agent costs USD 0.0072 per case (24K tokens on A100) with 24-second latency, 35-45% cheaper than Claude Sonnet 4.5 (USD 0.0110) and Gemini 3.1 Pro (USD 0.0128) while outperforming them by +9.70pp and +9.17pp. Harnessing can also correct frontier model failures; workflow constraints can outweigh parameter count or API cost.
  Beyond aggregate accuracy, the pipeline produces structured intermediate artifacts that make each stage inspectable and support error localization. These properties support high-stakes settings where traceability, reproducibility, and auditable evidence matter alongside benchmark performance.

</details>


### [86] [MIITA: Memory-Induced Inference-Time Adaptation for Continual Learning with Small Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22556)
*Dong Li,Yanchi Liu,Xujiang Zhao,Wei Cheng,Zhengzhang Chen,Xintao Wu,Zhong Chen,Chen Zhao,Haifeng Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MIITA is a continual-learning framework for small language models that stores compact, prototype-style memory and uses it at inference time to adapt without updating model weights, reducing forgetting under tight storage limits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Small language models deployed in the real world must continually adapt to new tasks and data, but directly fine-tuning their limited parameters leads to catastrophic forgetting of prior knowledge. Existing memory-based continual learning methods are tailored for large language models, assuming abundant storage and strong in-context learning, which small models do not have. There is a need for a continual learning approach that works under strict memory and compute constraints, avoids destructive weight updates, and still retains and reuses supervision from past tasks.

Method: The paper proposes MIITA, a Memory-Induced Inference-Time Adaptation framework for supervised continual learning with constrained storage. MIITA encodes past supervised examples as compact ‘correction-direction’ prototypes paired with semantic anchors. At inference, it retrieves relevant prototypes using both semantic similarity and model uncertainty signals. The retrieved directions are then applied through gated, temporary adaptation of hidden states during forward passes, without changing backbone parameters, extending prompts, or performing test-time backpropagation. The authors provide a local theoretical analysis showing how these retrieved directions approximate first-order loss reduction, motivate the uncertainty-based retrieval strategy, and argue that good directional coverage helps retain knowledge from previous stages.

Result: Across multiple supervised continual learning benchmarks and scenarios, MIITA is reported to consistently raise final task performance and reduce catastrophic forgetting compared with baselines, given the same fixed memory budget. The method demonstrates that storing compact prototype corrections and applying them at inference can be an effective form of continual adaptation for small language models under resource constraints.

Conclusion: MIITA enables non-destructive continual learning for small language models by offloading knowledge retention to a compact memory and performing inference-time hidden-state adaptation instead of parameter updates. Its theoretically motivated design and empirical results suggest that such memory-induced adaptation is a practical way to handle evolving tasks and mitigate forgetting when both storage and model capacity are limited.

Abstract: Continual learning (CL) is essential for small language models (SLMs) to adapt to evolving real-world needs in resource-constrained deployments. However, directly updating their limited parameter space causes catastrophic forgetting. While memory-based methods naturally address this by decoupling knowledge retention from parameters, existing approaches designed for large language models (LLMs) rely on abundant storage and strong in-context reasoning that SLMs lack. To address these challenges, we propose MIITA, a Memory-Induced Inference-Time Adaptation framework for supervised CL under constrained storage. MIITA stores supervised experiences as compact correction-direction prototypes with semantic anchors, and retrieves them at inference time using semantic and uncertainty-based cues. The retrieved directions are applied through gated temporary hidden-state adaptation, enabling non-destructive reuse of past supervision without backbone updates, prompt extensions, or test-time backpropagation. A local theoretical analysis links this design to first-order loss reduction, uncertainty-guided retrieval, and directional coverage for retaining old-stage knowledge. Extensive experiments across diverse supervised CL settings show that MIITA consistently improves final performance and mitigates forgetting under fixed memory budgets.

</details>


### [87] [Codifying the Judge: Scalable Evaluation via Program Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22561)
*Tzu-Heng Huang,Shengqi Qiu,Frederic Sala*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes PAJAMA, a system that distills an LLM judge into transparent programmatic judges plus a selective LLM fallback, achieving LLM-level evaluation and reward modeling performance at much lower cost and higher throughput.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-as-a-judge is widely used for evaluating model outputs and providing reward signals, but it is expensive, slow, and opaque. These drawbacks limit scalability for large-scale evaluation and reinforcement learning from AI feedback, and make it hard to inspect or control the evaluation criteria. The authors seek a cheaper, faster, and more interpretable alternative that preserves the strong performance of LLM judges.

Method: They apply program distillation: instead of calling an LLM judge at inference time, they learn a committee of programs that replicate its decision logic. The system, PAJAMA, (1) synthesizes multiple programmatic judges, (2) aggregates their scores into a joint verdict, and (3) uses these program outputs as routing signals, escalating only uncertain or low-confidence cases to an LLM judge. The programs are directly executable scoring functions, making judgments transparent and editable. They further use the programmatic judges’ outputs as labels to train reward models.

Result: Across five datasets and four model families, the programmatic judges match the performance of a 13B-parameter LLM judge. Using the programs’ scores to decide which cases to route to an LLM improves both accuracy and throughput, advancing the cost–quality Pareto frontier. For reward modeling on RewardBench, a reward model trained on labels from the programmatic judges outperforms a reward model trained on labels from a proprietary LLM judge, while reducing API costs by about 100×.

Conclusion: Program distillation into programmatic judges is a practical alternative to pure LLM-as-a-judge evaluation. PAJAMA achieves comparable or better evaluation and reward modeling performance while being cheaper, faster, and more interpretable, thanks to executable programs and selective LLM fallback. This approach can scale automated evaluation and reward signal generation without relying heavily on expensive, opaque LLM calls.

Abstract: LLM-as-a-judge has become the standard for automated evaluation, but it suffers from high cost, significant latency, and opaque decisions -- limitations that undermine its scalability and reliability. We address these with a simple, efficient alternative: program distillation. Instead of prompting an LLM at the evaluation time, we distill its decision logic into a committee of programs that score candidates directly. These programmatic judges offer transparency, are easily inspected or edited, and eliminate per-sample API costs. Building on this notion, we introduce PAJAMA, a system that synthesizes programs as judges, aggregates their decisions into a joint verdict, and incorporates a fallback mechanism to selectively escalate low-confidence cases to an LLM. Across five datasets and four model families, we show that programmatic judges can match the performance of a 13B-size LLM judge. When using program outputs as routing signals, PAJAMA improves both accuracy and throughput and advances the Pareto frontier. Beyond evaluation, programmatic judges produce cheap and effective reward signals: on RewardBench, a reward model distilled from programs' verdicts outperforms one trained on a proprietary LLM's labels at two orders of magnitude lower API cost.

</details>


### [88] [SF-AMS: Strategic Forgetting for Structured Memory in LLM Agent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22562)
*Ning Yang,Siqi Li,Miaoxin Shen,Yuan Zhou,Meng Zhang,Tong Li,Haijun Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes SF-AMS, a strategic forgetting framework that dynamically maintains compact, high-utility memory for LLM agents, improving long-context reasoning by modeling and updating memory importance as a utility signal.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-context reasoning in LLM agents suffers when agents must process large, noisy histories where redundant and irrelevant information accumulates. Existing approaches rely on static retrieval or simple decay heuristics, which do not adequately distinguish between enduringly important information and transient noise. This leads to degraded multi-step and multi-hop reasoning performance, especially in tasks that require robust use of long-term context. The paper aims to address this bottleneck by making memory management itself intelligent and utility-aware.

Method: The authors introduce SF-AMS (Strategic Forgetting for Agent Memory Systems), which models each memory unit with a dynamic importance score reflecting its long-term utility. Instead of fixed retrieval rules or heuristic time-based decay, SF-AMS uses a survival mechanism: memory importance is updated based on observed usage redundancy (how often and how meaningfully an item is used) and temporal signals (recency and temporal patterns). This induces a hierarchical memory structure that promotes stable, entity-consistent information and prunes noisy or low-utility content. Additionally, they propose Composite Importance Scoring, which combines semantic-level and entity-level signals to compute the overall importance score for memory retrieval, improving robustness when selecting relevant memories for a given query.

Result: On benchmark suites LoCoMo and LongMemEval-s, SF-AMS consistently outperforms strong long-context baselines such as LightMem, MemO, and A-Mem across various models and tasks. Notably, under the Qwen2.5-7B backbone, SF-AMS yields a +9.65 F1 improvement over the strongest baseline on multi-hop reasoning tasks. Under GPT-4o-mini, it improves temporal reasoning performance by +6.91 F1 and open-domain task performance by +6.53 F1. These gains indicate both effectiveness on challenging long-context settings and strong cross-backbone generalization.

Conclusion: Modeling memory importance as a dynamic, utility-based signal and using it to drive strategic forgetting and retrieval significantly improves long-context reasoning in LLM agents. SF-AMS creates a compact, high-utility memory hierarchy that preserves consistent, important entity information while filtering out noise and redundancy. The empirical gains across backbones and task types suggest that intelligent, utility-driven memory management is critical for building reliable LLM agents that operate over long and evolving contexts.

Abstract: Managing long-context dependencies remains a primary bottleneck in LLM agents, as redundant and irrelevant information can degrade multi-step reasoning. Strategic Forgetting for Agent Memory Systems (SF-AMS) is proposed as a framework for maintaining compact high-utility memory by modeling the long-term importance of memory units. SF-AMS replaces static retrieval and heuristic decay with a utility-driven survival mechanism that updates memory importance from usage redundancy and temporal signals, inducing a hierarchical memory structure that prioritizes stable entity-consistent information while filtering noise. On top of this, Composite Importance Scoring integrates semantic and entity level signals to improve retrieval robustness. Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-s show consistent gains over strong state of the art baselines including LightMem MemO and A-Mem. The largest improvement appears in multi-hop reasoning under Qwen2.5-7B where SF-AMS achieves plus 9.65 F1 over the strongest baseline followed by temporal reasoning under GPT-4o-mini plus 6.91 F1 and open-domain tasks plus 6.53 F1 demonstrating strong cross backbone generalization. These results show that modeling memory importance as a dynamic utility signal is critical for reliable long-context reasoning.

</details>


### [89] [Synthetic Scenario Generation for Evaluation of Industry 4.0 Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22563)
*Sagar Chethan Kumar,Rohith Kanathur,Dhaval Patel,Kaoutar El Maghraoui*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They extend an existing industrial-agent benchmark with a new Smart Grid Transformer asset class and propose a synthetic scenario generation pipeline that efficiently produces high-quality, standards-grounded evaluation scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing industrial-agent benchmarks like AssetOpsBench rely on manually created scenarios, which are labor-intensive, limited in asset coverage, and may not fully reflect realistic operational and diagnostic complexity. There is a need to scale benchmarks across more asset classes (e.g., smart grid transformers) and scenario varieties while maintaining realism, standards-compliance, and data richness for evaluating industrial agents.

Method: (1) Extend AssetOpsBench by adding a Smart Grid Transformer asset class.
(2) Implement four diagnostic tools grounded in IEC standards for transformer health-index prediction, dissolved-gas analysis, winding-temperature assessment, and load-profile assessment.
(3) Introduce ScenarioGeneratorAgent, a synthetic scenario generation pipeline that: (a) builds evidence-grounded asset profiles; (b) allocates a scenario budget across operational domains while aiming for good coverage; and (c) generates candidate scenarios via a hybrid validation-and-repair loop that enforces schema correctness, tool reachability, physical plausibility, alignment with standards, and deduplication.
(4) Improve scalability through several engineering optimizations: two-level caching, parallel generation using focus groups, thread-pool offloading, batched LLM calls, and early rejection filters.
(5) Empirically evaluate runtime and quality on Smart Grid Transformer scenario generation for 50 scenarios, comparing optimized vs. unoptimized pipelines using a composite quality score.

Result: On the Smart Grid Transformer case, the optimized ScenarioGeneratorAgent pipeline achieves an 8× reduction in end-to-end runtime for generating 50 scenarios, while maintaining essentially the same scenario quality. The composite quality score is 74.2 ± 1.9 for the optimized version versus 73.8 ± 3.0 for the baseline, indicating no degradation and possibly slightly improved consistency.

Conclusion: Standards-grounded synthetic scenario generation can reliably and efficiently expand industrial-agent benchmarks. By incorporating domain standards, realistic diagnostics, and a robust validation-and-repair loop, the proposed pipeline scales scenario creation to new asset classes (like smart grid transformers) without sacrificing scenario realism or quality, enabling broader and more practical evaluation of industrial agents.

Abstract: Industrial agent benchmarks require realistic evaluation scenarios that integrate telemetry, failure modes, maintenance records, and domain standards. However, existing benchmarks such as AssetOpsBench rely on manually authored scenarios and cover a limited set of asset classes. We extend AssetOpsBench with a Smart Grid Transformer asset class and four IEC-grounded diagnostic tools for health-index prediction, dissolved-gas analysis, winding-temperature assessment, and load-profile assessment. We further introduce ScenarioGeneratorAgent, a pipeline for synthetic industrial-agent scenario generation. The pipeline constructs evidence-grounded asset profiles, allocates coverage-aware scenario budgets across operational domains, and generates candidates through a hybrid validation-and-repair loop that enforces schema validity, tool reachability, physical plausibility, standards alignment, and deduplication. To improve scalability, we apply two-level caching, parallel focus-group generation, thread-pool offloading, batched LLM calls, and early rejection filtering. On Smart Grid Transformer scenario generation, these optimizations reduce end-to-end runtime by $8\times$ for 50 scenarios while preserving quality, achieving a composite quality score of $74.2 \pm 1.9$ compared with $73.8 \pm 3.0$ for the unoptimized baseline. These results show that standards-grounded synthetic scenario generation can efficiently expand industrial-agent benchmarks without sacrificing scenario quality.

</details>


### [90] [Loss-Aware Feature-Map Pruning in Convolutional Neural Networks Using Multi-Armed Bandits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22564)
*Salem Ameen,Sunil Vadera*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a bandit-based, loss-aware framework to prune redundant feature maps in CNNs, achieving substantial computation reduction while preserving accuracy close to unpruned models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Convolutional neural networks often have many redundant feature maps, which increase storage and inference costs without proportional gains in accuracy. Existing pruning methods can be greedy, magnitude-based, or costly oracle-style evaluations, and may not effectively balance pruning aggressiveness against accuracy preservation. There is a need for a principled, data-driven, and computationally efficient way to identify which entire feature maps (structured pruning) can be safely removed with minimal impact on performance.

Method: The paper frames feature-map pruning as a multi-armed bandit problem, where each candidate feature map (output channel) is an arm. At each play, the method temporarily masks one feature map in a trained CNN, evaluates the impact on loss over a sampled mini-batch, and converts the observed loss change into a reward that reflects how safe it is to remove that map. The map is then restored. Using a fixed budget of such plays, bandit algorithms (UCB1 and Thompson Sampling) learn a score for each map, trading off exploration and exploitation. After exhausting the play budget, maps are ranked by their learned scores, and the top-k maps (those judged safest to remove) are permanently pruned along with their associated filters, biases, and corresponding kernels in the following layer. The framework is evaluated against direct/oracle evaluations and baseline pruning methods on multiple CNN architectures and datasets.

Result: Experiments on LeNet/MNIST and several benchmark datasets (MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN, CUB-200-2011, Oxford Flowers 102) show that bandit-based pruning with UCB1 and Thompson Sampling can remove a significant number of feature maps and reduce convolutional computation while keeping classification accuracy close to that of unpruned networks. Statistical analyses using Friedman and Nemenyi tests indicate that UCB1 yields the best average rank in performance, followed by Thompson Sampling, and that both significantly outperform greedy and magnitude-based pruning strategies, while remaining statistically indistinguishable from the original unpruned models in many settings.

Conclusion: The study concludes that casting feature-map pruning as a multi-armed bandit problem enables effective, loss-aware, structured pruning of CNNs. UCB1 and Thompson Sampling provide an efficient way to estimate the impact of removing each feature map under a limited evaluation budget, leading to substantial model compression and computational savings without compromising accuracy. This bandit-based framework is shown to be statistically superior to common baselines and offers a principled tool for practical CNN pruning across diverse datasets and architectures.

Abstract: Convolutional neural networks often contain redundant feature maps that increase storage and inference cost. This paper presents a loss-aware feature-map pruning framework using multi-armed bandits. Feature-map pruning is structured because it removes complete convolutional output channels and their producing filters rather than isolated scalar weights. Each candidate feature map is treated as an arm. At each play time, one map is temporarily masked and evaluated on a sampled mini-batch; the map is then restored and the observed loss change is converted into a safe-removal reward. After a fixed play budget, candidate maps are ranked by learned scores and the top-k maps are permanently removed with their filters, biases and corresponding next-layer input-channel kernels. The study evaluates UCB1 and Thompson Sampling, compares them with direct/oracle-style evaluation on LeNet/MNIST, and extends the evaluation to MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN, CUB-200-2011 and Oxford Flowers 102. Results show that UCB1 and Thompson Sampling preserve accuracy close to unpruned models while removing feature maps and reducing convolutional computation. Friedman and Nemenyi tests show that UCB1 obtains the highest mean rank, followed by Thompson Sampling; both significantly outperform greedy and magnitude-based pruning while remaining statistically comparable to the original unpruned model.

</details>


### [91] [DSTFView: Multi-View Cloud-Edge Workload Forecasting with Dual-Input Spatio-Temporal-Frequency Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22565)
*Qingzhong Li,Hui Ma,Yajun Zhang,Qingchang Ma,Zhou Long*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DSTFView is a dual-input spatio-temporal-frequency multi-view workload forecasting framework for collaborative cloud-edge environments that achieves better accuracy and robustness than baselines on CPU and TP traces.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Edge platforms running AI inference must handle latency-sensitive, highly concurrent, and reliability-critical workloads. In collaborative cloud-edge environments, accurately forecasting workloads is hard because it requires capturing multiple types of dependencies (spatial, temporal, frequency, closeness, and periodicity) while keeping the model efficient enough for practical deployment. Existing methods either under-model these multidimensional features or are too heavy for efficient forecasting, motivating a new approach.

Method: The paper proposes DSTFView, a dual-input, multi-view workload forecasting framework. It jointly models short-term closeness and longer-term periodic dependencies in workload time series. The framework extracts dependencies from three domains: spatial (relationships across edge/cloud nodes or services), temporal (evolution over time), and frequency (periodic and spectral patterns). Multiple “views” corresponding to these dimensions are learned, and an adaptive fusion mechanism dynamically adjusts the contribution of each view, allowing the model to better capture abrupt changes and varying patterns in the workload.

Result: On CPU and TP (throughput or task processing) datasets, DSTFView is empirically evaluated against several representative baseline forecasting methods across different prediction horizons and metrics. In all tested settings, DSTFView achieves consistently better performance, indicating higher forecasting accuracy and robustness.

Conclusion: DSTFView effectively addresses the challenge of multidimensional workload modeling in collaborative cloud-edge environments by combining dual-input spatio-temporal-frequency views with adaptive fusion. The framework improves forecasting quality over existing approaches across datasets and horizons, suggesting it is well-suited for latency-sensitive and reliability-critical edge AI applications that depend on accurate workload prediction.

Abstract: With the widespread deployment of edge-side AI inference, edge platforms are increasingly required to support latency-sensitive, highly concurrent, and reliability-critical applications. However, existing methods often struggle to balance multidimensional feature modeling and forecasting efficiency in collaborative cloud-edge environments. To address this issue, we propose DSTFView, a dual-input spatio-temporal-frequency multi-view workload forecasting framework for collaborative cloud-edge environments. It jointly models closeness and period dependencies and extracts spatial, temporal, and frequency-domain dependencies. Besides, it designs an adaptive fusion mechanism and adjusts the contribution of each view to capture abrupt changes. Experimental results on the CPU and TP datasets demonstrate that DSTFView consistently outperforms representative baselines across multiple forecasting horizons and evaluation metrics.

</details>


### [92] [MedLoCoMo: A Long-Context Multi-Session Medical Dialogue Benchmark for Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22566)
*Zeyu Zhang,Ziqing Wang,Kaize Ding*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MedLoCoMo introduces a benchmark to test how well LLMs perform patient-specific clinical reasoning over very long, multi-visit medical dialogues, especially across admissions and with unanswerable cases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most existing medical QA benchmarks focus on short contexts or single documents, so we do not know if LLMs can reliably use and integrate information from long, longitudinal patient histories, or correctly abstain when information is missing. This is critical for real-world clinical use, where data is fragmented over many admissions and notes.

Method: The authors construct MedLoCoMo from deidentified MIMIC-IV and MIMIC-IV-Note data. They (1) build admission-level clinical packets, (2) synthesize realistic doctor–patient conversations grounded in these packets, and (3) generate QA items that are explicitly linked to supporting evidence. Questions cover three settings: single-admission reasoning, cross-admission reasoning that requires linking information across visits, and adversarial unanswerable cases where the correct behavior is to abstain. They then evaluate multiple baseline models, including those with long context windows and with external memory/retrieval mechanisms.

Result: The benchmark consists of 100 patient timelines, each with on average about 1,670 dialogue turns, ~30 sessions, and ~74k tokens per conversation, providing a very long-context testbed. Experimental results show that all evaluated baselines find cross-admission reasoning substantially more difficult than questions answerable from localized, single-admission evidence, even when models are equipped with long context windows or external memory/retrieval tools.

Conclusion: MedLoCoMo demonstrates that current LLMs struggle with patient-specific, long-horizon clinical reasoning across multiple admissions, particularly when information must be integrated over time or when recognizing that a question is unanswerable. The released benchmark and code offer a standardized way to develop and evaluate methods for long-context medical reasoning and safe abstention in realistic multi-admission clinical settings.

Abstract: MedLoCoMo is a Medical Long-Context Memory benchmark for patient-specific clinical reasoning over multi-admission medical dialogue. Existing medical QA benchmarks largely test short context knowledge or single document grounding, leaving open whether LLMs can use, connect, and abstain over longitudinal patient histories. We build MedLoCoMo from deidentified MIMIC-IV and MIMIC-IV-Note records by constructing admission-level clinical packets, synthesizing grounded doctor-patient conversations, and generating evidence linked QA items over single-admission, cross-admission, and adversarial unanswerable settings. The benchmark contains 100 patient timelines averaging 1,669.8 turns, 29.7 sessions, and 74,512.2 tokens per conversation. Across the evaluated baselines, cross-admission reasoning is consistently harder than localized evidence use, even when models have long context windows or use external memory or retrieval methods. The code and MedLoCoMo benchmark release is available at https://github.com/leozzy13/MedLoCoMo for use and reproducibility.

</details>


### [93] [Keyword Matters: Unveiling the Energy Sensitivity of On-Device LLM Prompting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22568)
*Ruiyi Tao,Xiaolong Tu,Haoxin Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Study shows prompt wording affects energy usage of on-device LLMs, making prompt engineering a simple way to save energy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLMs move onto mobile and embedded devices, their high energy demand conflicts with limited battery capacity and thermal constraints. Existing work focuses mostly on compression and inference acceleration, but largely ignores how different ways of asking the same thing (prompt design) might change decoding behavior and thus energy use. Understanding this relationship could enable software-only, easy-to-deploy optimizations for greener and longer-lasting on-device AI.

Method: The authors run controlled experiments with LLMs deployed on a smartphone, directly measuring power draw during inference. They systematically vary the linguistic form of prompts—especially imperative verbs and instruction structures—while holding task intent constant. They then analyze how these linguistic features influence decoding length and total energy consumption, correlating specific wording patterns with measured energy profiles across multiple tasks and verbs.

Result: They observe consistent, measurable energy differences between prompts that are semantically similar but linguistically different. Certain imperative verbs and instruction formats lead to shorter decoding lengths and lower total energy use, while others cause longer outputs and higher consumption. These patterns are stable across tasks, demonstrating that small wording changes can materially affect energy usage on-device.

Conclusion: Prompt design is not only a tool for accuracy and alignment but also for resource efficiency. On-device LLM energy consumption can be reduced through careful choice of verbs and instruction structures, without modifying model weights or hardware. Prompt engineering thus emerges as a lightweight, software-only lever to improve the sustainability and practicality of LLM deployment on mobile and embedded systems.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed on mobile and embedded devices to improve privacy and reduce network latency. Yet on-device inference faces a fundamental constraint: high energy consumption on battery-powered, resource-limited hardware. While model compression and runtime acceleration have been widely studied, the effect of \emph{prompt design} on energy efficiency remains underexplored. This paper presents an empirical study of the relationship between prompt wording and energy consumption for on-device LLMs. Using real power measurements collected on a smartphone, we quantify how linguistic features, particularly imperative keywords and instruction structure, affect decoding length and total energy. Our results show consistent energy differences across verbs and tasks, indicating that prompt engineering is a lightweight lever for improving energy efficiency.

</details>


### [94] [Execution-Grounded Security Testing for Coding Agents in Software Engineering Pipelines](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22569)
*Yifei Ge,Weisong Sun,Jinkun Xiao,Yuchen Chen,Yebo Feng,Peizhuo Lv,Xia Feng,Chunrong Fang,Zhihong Zhao,Zhenyu Chen,Yang Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces an execution-grounded red-teaming framework to test how coding agents perform unsafe actions in real system environments, revealing high rates of verified unsafe behavior when risky intents are disguised as normal software engineering tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Coding agents are being integrated directly into system operations, where their tool use can persistently modify code, configs, and environments in ways that may create lasting, privilege-abusing security risks. Existing evaluations often focus on what models say rather than what they actually do to the surrounding system, missing execution-layer vulnerabilities, especially when harmful intent is hidden in seemingly benign tasks.

Method: The authors design an execution-grounded red-team framework that runs agents inside observable sandboxes and evaluates them based on concrete system-side evidence such as tool calls, runtime traces, and filesystem diffs. They embed unsafe target operations into standard software-engineering workflows (unit/regression tests, crash reproduction, validation) so that harmful actions are disguised as plausible tasks. An execution oracle then guides iterative refinement of probes when the agent initially fails or its attempt is rejected, enabling more effective elicitation of unsafe executions. They apply this framework across multiple agent frameworks and model backbones, and measure verified unsafe behavior on both code-based and text-based task carriers.

Result: Using the red-team workload reformulation, the framework substantially increases the rate of verified unsafe executions, achieving up to 73.61% on code carriers and 53.93% on text carriers across various coding agent setups. These empirical results demonstrate that agents frequently perform unsafe system modifications when risky goals are embedded within realistic engineering workflows.

Conclusion: Coding agents operating within system contexts remain insecure when facing disguised harmful objectives: once risky intentions are embedded in routine engineering tasks, agents can be reliably induced to execute unsafe system actions. Therefore, execution-grounded security testing and stronger safeguards are necessary, as prompt-level safety alone is insufficient to protect system operations from agent-induced vulnerabilities.

Abstract: Coding agents are increasingly integrated into system operations, where their tool use can directly modify project artifacts, execution environments, and the underlying system. For example, if a coding agent inserts a hook into a system startup or configuration script, that change can persist after the interaction, be triggered later, and abuse delegated user or system privileges to modify the system. This makes security testing a system problem: the key question is not only what the agent says, but what it actually does to the surrounding environment. We present an execution-grounded red-team testing framework for probing this execution-layer security boundary using observable sandbox evidence, including tool invocations, runtime traces, and file-system diffs. Our framework embeds target unsafe operations into routine software engineering workloads, including unit testing, regression testing, crash reproduction, and validation, and uses an execution oracle to guide refinement when an initial probe is rejected or fails. Across multiple agent frameworks and model backbones, our red-team workload reformulation substantially increases verified unsafe execution, reaching 73.61% on code carriers and 53.93% on text carriers. These results show that coding agents in system operations remain insecure under task disguise: once risky intent is hidden inside plausible engineering tasks, the agent can be induced to carry out unsafe actions on the surrounding system. More broadly, coding agents in system operations still demand stronger security testing and safeguards.

</details>


### [95] [Reference Feature Atlases for Mechanistic Auditing of Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22570)
*Rui Wu,Tong Che*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Describe your article briefly in one sentence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Describe your motivation for this article in two or three sentences.

Method: Describe the methods you used in your article in two or three sentences.

Result: Describe your findings of this article in two or three sentences.

Conclusion: Describe your conclusions of this article in one or two sentences.

Abstract: Auditing a new language model usually means relearning and reinterpreting its internal features from scratch. We propose a reference feature atlas: a sparse feature library trained once on a reference panel and reused for new targets, which attach by fitting only a linear decoder. This yields two complementary views. The atlas channel reads the target on already interpreted panel features, providing a stable coordinate system across models. The residual channel learns features only from what the atlas fails to reconstruct, making "outside the reference panel" an explicit audit signal.
  We train leave-one-out atlases over five 7-9B instruction-tuned models and audit held-out Mistral and Qwen targets. On three controlled LoRA hidden objectives injected into both targets, the residual channel makes the planted mechanism perfectly controllable at runtime while matched controls stay unaffected and recovers the planted objective as the top-ranked latent across both targets; on Mistral, where the per-target SAE and pairwise crosscoder baselines are retrained for a head-to-head benchmark, both baselines fail to do so. On Qwen-2.5, the same channel additionally reveals a panel-relative political-framing cluster; steering it shifts the audited framing metrics while out-of-domain controls remain unchanged.

</details>


### [96] [SCAIR: Schema-Conditioned Agentic Iterative Reasoning for Enterprise Knowledge Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22571)
*Prateek Chaturvedi,Yuqicheng Zhu,Hongkuan Zhou,Dongzhuoran Zhou,Yunjie He,Steffen Staab,Fei Du,Jie Tang,Evgeny Kharlamov*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They introduce SCAIR, a training-free, schema-aware reasoning framework that makes KG-RAG work better on dense, operational enterprise Knowledge Graphs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing KG-RAG and agentic reasoning methods that look strong on public benchmarks fail to generalize to real enterprise Knowledge Graphs, which are dense, governed by strict schemas, and subject to operational constraints. Enterprises need reliable, controllable reasoning over their KGs without costly retraining, and current generic agents do not adequately respect the structure and business logic embedded in these graphs.

Method: They propose SCAIR (Schema-Conditioned Agentic Iterative Reasoning), a framework that guides an LLM-based agent with schema-conditioned structural priors and enforces schema-aware traversal for multi-hop reasoning. The approach combines explicit structured planning with controlled, iterative reasoning steps over the KG, constraining the agent’s actions to those that are valid under the enterprise schema and operational rules. The framework is training-free: it wraps and constrains existing models rather than fine-tuning them.

Result: On an enterprise-oriented benchmark built from a real-world Configuration Management Database (CMDB), SCAIR significantly outperforms existing KG-RAG baselines. The performance gains are attributed to better adherence to the KG’s schema and operational constraints during multi-hop reasoning, leading to more accurate and reliable answers in enterprise settings.

Conclusion: Generic agentic KG-RAG designs are insufficient for robust enterprise graph reasoning. Effective systems must explicitly encode and enforce the target domain’s structural and operational constraints within the reasoning process. By aligning the agent’s design with business logic and schema, substantial performance improvements can be achieved without retraining the underlying models, making SCAIR a practical and scalable solution for enterprise KG-RAG.

Abstract: Knowledge Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation (KG-RAG) enables natural language interaction with structured enterprise knowledge, yet existing agentic approaches that perform well on public benchmarks often fail to generalize to real-world enterprise Knowledge Graphs (KGs), which are dense, schema-driven, and operationally constrained. To address these limitations, we propose SCAIR (Schema-Conditioned Agentic Iterative Reasoning), a training-free framework that integrates structured planning with controlled iterative reasoning by injecting schema-conditioned structural priors and enforcing schema-aware traversal during multi-hop reasoning. Experiments on an enterprise-oriented benchmark constructed from a real-world Configuration Management DataBase (CMDB) demonstrate that SCAIR substantially improves performance over existing KG-RAG methods. Crucially, our study highlights that reliable enterprise graph reasoning cannot rely on generic agentic designs; instead, it must explicitly incorporate the target domain's structural and operational constraints into the reasoning process. We demonstrate that by aligning agent design with business logic, substantial performance gains can be achieved without the need for costly model retraining.

</details>


### [97] [Schema-Aware Localisation (SAL): Live Schema Grounding and Hallucination Validation for Oracle NL2SQL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22572)
*Sanjay Mishra,Divya Chukkapalli,Ganesh R. Naik*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SAL is a lightweight middleware that grounds LLM-generated SQL in the live Oracle schema and auto-corrects identifier issues, boosting execution-correct NL2SQL accuracy on real databases without retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs can produce fluent SQL, but on real enterprise Oracle databases they often fail at execution despite looking syntactically plausible. The main issue is hallucinated tables/columns and missed Oracle-specific syntax, largely due to a lack of grounding in the actual database schema. Existing fixes like retraining or heavy engineering are costly; the paper aims for a simple, retraining-free way to make NL2SQL reliable on live Oracle systems.

Method: The authors propose Schema-Aware Localisation (SAL), a middleware layer between the user and the LLM. SAL queries Oracle’s USER_TAB_COLUMNS catalog to build an up-to-date schema map. For each natural language question, it selects a relevant subset of tables (or the full schema for multi-table queries) and injects this schema context into the LLM prompt. After the LLM generates SQL, SAL applies the Hallucination Index (Hidx): it validates every alias.column against the live catalog, automatically rewrites predictable prefix-related errors, and if issues remain it triggers a structured retry with explicit, itemised corrections fed back to the model. This operates without retraining the underlying model.

Result: On 500 TPC-H natural language questions over a live Oracle Autonomous Database 23c, using GPT-4o-mini, unguided NL2SQL achieves only 2.2% execution-grounded truth (EGT). Adding a hand-written static schema hint raises EGT to 62.0%. SAL, using automatically derived schema grounding and Hidx-based validation/correction, reaches 62.6% EGT overall, with 96% on simple, 95% on medium, and 40.7% on complex queries. Execution failures drop from 97.6% to 2.6%.

Conclusion: Schema grounding is the dominant bottleneck for LLM-based NL2SQL on real Oracle databases. A lightweight middleware approach—SAL—can nearly match carefully hand-crafted schema hints without any manual schema curation or model retraining, dramatically reducing execution errors. This suggests that robust catalog-driven grounding and post-generation validation/correction are highly effective, practical strategies for deploying NL2SQL in enterprise Oracle environments.

Abstract: Large language models can generate fluent SQL from natural language, but on real enterprise Oracle databases they frequently fail at execution time: columns and aliases are hallucinated and dialect-specific syntax is missed, leading to ORA-00904 invalid-identifier errors. In this setting, failures are primarily due to missing schema grounding: the model cannot know which tables and columns actually exist. This paper introduces Schema-Aware Localisation (SAL), a lightweight middleware layer for Oracle NL2SQL that requires no model retraining. SAL queries Oracle's USER_TAB_COLUMNS catalog to build a live schema map, selects a relevant table subset for each question (falling back to the full schema for multi-table queries), and injects this ground-truth context into the LLM prompt. Generated SQL is then checked by the Hallucination Index (Hidx), which validates every alias.column reference against the live catalog, automatically rewrites predictable prefix errors, and otherwise triggers a structured retry with itemised corrections. We evaluate SAL on 500 TPC-H natural language questions executed against a live Oracle Autonomous Database 23c instance using GPT-4o-mini. Without any schema grounding, execution-grounded truth (EGT; executes and matches the reference result set) is 2.2% (12/500). A hand-written static schema hint brings EGT to 62.0%. SAL, with no manual schema curation, achieves 62.6% EGT (96% simple, 95% medium, 40.7% complex) while reducing execution failures from 97.6% to 2.6%.

</details>


### [98] [PhononBench-MP40: a spectrum-resolved benchmark dataset for phonon stability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22573)
*Wen-Kao Li,Ze-Feng Gao,Zhong-Yi Lu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They introduce PhononBench-MP40, a large, labeled benchmark dataset of phonon spectra and stability for ~47k Materials Project structures, enabling systematic studies of workflow-defined phonon stability and related analyses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Imaginary phonon modes make many otherwise promising computationally predicted materials dynamically unstable within a given workflow, creating a bottleneck for high-throughput materials screening. There is a lack of standardized, auditable benchmark data that links phonon spectra, workflow-defined stability labels, and failure cases, which hinders method development, threshold analysis, and robust screening strategies.

Method: Starting from 47,969 phonon calculation tasks based on the Materials Project MP40 workflow, the authors collected and curated results into a benchmark dataset. For each successfully completed task, they stored the full local phonopy YAML phonon spectrum and derived stability labels from it, including the lowest sampled phonon frequency and any label changes under chosen thresholds. They explicitly separate fully completed phonon calculations, locally dynamically unstable results, and relaxation failures, and provide code and utilities in a companion GitHub repository for accessing and reproducing the workflow.

Result: The final dataset, PhononBench-MP40, contains 46,899 completed phonon records with paired stability labels and phonon spectra: 16,683 structures labeled as phonon-stable and 30,216 labeled as unstable according to the MP40 phonon workflow. Additionally, 1,067 relaxation failures are reported as a distinct category outside the completed-phonon set. All records use a common data schema centered on the local phonopy YAML spectrum, from which stability labels and minimum frequencies are derived.

Conclusion: PhononBench-MP40 serves as an open, auditable reference dataset for studying workflow-defined phonon stability, minimum-frequency statistics, threshold-dependent stability criteria, and strategies that explicitly account for calculation failures in high-throughput screening. By making the workflow, schema, and interpretation boundaries explicit and providing both data and code, the resource supports reproducible method benchmarking and development in computational materials science.

Abstract: Imaginary phonon modes remain a practical bottleneck in computational materials screening because otherwise plausible structures can be locally dynamically unstable under a chosen workflow. Here we present PhononBench-MP40, a spectrum-resolved benchmark dataset of Materials Project-derived crystals for workflow-defined phonon stability. The dataset starts from 47,969 MP40 workflow tasks and provides 46,899 completed records with paired stability labels and local phonopy YAML spectra, including 16,683 Stable records and 30,216 completed-phonon unstable records. A further 1,067 relaxation failures are reported separately rather than merged into the completed phonon denominator. The release centers on the local YAML spectrum: the stability label, the lowest sampled frequency and any threshold-dependent relabeling are derived from that spectrum. The dataset is openly available through Science Data Bank at https://doi.org/10.57760/sciencedb.38735. A companion GitHub repository provides the calculation code and lightweight access utilities. PhononBench-MP40 provides an auditable reference for workflow-defined stability classification, minimum-frequency analysis, threshold studies and failure-aware triage, while keeping the reference workflow, data schema and interpretation boundaries explicit.

</details>


### [99] [Too much evidence, too little time: From text to actionable recommendations through multi-objective evidence reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22574)
*Adela Bara,Simona-Vasilica Oprea*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They build an automated pipeline (SCEPTER) that turns complex clinical cases into a small set of evidence-based, literature-grounded treatment recommendations, dramatically shrinking the PubMed search space while preserving evidence diversity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Clinicians must make evidence-based decisions but PubMed searches for complex cases return hundreds of papers, which are impossible to fully review under time pressure. Existing tools don’t fully integrate retrieval, critical appraisal, contradiction handling, and recommendation generation into a single automated reasoning system tailored to single-patient cases.

Method: They design SCEPTER, a multi-stage framework: (1) retrieve literature from PubMed, (2) rerank using PubMedBERT for semantic relevance, (3) use LLMs to extract and structure claims from papers, (4) weight claims by evidence level, (5) detect contradictions between claims, (6) perform consensus analysis, and (7) apply multi-objective Pareto optimization to select a small set of claims that jointly optimize support, consistency, and diversity, from which final recommendations are generated. A Paper Q&A component lets users interactively query individual selected papers.

Result: On 150 clinical case studies, SCEPTER reduced the initial average of 576 retrieved PubMed papers down to 53 kept papers, 7 Pareto-optimal claims, and 3 final recommendations per case, achieving about 192:1 compression of the search space while maintaining high diversity of evidence (reported entropy 0.901). Ablation experiments showed that the Pareto-based selection improved diversity and practical utility of recommendations versus standard ranking-based baselines.

Conclusion: SCEPTER demonstrates that an integrated, multi-objective reasoning pipeline can transform raw PubMed results into compact, diverse, and actionable evidence syntheses for single-patient decision support. The combination of semantic reranking, LLM-based claim extraction, contradiction-aware reasoning, and Pareto-based selection is more effective than simple ranking in producing useful clinical recommendations while retaining diverse supporting evidence.

Abstract: Evidence-based clinical decision making requires specialists to identify, evaluate and synthesize relevant scientific literature. However, PubMed searches for complex clinical cases often return hundreds of publications that cannot be reviewed manually under time constraints. This study proposes SCEPTER (Single-Case Evidence-driven PubMed-To-rEcommendation Reasoner), a framework for transforming clinical case descriptions into evidence-based recommendations. SCEPTER combines PubMed retrieval, PubMedBERT semantic ranking, large language model (LLM)-based claim extraction, evidence-level weighting, contradiction detection, consensus analysis and multi-objective Pareto claim selection. The framework generates structured evidence syntheses and grounded actionable recommendations. A Paper Q&A module further enables interactive exploration of selected publications. The proposed framework introduces multi-objective reasoning model that integrates literature support, contradiction analysis and interactive literature interrogation into a unified clinical decision-support pipeline. Evaluation on 150 case studies demonstrated that the framework reduced an average search space of 576 papers to 53 retained papers, 7 Pareto-optimal claims and 3 final recommendations, corresponding to an overall compression ratio of 192:1. Despite this reduction, the retained evidence maintained high diversity (entropy=0.901). The ablation study showed that Pareto-based selection increased evidence diversity and recommendation utility compared with conventional ranking approaches.

</details>


### [100] [Temporal Context Reinstatement Drives Episodic-Like Order Memory in Long-Context Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22575)
*Mathis Pink,Vy Ai Vo,Qinyuan Wu,Jianing Mu,Javier Turek,Uri Hasson,Kenneth A. Norman,Sebastian Michelmann,Alexander Huth,Mariya Toneva*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper tests whether long-context LLMs show human‑like temporal order memory over extended narratives and reveals a simple temporal coding mechanism underlying their behavior.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Human episodic memory can retrieve events over long timescales, but we lack mechanistic explanations because it is hard to probe human long-term memory at the circuit/computational level. Long-context LLMs can process long narratives and are fully observable and manipulable, making them attractive models to test hypotheses about episodic memory mechanisms, particularly how temporal order information is represented and used for retrieval.

Method: The authors design a temporal order memory task based on a full-length novel and collect human behavioral data on people’s memory for the order of events in the story. They then give analogous tasks to long-context LLMs and compare performance patterns, especially the distance effect (how accuracy changes with temporal separation between events). Using mechanistic interpretability tools on the LLMs, they analyze internal representations and attention patterns to identify how temporal information is encoded and reinstated during retrieval, focusing on specific attention heads and latent dimensions that correlate with temporal position.

Result: LLMs display the same characteristic distance effect in temporal order judgments as humans do when recalling events from the novel. Mechanistic analysis reveals that the model’s success depends on a low-dimensional—essentially one-dimensional—temporal code that tracks when events occurred. During retrieval, a specific “time-reinstatement” attention head reactivates this temporal code, which in turn supports accurate temporal order decisions.

Conclusion: Long-context LLMs can reproduce key behavioral signatures of human episodic temporal order memory, and their internal computations appear to rely on temporal context reinstatement via a simple one-dimensional temporal code and a specialized attention head. This suggests that temporal context reinstatement may be a general and efficient mechanism for encoding and retrieving long-timescale episodic information, offering a concrete computational hypothesis that may inform both artificial models and theories of biological episodic memory.

Abstract: Human episodic memory supports the retrieval of experiences that unfold over extended timescales, yet the computational mechanisms underlying this ability remain debated due to the limited mechanistic accessibility in long-term memory experiments in humans. Long-context LLMs may offer promising ways to reveal plausible computational mechanisms that drive this type of retrieval. Here, we investigate whether and how LLMs capture the core behavioral signatures of episodic memory via a temporal order memory task. Using a new dataset of human behavior based on memory of a full-length novel, we show that models exhibit the same characteristic distance effect observed in humans on this task. We next apply long-context mechanistic interpretability analyses to uncover how models solve this task, and find that model performance relies on a one-dimensional temporal code that is reinstated during retrieval by a single time-reinstatement attention head. These findings support temporal context reinstatement as an important mechanism for episodic-like temporal-order memory in LLMs, offering new insights into how temporal aspects of long-term episodic memory may be instantiated in both artificial and biological systems.

</details>


### [101] [cMoLLM at Scale: Horizontal Scaling Laws for Mixture-of-LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22577)
*Xin Yang,Yemin Wang,Mingda Liu,Letian Li,Shuaishuai Cao,Zhengxiao He,Ryan Dong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose cMoLLM, a convolutionally gated mixture-of-LLMs architecture that reformulates MoE routing as dynamic convolutions across full model streams, improving perplexity and downstream performance under matched compute versus prior pipeline-level mixture methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dense Transformers activate all parameters for every token, so both training and inference cost grow linearly with parameter count. This is a major bottleneck when scaling to near-trillion-parameter models. Existing attempts to introduce mixture-of-experts at the pipeline level (ParaScale, AltUp) either incur high overhead, suffer from routing/gradient issues, or provide limited adaptivity and slow convergence. The authors want a way to increase model capacity without proportionally increasing computation, by using more effective mixture mechanisms throughout the LLM pipeline.

Method: They show that standard MoE layers can be viewed as variable-kernel dynamic convolutions, with each expert as a 1×1 convolution kernel and routing as input-conditioned kernel aggregation. Using this equivalence, they design cMoLLM, a convolutionally gated mixture-of-LLMs that routes among end-to-end model streams via fully differentiable dynamic convolution instead of discrete expert selection. This provides pipeline-level mixture with continuous gating and avoids some of the routing instability and overhead of prior work such as ParaScale and AltUp.

Result: On GPT-2-style architectures trained on the FineWeb corpus, cMoLLM achieves lower language modeling perplexity and higher accuracy on downstream benchmarks like GLUE and SQuAD compared with ParaScale- and AltUp-style baselines when compute is matched. It also shows better utilization of the different streams, more stable optimization behavior, and more favorable scaling properties as model capacity increases.

Conclusion: Reinterpreting MoE as dynamic convolution enables a new pipeline-level mixture design—cMoLLM—that can scale LLM capacity more efficiently than dense Transformers while avoiding key drawbacks of earlier pipeline mixture approaches. The proposed architecture yields empirical gains in perplexity, downstream task performance, and training dynamics under the same computational budget, suggesting it is a promising direction for building higher-capacity yet compute-efficient LLMs.

Abstract: Scaling large language models (LLMs) has driven their success, yet dense Transformers couple capacity and computation: every parameter is activated for every token, making training and inference costs grow linearly with model size-a critical bottleneck as models approach trillion-parameter regimes. We aim to scale capacity through MoE-style mixture throughout the LLM pipeline rather than only the FFN. Prior pipeline-level approaches include ParaScale, which introduces virtual tokens and parallel streams but incurs substantial overhead and suffers from homogenized routing and gradient collapse, and AltUp, which uses an auxiliary prediction branch but offers limited adaptivity and slow convergence. We establish that MoE-style mixture layers can be reformulated as variable-kernel dynamic convolutions, where each expert corresponds to a $1{\times}1$ convolutional kernel and routing implements input-conditioned kernel aggregation. Building on this equivalence, we introduce cMoLLM: a convolutionally gated mixture-of-LLMs that routes over end-to-end streams through fully differentiable dynamic convolution. In GPT-2-style models trained on FineWeb, cMoLLM improves language modeling perplexity and downstream GLUE and SQuAD accuracy under matched compute, with better stream utilization, more stable optimization, and favorable scaling compared to ParaScale- and AltUp-style baselines.

</details>


### [102] [HeraSys: Collaborative Serving of Multiple LLM Workflows via Fine-Grained End-to-End Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22578)
*Size Li,Zhiqing Tang,Hongrui Liang,Jianxiong Guo,Jiong Lou,Tian Wang,Weijia Jia*

Main category: cs.AI
