TL;DR: HeraSys is an LLM serving system that optimizes concurrent, multi-tenant workflows by reusing redundant computation across workflows and using smarter, load-aware scheduling to reduce tail latency and boost throughput.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM serving systems focus mainly on optimizing each workflow in isolation (intra-workflow optimization), even though real deployments must handle many concurrent, multi-tenant workflows. This creates redundant computation across workflows and poor scheduling under load, leading to high tail latency and limited throughput. There is a need for a system that can jointly optimize across workflows while respecting strict latency constraints.

Method: The paper designs HeraSys, which (1) performs fine-grained orchestration of LLM agent workflows to detect shared structure across different workflows and merge or reuse overlapping computation nodes; (2) introduces a load-aware joint scheduling policy that considers both inter-query (across workflows) and intra-query (within a workflow) priorities to decide execution order; and (3) combines a resource skewing mechanism with adaptive batching and pipeline decomposition to better utilize hardware, balance load, and control tail latency.

Result: Experiments with concurrent LLM workflows show that HeraSys can reduce P99 latency by up to 2.17× and increase overall serving throughput by up to 1.85×, while still meeting strict latency guarantees.

Conclusion: Cross-workflow optimization is crucial for modern high-concurrency LLM serving. By merging redundant computation across workflows and using a load-aware, joint scheduling strategy integrated with resource skewing, batching, and pipeline decomposition, HeraSys significantly improves both tail latency and throughput compared with existing intra-workflow–focused systems.

Abstract: The proliferation of Large Language Models (LLMs) has shifted serving systems from processing isolated requests to orchestrating high-concurrency, multi-tenant agentic workflows. However, existing solutions typically prioritize intra-workflow optimization, largely neglecting the significant potential for inter-workflow optimization. In this paper, we propose HeraSys, an LLM serving system designed to optimize the end-to-end performance of concurrent workflows. Through fine-grained orchestration, HeraSys eliminates cross-workflow computational redundancy via structural node merging and reuse. Furthermore, HeraSys introduces a load-aware joint scheduling policy that dynamically manages execution order by evaluating both inter- and intra-query priorities. By integrating a resource skewing mechanism with adaptive batching and pipeline decomposition, HeraSys effectively mitigates tail latency while maintaining low average latency, thereby substantially improving system throughput. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HeraSys reduces P99 latency by up to 2.17$\times$ and increases serving throughput by up to 1.85$\times$ under strict latency guarantees.

</details>


### [103] [Multi-Objective Structured Pruning of LLMs for Latency and Model Size Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22583)
*Muhammad Junaid Ali,Smail Niar,El-Ghazali Talbi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A hardware-aware, multi-objective structured pruning framework for LLMs that jointly prunes layers, attention/MLP blocks, and dimensions to meet edge-device latency and size constraints while preserving reasoning performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are powerful but too large and computationally intensive for embedded and edge devices with strict constraints on latency, memory, and energy. Existing pruning methods struggle to jointly optimize different structural components (layers, heads, MLPs) because the combined design space is huge, costly to explore, and prone to suboptimal or unstable configurations. There is a need for a principled, hardware-aware pruning approach that explicitly optimizes latency and model size without sacrificing key abilities like commonsense reasoning and zero-shot performance.

Method: The paper proposes a two-stage, hardware-aware, multi-objective structured pruning framework. Stage 1 is coarse-grained, performing multi-objective depth pruning by removing entire attention and MLP blocks to substantially cut compute and memory. Stage 2 is fine-grained: a Parallel Bayesian Optimization (PBO) procedure searches the space of layer-wise pruning ratios under hardware latency constraints, while importance-based ranking within each layer selects which heads/MLP components to prune given that layer’s pruning budget. The framework jointly considers accuracy, latency, and model size, and is applied to multiple LLMs at different global pruning ratios.

Result: Experiments on multiple LLMs show that the method can prune 37.5% and 50% of model parameters while achieving better performance on commonsense reasoning benchmarks and zero-shot tasks than existing pruning approaches under similar pruning ratios. It significantly reduces inference cost (latency and model size) while maintaining or mildly degrading accuracy, demonstrating suitability for edge deployment.

Conclusion: A structured, hardware-aware, two-stage pruning framework using coarse depth pruning plus PBO-driven fine-grained pruning can effectively shrink LLMs for edge devices while preserving important reasoning capabilities. By explicitly optimizing latency and size alongside accuracy, it achieves a superior accuracy–efficiency trade-off compared to prior methods, suggesting a practical route to deploying LLMs in resource-constrained environments.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved widespread adoption because of their strong reasoning and query-response capabilities. However, deploying them in embedded and edge computing environments remains challenging because of strict latency, memory, and energy constraints. Their large parameter counts and computational demands hinder efficient execution on resource-constrained platforms. Although model pruning has emerged as a viable solution for reducing scale while preserving performance, jointly optimizing layers, attention heads, and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) dimensions remains highly complex. Exhaustively exploring this combined design space is computationally expensive and often leads to local optima or unstable configurations. To address these limitations, we propose a hardware-aware, multi-objective structured pruning framework. The proposed two-stage method explicitly targets latency and model size for efficient deployment on edge devices. In the coarse-grained stage, multi-objective depth pruning removes entire attention and MLP blocks to reduce computational load and memory usage. In the subsequent fine-grained stage, Parallel Bayesian Optimization (PBO) searches for the optimal layer-wise pruning ratios for pruning under latency constraints, while importance-based strategies rank the specific components to be pruned within each layer's allocated budget. Experimental results show that our approach reduces model complexity with minimal impact on commonsense reasoning tasks and zero-shot performance. Our method achieves a favorable trade-off among accuracy, latency, and model size, making it suitable for edge deployment. Across multiple LLMs at 37.5% and 50% pruning ratios, the proposed approach achieves better performance on commonsense reasoning tasks than existing methods while significantly reducing inference cost.

</details>


### [104] [Source-Aware Reranking for Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Reliability Prior Approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22584)
*Yuktha Tata Koganti,Hugo Garrido-Lestache Belinchon*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They modify standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) ranking by weighting document similarity scores with simple source-reliability priors, and show this boosts precision and reduces retrieval of adversarial documents in a small health-domain corpus.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard RAG systems rank documents purely by semantic similarity, ignoring how trustworthy different sources are. This can surface low-credibility or adversarial content, which is especially problematic in sensitive domains like health. The authors want a simple, interpretable way to incorporate domain knowledge about source reliability directly into the retrieval step to improve answer quality and robustness.

Method: They define a source-specific reliability prior λ(s) for each document based on its source type. For a query q and document d from source s, the final retrieval score is score(q,d) = sim(q,d) * λ(s), where sim is the usual semantic similarity. They evaluate this source-aware reranking against a similarity-only baseline on a 120-document health-domain corpus in a controlled setting, under a threat model where low-credibility sources are identifiable via metadata. All experiments are run on an HPC cluster (Rosie) for reliable, reproducible execution.

Result: In this health-domain corpus, incorporating source priors improves Precision@5 from 0.48 to 0.72 versus similarity-only ranking, and decreases the average retrieval of adversarial documents, given the assumed ability to detect low-credibility sources via metadata.

Conclusion: A very simple, multiplicative source-aware reweighting of similarity scores can substantially improve top-k retrieval quality and reduce adversarial document inclusion in RAG for this controlled health-domain scenario. While limited by the small corpus and strong assumptions about metadata availability, the approach appears to be a promising mitigation strategy against source quality degradation in RAG pipelines.

Abstract: Standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation pipelines rank retrieved documents by semantic similarity alone, without accounting for source provenance or credibility. This work evaluates a simple and interpretable modification to RAG retrieval ranking that incorporates domain-informed source reliability priors. Each document is assigned a prior lambda(s) based on its source type, and retrieval scores are reweighted using score(q, d) = sim(q, d) * lambda(s). The framework is evaluated against a similarity-only baseline on a 120-document health-domain corpus. In this controlled setting, source-aware reranking improves Precision@5 from 0.48 to 0.72 and reduces average adversarial document retrieval under the evaluated threat model, where low-credibility sources are identifiable via metadata. All experiments were executed on Rosie, the high-performance computing cluster at the Milwaukee School of Engineering, which provided the GPU-accelerated infrastructure necessary to run the full experimental pipeline reliably and reproducibly. These results suggest a potential mitigation strategy for source quality degradation in RAG pipelines, within the limits of the experimental setup described.

</details>


### [105] [The Scaffold Effect in Coding Agents: Harness Choice as a Hidden Variable in Coding-Agent Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22585)
*Naman Vats,Oleg Golev*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper shows that for coding agents, the surrounding harness (scaffold) can dramatically change efficiency (up to 40x tokens per solved task) while leaving pass rates relatively similar, so evaluations must treat harness+model as the real comparison unit.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Public coding-agent leaderboards mostly report model names and pass rates, implicitly assuming the harness is either fixed or unimportant. In practice, harnesses differ in how they issue tools, manage context, and decide when to stop, which may strongly affect both performance and efficiency. The authors aim to disentangle model effects from harness effects and highlight how this impacts real-world usability, cost, and latency of coding agents.

Method: They evaluate two models (Qwen 3.6 Plus and MiniMax M2.5) across three different open-source harnesses (Goose, OpenCode, OpenHands-SDK). The benchmark is a stratified 50-task subset of Terminal-Bench Pro. They measure pass rate, tokens per solved task, and analyze error/failure patterns. They use paired-task bootstrap confidence intervals to compare pass rates and examine repeated failure modes across models to infer harness-level biases.

Result: Harness choice causes very large differences in efficiency: up to 40x differences in tokens per solved task between harnesses. Yet, for a given model, pass-rate differences across harnesses are modest (0–8 percentage points) and the paired-task confidence intervals mostly include zero, meaning no statistically clear difference except for the largest gap. Failure patterns (“fingerprints”) are similar for both models within the same harness (e.g., REASON failures for Goose, VERIFY/MAX_TURNS for OpenHands-SDK, idle-loop/TIME for OpenCode), implying that many failure modes come from the harness itself, not the underlying model.

Conclusion: The effective unit to compare in human-centered coding-agent evaluations is the harness–model pair, not the model alone. Harness design substantially drives efficiency, cost, latency, and oversight burden, even when pass rates are similar. The authors recommend selecting harness–model combinations based on pass rate subject to token and latency budgets, and urge that future work report token usage, latency, and detailed harness specifications along with any model comparisons. They also release configs, logs, snapshots, and analysis scripts to support reproducibility and further study.

Abstract: Public leaderboards for coding agents typically rank systems by model name and pass rate, while the surrounding harness (the scaffold that issues tools, manages context, and decides when to stop) is often under-specified. Model-to-model comparison is valid when the harness is fixed; when it varies, performance and efficiency conflate model and scaffold effects. We evaluate Qwen 3.6 Plus and MiniMax M2.5 across three open-source harnesses (Goose, OpenCode, OpenHands-SDK) on a stratified 50-task subset of Terminal-Bench Pro. Harness choice induces up to a 40x difference in tokens per solved task, while paired within-model pass-rate differences remain 0-8 percentage points (95% paired-task bootstrap CIs include zero except for the largest gap). Failure fingerprints replicate across models (REASON for Goose, VERIFY/MAX_TURNS for OpenHands-SDK, idle-loop/TIME for OpenCode), indicating harness-level biases that are largely model-independent. For human-centered coding-agent evaluation, model name alone is an incomplete comparison unit: harness-model pairs determine real-world cost, latency, and oversight burden; no-action turns are a per-task wait tax, not just a token tax. We therefore recommend selecting harness-model pairs by pass rate under token/latency budgets, and reporting token usage, latency, and full harness specifications alongside any model comparison. We release anonymized configs, raw trial logs, aggregated snapshots, and analysis scripts.

</details>


### [106] [MM-ShiftKV: Decode-Aware Prefill-Stage KV Selection for Multimodal Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22586)
*Jinsong Shu,Chenyang Wu,Zhongle Xie,Baokun Wang,Lidan Shou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces MM-ShiftKV, a training-free method to more accurately select which key-value (KV) cache entries to keep in multimodal LLMs, by making prefill-time KV importance estimation better reflect decoding-time behavior, thereby improving performance under strict memory budgets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: KV caching enables fast inference in MLLMs but its memory usage grows linearly with context length, and multimodal inputs add many visual tokens, making memory a bottleneck. Existing KV selection methods decide which KVs to keep using only prefill statistics and assume these are representative of decoding-time queries. The authors show this assumption fails in multimodal settings because decoding queries have much larger variance, so small ranking errors when pruning KVs can remove crucial visual tokens and hurt grounding and reasoning, especially under tight cache budgets. They want a prefill-only method that is robust to this decode-time shift.

Method: They propose MM-ShiftKV, a training-free, decode-aware yet strictly prefill-only KV selection approach. During the prefill stage, MM-ShiftKV constructs variance-expanded proxy queries that approximate the higher-variance behavior of decoding-time queries. It then uses these proxy queries to compute aggregated attention mass over the prompt tokens and estimate each token’s KV importance. Based on this importance ranking, the method selects which KVs (especially visual ones) to retain in the cache under a given memory budget, without modifying the underlying MLLM or requiring additional training.

Result: On multiple multimodal benchmarks, MM-ShiftKV achieves consistently better performance than prior KV selection and compression methods when operating under strict KV-cache memory budgets. It particularly improves multimodal grounding and reasoning quality compared to existing prefill-based selection baselines, showing more stable performance as the cache size is reduced.

Conclusion: The work demonstrates that the distribution shift between prefill and decoding queries is critical for KV selection in multimodal LLMs and that ignoring this shift leads to unstable importance estimates and degraded performance under tight cache budgets. By approximating decode-time query variance through proxy queries at prefill, MM-ShiftKV provides a practical, training-free, prefill-only solution that more reliably preserves semantically important visual tokens and improves MLLM performance within limited memory. The approach is validated empirically and released as open-source code.

Abstract: Key-Value (KV) caching is essential for efficient inference in multimodal large language models (MLLMs), yet its memory footprint grows linearly with context length and becomes a major bottleneck due to the large number of visual tokens. Recent prefill-stage KV selection methods estimate KV importance from prefilling statistics, implicitly assuming that prefilling-time queries are representative of those encountered during decoding. We show that this assumption breaks down in multimodal inference, where decoding-time queries exhibit substantially larger variance than prefilling-stage representations, leading to unstable KV importance estimation under tight cache budgets. As a result, small ranking errors can disproportionately discard semantically critical visual tokens and degrade grounding and reasoning performance. We propose MM-ShiftKV, a training-free, decode-aware and strictly prefill-only KV selection method. MM-ShiftKV approximates decoding-time query behavior during prefilling by constructing variance-expanded query proxies and estimates prompt KV importance based on their aggregated attention mass. Experiments on multimodal benchmarks demonstrate that MM-ShiftKV consistently outperforms existing methods under strict KV-cache budgets. Our code is available at https://github.com/zjuDBxAI/MM-ShiftKV.

</details>


### [107] [TriSP: Tri-Signal Structured Pruning for Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22587)
*Manel Kara laoua,Soumia Bouyahiaoui,Aicha Boutorh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TriSP is a structured pruning method for LLMs that combines three signals to score channels and, together with adaptive layer budgets and LoRA recovery, yields smaller, faster models with strong performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deploying large language models is costly in memory and compute, limiting their practical use. Structured pruning can reduce model size and speed up inference by removing entire components (e.g., heads, neurons), but current approaches either need expensive gradient computations or rely on indirect activation statistics and often ignore how pruning criteria interact with recovery strategies. A better importance metric and a more principled pruning+recovery pipeline are needed to get efficient yet accurate pruned LLMs.

Method: The paper introduces TriSP (Tri-Signal Structured Pruning), which defines an importance score for each channel (e.g., attention head or MLP neuron) as the geometric mean of two main terms: (1) weight magnitude scaled by the norm of the corresponding activations, and (2) a first-order gradient-based loss-sensitivity measure. This yields a unified channel-level importance metric reflecting both structural properties and sensitivity of the loss to removal. TriSP is combined with an adaptive, per-layer pruning budget allocation strategy and a LoRA-based post-pruning recovery phase to fine-tune the pruned model efficiently.

Result: On LLaMA-7B, TriSP achieves 6.80 perplexity on WikiText-2 at 20% structured pruning, outperforming alternative pruning criteria and recovery combinations across all tested configurations in terms of both perplexity and zero-shot accuracy. At 50% pruning, inference throughput improves by 82% while the model maintains competitive performance, demonstrating that substantial efficiency gains are possible without dramatic degradation in quality.

Conclusion: A tri-signal, channel-level importance metric that fuses structural and gradient-based information, when paired with adaptive layer-wise pruning and LoRA recovery, leads to pruned LLMs that are significantly faster and smaller while preserving strong perplexity and zero-shot accuracy. This shows that carefully designed scoring and recovery strategies can make structured pruning a practical path for efficient LLM deployment on standard hardware.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve strong performance across diverse tasks but their deployment is constrained by the memory and compute cost of their parameters. Structured pruning addresses this by removing entire structures such as attention heads and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) neurons to produce smaller dense models that run efficiently on standard hardware. However, existing methods rely on either gradient-based importance estimation, which is memory-prohibitive, or activation-based statistical proxies, which do not directly measure the effect of removal on the loss. Furthermore, the interaction between the importance criterion and the post-pruning recovery strategy has not been systematically studied. We propose TriSP (Tri-Signal Structured Pruning), an importance metric that combines weight magnitude scaled by activation norm with first-order gradient sensitivity via a geometric mean, producing a channel-level score that captures both structural and loss-sensitivity signals. Combined with adaptive per-layer budget allocation and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) recovery, TriSP achieves the lowest perplexity and highest zero-shot accuracy across all tested configurations, reaching 6.80 WikiText-2 perplexity at 20% pruning on LLaMA-7B. Inference throughput improves by 82% at 50% pruning, while still maintaining competitive performance.

</details>


### [108] [ParBench: A Benchmark for Reliable Evaluation of LLM Parallel Code Translation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22588)
*Samyak Jhaveri,Erel Kaplan,Tom Yotam,Le Chen,Tomer Bitan,Niranjan Hasabnis,Gal Oren*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ParBench is a benchmark suite to rigorously test how well LLMs translate parallel code between GPU/parallel APIs while preserving low-level semantics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As code must be migrated between evolving accelerator ecosystems and APIs (CUDA, OpenMP, OpenCL, OpenMP target offload), LLMs and coding agents are being used to automate translation. However, there is no reliable way to measure whether these models preserve crucial low-level parallel behavior like thread indexing, synchronization, memory and host-device coordination, and API-specific execution structures. A dedicated, executable benchmark is needed to rigorously evaluate semantic preservation in such translations.

Method: The authors design ParBench, a kernel-centric benchmark framework. It standardizes build, run, and verification via declarative benchmark specifications so models only translate the core computational kernels. Benchmarks are drawn from multiple open-source HPC suites and span several cross-API translation directions between CUDA, OpenMP, OpenCL, and OpenMP target offload. To reduce the chance that models succeed via memorization rather than robust understanding, ParBench applies AST-driven, behavior-preserving source augmentations that are validated against baselines before use.

Result: Using ParBench, the authors evaluate several state-of-the-art open and proprietary LLMs on parallel API translation tasks. The results show that current models struggle to reliably preserve parallel semantics. Specific issues include asymmetry between translation directions, problems coordinating code across multiple files, failures to fully adapt to target APIs, and sensitivity to minor source-level changes despite intended behavior-preserving transformations.

Conclusion: ParBench exposes significant remaining challenges in using LLMs for trustworthy parallel code translation across accelerator APIs. Even advanced models frequently break low-level semantics, and their performance can be brittle to small source perturbations. The benchmark provides an executable, reproducible way to measure and compare model robustness in this domain, pointing to the need for more semantically aware approaches. The code and framework are publicly released for the community to use and extend.

Abstract: Modern compute-intensive software must migrate across a changing ecosystem of accelerators, programming APIs, compiler stacks, and portability layers, including CUDA, OpenMP, OpenCL, and OpenMP target offload. Large language models and autonomous coding agents are increasingly proposed for such migration, but the field lacks reliable ways to measure whether they preserve the low-level parallel semantics that make translations behaviorally valid, including thread indexing, synchronization, memory management, host-device coordination, and API-specific execution structure.
  We present ParBench, a kernel-centric benchmark framework for evaluating LLM-based parallel API translation under executable, reproducible conditions. ParBench fixes the surrounding build, run, and verification infrastructure through declarative benchmark specifications and asks models to translate only the computational kernels. It draws on multiple open-source HPC suites and covers representative cross-API translation directions among CUDA, OpenMP, OpenCL, and OpenMP target offload. To test whether success reflects robust translation rather than surface-form memorization, ParBench includes AST-driven, intended behavior-preserving, baseline-validated source augmentation. Evaluations on state-of-the-art open and proprietary LLMs show persistent barriers to reliable parallel code translation, including direction asymmetry, multi-file coordination, incomplete API adaptation, and uneven robustness to source-level perturbations. Code is available at https://github.com/Scientific-Computing-Lab/ParBench.

</details>


### [109] [Lexical discovery in unknown environments orchestrated by Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22591)
*Rafael Sendra-Arranz,Iñaki Dellibarda Varela,Eduardo Rocon,Álvaro Gutiérrez,Manuel Cebrian*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Framework where multiple LLM-based agents explore images and autonomously build a shared “alien” vocabulary for previously unnamed visual entities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous agents in unexplored environments (like other planets or deep sea) will encounter novel entities lacking names in human language, yet must communicate about them and keep their vocabularies interpretable for humans.

Method: Introduce the Neuro-Symbolic Lexical Discovery (NSLD) framework: a population of agents, each with a frozen CLIP vision encoder, a private FAISS vector index, and a text-only LLM, plays a referential game over out-of-distribution visual referents. Agents invent and adapt lexical items while grounding them via semantic proximity in a shared embedding space, enabling alignment with natural language. They then analyse convergence using three analytical models, each explaining the dynamics of lexicon emergence with high goodness of fit (R^2>0.95).

Result: In simulations with up to 20 agents and 10 novel visual referents, agents self-organise a consistent shared “alien” lexicon. The new invented words are systematically aligned with human language concepts through embedding similarities, and the convergence of the lexicon is well described by their analytical models (R^2>0.95).

Conclusion: NSLD demonstrates that populations of LLM-based agents can autonomously invent and agree on names for previously unknown visual entities while keeping those names interpretable via semantic anchoring to natural language. This offers a foundation for planning and analysing communication systems in future autonomous exploration missions.

Abstract: Populations of autonomous agents deployed in unknown environments (e.g. planetary or deep-sea exploration) must develop shared vocabularies to refer to entities that have no name in any human language. We propose the Neuro-Symbolic Lexical Discovery (NSLD) framework, in which a population of LLM-based agents plays a referential game over out-of-distribution visual referents, autonomously self-organising a shared alien lexicon. Each agent combines a frozen CLIP vision encoder with a private FAISS vector index and a text-only LLM. Crucially, discovered alien words are anchored to natural language via semantic proximity in the embedding space, enlarging the human vocabulary with new perceptually grounded words. Consensus is reached in simulations with populations of up to twenty agents and ten visual referents. Convergence dynamics are characterised through three analytical models achieving R^2 > 0.95, representing a first step towards pre-deployment planning in autonomous exploration missions.

</details>


### [110] [Structure Over Scale: Schema-Constrained Causal Graphs for RAG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22592)
*Marc Saouda,Rajprakash Bale,Eren Aldis,Cloves Almeida*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes HCG-RAG, a hierarchical causal graph-based RAG system that uses a schema-constrained causal vocabulary to build compact, auditable graphs, achieving similar or better answer quality to entity-relation GraphRAG baselines at much lower construction cost, and showing that structured causal organization matters more than graph size.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing graph-based RAG systems typically perform open-ended extraction of entities and relations, creating large graphs whose size and building cost scale with the length of the entire corpus rather than the complexity of the query’s reasoning needs. These graphs are expensive to construct, hard to audit, and may not offer proportionate gains over simpler retrieval. The authors aim to design a more efficient, interpretable, and targeted structured retrieval method that leverages causal and hierarchical structure, particularly valuable in domains like medicine where expert oversight and compact, meaningful structure are critical.

Method: The authors introduce HCG-RAG (Hierarchical Causal Graph RAG), which replaces unconstrained entity-relation extraction with a schema-constrained causal representation. First, an automated pipeline distills the corpus into a fixed, typed vocabulary of causal variables (i.e., pre-specified variable types rather than arbitrary entities). Then it materializes a compact two-tier hierarchical causal graph over these variables. This causal graph is used as a structured filter for retrieval in a RAG pipeline, controlling what information is retrieved and in which causal/hierarchical relations. The approach is evaluated against entity-relation GraphRAG baselines, including MS-GraphRAG, on medical and clinical benchmarks and with an ablation that isolates the effect of the causal graph versus embedding-only retrieval.

Result: Compared with entity-relation graph baselines, HCG-RAG achieves comparable or better answer quality with substantially reduced graph size and construction cost: 3–20× fewer nodes and 8–135× fewer build-time LLM calls than MS-GraphRAG. The resulting graphs are compact enough for domain experts to audit, correct, and extend. On medical/clinical datasets, including a neurologist-validated epilepsy dataset, HCG-RAG matches or outperforms state-of-the-art entity-relation systems. Ablation experiments show that using the causal graph as a structured retrieval filter yields a +6 percentage point performance gain over embedding-only retrieval. Across domains, the experiments indicate that methods imposing meaningful hierarchical causal structure are the only ones that consistently outperform flat entity-relation retrieval.

Conclusion: The study concludes that schema-constrained hierarchical causal graphs provide a more efficient and interpretable basis for graph-based RAG than open-ended entity-relation extraction. HCG-RAG demonstrates that compact, causally organized graphs can match or exceed the performance of much larger entity-relation graphs while being cheaper to build and easier for experts to inspect and refine. The findings highlight that the quality and organization of information encoded in the graph—especially hierarchical causal structure—matters more than graph size or density, suggesting future graph-RAG research should focus on higher-level, domain-aligned structure rather than exhaustive extraction.

Abstract: Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG) grounds answers in structured knowledge, but current systems extract entities and relationships exhaustively, producing graphs whose size and construction cost scale with corpus length rather than with the reasoning a query requires. We introduce HCG-RAG (Hierarchical Causal Graph RAG), which replaces open-ended extraction with schema-constrained causal graphs: an automated pipeline distills a corpus into a fixed, typed vocabulary of causal variables and materializes a compact two-tier graph over it. Our schema-constrained graphs match entity-relation baselines on answer quality at a fraction of the cost: 3-20x fewer nodes, 8x-135x fewer build-time LLM calls than the most LLM-intensive baseline (MS-GraphRAG), and graphs compact enough for a domain expert to audit, correct, and extend. On medical and clinical benchmarks, including a neurologist-validated epilepsy dataset, HCG-RAG matches or exceeds the best entity-relation systems. An ablation isolates the causal graph as a structured retrieval filter, contributing +6 percentage points (pp) over embedding-only retrieval. Across all domains with discoverable hierarchical causal structure, only methods imposing higher-level organization outperform flat entity-relation retrieval, indicating that what is placed in the graph matters more than how many nodes it contains.

</details>


### [111] [xMIx: High-Performance Serving-Time Platform for Mechanistic Interpretability Apps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22595)
*Michael Blum,Mark Silberstein,Yaniv David*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: xMIx is a serving-native framework that lets mechanistic interpretability (MI) applications run inline with production LLM inference with negligible overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing mechanistic interpretability tools are too slow and operationally clumsy for production serving. They typically require separate runs, disrupt batching and CUDA-graph optimizations, and force model restarts or separate stacks, making practical deployment for tasks like jailbreak detection or hallucination monitoring infeasible.

Method: Design a serving-native framework (xMIx) that hooks MI functions into predefined points in the model runtime (layers, residual streams). Compile multiple MI apps into the same serving path but activate them conditionally and dynamically based on intermediate activations, without spinning a separate model instance or execution stack. Integrate this into the vLLM serving system and evaluate across multiple models and MI workloads.

Result: When integrated with vLLM and tested on three major models and seven MI applications, xMIx preserves almost all serving performance: ~1.3% overhead in mean inter-token latency, 1.2% in P99 ITL, 2.6% in time to first token, and 1.6% in total token throughput, compared to vanilla vLLM.

Conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability can be embedded directly into production LLM serving with minimal performance penalty by compiling MI computations into the serving path and activating them conditionally at runtime. This makes MI-based monitoring and interventions (e.g., jailbreak or hallucination detection) practical in real-world deployments.

Abstract: Mechanistic interpretability (MI) has emerged as a powerful approach for analyzing and intervening in inference computations, with a growing number of applications such as jailbreak attempt detection, truthfulness evaluation, and hallucination detection. Unfortunately, MI deployment in production model-serving systems is currently not practical, as most existing MI frameworks introduce prohibitively high runtime overheads. The fundamental problem is that MI functions do not compose cleanly with served models: they fragment deployment, often force draining requests and rebuilding serving state, and conflict with critical performance optimizations such as continuous batching and CUDA-graph execution, essential for production deployments.
  We present xMIx, a serving-native framework for deploying MI applications in production inference serving environments. xMIx enables attaching MI functions to a predefined set of locations in the model runtime, interposing on activations within the layers and residual streams. xMIx supports conditional invocation of MI functions depending on the outputs in preceding model layers. Multiple MI applications can be deployed in a single model instance. xMIx compiles them all into the serving path but activates them dynamically at runtime only when necessary, with negligible performance cost, and without requiring a separate model instance or alternative execution stack.
  We integrate xMIx with the vLLM serving system and evaluate it across three major models and seven diverse MI applications. xMIx achieves performance comparable to native vLLM execution, incurring a slowdown of 1.3% mean inter-token latency (ITL), 1.2% for tail P99 ITL, 2.6% for mean time to first token (TTFT), and 1.6% for mean total token throughput (TTT).

</details>


### [112] [An Agentic Orchestration of Atomistic Simulations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22596)
*Rahul Somasundaram,Adela Habib,Khanh Dang,Sachin Shivakumar,Ryley G. Hill,Golo Wimmer,Avanish Mishra,Aleksandra Pachalieva,Arthur Lui,Hari Viswanathan,Michael Grosskopf,Saryu Fensin,Russell Bent,Nathan DeBardeleben,Earl Lawrence*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: An agent-based system automates complex atomistic simulation workflows in LAMMPS, improving rigor, reproducibility, and scalability by autonomously handling setup, execution, and validation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Atomistic simulations are powerful for materials design but currently require complex, multi-step workflows and substantial expert human intervention, including selecting interatomic potentials, configuring simulations, and managing failures. This complexity hampers efficiency, rigor, reproducibility, and scalability, especially in high-throughput or non-expert settings. The paper aims to reduce this manual overhead and make atomistic modeling more autonomous and reliable.

Method: The authors develop an agent-based system within the URSA (Universal Research and Scientific Agent) framework that encapsulates domain knowledge and decision logic to control LAMMPS-based simulations. The agent automatically selects appropriate interatomic potentials, constructs simulation inputs, executes simulations, and monitors them in a closed-loop fashion. It performs iterative error detection and recovery, adjusting parameters or workflows as needed. The system’s scientific reliability is benchmarked by comparing its results against those from LAVA, a high-throughput LAMMPS toolkit, and from VASP calculations used as higher-fidelity references.

Result: The agent-based framework successfully designs and runs atomistic simulations in LAMMPS with minimal human intervention, handling potential selection, input generation, and automated error recovery. Benchmarking shows that the outputs are scientifically reliable and consistent with results from LAVA workflows and VASP calculations, indicating that the autonomous agent can reproduce accepted computational materials results. The workflow demonstrates reduced need for trial-and-error and manual tuning.

Conclusion: Embedding an agent-based system into the URSA framework enables robust automation of atomistic simulation workflows in LAMMPS. By autonomously managing setup, execution, and validation, the system reduces manual effort, decreases trial-and-error, and enhances rigor, reproducibility, and scalability in atomistic modeling. This approach points toward more autonomous, agent-driven computational materials research pipelines.

Abstract: Atomistic simulations are central to materials design, but their execution involves complex, multi-step workflows that require significant human expertise. Here, we present an agent-based system embedded within the URSA (Universal Research and Scientific Agent) framework that automates the design, execution, and validation of atomistic simulations, demonstrated using the Large-scale Atomic/Molecular Massively Parallel Simulator (LAMMPS) tool. Our system autonomously selects interatomic potentials, constructs and runs simulations, and performs iterative error recovery within a closed-loop workflow. We evaluate the scientific reliability of the agent by benchmarking its outputs against LAVA, a high-throughput toolkit for LAMMPS and the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP) calculations. Our framework reduces manual intervention and trial-and-error, thereby improving the rigor, reproducibility, and scalability of atomistic modeling.

</details>


### [113] [HyCE-RAG: Hypergraph Chain-of-Evidence Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Explainable Multi-hop Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22597)
*Hong-Yu An,Yun-Jian Zhang,Chen-Wei Liang,Tian-Yi Zhang,Jian Ding,Yi-Lun Wu,Ao-Bo Li,Wei-Cong Su,Saifullah,Mujiangshan Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HyCE-RAG is a hypergraph-based retrieval-augmented generation framework that builds structured chains of evidence for multi-hop question answering, improving accuracy and explainability over standard and graph-based RAG.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RAG systems for multi-hop QA mostly rely on semantic similarity search and simple graph structures, which struggle to capture higher-order relations among multiple entities and evidence pieces, leading to missing or incoherent reasoning chains and less faithful answers.

Method: The authors construct a query-aware evidence hypergraph where entities, relations, and contextual evidence are grouped into hyperedges. They perform confidence propagation over the entity–hyperedge incidence structure, then use a confidence-guided evidence assembly mechanism to select, connect, and rank evidence paths. Scoring integrates semantic relevance, entity connectivity, evidence coverage, relation reliability, extraction confidence, and propagated confidence before feeding structured evidence chains to a language model for answer generation.

Result: On several multi-hop QA benchmarks (HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, MuSiQue, and GraphRAG-Bench subsets), HyCE-RAG achieves consistently higher answer accuracy, more relevant retrieved context, and more faithful reasoning compared with standard RAG and graph-based RAG baselines.

Conclusion: Organizing post-retrieval evidence as a hypergraph and explicitly constructing confidence-scored chains of evidence leads to more accurate and interpretable multi-hop QA, indicating that hypergraph-based structures are a promising direction for complex reasoning beyond traditional pairwise graph or flat passage retrieval approaches.

Abstract: Multi-hop question answering requires systems to retrieve evidence from multiple documents and connect scattered facts into a coherent reasoning process. Standard retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) mainly relies on semantic similarity between a query and text chunks, and therefore often fails to model structural relations among entities, facts, and evidence units. Graph-based RAG improves this by introducing graph-structured knowledge, but pairwise edges are still limited in representing higher-order associations involving multiple entities and contexts. We propose HyCE-RAG, a Hypergraph Chain-of-Evidence Retrieval-Augmented Generation framework for explainable multi-hop question answering. HyCE-RAG organizes entities, relations, and contextual evidence into hyperedges, builds a query-aware evidence hypergraph, and performs confidence propagation over entity--hyperedge incidence structures. It then uses confidence-guided evidence assembly to select, connect, and rank evidence paths before answer generation. The scoring process jointly considers semantic relevance, entity connectivity, evidence coverage, relation reliability, extraction confidence, and propagated confidence. By providing the language model with structured evidence chains rather than flat retrieved passages, HyCE-RAG supports more faithful and interpretable reasoning. Experiments on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, MuSiQue, and two GraphRAG-Bench subsets show that HyCE-RAG consistently outperforms standard RAG and graph-based RAG baselines in answer accuracy, context relevance, and faithfulness. These results suggest that hypergraph-based evidence organization is a promising direction for post-retrieval reasoning in complex question answering.

</details>


### [114] [Differencing the Diffusion Trajectory toward Uncertain Components for Time Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22599)
*Chen Su,Yuanhe Tian,Yan Song*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DiffDiff is a diffusion-based time series forecasting framework that embeds the asymmetry between predictable low-frequency trends and uncertain high-frequency components directly into the diffusion trajectory, improving probabilistic forecasts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard diffusion models for time series treat all parts of the future trajectory symmetrically during corruption and denoising, even though in forecasting the near-future low-frequency behavior is strongly constrained by past observations while high-frequency components remain uncertain. Existing methods handle this via external rules (e.g., predicting residuals), so the diffusion process itself is unaware of what the history already determines, potentially wasting model capacity and sampling steps on reconstructing predictable, history-anchored content. The motivation is to design a diffusion process that inherently focuses generative effort on the most uncertain components of the future while preserving compatibility with standard samplers.

Method: The authors introduce DiffDiff, which modifies both the forward diffusion operator and the conditioning pathway. In the forward process, the corruption operator becomes step-dependent: early in the trajectory, the noisy state stays close to the original target values; as time progresses, the state is transformed to emphasize the second-order differenced structure (i.e., higher-frequency, less predictable components). In parallel, the denoiser is conditioned on two types of history information—raw value-domain history and differential (e.g., differenced) history—combined using a stage-adaptive gating mechanism at each diffusion step to balance their contributions depending on the noise level. The design ensures that the terminal distribution still converges to a standard Gaussian so standard diffusion samplers can be used.

Result: On seven time series forecasting benchmarks and across four prediction horizons, DiffDiff is empirically compared to six existing diffusion-based forecasting baselines. DiffDiff achieves superior performance on these tasks, indicating better calibrated probabilistic forecasts. Additional analysis shows that the method successfully concentrates generative capacity on uncertain, high-frequency components of the future and avoids redundantly regenerating slowly-varying content that is already determined by the observed history.

Conclusion: Embedding the forecasting asymmetry between predictable low-frequency trends and uncertain high-frequency variations directly into the diffusion process leads to more effective probabilistic time series forecasting. DiffDiff’s step-dependent forward operator and stage-adaptive conditioning allow the model to focus on uncertain components while remaining compatible with existing sampling schemes. The approach outperforms several diffusion baselines, suggesting that making the diffusion trajectory itself history-aware is a promising direction for future diffusion-based forecasting models.

Abstract: Diffusion models have become a widely used framework for probabilistic time series forecasting, modeling the distribution of future values given an observed history. In time series forecasting, however, the future continues the observed history, creating an asymmetry the standard diffusion process leaves unaddressed, with slowly-varying content largely determined by the observed continuity while higher-frequency dynamics carry most of the residual uncertainty. Existing diffusion-based forecasters decouple this asymmetry through an external rule before generation, leaving the corruption trajectory blind to which parts of the target the history can already anchor. We propose DiffDiff, a diffusion framework that embeds this predictability asymmetry into the diffusion trajectory itself, so that a single end-to-end diffusion process becomes aware of which parts of the target the history can already anchor. DiffDiff makes the forward operator step-dependent so that the noisy intermediate state progressively shifts from the target itself toward its second-order differenced structure, while a conditioning pathway supplies the denoiser with both value-domain and differential history information balanced by a stage-adaptive gate at each diffusion step. The terminal distribution approaches a standard Gaussian, preserving compatibility with existing samplers. On seven benchmarks across four prediction horizons, DiffDiff outperforms six diffusion baselines, and our analysis confirms that DiffDiff concentrates the diffusion's generative effort on the most uncertain components of the target while relieving it from rebuilding the history-anchored content.

</details>


### [115] [Chart Deception in Vision-Language Models: From Vulnerability to Mitigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22600)
*Ridwan Mahbub,Mohammed Saidul Islam,Md Tahmid Rahman Laskar,Mizanur Rahman,Mir Tafseer Nayeem,Enamul Hoque*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces VisDeception, a benchmark and metric to test how easily vision-language models are fooled by misleading chart designs, and a mitigation method that makes them more robust by grounding in chart metadata.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As charts are widely used for data communication, deceptive but data-faithful design choices can mislead human viewers and, increasingly, vision-language models used for chart understanding. With VLMs being deployed for analytical reasoning, it is important to know whether they are robust to such visual deceptions and how to mitigate vulnerabilities, but there has been no systematic, controlled benchmark to evaluate this.

Method: The authors create VisDeception, a benchmark of 1,600 chart pairs where each misleading chart is matched with a faithful version generated from the same data, covering eight common categories of deceptive visualization tactics. They define a paired metric, the Deception Score, to measure how much misleading charts shift a model’s answers away from the faithful interpretation. They then run 10 state-of-the-art VLMs on 32,000 chart-question pairs and analyze performance. Finally, they design an inference-time multi-agent mitigation framework that first extracts structured chart metadata from the visualization and then bases reasoning on this metadata during answer generation, aiming to dampen the impact of deceptive visual cues.

Result: Experiments show that current state-of-the-art VLMs are highly susceptible to deceptive visualization tactics, with misleading charts significantly altering their interpretations relative to faithful charts, as quantified by the Deception Score. The proposed metadata-grounded multi-agent inference framework improves robustness, reducing the influence of deceptive chart features without needing extra instructions from users.

Conclusion: The work demonstrates that existing VLMs have serious reliability gaps when interpreting deceptive information visualizations, even when the underlying data is unchanged. VisDeception, along with the Deception Score, offers a principled way to evaluate and compare model robustness. The structured, metadata-grounded reasoning framework is a promising mitigation strategy, and the authors argue that future chart-understanding systems should incorporate benchmark-driven evaluation, deception-aware metrics, and structured reasoning to build more trustworthy visual analytics tools.

Abstract: Information visualizations are widely used to communicate patterns, trends, and outliers, yet deceptive design choices-such as truncated or inverted axes, distorted aspect ratios, inappropriate encodings, and misleading color mappings-can systematically alter interpretation while preserving the underlying data. As Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly used for chart understanding and analytical reasoning, assessing their robustness to such deceptive visualizations has become critical for trustworthy data analysis. We introduce VisDeception, the first controlled paired benchmark for evaluating the robustness of VLMs to misleading chart designs. The benchmark contains 1,600 paired faithful and misleading charts spanning eight major categories of deceptive visualization tactics, where each misleading chart is paired with a faithful counterpart generated from the same underlying data. To isolate deception-induced reasoning errors from baseline chart-understanding errors, we introduce the Deception Score, a paired evaluation metric that quantifies how misleading visualizations shift model responses away from the faithful interpretation of the data. Across 32,000 responses from 10 state-of-the-art VLMs, we find that even advanced models remain highly vulnerable to deceptive visual manipulations. To improve robustness, we further propose an inference-time multi-agent mitigation framework that grounds reasoning in structured chart metadata extracted from the visualization before answer generation, enabling models to reduce the influence of deceptive visual cues without requiring explicit user instructions. Together, our findings reveal important reliability gaps in current chart-understanding systems and establish benchmark-driven evaluation, deception-aware metrics, and structured reasoning as promising directions for developing more trustworthy VLMs for visual analytics.

</details>


### [116] [DeepLook: Deeper Thinking with Lookahead](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22602)
*Tingxin Yang,Zefeng Wang,Mengyue Wang,Xingcheng Zhou,Yunpu Ma*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DeepLook is a training-free decoding framework that selectively allocates extra inference-time compute only at uncertain parts of a model’s reasoning trace, improving accuracy–cost trade-offs on math benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Inference-time scaling improves reasoning by spending more compute during generation, but current methods typically allocate this extra compute uniformly across the whole reasoning trace. This is inefficient because many tokens are easy and don’t need additional exploration. Empirically, reasoning failures often show an early drop in model confidence before an explicit error appears, suggesting that we could detect and focus on these ‘uncertainty bottlenecks’. The paper aims to exploit this structure to get more benefit from the same or less compute.

Method: The authors propose DeepLook, a training-free ‘monitor-and-intervene’ decoding framework. During generation, DeepLook monitors token-level confidence and aggregates it into segment-level confidence scores. It tracks recent confidence history and triggers an intervention when current confidence drops significantly, signaling uncertainty. At each trigger point, it performs fixed-horizon lookahead: it rolls out multiple candidate continuations (branches) for a limited number of steps. Each branch is scored using Average Lookahead Confidence (ALC), defined as the average segment-level confidence over its lookahead continuation. Low-ALC branches are pruned; the remaining branches are combined via voting to decide which continuation to follow. This process selectively applies extra compute only at detected uncertainty points, without modifying the base model or requiring extra training.

Result: On four competition-style math benchmarks and four LLM backbones (DeepSeek-R1-8B, Qwen3-32B, GPT-OSS-20B, GPT-OSS-120B), DeepLook consistently improves the accuracy–token-cost Pareto frontier relative to a strong inference-time baseline (DeepConf-low). It improves accuracy in 11 out of 16 model–benchmark settings while cutting dataset-level token generation by an average of 87.3%. Notable gains include +3.1 accuracy on AIME25 with Qwen3-32B and +8.8 on BRUMO25 with GPT-OSS-20B, achieved despite large reductions in generated tokens.

Conclusion: Selective, uncertainty-triggered lookahead is more effective than uniformly scaling complete reasoning trajectories. By monitoring confidence, intervening only when confidence drops, and ranking candidate branches with Average Lookahead Confidence, DeepLook delivers substantially better accuracy–cost trade-offs without any additional training. This demonstrates that future-aware, targeted inference-time computation can push LLM reasoning performance more efficiently than naive inference-time scaling.

Abstract: Inference-time scaling has emerged as a powerful paradigm for improving large language model reasoning, often delivering larger gains on difficult reasoning tasks than parameter scaling alone. However, existing approaches remain inefficient in how compute is allocated within a reasoning trace. Motivated by the observation that reasoning failures often exhibit an early onset of uncertainty before a wrong answer become explicit, we introduce DeepLook, a training-free monitor-and-intervene decoding framework that concentrates lookahead compute at uncertainty bottlenecks. DeepLook aggregates token-level confidence into segment-level signals, triggers when confidence drops relative to recent history, and explores candidate continuations with fixed-horizon lookahead. Branches are ranked by Average Lookahead Confidence (ALC), the average segment-level confidence over rollout continuations, then pruned and aggregated through voting. On four competition-style mathematics benchmarks across DeepSeek-R1-8B, Qwen3-32B, GPT-OSS-20B, and GPT-OSS-120B, DeepLook shifts the accuracy--token-cost Pareto frontier: it improves accuracy over DeepConf-low in 11 of 16 settings while reducing dataset-level token generation by 87.3% on average, including gains of +3.1 on AIME25 with Qwen3-32B and +8.8 on BRUMO25 with GPT-OSS-20B. These results show that selective, future-aware intervention yields substantially stronger accuracy--cost trade-offs than uniformly scaling complete reasoning trajectories. Code is available here.

</details>


### [117] [Group Preference Collapse in Personalized Multimodal Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22603)
*Fan Lyu,Wenqi Zhang,Joost van de Weijer*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces PrefMoE, a framework to prevent 'group preference collapse' in personalized multimodal LLMs so they remain sensitive to each individual’s preferences instead of defaulting to majority choices.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing personalized multimodal LLMs mostly use coarse, profile-level information and fail to capture fine-grained, diverse user preferences. When trained on multiple users, models tend to ignore weaker or minority preference signals and converge to dominant, population-level behaviors, causing 'group preference collapse.' The authors aim to diagnose this phenomenon and design a method to preserve and utilize individualized preference information during generation.

Method: The authors propose PrefMoE, a preference-centric architecture that explicitly disentangles user information into (1) stable profile features and (2) preference-related representations. Within the preference space, PrefMoE decomposes each user’s preferences into shared prototypes (capturing common patterns) and personalized residuals (user-specific deviations). To keep these residuals informative and robust, they use three techniques: (a) imbalance-aware learning to handle skewed preference distributions and prevent minority preferences from being overwhelmed; (b) counterfactual pseudo-user augmentation to synthetically generate users with varied preference combinations, strengthening the model’s ability to recognize and use preference signals; and (c) residual decorrelation to reduce redundancy and interference between residual components. For adaptation, PrefMoE routes profile and preference factors through separate LoRA paths, effectively creating a mixture-of-experts–like mechanism specialized for different aspects of personalization.

Result: On multiple multimodal LLM backbones and personalization benchmarks, PrefMoE yields stronger preference-sensitive personalization, meaning it follows individual user preferences more accurately and consistently. It also empirically shows much lower levels of group preference collapse—models remain responsive to non-dominant and minority preferences instead of defaulting to majority patterns—while maintaining or improving overall response quality.

Conclusion: Separating stable profile information from fine-grained preference signals and explicitly modeling preferences via shared prototypes plus personalized residuals is an effective way to combat group preference collapse in personalized MLLMs. By preserving individualized residuals with specialized training (imbalance-aware learning, pseudo-user augmentation, and decorrelation) and using separate LoRA routes for profiles vs. preferences, PrefMoE improves the fidelity and robustness of user-specific generation across different model backbones.

Abstract: Personalized multimodal large language models (MLLMs) aim to generate user-specific responses, but existing methods mainly rely on profile-level information and overlook diverse user preferences. We identify group preference collapse, where multi-user personalized MLLMs become insensitive to individual preferences and drift toward dominant population-level choices due to suppressed preference signals and unreliable preference use during generation. We propose PrefMoE, a preference-centric framework that separates stable profile information from preference-related representations. PrefMoE decomposes preferences into shared prototypes and personalized residuals, preserves individualized residuals with imbalance-aware learning, counterfactual pseudo-user augmentation, and residual decorrelation, and routes profile and preference factors through separate LoRA adaptation paths. Experiments across multiple MLLM backbones show that PrefMoE improves preference-sensitive personalization while substantially reducing preference collapse. Project page: https://prefmoe.github.io/.

</details>


### [118] [Evaluating LLMs as Interpretable Controllers for Dynamical Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22609)
*Aleksander Østensen,Alberto Mino Calero,Anastasios M. Lekkas,Adil Rasheed*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper evaluates whether large language models can serve as interpretable controllers for a thermal environment, finding that sufficiently large, tool-augmented LLMs can track temperature setpoints, use actuators efficiently, and explain their decisions coherently.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While LLMs are widely used for reasoning and decision-making, their application as direct controllers of physical systems is underexplored. Traditional controllers (e.g., PID, MPC) are effective but opaque to non-experts and hard to align with rich, natural-language objectives. The authors want to know if LLMs can bridge this gap by acting as controllers that both manage dynamics and provide human-understandable rationales, especially under constraints like energy penalties and complex actuator interactions.

Method: The authors set up a dynamic thermal environment with actuators (heater, fan) and define tasks such as following temperature setpoints and responding to natural-language commands. They test five LLMs of different sizes as controllers across scenarios: (1) pure tracking, (2) tracking under penalties on actuator usage, and (3) tracking with access to a physics-based prediction tool. They log actions, temperature evolution, and model-generated explanations, and construct a reasoning taxonomy to characterize how models understand actuator dynamics and temporal causality.

Result: Control quality strongly correlates with model scale. Smaller and mid-sized LLMs often misinterpret how actuators affect temperature, issue unstable or inconsistent control signals, and produce incoherent explanations. Larger models (e.g., Qwen-3 14B and GPT-4o) achieve accurate temperature tracking, maintain stable actuator usage, and give explanations consistent with physical laws. When a physics-based prediction tool is available, the controllers exhibit smoother control trajectories, better energy efficiency, and more anticipatory decisions.

Conclusion: Sufficiently capable LLMs can function as interpretable controllers for physical systems like thermal environments, especially when grounded with domain knowledge through tools. There is a clear reasoning progression from smaller to larger models, moving from causal confusion to temporally aware, physically grounded reasoning. This suggests a promising direction for hybrid control architectures that pair model-based prediction with language-driven decision layers capable of generating human-legible explanations.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used for decision-making and reasoning tasks, yet their potential as controllers for physical systems remains largely unexplored. This work investigates whether LLMs can function as interpretable controllers for a dynamic thermal environment, examining their ability to follow setpoints, interpret natural-language commands, reason about actuator effects, and incorporate prior model-based knowledge. Five LLMs of varying scales are evaluated under multiple scenarios, including settings with penalties on heater or fan usage and cases where the models have access to a physics-based prediction tool. The results show that control performance depends on model complexity: while low- and mid-scale models frequently misinterpret actuator dynamics or generate inconsistent reasoning, high-complexity models such as Qwen-3~14B and GPT-4o achieve accurate temperature tracking, stable actuator usage, and coherent explanations aligned with physical principles. Incorporating a physics-based model significantly improves control smoothness and energy efficiency by enabling anticipatory decision-making. A detailed reasoning taxonomy further reveals a clear progression from causal misinterpretation in smaller models to cohesive and temporally aware reasoning in larger ones. The findings demonstrate that LLMs can act as interpretable controllers when sufficiently capable and appropriately grounded in domain knowledge, highlighting promising opportunities for hybrid model-based and language-driven control strategies that can provide plausible explanations.

</details>


### [119] [Tokengeist: Multi-Turn Attribution Tracing in Agentic Conversations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22610)
*Jessica Tang,Shraddha Barke,Sharad Agarwal*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces Multi-Turn Context Attribution (MTCA) and a framework called Tokengeist to trace how tokens in a language model’s multi-turn response depend on tokens in previous turns, revealing deep, multi-hop provenance paths that standard, single-pass attribution methods miss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing context attribution methods treat the entire dialogue context in a single pass and only capture shallow, surface-level dependencies. They fail to explain how information and reasoning propagate across multiple turns in real-world conversations, especially when responses depend on chains of earlier context. The authors want a principled way to reconstruct these layered, multi-hop dependency structures and to evaluate attribution methods on this capability.

Method: They define the MTCA task: starting from a target text span in a model’s response, recursively trace back which previous turns influenced it and how those turns themselves depended on even earlier context. They propose Tokengeist, a general, attribution-method-agnostic framework that represents a conversation as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) over turns and recovers full dependency paths by recursively traversing this DAG, instead of doing one flat attribution pass. They also build MTCABench, a benchmark of 3,845 annotated target spans across 665 multi-turn conversations, each with gold provenance graphs up to depth 14, covering four types of dependency.

Result: On four open-weight language models, standard flat attribution methods achieve less than 20% source recall on multi-hop dependencies in MTCABench, indicating they largely miss the true provenance paths. Tokengeist, in contrast, achieves around 90% source recall, demonstrating that recursive, graph-based attribution can reliably recover deep, multi-turn dependency structures.

Conclusion: Single-pass, flat context attribution is inadequate for explaining model behavior in multi-turn dialogues, as it suffers from "provenance collapse"—a failure to capture multi-hop, layered dependencies. Recursive, DAG-based approaches like Tokengeist are far more effective at reconstructing full provenance paths, and benchmarks such as MTCABench are necessary to drive the development and evaluation of such multi-turn attribution methods.

Abstract: When a language model produces a response in a multi-turn conversation, which tokens from prior turns shaped that answer, and how did those dependencies propagate across prior turns? Existing context attribution methods process the full context in a single pass, recovering surface-level dependencies but missing the layered, non-linear structure of real-world dialogues and multi-step reasoning tasks. We introduce multi-turn context attribution (MTCA): given a target span in a model response, the task of tracing attribution backward across turns to identify not only which prior turns were directly relevant, but also how those turns themselves depended on earlier context. We propose Tokengeist, an attribution-method-agnostic and scalable framework that recovers full dependency paths by casting attribution as a recursive traversal of a directed acyclic graph (DAG) over conversation turns. We will release MTCABench, a benchmark of 3,845 target spans across 665 multi-turn conversations, annotated with gold provenance graphs reaching depths of up to 14, across four dependency types. Across four open-weight models, flat attribution methods fail to recover multi-hop dependencies, achieving under 20% source recall, while Tokengeist reaches 90%. Our results reveal systematic failure modes of single-pass attribution -- which we term provenance collapse -- and motivate attribution methods that reason recursively across turns.

</details>


### [120] [Decentralized Granular Access Control for Agentic AI Systems in Critical Infrastructure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22611)
*Arun Malik,Deepal Jayasinghe,Bradley Klemick,Prachi Shah,Nitish Talasu,Vineet Tushar Trivedi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces and deploys a decentralized, multi-layered access control architecture tailored for autonomous AI agents managing critical cloud infrastructure, achieving fine-grained control with no unauthorized writes over eight months in production.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional RBAC and trust models assume deterministic, human-initiated actions and thus fail to adequately secure stochastic, autonomous AI agents that operate continuously and may take complex, non-obvious actions on critical systems. As AI agents are introduced into production cloud and network operations, there is a need for a security architecture that can constrain their behavior, prevent privilege escalation, and align their actions with delegated human authority while addressing emerging threats cataloged for LLM applications.

Method: Design and implementation of a decentralized, multi-layered access control framework for agentic AI in cloud infrastructure. The framework includes: (1) a compound identity model binding each agent action to a human delegator; (2) a hierarchical permission model with five levels of granularity, down to per-parameter constraints; (3) decentralized policy ownership where each tool or service team manages its own authorization boundaries; and (4) progressive trust escalation with safety interlocks that gate high-risk operations. The design is mapped explicitly to the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025) threat taxonomy, and evaluated through real-world deployment metrics.

Result: In production at a major cloud provider managing network infrastructure across hundreds of data centers, the system secures more than 20 specialized AI agents and over 60 deterministic playbooks. It processes thousands of operations daily while reporting zero unauthorized write operations over an eight-month period. The authors provide empirical statistics on how access is used in practice, the rate and patterns of access denials, and show that layered authorization effectively blocks privilege escalation attempts by non-deterministic AI actors.

Conclusion: A traditional RBAC-centric approach is inadequate for securing autonomous AI agents in critical infrastructure. A decentralized, multi-layered access control architecture tailored to agentic behavior can provide fine-grained, context-aware control and strong safety guarantees. The presented framework, grounded in a modern LLM threat taxonomy and validated at cloud scale, demonstrates that it is possible to integrate powerful autonomous agents into production operations while maintaining strict security and preventing unauthorized high-risk actions.

Abstract: The deployment of autonomous AI agents in production infrastructure introduces fundamental security challenges that traditional role-based access control (RBAC) models cannot address. Unlike deterministic automation, AI agents exhibit stochastic behavior, making conventional trust models insufficient for governing their access to critical systems. This paper presents a decentralized, multi-layered access control architecture designed specifically for agentic AI systems operating in critical cloud infrastructure. Our framework introduces four key innovations: (1) a compound identity model that binds agent actions to delegated human authority, (2) a hierarchical permission system spanning five granularity levels from global platform access to per-parameter constraints, (3) a decentralized policy ownership model where tool teams independently govern their authorization boundaries, and (4) progressive trust escalation with safety interlocks that prevent autonomous agents from executing high-risk operations. We ground our design in the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025) threat taxonomy and demonstrate how each architectural decision mitigates specific attack vectors. Deployed in production at a major cloud provider managing network infrastructure across hundreds of datacenters, the system enforces granular access control for 20+ specialized AI agents and 60+ deterministic playbooks processing thousands of operations daily while maintaining zero unauthorized write operations over eight months of production deployment. We present empirical data on access pattern distributions, denial rates, and the effectiveness of layered authorization in preventing privilege escalation by non-deterministic actors.

</details>


### [121] [DynaResize: Runtime GPU Reallocation for Disaggregated LLM Post-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22614)
*Hanlin Du,Zhiyuan Yan,Haiquan Chen,Jiarui Fang,Yungang Bao,Sa wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DynaResize is a runtime GPU reallocation system that dynamically balances rollout and training GPUs in RL-based LLM post-training to remove pipeline bubbles and boost throughput.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In RL-based LLM post-training, rollout and training are often run on separate GPU pools. Because rollout latencies have a long-tail distribution, any static partitioning of GPUs between these stages leads to severe pipeline bubbles and low utilization, limiting end-to-end throughput even if the static split is tuned. A dynamic mechanism is needed to rebalance GPU resources across stages without changing RL semantics.

Method: DynaResize is a runtime system that dynamically reallocates GPUs between Rollout and Training. It decomposes resizing into fine-grained operations so GPUs can change roles with minimal interruption. It shortens the critical path of role switching via three main techniques: communicator reuse to avoid expensive reinitialization of communication primitives, bounded state staging so only necessary state is transferred during resizing, and hysteresis-based resizing policies to avoid frequent oscillations and to stabilize decisions.

Result: Experiments show that DynaResize improves end-to-end throughput by 66.5% and reduces total execution time by 33% compared to the best possible static GPU configuration. It also hides 27% of the role-switching overhead, demonstrating that its design substantially mitigates the performance penalties of dynamic resizing.

Conclusion: Dynamic GPU reallocation between rollout and training in RL-based LLM post-training can significantly outperform even optimally tuned static partitions.
