By structuring resizing as fine-grained operations and optimizing the critical path with communicator reuse, bounded state staging, and hysteresis-based control, DynaResize reduces pipeline bubbles and achieves large gains in throughput and total runtime without changing RL semantics.

Abstract: RL-based LLM post-training increasingly disaggregates Rollout and Training across separate GPU resources, but static GPU partitioning suffers from severe pipeline bubbles under long-tail rollout latency. We present DynaResize, a runtime GPU reallocation system that dynamically switches GPUs between Rollout and Training to balance stage execution times without changing RL semantics. DynaResize decomposes resizing into fine-grained operations and removes non-startup-critical work from the critical path through communicator reuse, bounded state staging, and hysteresis-based resizing. Experimental results show that DynaResize can improve end-to-end throughput by 66.5% and reduce total execution time by 33% over the optimal static configuration, while hiding 27% of role-switching overhead.

</details>


### [122] [Opti-Q: A Constraint-Based Optimization Framework for Multi-LLM Question Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22621)
*Aamir Hamid,Bharg Barot,Satvik Racharla,Tim Finin,Primal Pappachan,Roberto Yus*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OPTI-Q is a cost-based optimizer that orchestrates multiple LLMs to maximize answer quality under budgets for money, latency, and energy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deploying LLM-based QA in practice is hard because models are nondeterministic, have different cost/latency/energy profiles, and users often have strict resource budgets. Existing systems typically use fixed pipelines or heuristics and fail to adapt per-question or to jointly optimize quality and multiple resource constraints. The paper aims to bring principled, database-style query optimization to multi-LLM orchestration so that each question is answered with the best possible quality given user-specified budgets.

Method: The authors design OPTI-Q, which treats LLM calls as physical operators in a DAG (e.g., sequential calls that pass intermediate answers as context, and parallel/blend calls that run multiple models and merge their outputs). For each question, OPTI-Q searches over possible execution plans using a cost-based optimizer that relies on PERFDB, a statistics catalog built from benchmarks and execution traces. PERFDB stores estimates of answer quality (QoA) and resource usage (cost, latency, energy) for operators and subplans. Using these estimates, OPTI-Q performs a Pareto-frontier search over the plan space, then selects a plan according to user preferences and constraints on resources.

Result: On MMLU-Pro and SimpleQA benchmarks with user-specified resource budgets, OPTI-Q achieves substantially higher answer quality than baselines while maintaining comparable cost. The abstract reports average QoA improvements of about 58% on MMLU-Pro and 41% on SimpleQA relative to baselines at similar resource usage, showing that principled planning outperforms naive or static orchestration strategies.

Conclusion: Database-style, cost-based optimization is effective for orchestrating multiple LLMs in QA settings under multi-dimensional resource constraints. By modeling LLM calls as operators, estimating their quality and costs via a statistics catalog, and searching the Pareto frontier of plans, OPTI-Q can significantly improve quality-resource trade-offs. This suggests that future LLM systems should incorporate plan-before-execute optimizers rather than fixed pipelines, especially in budgeted or production deployments.

Abstract: While large language models (LLMs) enable strong question answering (QA), budgeted deployment is complicated by nondeterminism and heterogeneous resource profiles (cost, latency, and energy). We present OPTI-Q, a database-inspired, cost-based optimizer that implements a plan-before-execute paradigm for multi-LLM orchestration. OPTI-Q models LLM invocations as physical operators in an execution DAG and, for each question, searches for plans that optimize answer quality (QoA) while trading off financial cost, latency, and energy under user-specified resource constraints. Plans can include sequential operators that pass intermediate answers as context and parallel/blend operators that run models concurrently and merge their outputs. To search this space without executing each candidate plan, OPTI-Q uses PERFDB, a statistics catalog populated and refreshed from benchmarks and execution traces, to estimate the QoA and resource costs of both individual operators and composed subplans. Using these estimates, OPTI-Q performs Pareto-frontier search and selects a final plan based on user preferences. On MMLU-Pro and SimpleQA under user-specified budgets, OPTI-Q improves average QoA by ~58% and ~41% over baselines at comparable cost, demonstrating that database-style planning yields better quality-resource trade-offs for multi-LLM QA.

</details>


### [123] [CHS-SQL: A Text-to-SQL approach based on Confidence-Guided Heuristic Search Schema Linking process](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22624)
*Minghao Yang,Yanjun Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes CHS-SQL, a framework for fine-tuning small language models (SLMs) on Text-to-SQL that optimizes schema linking via a precision–recall–aware heuristic search and model confidence, achieving SOTA SLM results.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Text-to-SQL methods with small language models can approach large-model performance but mainly improve accuracy by filtering redundant schema elements. They usually treat schema selection as a one-sided filtering problem and ignore the precision–recall trade-off in schema linking. The authors observe that both high precision and high recall in schema linking are crucial for final SQL accuracy, and that current methods often either include too much noise (low precision) or miss necessary schema elements (low recall). This gap motivates a more principled schema selection mechanism tailored for SLM fine-tuning under limited compute and data-security constraints.

Method: They introduce CHS-SQL, a fine-tuning framework for SLMs on Text-to-SQL. The key idea is a new schema linking mechanism that treats schema selection as a precision–recall optimization problem. It uses a heuristic search over candidate tables and columns guided by the model’s internal confidence scores. This search aims to pick a subset of schema elements with an optimal balance of precision and recall—maximizing relevant elements while suppressing irrelevant ones. The same heuristic and confidence-guided selection strategy is also applied during SQL generation, where multiple candidate SQLs are refined and filtered to avoid local optima and reduce error propagation. All of this is designed to run efficiently on a single RTX 4090 GPU.

Result: CHS-SQL attains state-of-the-art performance among methods based on small language models for Text-to-SQL benchmarks. It improves final SQL accuracy by better aligning schema-linking precision and recall, outperforming prior SLM-based approaches that use simpler schema filtering or linking heuristics, all while remaining computationally efficient and preserving data security benefits.

Conclusion: Balancing precision and recall in schema linking is critical for Text-to-SQL performance, especially when using SLMs. By combining heuristic search with model-internal confidence to optimize this balance, CHS-SQL can significantly improve SQL generation accuracy and reach SOTA results within the SLM regime on modest hardware. The approach shows that smarter schema selection and generation-time refinement can partially close the gap between small and large models without increasing computational requirements.

Abstract: Recently, there have been several works in the Text-to-SQL domain that utilize Small Language Models (SLMs) for training. These approaches achieve performance close to that of large models in generating SQL, using only the computational power of a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU, while also ensuring data security. Most existing methods filter out redundant tables and columns during Schema Linking to improve Text-to-SQL accuracy. However, they do not consider the precision-recall trade-off when selecting the candidate schema subset. Our research found that both the precision and recall of Schema Linking directly affect the final SQL accuracy. Therefore, we propose a novel framework for efficiently fine-tuning SLMs on Text-to-SQL tasks, CHS-SQL, that not only balances precision and recall but also improves overall performance on Text-to-SQL tasks. Its main innovation lies in the Schema Linking phase, where a heuristic search combined with model internal confidence is employed to achieve an optimal precision-recall trade-off. This elaborated mechanism maximizes the precision of relevant schema candidates for the generated SQL queries while suppressing irrelevant noise. The same strategy is further applied during SQL generation to refine candidate queries while helping the SLM to avoid trapping in a local optimum. Our method achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) results on Text-to-SQL tasks via SLMs.

</details>


### [124] [TokenMem: Faithful Knowledge Injection for Frozen LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22625)
*Chengzhang Yu,Chenyang Zheng,Zening Lu,Yingru He,Yutong Huang,Yiming Zhang,Yue Xu,Zhanpeng Jin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TokenMem is a lightweight memory module that feeds retrieved knowledge into frozen LLMs via a separate cross‑attention channel, greatly improving their ability to follow external knowledge even when it conflicts with parametric memory.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard RAG makes retrieved documents and the model’s internal (parametric) knowledge compete in the same self‑attention pathway, leading to unstable or incorrect behavior when they disagree. The authors want a way to integrate external knowledge that avoids this competition and yields predictable, controllable use of retrieved information, especially in counterfactual or conflicting settings.

Method: They introduce TokenMem, which adds a dedicated cross‑attention channel plus a small gating adapter (3–7M parameters) to a frozen base LLM. Training uses a two‑phase curriculum: (1) teach the gate how to generally utilize retrieved knowledge, and (2) specifically train it to obey retrieved, possibly counterfactual knowledge over the model’s parametric memory. Only the gating adapter is trained; the base model stays frozen. They evaluate TokenMem across several LLM families and perform ablations and mechanistic analyses of the learned gating behavior.

Result: Across five models (Qwen3-4B/8B/14B, LLaMA-3.1-8B, OLMo-3-7B), TokenMem reaches 69–70% Knowledge Compliance on counterfactual benchmarks, versus 20–52% for standard RAG, giving improvements up to 49 percentage points. Removing the second curriculum phase causes Knowledge Compliance to drop to nearly zero. Mechanistic probes show that the adapter learns to inject retrieved knowledge in a conflict-aware and layer‑specific way despite the lack of explicit supervision on when or where to inject.

Conclusion: Separating retrieved knowledge from parametric memory via a dedicated cross‑attention channel and training only a small gating adapter enables frozen LLMs to follow external knowledge far more reliably in conflicting scenarios. The two‑phase curriculum is essential, and the learned gate naturally develops a nuanced, layer‑dependent conflict-resolution strategy. This architecture offers a more robust alternative to vanilla RAG for counterfactual and knowledge‑conflict settings.

Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enhances large language models (LLMs) with external knowledge, but suffers from knowledge conflicts: when retrieved information contradicts parametric memory, the shared self-attention pathway produces unpredictable outputs. We present TokenMem, a lightweight memory system that injects knowledge into frozen LLMs through a dedicated cross-attention channel, bypassing competition with parametric memory in the residual stream. TokenMem trains only a thin gating adapter ($\sim$3-7M parameters) via a two-phase curriculum: first learning general knowledge utilization, then strengthening faithful compliance under counterfactual knowledge. In controlled experiments on five models spanning three families (Qwen3-4B/8B/14B, LLaMA-3.1-8B, OLMo-3-7B), TokenMem achieves 69-70% Knowledge Compliance (KC) on counterfactual benchmarks, compared to 20-52% for vanilla RAG, a gap of up to 49 percentage points. Ablation studies show that the two-phase curriculum is critical: removing Phase 2 collapses KC to near-zero. Mechanistic analysis reveals that the gate adapter learns a conflict-aware, layer-specific injection strategy without explicit supervision.

</details>


### [125] [Masked Distillation: Internalizing the Chain-of-Thought in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22629)
*Durgesh Kalwar,Vardhan Palod,Subbarao Kambhampati*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a training method to turn long chain-of-thought reasoning done at inference into internalized knowledge in the model parameters, allowing shorter or no reasoning traces while keeping accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large Reasoning Models rely on long, explicit chains of thought at inference, which are expensive in latency, memory, and cost. Moreover, correctness of the final answer is not tightly linked to the correctness or length of the reasoning trace. The authors want to know if the computation currently performed in these long intermediate traces can instead be internalized into the model’s parameters so that it can answer directly or with much shorter traces, reducing serving costs while maintaining performance.

Method: They introduce masked distillation, a knowledge distillation framework where a student language model is trained to predict only the final solution tokens, while a reasoning teacher has access to both the question and its own chain-of-thought (CoT) trace. The student learns from teacher feedback on the student’s outputs without directly seeing the full CoT. They explore two setups: (1) self-distillation, where one model acts as both teacher (with CoT) and student (without CoT) in different modes; and (2) dual-model distillation, where a larger reasoning teacher supervises a smaller non-thinking student. They also vary how many intermediate tokens the student is supervised on, treating the teacher’s CoT as a scaffold, and interpolate between full internalization (student produces only answers) and no internalization (student reproduces full traces plus answers).

Result: In controlled experiments on GSM8K (grade-school math word problems) and the Countdown number puzzle task, the masked distillation framework successfully trains students that can solve problems while emitting fewer intermediate reasoning tokens. This shows that much of the computation expressed in explicit chains-of-thought can be transferred into the student’s parameters, reducing dependence on long traces. Performance is benchmarked across different degrees of scaffolding to characterize the trade-offs between trace length and accuracy.

Conclusion: Masked distillation is an effective way to compress explicit reasoning traces into a model’s parameters, enabling shorter or even trace-free inference with comparable performance. By using reasoning teachers (either the same model in thinking mode or a larger model) and treating CoT as a scaffold over solution tokens, the approach offers a principled way to trade off interpretability and token cost against efficiency and accuracy in reasoning tasks.

Abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) produce long, explicit chains of intermediate steps before generating a final answer at inference time. These intermediate traces dominate latency, memory usage, and serving cost, even though the final answer correctness is not causally related to the trace correctness and the trace length is not a reliable indicator of the problem complexity. This raises a natural question: can the computation expressed in these intermediate tokens be internalized into the parameters of a language model, enabling it to produce answers directly (or with much shorter intermediate traces)? We introduce \textit{masked distillation}, a knowledge-distillation framework in which a student LLM is trained to predict only the solution tokens conditioned on the question, while a reasoning teacher provides feedback on the student's responses after conditioning on the question and its own CoT trace. We instantiate this framework in two settings: (i) a \textit{self-distillation} setting, in which the same model serves as the teacher in thinking mode and as the student in non-thinking mode, and (ii) a \textit{dual-model} setting, in which a larger reasoning teacher supervises a separate smaller non-thinking student over the solution tokens. By treating intermediate tokens as a scaffold which reasoning models use to fit over the solution tokens, We additionally vary the length of intermediate-token scaffolding the student is supervised on, interpolating between full internalization (the student emits only the solution) and no internalization (the student emits the full trace before the answer). We evaluate the framework through controlled experiments on two reasoning domains: GSM8K (grade-school arithmetic) and Countdown (a number-puzzle search task).

</details>


### [126] [VlogReward: Learning Multi-Dimensional Evaluation for Vlog Editing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22632)
*Yexiang Liu,Wen Zhong,Sijie Zhu,Xin Gu,Fan Chen,Junxian Duan,Jie Cao,Longyin Wen,Zhenfang Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a standardized framework, dataset, benchmark, and reward model (VlogReward) for automatically evaluating and improving vlog editing quality across six key dimensions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vlog editing quality is important but hard to assess automatically because it is subjective and lacks standardized criteria, public datasets, benchmarks, and effective reward models for training agents or assistants. Existing multimodal LLMs are not well aligned to nuanced vlog editing quality, limiting their usefulness for creators and automated editing systems.

Method: 1) Work with professional vlog creators and product managers to define a six-dimension evaluation taxonomy: Creativity, Consistency, Concept Design, Cinematography, Narration, and Pacing. 2) Build a large-scale dataset of 100k vlog edits plus a benchmark, VRMBench, for testing the reward capabilities of multimodal LLMs. 3) Propose VlogReward, a reward model that outputs fine-grained multi-dimensional scores and textual feedback for iterative refinement. 4) Improve the Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) training framework by adding an adjustable inter-group comparison reward to reduce "direction blindness" and better separate high- and low-quality edits.

Result: VlogReward, trained with the improved GRPO framework and the curated dataset, achieves state-of-the-art performance on VRMBench and surpasses strong multimodal LLM baselines such as GPT-5 and Gemini-3-Pro in assessing vlog edits and providing guidance for improvement.

Conclusion: A principled framework, large-scale data resource, dedicated benchmark, and enhanced GRPO-based reward model can significantly improve automatic vlog evaluation. VlogReward demonstrates that specialized reward models tailored to creator-centric criteria can outperform general-purpose MLLMs and support iterative refinement of vlog editing plans, helping both human creators and future automated editing systems.

Abstract: The rapid rise of vlogs as a personalized storytelling medium has created a demand for automated systems to evaluate and refine vlog editing plans. However, vlog assessment is highly subjective and remains challenging due to a lack of standardized criteria, dataset and benchmark, and effective reward models. To address these challenges, we define a comprehensive vlog evaluation framework guided by professional vlog creators and product managers, establishing a taxonomy of six key dimensions, i.e., Creativity, Consistency, Concept Design, Cinematography, Narration, and Pacing. Subsequently, we curate a large-scale dataset of 100k vlog edits and a dedicated benchmark, VRMBench, to evaluate the vlog rewarding capabilities of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Finally, we present VlogReward, a robust vlog reward model that can provide both fine-grained multi-dimensional scores and actionable feedback for iterative refinement. Technically, we enhance the Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) framework by introducing an adjustable inter-group comparison reward, which mitigates the "direction blindness" issue of standard GRPO and enables the model to better distinguish varied-quality edits. VlogReward achieves state-of-the-art results that significantly outperform existing MLLMs, including GPT-5 and Gemini-3-Pro. We hope that our study can help vlog creators and foster automated vlog evaluation and refinement systems.

</details>


### [127] [Evolving from Lessons: Skill-Augmented Table Graph Reasoning for Operation-wise Table Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22633)
*Guixin Su,Qiankun Pi,Mayi Xu,Wenli Li,Ming Zhong,Yuanyuan Zhu,Jiawei Jiang,Tieyun Qian*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces an operation-wise evaluation and a new framework, SkillTGR, for table question answering, improving complex reasoning with structured table graphs and learned reusable skills.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing TableQA work treats all questions uniformly and uses only overall accuracy, which hides the large gap between how well LLMs handle simple lookup questions versus complex operations like aggregation and arithmetic. Furthermore, current models linearize tables into text, breaking the natural table structure and worsening cross-row reasoning, and they generally reason from scratch each time without reusing common reasoning patterns.

Method: The authors define an Operation-wise TableQA task with a fine-grained taxonomy of question types and build two benchmark datasets (WikiTQ-ow and TabFact-ow). They propose SkillTGR, which represents tables as attributed graphs capturing row, column, and cell relationships. LLMs are used to plan and execute dynamic reasoning chains that select evidence subgraphs and perform graph traversal reasoning. On top of this, SkillTGR maintains a hierarchical SkillBank that abstracts past reasoning trajectories into reusable skills guided by cognitive heuristics. During inference, it retrieves both successful and failed skills for contrastive, skill-augmented reasoning, enabling continual self-improvement.

Result: SkillTGR outperforms existing TableQA methods with an average gain of 5.91% in overall accuracy and 6.03% in operation-wise performance across benchmarks. It also substantially improves efficiency by cutting token usage by 19.76% and reducing inference latency by 27.64%.

Conclusion: Operation-wise evaluation reveals that LLM-based TableQA systems struggle disproportionately with complex reasoning operations. By modeling tables as graphs and building a reusable hierarchical SkillBank of reasoning patterns, SkillTGR provides more accurate and efficient structured reasoning, leading to consistent performance improvements across different operation types while also lowering computational costs.

Abstract: Table Question Answering (TableQA) aims to reason over tables to answer user queries. Existing research treats all questions uniformly and evaluates solely through overall accuracy, obscuring a critical reality that LLMs excel at simple lookups yet struggle with complex operations like aggregation and arithmetic. To reveal this disparity, we introduce a novel \emph{Operation-wise TableQA} task with a fine-grained question taxonomy and release two datasets named WikiTQ-ow and TabFact-ow for evaluation. As for modeling bottlenecks, existing methods flatten tables into linearized texts, disrupting inherent structures and inducing the ``lost-in-the-middle'' issue, which poses a primary barrier to complex cross-row reasoning. Moreover, they typically reason from scratch, neglecting reusable patterns shared across similar operations. To address these limitations, we propose a Skill-augmented Table Graph Reasoning (SkillTGR) framework for self-evolving structured reasoning. Specifically, SkillTGR represents tables as attributed graphs with explicit row-column-cell structures, where LLMs plan and execute dynamic chains to retrieve evidence subgraphs for graph traversal reasoning. Based on this, SkillTGR builds a hierarchical SkillBank to distill reason trajectories into abstract skills under cognitive heuristics, then hybrid retrieves both successful and failed skills for contrastive augmented table graph reasoning, thereby enabling the continual self-evolution. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SkillTGR achieves superior performance with an average of 5.91\% overall and 6.03\% operation-wise improvement, also reducing 19.76\% token consumption and 27.64\% inference latency. Our codes and data will be released upon publication.

</details>


### [128] [PRESTO: Prefix-Aligned Tree Drafting for Diffusion Speculative Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22634)
*Zheng Wang,Zhifan Ye,Qi Cheng,Yonggan Fu,Ziyan Wang,Feng Zhu,Haozhe Zhao,Jan Kautz,Pavlo Molchanov,Humphrey Shi,Minjia Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose PRESTO, a tree-based speculative decoding framework tailored for diffusion LLMs that better exploits their multi-candidate outputs and aligns draft scoring with autoregressive verification, yielding notable speedups.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion LLMs can generate many token candidates in parallel and are strong draft models for speculative decoding, but current methods use only simple linear drafting and ignore the rich combinatorial space of candidate paths. Moreover, naive tree-based use of diffusion LLMs is ineffective because diffusion token probabilities are not conditioned on prefixes the way autoregressive verifiers are, causing poor ranking and low acceptance lengths. There is a need for a drafting method that both exploits the multi-candidate structure and respects the prefix-based nature of AR verification, to improve decoding efficiency and throughput.

Method: They introduce PRESTO, a framework that applies tree-based drafting to diffusion LLMs while correcting the mismatch between diffusion marginals and prefix-based AR verification. PRESTO has two core ideas: (1) prefix-aligned scoring that redefines how candidate paths are ranked so that the scores better reflect their likelihood of being accepted by the AR verifier; and (2) a priority-based tree search strategy that expands and explores paths according to their estimated verification potential, rather than uniformly or naively. This yields a structured speculative decoding process where diffusion-generated multi-candidate tokens drive a search over a tree of possible continuations, guided by AR-compatible confidence scores.

Result: In experiments on state-of-the-art diffusion drafters and self-speculative diffusion LLMs across multiple benchmarks, PRESTO improves decoding efficiency. Specifically, it achieves up to an average 1.5× end-to-end throughput speedup over the strongest existing diffusion-based speculative decoding and about 1.12× speedup on self-speculative diffusion LLMs, indicating higher acceptance lengths and better utilization of the diffusion drafts.

Conclusion: PRESTO shows that diffusion LLMs can be more effectively used as draft models by moving from linear to tree-based speculative decoding and, crucially, by aligning draft scoring with the prefix-based behavior of autoregressive verifiers. By prioritizing candidate paths with high verification potential, PRESTO increases accepted token lengths and boosts throughput, demonstrating a practical path toward faster decoding with diffusion-based language models.

Abstract: Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive (AR) LLMs, generating tokens in parallel. This makes them effective draft models for speculative decoding (SD), producing an entire block of draft tokens in a single forward pass. Yet existing diffusion-based drafting methods rely on linear drafting, even though dLLMs emit multiple candidate tokens across positions, inducing a large combinatorial space of decoding paths. Consequently, they limit acceptance length and decoding efficiency. To exploit this multi-candidate structure, we apply tree-based drafting to diffusion drafters, enabling exploration of diverse candidate paths. However, we find that naive tree drafting is suboptimal: diffusion marginals are prefix-blind, mismatching the prefix-based AR verification and yielding unreliable path ranking. We propose PRESTO, a principled framework that extends tree-based drafting to diffusion drafters while resolving the fundamental mismatch between diffusion draft confidence and prefix-based AR verification through PREfix-aligned Scoring and priority-based Tree search for diffusion speculative decOding. The key principles behind PRESTO are that (1) candidate ranking should align with the prefix-based nature of AR verification, and (2) tree construction should prioritize candidate paths with high verification potential to maximize acceptance length. Extensive experiments show that PRESTO achieves up to an average of $1.5\times$ end-to-end throughput speedup on the state-of-the-art dedicated diffusion drafter SD and an average of $1.12\times$ on self-speculative diffusion LLMs across diverse benchmarks.

</details>


### [129] [CallBench: A Benchmark for Dual-Goal Coordination in Phone Call Assistants](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22635)
*Xuzhao Geng,Haozhao Wang,Xuelian Li,Zhenyu Yang,Haonan Lu,Rui Zhang,Ruixuan Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They build a Chinese benchmark, CallBench, to test phone call assistants that must juggle both the phone owner’s preset goals and the caller’s changing goals, and show current dialog systems perform poorly.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most target-oriented dialog systems assume a single, explicit user goal, but real phone assistants work as proxies: they must honor the device owner’s preset instructions while also reacting to a caller whose goal is implicit, dynamic, and sometimes conflicting. There was no large-scale benchmark to study and evaluate this dual-goal coordination problem, especially in realistic phone call scenarios.

Method: The authors construct CallBench, a large Chinese dataset of 50,000 full multi-turn phone call dialogues in six everyday scenarios (takeout, delivery, taxi, work, life, harassment). They design the data to cover different preset situations (regular preset, emergent preset, no preset) and different relationships between the phone owner’s and caller’s goals (aligned, complementary, irrelevant, conflicting). They also propose a preset-aware, turn-level evaluation protocol that scores dialog systems along multiple dimensions: semantic understanding, context usage, active guidance, response quality, compliance with presets, dialogue rhythm, and safety. They then run experiments with representative dialogue system methods on this benchmark.

Result: The constructed CallBench benchmark reflects diverse and realistic dual-goal situations in phone calls and supports fine-grained, turn-level evaluation. Experimental results show that existing dialogue approaches perform unsatisfactorily on many of the new metrics, particularly in reliably balancing the owner’s presets against the caller’s goals under proxy constraints.

Conclusion: Dual-goal coordination in phone call assistants is a substantially harder problem than traditional single-goal dialog, and current models are not yet adequate. CallBench provides a challenging, structured benchmark and evaluation protocol to drive research on assistants that can reason at each turn about two independent goals, follow the owner’s presets, and still manage effective conversations with callers.

Abstract: Target-oriented dialogue systems have demonstrated strong capabilities in completing user goals through interactive conversations. However, existing studies are primarily designed for single, explicit goal completion, while phone call assistants face a proxy setting that requires coordinating the device owner's explicit preset goal with the caller's implicit and dynamic goal. We introduce \textsc{CallBench}, a Chinese benchmark for evaluating dual-goal coordination in phone call assistants. \textsc{CallBench} contains 50,000 complete multi-turn phone call dialogues across six scenarios: takeout, delivery, taxi, work, life, and harassment. It covers regular presets, emergent presets, and no-preset cases, and includes diverse relations between owner-side and caller-side goals, such as alignment, complementarity, irrelevance, and conflict. We further design a preset-aware turn-level evaluation protocol covering semantic understanding, context use, active guidance, response quality, preset compliance, dialogue rhythm, and safety. Experiments on representative dialogue methods show that existing approaches still struggle with this task, highlighting the need for phone call assistants that can make reliable turn-level decisions between two independent goals under proxy constraints.

</details>


### [130] [Answering Path Queries under Linear and Guarded Existential Rules](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22636)
*Jean-François Baget,Meghyn Bienvenu,Marie-Laure Mugnier,Michaël Thomazo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies how hard it is, computationally, to answer expressive path queries over databases enriched with certain logical rules (ontologies), and precisely characterizes the complexity in several settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most existing work in ontology-mediated query answering focuses on simple conjunctive queries, but many applications need navigational queries that follow paths in graph-like data. There is a gap in understanding the complexity of answering such two-way regular path queries when the ontology is expressed as guarded existential rules. The authors aim to fill this gap and compare the cost of ontology-mediated path queries with both plain graph databases and standard conjunctive queries.

Method: The authors analyze ontology-mediated query answering where the ontology is a set of guarded existential rules, and the queries are two-way regular path queries and their conjunctive variants. They first restrict to linear existential rules and derive tight data and combined complexity bounds, leveraging known results for graph databases. For the more general guarded rules, they design a non-trivial reduction that transforms the problem into an equivalent one under linear rules, which lets them lift the linear-case complexity characterization to the guarded setting. They also distinguish between general and bounded-arity predicates to refine combined complexity results.

Result: For linear existential rules, answering two-way (conjunctive) regular path queries is NL-complete in data complexity, matching the complexity of answering regular path queries over plain graph databases. In combined complexity, under linear rules, RPQ and CRPQ answering are ExpTime-complete in general; when predicate arity is bounded, RPQ answering drops to PTime-complete and CRPQ answering to PSpace-complete. For guarded rules, using the reduction to the linear case, they show that (C)RPQ answering has the same complexity as conjunctive query answering: 2ExpTime-complete in combined complexity (ExpTime-complete with bounded arity) and PTime-complete in data complexity.

Conclusion: Ontology-mediated answering of two-way regular path queries under guarded existential rules is no harder in data complexity than answering such queries on plain graph databases and matches the known bounds for conjunctive queries in the guarded setting. Linear rules preserve low data complexity and allow for finer-grained combined complexity results, especially under bounded arity. Overall, the paper delineates precise complexity boundaries for ontology-mediated navigational querying under guarded and linear existential rules, aligning them with existing results for conjunctive queries and plain graph databases.

Abstract: Ontology-mediated query answering is concerned with the problem of answering queries over knowledge bases consisting of a database instance and an ontology. While most work in the area focuses on conjunctive queries (CQs), navigational queries have gained increasing attention. In this paper, we investigate the complexity of answering two-way (conjunctive) regular path queries ((C)RPQs) over knowledge bases whose ontology is given by a set of guarded existential rules. We first consider the subclass of linear existential rules and show that (C)RPQ answering is NL-complete in data complexity, which matches the data complexity of answering RPQs over plain graph databases (i.e., without an ontology). In combined complexity, both tasks are ExpTime-complete in the general case, but RPQ and CRPQ answering drop to PTime-complete and PSpace-complete respectively if there is a bound on predicate arity. For guarded rules, we provide a non-trivial reduction to the linear case, which allows us to show that the complexity of (C)RPQ answering is the same as for CQs, namely 2ExpTime-complete in combined complexity (ExpTime-complete in the bounded-arity case) and PTime-complete in data complexity.

</details>


### [131] [Fast Cross-Scenario Adaptation of CSI Models via Channel Conditional Parameter Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22637)
*Xudong Zou,Siyu Wu,Zunlei Feng,Jie Song,Yuanyu Wan,Mingli Song,Jiacong Hu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces CCPG, a system that can quickly adapt Massive MIMO CSI deep learning models to new wireless environments in seconds using generated lightweight LoRA parameters, avoiding costly retraining while maintaining near state-of-the-art performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep learning-based CSI feedback and channel estimation models perform well but are fragile to changes in wireless environments (new scenarios, topologies, channels). Conventional domain adaptation needs labeled data and heavy online fine-tuning in the target scenario, which is impractical for dynamic large-scale 6G systems. There is a need for a method that can rapidly adapt pre-trained CSI models to unseen environments with minimal computation and without target-domain training data.

Method: The authors propose Channel Conditional Parameter Generation (CCPG), an end-to-end framework that generates scenario-specific adaptation parameters for CSI models. They first identify which parts of the base model are most scene-sensitive via component-freezing experiments, then restrict adaptation to lightweight LoRA (low-rank) weights instead of the full network. High-dimensional channel features from the new environment are compressed into low-dimensional latent conditions using cascaded SVD and a Perceiver Resampler. To make generated LoRA parameters consistent, they introduce an energy-based canonicalization mechanism to resolve permutation and sign ambiguities. Finally, they use a diffusion-based generator with structural priors and an asymmetric size-aware loss to synthesize topology-aware LoRA weights conditioned on the compressed channel representation.

Result: On the DeepMIMO and WAIR-D benchmarks for CSI feedback and channel estimation, CCPG can adapt a pretrained model to a previously unseen scenario with only a single forward pass of the parameter generator, taking about 3 seconds and requiring no target-scenario training or fine-tuning. The adapted models achieve cross-domain reconstruction and estimation accuracy comparable to or close to traditional online adaptation methods that require substantial computation and target-domain supervision, significantly reducing deployment cost and latency.

Conclusion: CCPG shows that it is possible to decouple CSI model training from scenario-specific adaptation by generating only small LoRA-based adaptation modules from a compact representation of the channel environment. This allows Massive MIMO CSI models to be rapidly and efficiently deployed across diverse, dynamic wireless settings, supporting the scalability and flexibility demanded by future intelligent 6G communication systems.

Abstract: Deep learning has shown strong potential for massive multiple-input multiple-output (Massive MIMO) physical-layer tasks, including channel state information (CSI) feedback and channel estimation. However, environmental heterogeneity can severely degrade CSI models in unseen scenarios, while conventional adaptation requires target-domain data and substantial computation. This paper proposes Channel Conditional Parameter Generation (CCPG), an end-to-end pipeline for rapid deployment of CSI models in dynamic wireless environments. CCPG identifies scene-sensitive adaptation bottlenecks through component-freezing experiments and generates only lightweight LoRA weights instead of full model parameters. It compresses high-dimensional channel features into compact latent conditions using cascaded SVD and a Perceiver Resampler. An energy-based canonicalization mechanism mitigates permutation and sign ambiguities in LoRA weights, while a diffusion-based generator incorporates structural information and an asymmetric size-aware loss for topology-aware parameter generation. Experiments on DeepMIMO and WAIR-D for CSI feedback and channel estimation show that CCPG adapts to new scenarios in about 3 seconds with a single forward pass, without target-scenario training or fine-tuning, and achieves cross-domain recovery performance comparable to costly online adaptation. These results demonstrate that CCPG enables efficient deployment of CSI models in large-scale dynamic wireless scenarios for intelligent 6G communications.

</details>


### [132] [TRACE: Business Rule-Grounded Reasoning Curriculum for Knowledge-Preserving Parametric Tool Retrieval in Enterprise LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22639)
*Sai Shruthi Sistla,Ashutosh Hathidara,Christopher Toukmaji,Mayank Shrivastava,Karthikeyan Asokkumar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TRACE is a two-stage training approach that preserves and improves tool knowledge while enabling fast, greedy-decoding parametric tool retrieval in large enterprise catalogs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing parametric retrieval methods like Toolsense assign tools to virtual tokens and train LLMs to output these via constrained beam search, but they suffer two key issues: they overwrite the model’s parametric tool knowledge during training, and their reliance on beam search makes inference too slow for real-time, production use. There is a need for an approach that both maintains/improves tool understanding and allows low-latency decoding over very large enterprise tool catalogs.

Method: TRACE uses a two-stage curriculum. Stage 1 reuses Toolsense’s multi-format memorization supervised fine-tuning (with LoRA) to seed parametric tool knowledge. Stage 2 trains the model to first generate an explicit reasoning trace (a ‘thinking trace’) and then output a JSON list of tool tokens. Training data for Stage 2 comes from two sources: (1) RRB (request–response–binding) pairs from Toolsense and (2) synthetic queries crafted to target business rules provided by domain experts. Both data sources are augmented with chain-of-thought style reasoning traces. The model is then decoded with single-beam greedy decoding, eliminating the need for constrained beam search.

Result: On an enterprise catalog of more than 8,300 tools across two product lines, TRACE’s Stage 2 training not only preserves but improves tool knowledge relative to Stage 1: multiple-choice probing accuracy increases by 3.2 percentage points and QA probing accuracy by 9 percentage points. For retrieval, TRACE attains about 86% recall on Domain A and about 60% recall on Domain B using single-beam greedy decoding, outperforming an embedding-based baseline that achieves only about 27% and 52% recall on the two domains, respectively.

Conclusion: TRACE resolves the trade-off in earlier parametric retrieval systems between preserving tool knowledge and achieving low-latency inference. By adding an augmented chain-of-thought stage that culminates in JSON tool-token lists, it maintains or improves tool understanding while enabling fast single-beam greedy decoding. This makes parametric tool retrieval feasible for real-time deployment over large enterprise tool catalogs, and it outperforms strong embedding-based retrieval baselines in recall.

Abstract: Parametric retrieval enables LLMs to retrieve tools implicitly by assigning each API a unique virtual token and training the model to generate it via constrained beam search. Toolsense shows that this regime has two critical drawbacks: it destroys parametric tool knowledge during training, and its beam-search decoding is too slow for real-time deployment. We introduce TRACE (Tool Retrieval via Augmented Chain-of-thought and Enterprise rules), a two-stage curriculum that resolves this dissociation. Stage 1 reuses the multi-format memorization SFT from ToolSense to seed tool knowledge with LoRA. Stage 2 is our core contribution: the model is trained to emit a thinking trace before producing a JSON list of tool tokens, using two data sources -- RRB pairs from ToolSense and queries synthesized to target business rules curated by domain experts -- both augmented with reasoning traces. This training objective preserves Stage 1 MCQ and QA probing accuracy while enabling single-beam greedy decoding at production latency. Evaluated on a combined enterprise catalog of 8,300+ tools across two enterprise product lines, TRACE training for Stage 2 not only preserves but improves tool understanding: MCQ accuracy gains +3.2 pp and QA probing gains +9 pp over Stage 1. On retrieval, TRACE achieves ~86% recall on Domain A and ~60% on Domain B -- compared to embedding baseline performance of ~27% & ~52% -- both with single-beam greedy decoding, making it directly deployable at production latency.

</details>


### [133] [CRAFT: Learn the Schema, Execute the Plan](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22642)
*Aakash Kolekar,Sahika Genc,Shahriar Shariat,Bunyamin Sisman,Tibor Mezi,Barbara Poblete,Shree Vandana Kachroo,Calvin Chi,Parth Parmar,Ari Singer,Prayaas Jain,Cindy Barker,Benoit Dumoulin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CRAFT is a two-stage post-training framework that turns LLMs into reliable, low-overhead coding agents for enterprise analytics without stuffing full schemas into every prompt.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing enterprise coding agents rely on injecting large volumes of schema and tool documentation into each prompt to translate natural-language analytics requests into code. This causes high token cost, makes it hard to evolve schemas, and leads to fragile multi-turn behavior. The authors want a way for agents to internalize stable schema knowledge and tool-use patterns through training so they can operate efficiently and reliably in production analytics settings.

Method: CRAFT uses a two-stage post-training pipeline on validated agent trajectories. (1) PLAN supervised fine-tuning: the model is trained on schema-stripped trajectories to learn domain-structured planning and executable behavior without seeing exhaustive schema in the prompt. (2) Execution-shaped reinforcement learning: the policy is further aligned via RL rewards that emphasize correct tool selection, high-quality code, consistency between plans and code, and recovery from execution failures. Training data is filtered by a Tri-Gate process that combines: execution validation, data-integrity checks, and an LLM-based reasoning audit to ensure high-quality supervision signals.

Result: In an enterprise advertising-analytics environment with beta APIs, 25 schema-linked entities, and 30 agentic workflows, CRAFT is compared to a baseline that receives schema-stuffed prompts. CRAFT improves a composite Agent Score by +9.6 percentage points, interaction consistency by +4.1 pp, and multi-turn coherence by +4.2 pp. It also reduces input-token usage by about 9x and decreases schema-discovery loops by up to 5x, indicating both efficiency gains and more robust schema-grounded behavior.

Conclusion: The study shows that enterprise coding agents can acquire stable schema knowledge and effective tool-use behavior via post-training rather than heavy prompt-time schema injection. CRAFT delivers better reliability, coherence, and efficiency for multi-turn analytics over proprietary APIs. The authors also highlight practical deployment considerations, including tradeoffs in reward shaping and the need for specialized training infrastructure to support multi-turn tool-use RL in production-like enterprise environments.

Abstract: Enterprise coding agents translate natural-language analytical requests into executable code over proprietary APIs, schemas, and metric definitions. Yet the prevailing deployment pattern injecting exhaustive schema and tool documentation into each prompt increases inference overhead, complicates schema evolution, and undermines reliability in multi-turn analysis. We investigate whether stable schema knowledge and tool-use behavior can instead be acquired through post-training while preserving the consistency required for production-facing analytics. We present CRAFT, a two-stage post-training recipe for schema-grounded coding agents. First, schema-stripped PLAN supervised fine-tuning learns domain-structured plans and executable behaviors from validated trajectories without exhaustive prompt-time schema injection. Second, execution-shaped reinforcement learning aligns the policy for tool selection, code quality, plan-code consistency, and recovery from failed executions. Training trajectories are curated through a Tri-Gate filter combining execution validation, data-integrity checks, and LLM-judge reasoning audit. We evaluate CRAFT for planned rollout in advertising analytics, covering campaign performance analysis, metric drill-downs, entity-level performance analysis, and multi-turn analytical refinement. The enterprise evaluation environment incorporates beta APIs as the agent-facing tool surface and spans 25 schema-linked core entities and 30 agentic workflows. Relative to a schema-stuffed baseline, CRAFT improves composite Agent Score by +9.6 pp, consistency by +4.1 pp, and multi-turn coherence by +4.2 pp, while reducing input-token burden by approximately 9x and schema-discovery loops by up to 5x. We further report deployment tradeoffs, reward-shaping limitations, and training-infrastructure extensions required for multi-turn tool-use reinforcement learning in enterprise settings.

</details>


### [134] [Reason Before You Retrieve: Agentic Planning for Multi-modal RAG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22643)
*Tianyu Yang,Shir Simon,Zhenzhen Li,Minhao Cheng,Xiangliang Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MM-R2 is a multimodal RAG framework that reasons about what to retrieve and where to search using an intent-grounded retrieval state and a structured KnowledgeMap, leading to better accuracy and interpretability than flat mRAG baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multimodal RAG systems usually retrieve directly from raw image-text input over a flat evidence space. This causes two major issues: (1) the retrieval target is under-specified because the question must first be grounded to the correct visual referent, and (2) the evidence space is weakly structured, forcing heterogeneous evidence to compete in one global ranking, which harms both precision and interpretability. The authors want a system that can explicitly reason about user intent and visual grounding, and can search over a structured knowledge space with better control and transparency.

Method: They propose MM-R2, a multimodal agentic retrieval framework with two key components: (1) an intent-grounded retrieval state constructed from the image-question pair, which encodes the information need, grounded visual referent, and retrieval constraints; and (2) retrieval over a structured KnowledgeMap, where the agent first chooses relevant retrieval units (subspaces or nodes in the knowledge structure) and then issues grounded queries within those units. To train this behavior, they build MM-R2-Traj, a large-scale dataset of multi-step retrieval trajectories, and apply a two-stage post-training pipeline combining supervised fine-tuning on trajectories with GRPO-based optimization.

Result: On the Infoseek and Encyclopedic VQA benchmarks, MM-R2 achieves substantially higher answer accuracy compared to strong multimodal RAG baselines. It also produces retrieval trajectories that are more interpretable and easier to verify, as its multi-step decisions and chosen retrieval units can be inspected and evaluated by humans.

Conclusion: Reasoning before retrieval and searching in a structured knowledge space significantly improves multimodal RAG. By modeling an intent-grounded retrieval state and operating over a KnowledgeMap, MM-R2 addresses under-specified retrieval targets and weakly structured evidence spaces, leading to better performance and more transparent retrieval processes. The trajectory dataset and two-stage post-training show that complex agentic retrieval behaviors can be effectively learned at scale.

Abstract: Multimodal retrieval-augmented generation (mRAG) aims to answer image-text queries with external knowledge, but most existing systems still retrieve directly from raw multimodal input over a flat evidence space. This design often struggles with two key challenges: the retrieval target is under-specified because the question intent must be grounded to the correct visual referent, and the search space is weakly structured, forcing semantically distinct evidence to compete in a single global ranking step. We propose MM-R2, a multimodal agentic retrieval framework that reasons before retrieval by explicitly modeling both what to retrieve and where to search. MM-R2 first constructs an intent-grounded retrieval state from the image-question pair, capturing the information need, grounded referent, and retrieval constraints. It then performs retrieval over a structured KnowledgeMap, where the agent selects relevant retrieval units before issuing grounded queries within them. To enable this capability, we build MM-R2-Traj, a large-scale trajectory dataset of multi-step retrieval processes, and adopt a two-stage post-training strategy with supervised fine-tuning and GRPO. Experiments on Infoseek and Encyclopedic VQA datasets show that MM-R2 substantially outperforms strong baselines on answer accuracy while also yielding more interpretable and verifiable retrieval trajectories.

</details>


### [135] [DocHRL: A Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning Framework for Cost-Optimised Document Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22644)
*Mohammed Yousif,Prabhjot Singh,Arjun Pankajakshan,Madhu Reddiboina*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DocHRL is a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework that dynamically chooses the cheapest effective mix of vision models, LLMs, OCR, and human review for each document, significantly cutting cost while keeping very high classification accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing document classification systems run the same fixed pipeline for every document, which wastes compute on easy cases and can still mishandle hard ones. There is a need for systems that can adapt processing depth and tool choice per document, trading off model cost, human effort, and misclassification risk in a principled way.

Method: The authors cast document classification as a sequential decision-making problem and design DocHRL, a two-level hierarchical RL agent. A high-level policy first picks a coarse processing option (e.g., visual classifier, OCR+text model, LLM, or human review). For each option, a sub-policy then chooses a specific model or tool instance to run. They define a reward as the negative total expected cost, combining inference cost, error cost, and human labeling cost, and train both levels jointly using Proximal Policy Optimisation on the RVL-CDIP dataset.

Result: On the RVL-CDIP benchmark with 16 classes, DocHRL attains a macro F1 score of 0.973 while achieving an average per-document cost of 2.74 normalized units, substantially lower than the costs of baselines that rely on single fixed classifiers or non-adaptive pipelines.

Conclusion: A hierarchical, cost-aware RL controller can effectively orchestrate heterogeneous tools and human reviewers for document classification, yielding both better accuracy and lower operational cost than static pipelines. This suggests that policy-learning approaches are promising for building adaptive, resource-efficient document understanding systems.

Abstract: Real-world document classification pipelines typically apply the same sequence of models to every incoming document, regardless of its complexity or type. This leads to inefficient use of compute and human resources: simple documents are over-processed while difficult ones may not receive enough scrutiny. We introduce DocHRL, a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework that learns to adaptively and dynamically select the most cost-effective classification policy on a per-document basis. DocHRL formulates document classification as a sequential decision problem with a two-level policy hierarchy: a top-level policy selects among broad options (vision classifiers, LLMs, OCR, and human-in-the-loop review), while option-specific sub-policies choose the concrete model or tool to invoke. The reward signal is the negative total expected cost, which captures inference cost, cost of misclassification, and cost of human labelling. Trained with Proximal Policy Optimisation on the RVL-CDIP benchmark, DocHRL achieves a macro F1 of 0.973 across 16 document classes while reducing average per-document cost to 2.74 normalised units compared to substantially higher costs incurred by fixed standalone classifiers. Our results demonstrate that cost-aware reinforcement learning can simultaneously improve classification performance and operational efficiency in document understanding systems.

</details>


### [136] [Extracting Algorithms in Pre-trained LLMs: A Case on Hidden Markov Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22646)
*Yijia Dai,Zhaolin Gao,Yahya Sattar,Jennifer J. Sun,Sarah Dean*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper investigates how large language models perform in-context learning for predicting sequences generated by Hidden Markov Models, identifies which algorithms best match their behavior, shows how those algorithms can be implemented in Transformers, and uses a new probing method to uncover the internal low-dimensional mechanisms that realize them.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large language models can surprisingly learn to predict the next observations from Hidden Markov Models purely from context, but it is unclear what internal algorithms they use to do this and how these algorithms are implemented inside Transformer architectures. Previous hypotheses are not agreed upon and are not directly linked to internal activations, leaving a gap in mechanistic understanding of in-context learning on structured probabilistic tasks such as HMMs.

Method: The authors use a three-stage approach: (1) empirically compare LLM predictions on HMM sequence tasks against a range of candidate inference algorithms, narrowing them down to three algorithmic classes though none fully explains all regimes; (2) derive theoretical correspondences between these algorithmic classes and in-context implementations within a Transformer, then validate these constructions on a small trained Transformer model; and (3) develop the Principal Activations Probe (PAP), a layer-wise probing and intervention technique that identifies low-dimensional activation subspaces corresponding to the algorithms, and use PAP on pre-trained LLMs to analyze how internal representations relate to in-context HMM prediction performance.

Result: The empirical analysis shows that LLM behavior is best approximated by three algorithmic classes across HMM regimes, but that no single algorithm fits all settings. Theoretical work demonstrates that each class can be implemented in-context by a Transformer, and these implementations are confirmed in a small trained Transformer. PAP identifies low-dimensional linear activation subspaces that both predict and causally affect model outputs on HMM tasks, with these representations varying systematically across different HMM regimes and sequence lengths. Distinct algorithmic stages of computation are localized to different layers of the model.

Conclusion: The study establishes a concrete link between the in-context behavior of large language models on HMM prediction tasks and specific internal algorithmic mechanisms implemented within Transformers. By introducing PAP and showing low-dimensional, causally relevant representations that track in-context learning performance and shift with HMM properties, the paper advances mechanistic understanding of how LLMs execute in-context learning and clarifies the algorithmic nature and layerwise organization of their HMM inference capabilities.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) display a striking ability to predict next observations from Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) via in-context learning (ICL), but the algorithm underlying this capability remains undetermined: prior work has proposed several candidates without consensus, and none has been grounded in the model's internal activations. We close this gap with a three-stage pipeline. First, we empirically compare LLM behavior against a suite of candidate algorithms and narrow the space to three classes -- though no single class explains LLM behavior across all HMM settings and sequence lengths. Second, we derive theoretical connections between the three classes and show how each can be implemented in-context by a Transformer, validating the construction in a small trained Transformer. Third, returning to pre-trained LLMs, we introduce the Principal Activations Probe (PAP), a layer-wise probing and intervention method that isolates algorithmic signals in model activations. PAP reveals low-dimensional linear representations that causally drive model predictions and track empirical ICL performance. PAP further reveals how these representations shift with properties of the underlying HMM regime; distinct computational stages are localized to different layers. Together, our results connect the in-context behavior of pre-trained LLMs to the underlying internal mechanisms and advance our understanding of how LLMs perform ICL on HMMs.

</details>


### [137] [PTStore (Prefix Tensor Store): Distributed Prefix Caching and Replication for High Throughput Inference Serving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22648)
*Meghana Maghyastha,Robert Underwood,Randal Burns,Bogdan Nicolae*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PTStore is a distributed system that caches and replicates popular KV-cache tensor prefixes across nodes/GPUs, improving LLM inference efficiency, scalability, and load balance versus baselines that cannot aggregate KV memory.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM inference on long-passage Q&A is bottlenecked by KV-cache size limits and imbalanced, high-latency access patterns; existing systems keep KV caches local to individual nodes/GPUs, forcing repeated regeneration and overloading servers holding popular prefixes.

Method: Borrowing ideas from CDN client caching, PTStore distributes and replicates popular tensor prefixes (KV cache segments) across the cluster, decentralizing memory and access so that clients can fetch reused KV prefixes with lower latency and less skew; it aggregates memory from different nodes/GPUs to effectively expand KV-cache capacity by orders of magnitude.

Result: By decentralizing and replicating popular KV-cache prefixes, PTStore achieves 5–6× higher efficiency for long-passage Q&A LLM inference compared with baselines that do not share/aggregate KV memory and thus must frequently regenerate the KV cache.

Conclusion: CDN-style distribution and replication of popular KV-cache prefixes across nodes/GPUs significantly reduces latency and load imbalance while dramatically increasing effective KV-cache capacity, yielding substantial (5–6×) efficiency gains for long-context LLM inference workloads such as long-passage Q&A.

Abstract: Inspired by the design of client caching in Content Delivery Networks (CDNs), PTStore distributes and replicates popular tensors that form reusable KV cache prefixes, which are the main technique used by state of art approaches to accelerate inferences. This reduces the latency of accessing the KV cache and alleviates load imbalance caused by a disproportionately large number of requests on servers containing popular tensors. Furthermore, thanks to decentralization, PTStore allows the expansion of the size of the KV cache for LLM inference by orders of magnitude. As a result, PTStore can execute inferences on long passage Q\&A datasets 5-6 times more efficiently than current baselines, which do not aggregate memory across different nodes and GPUs and therefore require regenerating the KV cache.

</details>


### [138] [STAIF: A Stage-wise Optimization for Complex Instruction Following](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22649)
*Jian Hong,Chen Cheng,Quan Liu,Yuhao Chen,Enhong Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose STAIF, a two-stage alignment framework that separates soft and hard constraint optimization, and build a complex multi-constraint bilingual dataset to show it outperforms existing methods on instruction-following benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs struggle to reliably follow complex instructions with many explicit constraints, especially when out-of-distribution or when multiple constraints must be satisfied. Existing alignment methods like DPO use holistic rewards, which can miss or underweight individual constraint satisfaction. The authors aim to achieve more reliable and strict adherence to both subjective and objectively verifiable constraints in complex instructions.

Method: They introduce STAIF, a stage-wise optimization framework. Stage 1 uses preference optimization with multiple negative samples to increase the model’s sensitivity to subjective, soft constraints in instructions. Stage 2 uses Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) to strictly enforce objectively checkable, hard constraints. They also create STAINSTRUCT, a bilingual (English, Chinese) dataset of ~31k complex instructions with multiple constraints, designed to support training and evaluation of the proposed method.

Result: Through extensive experiments, STAIF achieves state-of-the-art results on representative instruction-following benchmarks compared to strong baseline alignment methods. Analyses show that STAIF better satisfies both soft and hard constraints, particularly in multi-constraint and out-of-distribution scenarios. The new STAINSTRUCT dataset enables robust evaluation and training in bilingual, complex-instruction settings.

Conclusion: Separating the optimization of soft and hard constraints in a staged framework leads to better complex-instruction following for LLMs than holistic approaches like DPO. With STAIF and the accompanying STAINSTRUCT dataset, the authors demonstrate improved performance, strict constraint satisfaction, and better generalization, suggesting stage-wise verifiable-reward-based alignment is a promising direction for future LLM training.

Abstract: Following complex instructions with multiple explicit constraints remains a fundamental challenge for large language models (LLMs). Existing alignment methods, such as DPO, optimize holistic reward signals that often underemphasize strict satisfaction of individual constraints, particularly under out-of-distribution or multi-constraint settings. In this paper, we propose STAIF, a stage-wise optimization framework that decouples the alignment of subjective (soft) constraints from the optimization of objectively verifiable (hard) constraints. Stage 1 applies preference optimization with multiple negative samples to sharpen sensitivity to soft constraints, while Stage 2 applies Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) to enforce strict compliance with hard constraints. To support this method, we construct STAINSTRUCT, a high-quality bilingual (English, Chinese) dataset of approximately 31,000 complex multi-constraint instructions. Extensive analyses validate the design of STAIF and show state-of-the-art performance on representative benchmarks against strong baselines, as well as genuine generalization.

</details>


### [139] [ARdena: Scenario-driven control of real-time LLM agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22651)
*Luka Borozan,Domagoj Matijević*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A framework for controlling LLM agent behavior at runtime via layered, scenario-driven prompting instead of retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Controlling LLM-based conversational agents in real-time interactive and multimodal environments is hard because current methods depend on fine-tuning or alignment steps that are inflexible and hard to adapt when interaction requirements or contexts change.

Method: Proposes a layered, scenario-driven control framework that uses structured prompting with two main components: (1) a persistent context that encodes stable, global instructions for the agent, and (2) scenario-specific constraints that can be swapped or updated at runtime. This is instantiated in ARDena, a real-time multimodal embodied agent that combines speech, vision, tool use, and avatar-based responses. They then empirically evaluate control effectiveness, latency, and stability under different scenario definitions.

Result: Different scenario definitions, applied only through prompting layers and without modifying the underlying LLM, lead to substantially different and controllable interaction behaviors. At the same time, the agent maintains acceptable response latency and stable real-time operation across scenarios.

Conclusion: Scenario-driven, layered prompting is an effective way to control the behavior of LLM-based agents in real-time multimodal settings, enabling flexible runtime adaptation of interaction behavior without model retraining or architectural changes.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have enabled increasingly capable conversational agents, but reliably controlling their behavior in real-time interactive environments remains a significant challenge. Existing approaches often rely on model fine-tuning or alignment procedures that are difficult to adapt to changing interaction requirements. This paper introduces layered scenario-driven LLM control, a framework that enables runtime behavior control through structured prompting. By combining persistent context with scenario-specific constraints, the approach allows agent behavior to be modified during interaction without changing the underlying model. The framework is implemented in ARDena, a real-time multimodal embodied agent that integrates speech interaction, visual perception, tool use, and avatar-based response generation. The proposed approach is evaluated with respect to control effectiveness, response latency, and operational stability. The results demonstrate that scenario definitions alone can produce substantially different interaction behaviors while maintaining stable real-time operation, highlighting the effectiveness of scenario-driven prompting for controlling LLM agents.

</details>


### [140] [KG2Code: Bridging Knowledge Graphs and Large Language Models via Executable Code for Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22652)
*Yike Wu,Nan Hu,Guilin Qi,Guohui Xiao,Chen Jiang,Xinchun Zou,Yuchen Lu,Songlin Zhai,Yongrui Chen,Yuyang Zhang,Xiaoguang Li,Lifeng Shang,Jiaoyan Chen,Jeff Z. Pan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: KG2Code converts knowledge graphs into code so LLMs can answer KG questions as a code-generation task, producing verifiable reasoning that reduces hallucinations and improves generalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing ways of combining KGs and LLMs for KG question answering—RAG, agents, SPARQL—lose graph structure, often reason unfaithfully, and don’t generalize well. There is also an opportunity to better align KGs with LLMs’ strong capabilities on code, which could yield more explicit and verifiable reasoning over structured data.

Method: The paper introduces KG2Code, a representation that encodes KG entities, relations, and structure as code-like programs that align with code-pretrained LLMs. On top of this, the authors design KG2Code-QA, which recasts KGQA as a code generation task: given a question, the model outputs executable code over the KG2Code representation, yielding both an answer and its reasoning trace. They also build an automated pipeline to generate a large code corpus from KGs and QA pairs, then fine-tune open-source LLMs on this corpus so they can perform KGQA in zero-shot settings.

Result: Models trained with KG2Code-QA substantially outperform state-of-the-art KG-enhanced LLM baselines for KGQA, particularly on reasoning quality and robustness. The generated code provides verifiable reasoning traces and reduces hallucinations, and the approach generalizes well to previously unseen KGs.

Conclusion: Encoding KGs as code and formulating KGQA as code generation effectively preserves structural semantics, aligns with LLMs’ strengths, and yields faithful, verifiable reasoning. KG2Code and KG2Code-QA provide a flexible and general framework that improves KGQA accuracy and zero-shot generalization over prior KG–LLM integration methods, supported by strong empirical results.

Abstract: Recent research has explored the integration of knowledge graphs (KGs) with large language models (LLMs) to enhance their performance on downstream knowledge-intensive tasks, particularly knowledge graph question answering (KGQA). Existing approaches primarily combine LLMs with KGs through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)-based, agent-based, and SPARQL-based methods. Although these methods have achieved notable success, they still suffer from several limitations, including structural information loss, unfaithful reasoning, and limited flexibility and generalization. To address these challenges, this paper proposes KG2Code, a novel approach that transforms knowledge graphs into a code-based representation, preserving structural semantics while naturally aligning with the code-aware pretraining of modern LLMs. Based on KG2Code, KG2Code-QA is further introduced as a KGQA framework that formulates KGQA as a code generation task. This formulation enables the generation of verifiable reasoning traces and executable code, thereby substantially mitigating the impact of hallucinations. In addition, an automated pipeline is developed to construct a large-scale, high-quality code corpus for effectively training open-source LLMs on KG2Code-QA. After training, LLMs are able to perform KGQA in zero-shot scenarios. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly outperforms existing KG-enhanced LLM methods for KGQA, while exhibiting strong generalization to unseen KGs. The code and data are available at Github.

</details>


### [141] [Do Language Models Converge to Themselves? Recursive Self-Refinement as Textual Relaxation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22653)
*Xuening Wu,Qianya Xu,Yanlan Kang,Zeping Chen,Yubin Liu,Shenqin Yin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies how large language models behave when repeatedly refining the same text and finds that revisions quickly converge to a stable form rather than improving indefinitely.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recursive self-refinement with LLMs is widely used (e.g., for editing drafts or improving code), but it is unclear whether repeated revisions keep improving outputs or instead settle into some stable pattern. Understanding these dynamics helps decide how many refinement steps are useful and whether such workflows can be viewed as optimization processes.

Method: Using GPT-5.5, the authors generate 10-step refinement sequences for 50 ICML 2025 abstracts and 15 ICML 2020 abstracts under both default-temperature (stochastic) and deterministic decoding. They analyze: normalized edit distance between consecutive drafts; exact and approximate fixed points (texts that stop changing or change only minimally); word-count stability; whether edit magnitudes follow exponential relaxation; and quality via an external LLM-as-a-judge evaluating clarity, conciseness, style, and meaning preservation.

Result: They observe that most textual changes happen in the first few refinement steps; after that, the text enters a "soft fixed-point" region where only small surface edits occur. Deterministic decoding reaches exact fixed points sooner and with less residual fluctuation than stochastic decoding, but both modes show approximate convergence. The magnitude of edits over iterations fits an exponential decay pattern, indicating movement toward a stable equilibrium. External evaluations show that the final converged abstracts are clearer, more concise, and more stylistically polished, while keeping the original technical content intact.

Conclusion: Recursive self-refinement of text by LLMs behaves like a dynamical system converging toward model-preferred textual equilibria rather than exhibiting unbounded improvement. This supports viewing self-refinement as relaxation to a fixed point and suggests practical stopping rules based on when edit magnitudes saturate, so additional refinement steps give diminishing returns.

Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used in recursive refinement workflows, where an initial draft is repeatedly revised by the same model. Despite their growing use, the long-term dynamics of such workflows remain poorly understood. Does repeated refinement continue to improve outputs indefinitely, or does it converge toward a stable textual form?
  We study recursive self-refinement as a dynamical process in which repeated LLM revision drives text toward a model-preferred soft fixed-point region. Using GPT-5.5, we generate 10-step refinement trajectories for 50 ICML 2025 abstracts under both default-temperature and deterministic decoding, and additionally evaluate 15 ICML 2020 abstracts. We analyze normalized edit distance, exact and approximate fixed points, word-count stability, exponential relaxation, and external LLM-as-a-judge evaluation.
  Across all settings, refinement trajectories rapidly saturate. Most edits occur within the first few iterations, after which trajectories enter a soft fixed-point region with only minor surface-level changes.
