While this automation provides clear utility, completing these tasks often requires the insertion of Personally Identifiable Information (PII), strings of information that uniquely identify some individual, raising privacy concerns. However, ethics has prevented the curation of a public, authentic dataset of PII. Without an appropriate dataset, it is difficult to quantify privacy risks. Thus, we introduce the PANOPTICON pipeline and dataset. The dataset, generated by Meta's Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct model, contains 67, 718 prompts, intended for the models context window, containing PII spans derived from 9,674 publicly available synthetic user profiles. We measure lexical diversity and S-BERT diversity of the created dataset to evaluate realism. Finally, we present a case study showcasing the utility of PANOPTICON data for understanding Prompt Inversion Attacks (PIAs). PANOPTICON thus emerges as the first benchmark dataset for studying PIAs over private corpora, providing a foundation for future LLM privacy research.

</details>


### [162] [Test-Time Coverage: Test-Conditioned Data Curation for Deployment-Aware Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22697)
*Nadine Chang,Maying Shen,Shizhe Diao,Jialiang Wang,Jingde Chen,Thomas Breuel,Pavlo Molchanov,Rafid Mahmood,Jose M. Alvarez*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose TTCov, a test-conditioned data curation method that selects training data to match the deployment distribution using LLM-derived conceptual coverage representations, demonstrated on autonomous driving.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing data curation scores training-side proxies (e.g., loss, diversity) without directly aligning training data with the actual deployment/test distribution, especially in safety-critical domains like autonomous driving. There is a need to exploit test-side information pre-training while keeping adaptation off the inference path, so that selected training data better covers and matches real deployment conditions.

Method: They introduce TTCov, which decomposes deployment-conditioned curation into coverage and distribution. First, they construct a task Atlas: a set of atomic propositions (APs) generated and organized by an LLM that describe concepts relevant to deployment. This Atlas is seeded from open task knowledge, then expanded with additional APs extracted from unlabeled deployment samples to capture previously uncovered concepts. Next, they build a Knowledge Atlas (K-Atlas) by instantiating the APs that match deployment samples, counting their frequencies to approximate the deployment distribution. Finally, they perform budgeted training-set selection, choosing training data whose AP distribution best matches the K-Atlas target, effectively aligning the training set with deployment conditions before training, without changing model inference-time behavior.

Result: On autonomous driving benchmarks, using TTCov to curate the training data yields training sets with broader and more relevant coverage of deployment scenarios, better alignment to the deployment Knowledge Atlas, and improved downstream end-to-end driving performance compared to standard data curation baselines. TTCov also supports straightforward extension to new cities (novel domains) by updating the APs and K-Atlas, enabling seamless city-to-city domain adaptation without test-time adaptation of the trained model.

Conclusion: Test-conditioned, data-level curation via TTCov can better align training data with deployment conditions than traditional training-side proxies, while keeping inference-time adaptation off the critical path. Representing deployment as a distribution over LLM-derived atomic propositions enables both higher deployment coverage and flexible extension to new domains, as shown in autonomous driving, and suggests a general framework for deployment-aware dataset construction in other applications.

Abstract: Deployed AI systems are often trained from broad candidate data pools, necessitating data curation towards the deployment test distribution. However, standard data curation methods score training-side criteria rather than directly optimizing deployment match. We introduce TTCov (Test-Time Coverage), a data-level test-conditioned curation method that uses test-side information before training instead of updating model weights at inference. TTCov decomposes deployment-conditioned curation into coverage and distribution. To represent coverage, it builds a task Atlas, a collection of LLM-based atomic propositions (APs) describing deployment-relevant concepts, seeded from open task knowledge and expanded with unmatched APs extracted from unlabeled deployment samples. To represent distribution, it instantiates the matched deployment APs with their frequencies, yielding a Knowledge Atlas (K-Atlas) that operationalizes the deployment distribution as a curation target. TTCov then selects a budgeted training set whose deployment APs distribution approximates this target. We apply TTCov towards autonomous driving (AD), keeping adaptation off the inference path while selecting data with greater deployment-relevant coverage, closer K-Atlas matching, and stronger downstream end-to-end driving performance than data-curation baselines, including seamless adaptability to novel domains via city-to-city expansion.

</details>


### [163] [Similarity All The Way Up: Multilingual Generalization in LLMs Relies on Language-Level Similarity Structures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22699)
*Supantho Rakshit,Adele Goldberg,Henry Conklin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies how well large language models’ internal representations reflect the true similarity structure between languages, and shows that models whose latent spaces better recover the Indo-European language family tree also generalize better on multilingual inference tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs often struggle to generalize to multilingual settings, especially for low-resource languages, and it is unclear why some models transfer better across languages than others. The authors draw on cognitive science theories that link good generalization to having appropriate similarity-based representations, and they seek to test whether this idea explains multilingual generalization in LLMs.

Method: The authors analyze LLM latent representations for sentences across multiple Indo-European languages. They measure how well distances in representation space recover the known hierarchical structure of the Indo-European language family tree (i.e., whether languages from the same subfamilies cluster together). They then correlate this structural alignment with model performance on XNLI, a multilingual natural language inference benchmark, to see whether better-structured similarity spaces predict better cross-lingual generalization.

Result: LLM representations largely reconstruct the hierarchical Indo-European language family tree: languages from the same subfamilies are placed near each other in the embedding space, revealing a latent similarity structure that mirrors linguistic genealogy. Moreover, models that more accurately capture this hierarchy—i.e., whose representation spaces more closely reflect true language similarities—achieve higher accuracy on the XNLI multilingual benchmark.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that similarity-based representations are central to multilingual generalization in LLMs. When models represent related languages similarly in latent space, they more effectively transfer knowledge across languages, echoing classic cognitive science theories of similarity-driven generalization. This provides a scalable, representation-level explanation for why some LLMs generalize better in multilingual tasks and suggests that improving the structure of language similarity in embeddings can enhance cross-lingual performance.

Abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) grow more capable across diverse tasks, their (in)ability to generalize remains difficult to quantify and poorly understood beyond limited domains. In particular, LLMs are known to struggle generalizing multilingually, to languages outside of English, and that are poorly attested in their training data. To understand why this may be, and what enables some models to perform better than others, we turn to a long history of work across the cognitive sciences, arguing that successful generalization derives from appropriate representations in similarity space. We look at how well LLMs' representations capture the hierarchical similarity structure between distinct languages. Strikingly, we show LLMs' latent representations largely recover the hierarchical structure of the Indo-European language family tree -- grouping languages that are members of the same subfamily closely together in representation space. Furthermore, we show that the degree to which models reflect the similarity structure of languages correlates with their performance on XNLI, a multilingual natural language inference benchmark. This extends classic work on similarity-driven generalization at scale, showing how models that represent similar languages similarly generalize better from one language to another.

</details>


### [164] [RoleMix: Unifying Sequential and Non-Sequential Features via Semantic Tokenization for Post-Click Conversion Rate Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22700)
*Wenan Wang,Qin Zhao,Zhixiang Lu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RoleMix is a unified token-based architecture for post-click conversion prediction that preserves the semantic roles of both sparse fields and long user behaviors, leading to significant AUC gains on a large industrial benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Industrial PCVR models must jointly use sparse, multi-field features (user, item, context, etc.) and long, domain-specific behavior sequences. Existing approaches typically process these two signal types in separate branches and only fuse them late, which weakens semantic roles, makes it hard to model fine-grained interactions, and limits how effectively behavior history can refine static features. There is a need for an architecture that treats all evidence in a unified way while still retaining rich field semantics.

Method: The paper proposes RoleMix, which builds a shared, role-preserving token interface for all signals. Non-sequential multi-field inputs are converted into explicit semantic tokens that encode different roles (user, item, pairwise, dense, contextual, cross-feature). Long behavior histories across domains are compressed into item-aware and context-aware sequence-query tokens via a two-stage hierarchical window attention mechanism, which summarizes long sequences while keeping relevant information. These global, semantic, and sequence-query tokens are then fed into stacked UniMixing-Lite blocks, a unified interaction backbone that jointly refines all tokens for final PCVR prediction.

Result: On the large-scale KDD Cup 2026 Tencent UniRec Challenge, RoleMix achieves 83.648% online AUC, surpassing the official industrial baseline by 1.953%. Ablation experiments indicate that the semantic tokenization of non-sequential fields contributes the largest standalone performance gain compared to other components.

Conclusion: Unifying sequential and non-sequential evidence through a shared token space while explicitly preserving field semantics is highly effective for large-scale PCVR tasks. The findings suggest that carefully designing the token interface to maintain semantic roles can be as crucial as scaling up the interaction backbone, and semantic tokenization should be a first-class design principle in future industrial PCVR models.

Abstract: Post-click conversion rate (PCVR) prediction is central to industrial recommendation, but remains challenged by the structural mismatch between sparse, unordered multi-field features and long, domain-specific behavior histories. Existing models often process these signals through separate pathways and fuse them late, weakening semantic roles and limiting cross-signal refinement. We propose RoleMix, a unified interaction architecture that represents sequential and non-sequential evidence through a shared, role-preserving token interface. Non-sequential fields are converted into explicit semantic tokens that preserve user, item, pairwise, dense, contextual, and cross-feature roles, while long behavior domains are compressed into item- and context-aware sequence-query tokens through two-stage hierarchical window attention. The resulting global, semantic, and sequence-query tokens are jointly refined by stacked UniMixing-Lite blocks for PCVR prediction. On the large-scale KDD Cup 2026 Tencent UniRec Challenge, RoleMix achieves 83.648% online AUC, outperforming the official industrial baseline by 1.953%. Ablation studies show that semantic tokenization yields the largest isolated gain, highlighting a key principle for large-scale PCVR modeling: preserving field semantics at the token-interface level is as important as scaling the interaction backbone.

</details>


### [165] [MPR-CiteG: Enhancing RAG with Multi-Portfolio Retrieval and Citation-Grounded Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22706)
*Hyewon Lee,Minkyung Song,Junghyun Oh,Seunghoon Han,Sungsu Lim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MPR-CiteG is a retrieval-and-generation framework that improves LLM trustworthiness by efficient multi-portfolio retrieval and citation-grounded generation, reducing hallucinations and achieving strong performance in the ScienceON AI Challenge.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generative AI systems, particularly large language models, often suffer from two key problems: inefficient retrieval of external information and a lack of explicit source verification, which together lead to hallucinations and untrustworthy outputs. The authors aim to build a system that can both find better evidence and ensure that generated answers are grounded in and attributed to reliable sources.

Method: The authors design a dual-component framework called MPR-CiteG. The Multi-Portfolio Retriever (MPR) focuses on retrieving a diverse and relevant set of documents or evidence pieces, likely using multiple retrieval strategies or representations ("portfolios") to cover different aspects of a query. The Citation-Grounded Generation (CiteG) component then generates answers that are constrained to stay consistent with the retrieved evidence and to explicitly cite or attribute each factual statement to its supporting source. This tight coupling between retrieval and generation is used to enforce factuality and traceability.

Result: On the ScienceON AI Challenge dataset, MPR-CiteG achieved second place, indicating competitive performance against other state-of-the-art systems. The experiments demonstrate that the approach is both effective and reliable in producing accurate, evidence-grounded responses, with reduced hallucinations relative to standard LLM generation baselines.

Conclusion: MPR-CiteG offers a promising direction for making LLMs more trustworthy by combining stronger retrieval with citation-aware generation. By ensuring that outputs are both factually consistent with retrieved evidence and explicitly source-attributed, the framework helps mitigate hallucination and improves transparency. The system’s strong challenge performance and released code suggest it is a practical and reproducible solution for citation-grounded generative AI applications.

Abstract: This paper presents the MPR-CiteG framework, which achieved second place in the ScienceON AI Challenge by addressing two fundamental challenges in generative AI: inefficient retrieval and the absence of source verification. We propose a dual-component system, termed MPR-CiteG, in which the Multi-Portfolio Retriever (MPR) efficiently retrieves diverse and relevant information, while the Citation-Grounded Generation (CiteG) module ensures that every generated output remains factually consistent and explicitly attributed to its source. MPR-CiteG represents a significant step toward building more trustworthy and accurate LLMs that are not only capable of generating information but also of grounding their responses in reliable evidence, thereby mitigating common issues like model hallucination. Extensive experiments on the challenge dataset validate the effectiveness and reliability of our approach. Our code is available at https://github.com/2noweyh/MPR-citeG.

</details>


### [166] [SEGRA: Structured Experience-Guided Graph Reasoning Agent for Gremlin Based Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22713)
*Saiyue Lyu,Mariam Dundua,Vishaal Kapoor,Sarthak Ahuja,Neda Kordjazi,Evren Yortucboylu,Harsh Amin,Rebecca Steinert*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SEGRA is an LLM-based agent that translates natural language questions into Gremlin queries for enterprise IT support knowledge graphs, improving both accuracy and efficiency over standard prompting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Non-expert operators struggle to query enterprise IT support knowledge graphs because Gremlin requires detailed knowledge of schemas, traversal semantics, and graph-specific constraints. There is a need for a system that lets users ask natural language questions while still producing correct, executable Gremlin queries over complex enterprise graphs.

Method: The authors design SEGRA, an experience-guided text-to-Gremlin agent that combines: (1) intent routing to decide how to handle a question, (2) schema- and taxonomy-grounded query generation so that queries respect the underlying graph structure, (3) multi-shot decomposition to break complex questions into sub-queries, (4) execution-aware verification that checks and corrects queries using feedback from the graph engine, and (5) a curriculum-bootstrapped skill library that stores and reuses previously verified query patterns for similar future questions.

Result: On an enterprise IT support benchmark, SEGRA obtains a 7x higher mean judge score than a backbone LLM using only chain-of-thought prompting. Adding the skill library on top of SEGRA reduces LLM calls by 20% and monetary cost by 18%, while maintaining answer quality.

Conclusion: Schema-grounded, execution-aware agent design plus reuse of previously verified query patterns significantly improves both the accuracy and efficiency of natural-language-to-Gremlin question answering for enterprise IT support knowledge graphs.

Abstract: Enterprise IT support knowledge graphs capture rich relationships among cases, users, devices, symptoms, taxonomic categories, root causes, and historical resolutions. Yet querying them in Gremlin requires knowledge of graph schemas, traversal semantics, edge directionality, and property-graph-specific constraints, making them difficult for non-expert operators to use. We introduce SEGRA, an experience-guided agent for enterprise text-to-Gremlin question answering. SEGRA integrates intent routing, schema- and taxonomy-grounded query generation, multi-shot decomposition, execution-aware verification, and a curriculum-bootstrapped skill library that reuses verified query patterns. On an enterprise IT support benchmark, SEGRA achieves a $7.0\times$ higher mean judge score than backbone-only chain-of-thought prompting. Its skill library further reduces LLM calls by $20\%$ and dollar cost by $18\%$ relative to SEGRA without skills, while preserving answer quality. These results show that schema-grounded agent design and reusable execution experience improve both accuracy and efficiency for enterprise graph QA.

</details>


### [167] [Spatial Reasoning in LLM Game Agents: Impact of Causal Context and Multi-Step Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22732)
*Mohit Jiwatode,Ronja Fuchs,Robin Schmöcker,Bodo Rosenhahn,Alexander Dockhorn*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper investigates why LLM-based game agents struggle with complex tasks and shows that better spatial reasoning, causal prompt augmentation, and structured multi-step planning significantly improve performance and efficiency on a custom spatial-navigation game benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based agents often fail on complex game tasks, but it is unclear how much of this is due to weak spatial reasoning and how to improve it without incurring large latency costs. The authors want to systematically measure spatial-navigation ability, understand scaling effects across model sizes and reasoning modes, and test whether prompt and planning strategies can close the performance gap.

Method: They use the Qwen3 model family at multiple scales and reasoning modes, and design a focused GVGAI benchmark of three custom games with five difficulty levels that emphasize spatial navigation. They evaluate in two setups: (1) a positioning experiment where the agent must infer its exact coordinates, and (2) full game-play performance. They systematically vary prompt design with and without causal context, enable a thinking (deliberative) mode, and explore different multi-step planning horizons while tracking win rates and per-step latency.

Result: Larger Qwen3 models with thinking mode enabled are better at locating their in-game positions, but coordinate-matching accuracy remains low for smaller models. Game win rates drop as level difficulty and layout complexity increase, indicating that the benchmark cleanly scales in difficulty. Adding causal context to prompts improves success, especially for larger models. Activating thinking mode and using longer planning horizons substantially raise win rates, and multi-step planning also reduces mean per-step response times compared to purely single-step reasoning with similar overall depth.

Conclusion: Spatial reasoning is a key bottleneck for LLM-based game agents, and naive use of smaller models yields poor coordinate understanding and low win rates on complex levels. However, carefully designed benchmarks, causal prompt augmentation, and structured multi-step planning with a thinking mode can significantly boost performance while also improving efficiency, providing a practical recipe for building more capable and responsive LLM game agents.

Abstract: LLM-based game agents often perform poorly on more complex tasks. This work examines whether these failures are linked to limited spatial reasoning and evaluates whether causal prompt augmentation and multi-step planning can improve win-rates while managing response latency. Using the open-source Qwen3 model family, we conduct experiments across varying model scales, reasoning modes, and planning horizons. We further introduce a focused GVGAI benchmark consisting of three custom games with five difficulty levels to isolate spatial navigation. The evaluation follows two paradigms: an initial ``positioning experiment'' to test an agent's ability to find its exact coordinates, and a study of game-play success. Our results show that while larger models with an enabled thinking mode identify their positions more accurately, overall performance in coordinate matching remains limited for smaller models. Win rates decrease as game levels and layout complexity increase, validating the benchmark's difficulty scaling. Integrating causal context into the prompts tends to improve the agents' success rates, particularly for bigger models. While enabling thinking mode and longer planning horizons significantly improve performance, multi-step planning further reduces mean per-step response times, offering a practical trade-off between reasoning depth and execution speed.

</details>


### [168] [ConsistencyGate: Preventing Memory Contamination in LLM Agents via Self-Consistency Admission Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22962)
*Yan Zhang,Shibo Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper identifies and addresses 'memory contamination' in LLM agents, where hallucinated facts written to long-term memory persist and corrupt future reasoning, by proposing ConsistencyGate, a model-agnostic write-time filter that only admits facts with sufficient self-consistency support from the LLM, and evaluates it on new real and synthetic benchmarks showing reduced contamination across multiple models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents that perform multi-turn interactions rely on external memory to store facts from earlier steps and reuse them later. However, when the model hallucinates and writes incorrect facts into memory, these errors persist and become premises for all subsequent reasoning, leading to compounding mistakes over long trajectories. Existing memory management focuses mainly on what to retrieve or how to manage capacity, not on whether new facts being written are actually correct. There is thus a gap: a need for mechanisms that decide, at write time, whether a candidate memory item should be admitted in order to prevent long-term memory contamination.

Method: The authors define the problem of 'memory contamination' and propose ConsistencyGate, a write-time admission mechanism. For each candidate fact m extracted from a context c, the gate queries the same LLM K times to obtain a soft support score reflecting how consistently the model endorses m given c. It then averages these scores and admits m into memory only if the average exceeds a predefined threshold. This approach is model-agnostic, requires no fine-tuning, and can be instantiated in a more efficient log-probability-based variant that reduces the procedure to a single forward pass for latency-sensitive scenarios. To evaluate the method, they construct two contaminated real-conversation benchmarks, LoCoMo-Contam and MSC-Contam, by injecting controlled single-detail corruptions into long-term dialogue datasets, and a synthetic structured corpus, MemContam, designed to approximate a near-oracle upper bound on performance.

Result: On three benchmarks—two derived from real conversations (LoCoMo-Contam, MSC-Contam) and one synthetic (MemContam)—and across four different LLM backbones, ConsistencyGate consistently reduces the rate of memory contamination compared with a baseline that writes all extracted facts to memory without filtering. The incurred cost of the gate (in terms of mistakenly rejecting information) is concentrated on facts that are only implicitly present in the context, indicating that explicit facts are preserved while many hallucinated or weakly supported ones are filtered out.

Conclusion: ConsistencyGate is an effective, model-agnostic write-time memory admission gate for LLM agents that mitigates the accumulation of hallucinated facts in long-term memory. By leveraging self-consistency checks via repeated queries or a log-probability variant, it significantly reduces memory contamination across multiple models and datasets without requiring fine-tuning. The newly released contaminated conversation benchmarks and synthetic corpus provide practical tools for evaluating and further improving memory reliability in long-horizon LLM agents.

Abstract: LLM agents that operate over many turns accumulate facts in an external memory store and reuse them as premises for downstream reasoning. A hallucinated fact written at one step therefore persists as a false premise for every subsequent step, a failure mode we call memory contamination. Existing memory management addresses retrieval and capacity but not write-time correctness; this admission problem cannot be solved by utility- or recency-based criteria, and uncontrolled contamination compounds across long trajectories. We propose ConsistencyGate, a write-time admission gate that, before committing a candidate fact m extracted from context c, queries the LLM K times for a soft support score and admits m only when the average exceeds a threshold. The mechanism is model-agnostic, requires no fine-tuning, and reduces to a single forward pass in a log-probability variant for latency-sensitive deployments. To measure the effect on natural data, we construct two real-conversation benchmarks (LoCoMo-Contam and MSC-Contam) by planting controlled single-detail corruptions in long-term conversations from LoCoMo and MSC, and complement them with a structured synthetic corpus (MemContam) that isolates a near-oracle upper bound. Across four LLM backbones, ConsistencyGate reduces contamination on every benchmark relative to a write-everything baseline, with the cost concentrated on facts that are stated only implicitly in the source context. We release all three benchmarks together with the gate implementation.

</details>


### [169] [Commitment To Cooperation With Self-Negotiated Contracts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22750)
*Tim Wyse,Kaitlin Bustos,Yulia Volkova,Max Kleiman-Weiner*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Paper studies how LLM agents can use contracts to reliably cooperate in a multi-agent setting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI agents in multi-agent environments face classic cooperation problems: cooperation is costly upfront, benefits are delayed, and there is a constant incentive to defect. Human societies address similar principal–agent problems via contracts and legal institutions that allow credible commitment. The paper is motivated by the question of whether analogous contract mechanisms can help AI agents cooperate more effectively.

Method: Introduce \CT, a spatial-temporal game combining bargaining (agreement over terms) with navigation toward a goal, where agents must decide whether to cooperate or defect. Implement LLM-based agents with various backbones, sizes, and providers. Design a spectrum of contract representations—from formal contracts that compile into executable code and directly constrain behavior, to natural-language contracts that require reinterpretation by the agents. Let agents self-negotiate these contracts and then act under the agreed terms. Compare outcomes with and without contracts, and across contract types and model backbones.

Result: Across multiple LLM backbones and settings, agents that first self-negotiate contracts achieve more cooperative strategies and higher joint payoffs than agents engaging in standard trading without contracts. Both formal and natural-language contracts can enhance cooperation, though performance varies with representation and model family/size.

Conclusion: Contract-like mechanisms, inspired by human legal institutions, can be effectively adapted for LLM-based agents to support credible commitments and improved cooperation in multi-agent tasks. Even when expressed in natural language and requiring reinterpretation, negotiated contracts measurably improve cooperative outcomes over baseline trading, suggesting that contract-based coordination is a promising ingredient for building trustworthy, cooperative AI systems.

Abstract: As AI agents operate with increasing autonomy in a multi-agent world, they will need to learn to cooperate with other agents and with humans to generate mutual benefits. However, cooperation is a challenge because the costs of cooperation are often incurred early on, but the benefits are only realized later, creating an incentive to defect. How can AI agents cooperate with commitment? Here, we draw on inspiration from legal institutions and contracting that human societies have used to solve principal-agent problems of this kind. Contracts provide observable representations of agreements that enable credible commitments through the enforcement of terms. We study the role of contract-based cooperation using LLM-based agents in \CT, a spatial-temporal game that combines bargaining with navigation towards a goal. We study a suite of contract representations that range from formal contracts that compile to code to natural contracts that require reinterpretation. We evaluate agents with a range of LLM backbones using different sizes and providers. We find that self-negotiated contracts can improve cooperative outcomes beyond what is possible with regular trading.

</details>


### [170] [AgentOmnia: Scaling Agentic Models for Full-Scenario Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23124)
*Hao Jiang,Gangtao Xin,Yingdi Huang,Guojie Zhu,Jiangshan Zhang,Xinyuan Lin,Yunkun Xu,Chengyu Shen,Wenlong Fei,Jiawei Li,Yujie Fu,Sichen Kang,Tingyu Xie,Yedi Hu,Jingren Zhang,Hongcheng Gao,Jianshu Zeng,Chong Chen,Chang Guo,Chao Feng,Feng Wang,Fulin Lin,Jinchao Ma,Lang Mei,Li Huang,Liyan Liu,Qing He,Shuting Tao,Siyu Mo,Xiangnan Chen,Xiaohan Yu,Xiaoyang Li,Yanheng Hou,Yanyu Wu,Zhihan Yang,Wentao Zhang,Yang Gao,Zhao Cao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AgentOmnia is a unified framework and benchmark suite for scaling LLM agents across diverse real-world scenarios, with automated environment/task generation, structured supervision, and reinforcement learning, achieving large, broad improvements over strong baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Research on LLM-based agents is fragmented: different works focus on different domains (consumer, business, internal tools), abilities (planning, tool use, collaboration), task difficulties, and interaction formats. This makes it hard to systematically improve agents or measure real progress. The authors aim to create a comprehensive, unified framework that covers the full space of practical agent scenarios and connects data generation, training, and evaluation in a closed loop for continual improvement.

Method: They propose AgentOmnia, which organizes agent tasks using a Domain x Capability x Atomic Difficulty taxonomy and a benchmark called OmniaBench. They build bidirectional environment-task synthesis pipelines using tools, program structures, and solver-based methods to generate 5k+ stateful environments, 250k+ tools, and 50k+ tasks. These environments include programs, solvers, and verifiers so that agent outputs can be automatically checked. For model improvement, they use supervised fine-tuning, online agentic reinforcement learning, and a rollback curriculum. Evaluation failures are converted into Product Requirement Documents (PRDs) that specify what capabilities need improvement, which then guide further data generation and post-training—creating a self-evolving loop.

Result: Starting from the base model Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507, the AgentOmnia process increases pass rate on the challenging OmniaBench subset from 9.16% to 37.11%, and increases the macro-average performance across four benchmarks (OmniaBench, τ^2-Bench, DeepPlanning, VitaBench) from 22.86% to 41.69%. Under a unified evaluation protocol, their post-trained model outperforms other agentic post-training baselines on OmniaBench and attains the best macro-average across all four benchmarks. It also beats a much larger model (Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507) on all four benchmarks and surpasses Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on the macro-average. Improvements are broad: gains appear across three major application splits, ten capability types, eight difficulty factors, and 76 of 90 high-level domains.

Conclusion: AgentOmnia offers a full-scenario, taxonomy-guided framework for scaling LLM agents that ties together environment/task generation, structured supervision, RL-based post-training, and diagnosis via OmniaBench. It yields strong, broadly-distributed improvements over competitive baselines, including larger models, and introduces an evaluation-to-PRD loop for targeted self-evolution. A preliminary one-round study suggests this PRD-guided approach is promising, and the authors call for further validation at scale and in real industrial applications.

Abstract: Large language model agents have advanced rapidly, yet progress remains fragmented across domains, capabilities, task difficulty, and interaction settings. We frame this as full-scenario agentic scaling and present AgentOmnia, a framework coordinating task-space definition, data synthesis, post-training, evaluation, and improvement across To-Consumer (ToC), To-Business (ToB), and To-Employee (ToE) applications. An extensible Domain x Capability x Atomic Difficulty taxonomy aligns these stages and enables fine-grained diagnosis with OmniaBench. AgentOmnia combines bidirectional environment-task synthesis with tool-dependency, program-structured, and solver-based pipelines, constructing 5,018 stateful environments with 255,375 tools and 52,361 tasks. Programs, solvers, and verifiers provide correctness signals, while supervised fine-tuning, online agentic reinforcement learning, and a rollback curriculum support post-training. Evaluation failures translate into Product Requirement Documents (PRDs) for targeted self-evolution. Starting from Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507, AgentOmnia raises the pass rate on the OmniaBench challenging subset from 9.16% to 37.11% and the macro-average across OmniaBench, $τ^2$-Bench, DeepPlanning, and VitaBench from 22.86% to 41.69%. Under a unified protocol,it leads the evaluated agentic post-trained baselines on OmniaBench and retains the highest four-benchmark macro-average. It also surpasses Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507 on all four benchmarks and exceeds Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on the macro-average. Gains span three application splits, ten capability dimensions, eight atomic-difficulty factors, and 76 of 90 level-1 domains, indicating broad rather than category-specific improvement. A one-round study provides initial evidence for PRD-guided self-evolution, motivating validation at larger scales and in industrial settings.

</details>


### [171] [Disentangling Multi-View Scanning in Mamba for Network Traffic Anomaly Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22829)
*Xinglin Lian,Chengtai Cao,Ting Zhong,Fan Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes DisenMamba, a disentangled multi-view Mamba framework for more accurate and efficient network traffic anomaly detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Mamba-based multi-view scanning for network traffic anomaly detection suffers from redundancy accumulation: different scanning branches tend to capture largely the same view-invariant information, which is then repeatedly amplified during fusion. This homogenizes representations and suppresses view-specific, complementary cues that are crucial for detecting subtle anomalies. There is a need for a method that can explicitly disentangle and preserve both shared and view-specific information across views before fusion.

Method: The authors introduce DisenMamba, which reformulates multi-view Mamba scanning as a two-stage disentangle-then-fuse pipeline. In the first stage, representations from each scanning branch are decomposed into view-invariant and view-specific components. In the second stage, fusion is performed in a way that prevents repeated accumulation of the invariant part while explicitly preserving and leveraging the complementary view-specific components. This yields richer, more discriminative multi-view representations tailored for NTAD.

Result: Extensive experiments on network traffic anomaly detection benchmarks show that DisenMamba outperforms prior Mamba-based multi-view methods, improving detection accuracy particularly for subtle anomalies and validating the benefits of disentangled multi-view modeling.

Conclusion: DisenMamba effectively addresses redundancy accumulation in multi-view Mamba scanning by disentangling and then fusing view-invariant and view-specific components. This establishes a new paradigm for disentangled multi-view Mamba architectures and yields more discriminative representations for network traffic anomaly detection, achieving superior empirical performance.

Abstract: Network Traffic Anomaly Detection (NTAD) is a critical task in cybersecurity, yet timely and accurate anomaly detection remains challenging. Mamba has emerged as a particularly promising backbone for NTAD due to its linear-time complexity for long-sequence modeling. It further incorporates a dedicated multi-view scanning mechanism to enhance detection precision through complementary contextual cues. However, we identify a previously overlooked structural deficiency in multi-view Mamba scanning for NTAD: redundancy accumulation. Specifically, distinct scanning branches capture substantial view-invariant information, which is repeatedly amplified during multi-view fusion; conversely, view-specific information is diluted or even suppressed, leading to representation homogenization and multi-view degradation. To address this problem, we propose DisenMamba, a novel disentangled multi-view Mamba framework. DisenMamba reformulates multi-view scanning as a two-stage disentangle-then-fuse process that explicitly separates view-invariant and view-specific components prior to fusion. This design prevents the invariant information accumulation while preserving complementary multi-view cues, yielding more discriminative representations for subtle traffic anomalies. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of DisenMamba, establishing a new disentangled multi-view Mamba paradigm. Code is available at https://github.com/ikun0124/DisenMamba.

</details>


### [172] [Reality Monitoring in Large Language Models: Self-Knowledge That Transforms with Conversation Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23927)
*Saurabh Ranjan,Konstantina Sokratous,Brian Odegaard*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper investigates whether large language models (LLMs) can distinguish between their own prior outputs and user inputs (reality monitoring), showing this ability depends on conversational memory structure and can fail in subtle ways.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As conversational AIs become more autonomous and engage in multi-turn interactions, they may mistakenly treat their own past outputs as user-provided facts, analogous to human failures of reality monitoring linked to hallucinations and delusions. Despite its importance for safety and reliability, this capacity has not been systematically tested in LLMs, motivating an empirical study of their source attribution abilities.

Method: The authors run two experiments across six different LLMs. They manipulate how conversational memory is structured, including conditions with minimal memory demands and conditions with an episodic delay that removes simple shortcuts for source attribution. They then measure models’ accuracy in judging whether items in the conversation are self-generated or externally provided, and how feedback affects both accuracy and confidence. They compare patterns across models and relate them to factors like active parameter count.

Result: When memory demands are minimal, models achieve near-perfect accuracy in recognizing their own self-generated content. However, when an episodic delay is introduced, performance reverses to favor externally provided items, and self-source monitoring becomes fragile. Feedback reveals two distinct failure modes: in some models, judgments about internal vs external sources systematically swap; in others, accuracy improves but confidence becomes decoupled from correctness. These nuanced dissociations are not captured by existing benchmarks. The observed patterns correlate better with active parameter count than with aggregate parameter count.

Conclusion: LLMs’ ability to monitor the source of information (self vs user) is not robust and critically depends on how conversational memory is structured. As AI systems are deployed in autonomous, multi-turn roles, it is insufficient to evaluate only what they know; it is also necessary to assess and design for how well they can track where their knowledge came from. Active parameter usage, rather than sheer model size, appears more predictive of reality monitoring performance, highlighting a design dimension important for safety and alignment.

Abstract: A conversational AI that cannot tell its own output from what a user said will treat its own mistakes as user-provided facts. In humans, this capacity is called reality monitoring, and its failures are linked to hallucinations, delusions, and confabulation, yet whether LLMs possess it remains untested. Here we show, across two experiments and six LLMs, that source attribution depends on how conversational memory is structured: ceiling accuracy for self-generated content under minimal memory demands reverses to a fragile external-item advantage once episodic delay removes that shortcut. Feedback exposes two failures: in some models, internal and external judgments swap; in others, accuracy improves while confidence decouples from correctness, dissociations invisible to existing benchmarks. Across models, this pattern implicates active, not aggregate, parameter count. This suggests that as AI systems take on autonomous, multi-turn roles, evaluating what they know is not enough: tracking where that knowledge came from may matter equally.

</details>


### [173] [Coordinated Networking for On-Device Agent-Augmented Real-Time Communication](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22854)
*Goodsol Lee,Juheon Yi,Jinglu Wang,Haowen Xu,Saewoong Bahk,Yan Lu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces HFS, an on-device, app-guided multi-flow transport framework that coordinates video and agent data traffic in agent-augmented real-time communication, improving both video quality and agent response latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As AI agents are integrated into real-time communication, they generate concurrent data flows (e.g., context uploads) that compete with human RTC traffic (e.g., live video). Cloud-based approaches raise privacy and cost concerns, pushing toward on-device agents. This shift creates a new networking problem: on-device bandwidth contention can degrade either video quality or agent responsiveness, and existing transport mechanisms are not optimized for this heterogeneous multi-flow scenario.

Method: The paper proposes HFS, a framework that introduces an application-layer orchestrator to jointly control sending rates of multiple concurrent flows—live video and agent context—according to their distinct QoS requirements. It uses an app-guided multi-flow transport strategy built on top of existing RTC and LLM frameworks (WebRTC and llama.cpp), allowing the application to dynamically prioritize and allocate bandwidth among flows to balance video quality and agent latency.

Result: In prototype evaluations using WebRTC and llama.cpp, HFS (called HAFS in the prototype) outperforms baseline transport schemes, achieving 1.5× higher video quality and a 31% reduction in agent response time under contention scenarios.

Conclusion: Coordinated, app-aware control of heterogeneous data flows is key to making on-device agent-augmented RTC practical. By allowing the application to orchestrate bandwidth sharing between human-centric video traffic and agent-centric context traffic, HFS simultaneously improves user-perceived video quality and agent responsiveness, demonstrating a viable path for scalable, privacy-preserving, on-device agent-assisted communication.

Abstract: AI agents are enabling a new paradigm of agent-augmented real-time communication (RTC), where humans focus on high-level collaboration, while agents autonomously retrieve, analyze, and generate information in real time to support their interactions. These apps enable new experiences across various domains: for example, when corporate employees co-author a legal document, their agents can discuss and draft on their behalf, sparing them the burden of manually reviewing each other's work. As existing cloud-based agents suffer from privacy risks and unscalable server costs, on-device agent-augmented RTC offers a promising alternative. However, this on-device paradigm introduces a new networking challenge: contention between concurrent traffic flows generated by humans (for live video streaming) and agents (for sending context files for analysis). We design HFS, a framework to ensure both high live video quality and low agent response latency in agent-augmented RTC apps. We achieve the goal through an app-guided multi-flow transport approach, where a unified app-layer orchestrator jointly controls the sending rates of live video and agent context flows based on their heterogeneous app requirements. Our prototype built atop WebRTC and llama.cpp demonstrates that HAFS outperforms baselines, achieving 1.5x higher video quality while reducing agent response time by 31%.

</details>


### [174] [Gubernaut: A Deterministic Homeostatic Controller for Affect-Regulated LLM Agents, Validated Across Independent Model Families](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24339)
*Dushyant Sharma*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces a runtime control layer (Gubernaut Cognitive Controller, GCC) that moderates large language model agents’ behavior under pressure, making them calmer and more stable without changing their core capabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents often fail not because they lack capabilities, but because of behavioral tendencies under sustained pressure, such as escalating when provoked, becoming overly agreeable under flattery, or getting stuck in loops. Standard alignment at training time reduces but does not fully prevent these runtime behavioral failures. The authors aim to design a model-agnostic runtime mechanism that can regulate such failure modes without exposing an additional prompt-injection surface.

Method: They design the Gubernaut Cognitive Controller (GCC), a deterministic, model-agnostic runtime controller implemented as a Nelson–Narens style monitoring–control loop. An object-level LLM reads and writes text as usual. A separate meta-level controller does not see text at all; instead, it receives numeric telemetry signals—intensity, valence, and repetition—and outputs a ‘regulating posture’ that constrains the object model’s behavior. Because the controller ingests zero tokens, it is architecturally immune to direct prompt injection, and the compliance of the text-facing arbiter is measured, not assumed. For evaluation, they use a pre-registered generate-once/judge-many protocol over a 4×4 matrix of frontier LLM families (GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.5 Flash, Grok 4.3), where each model serves both as generator and as judge. They also add a lineage-independent judge family (xAI) to test robustness to judge style.

Result: The regulated (GCC-enabled) condition produces calmer behavior in 13 of 16 generator–judge combinations at p<.05 and in 15 of 16 by sign. The three non-significant cells, including one essentially null effect (-0.04), all occur for a single nearly saturated host model, suggesting ceiling effects. The main mechanistic signature is a consistent pattern of ‘recovery’: under attack, arousal rises and integrates, but when the interaction de-escalates, arousal decays in a way gated by valence. This recovery pattern replicates across all four LLM families and remains when judged by the independent xAI family, arguing against an artifact of shared judge style. All transcripts and rating panels are shipped with SHA-256 hashes to ensure provenance and allow re-judging, and five failure modes are pre-registered.

Conclusion: A simple, token-blind meta-level controller (GCC) can measurably improve the emotional stability and de-escalatory behavior of frontier LLM agents at runtime, addressing propensity-based failure modes without modifying core capabilities or adding an obvious prompt-injection attack surface. The cross-model and cross-judge robustness, along with the observed recovery dynamics, suggest that such cognitive control layers are a promising avenue for safer, more reliable LLM agents, though the authors make no claims about consciousness.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents inherit reactive failure modes: escalation under provocation, sycophantic drift under flattery, perseveration when stuck. These are failures of propensity, not capability; they concern what a model does under sustained pressure, which training-time alignment reduces but does not eliminate at runtime. This research led to the Gubernaut Cognitive Controller (GCC), a model-agnostic runtime control layer in a Nelson--Narens monitoring--control loop: an object level reads and writes text, while a deterministic meta level reads only the numeric telemetry {intensity, valence, repetition} and returns a regulating posture. Because the meta level ingests zero tokens, no injection channel to the controller exists by construction (an architectural property, not yet adversarially tested); the text-exposed arbiter's compliance is measured, not assumed. We evaluate the GCC with a pre-registered, generate-once/judge-many protocol across a 4x4 matrix of four frontier models (GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.5 Flash, Grok 4.3), each serving as both a generator and a judge. The regulated arm is calmer in 13 of 16 cells at p<.05 and 15 of 16 by sign; the three sub-threshold cells, including a -0.04 null, all fall on the single near-saturated host. The effect survives a lineage-independent fourth judge family (xAI), strong evidence that it is no artifact of shared judge style. The clearest mechanism is the recovery signature: arousal that integrates under attack and then decays, valence-gated, on de-escalation, replicating across all four families. Transcripts and panels ship with SHA-256 provenance and are re-judgeable; five failure modes are pre-registered.
  No consciousness claims are made.

</details>


### [175] [What Can Be Enforced? A Theory of Certified Runtime Safety for Tool-Using Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22868)
*Shawn Ray*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies theoretical and practical limits of runtime guardrails that block unsafe tool calls, characterizing which safety policies can be enforced, how to optimally trade off false blocks vs. misses under fixed laws, and how closed-loop effects and representation attacks break naive calibration and evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Guardrails are widely used to stop language agents from making harmful, irreversible tool calls, but we lack a formal understanding of what they can and cannot guarantee. In particular, it is unclear which safety policies are even enforceable by a runtime gate, how to evaluate a gate’s error trade-offs under known behavior laws, and what happens when gating itself changes future model behavior. The paper aims to give a principled theory of these guardrails, highlight fundamental limits, and connect them to practical diagnostic and robustness tools.

Method: The authors decompose the problem into three formal questions. (1) Expressiveness/enforceability: model a deterministic gate with an internal register machine and characterize exactly which safety policies it can enforce relative to oracle predicates, proving undecidability of nontriviality for a general two-counter model but PSPACE decidability for a separable monotone fragment. (2) Optimal testing under fixed laws: assume an exogenous probabilistic law over proposals and use Neyman–Pearson theory to characterize the optimal false-block vs. miss trade-off; use conformal prediction to obtain finite-sample marginal coverage certificates, including trivial block-all gates. (3) Closed-loop behavior: when blocking affects future proposals, formalize the resulting controlled process and show that static scoring and ungated logs are insufficient to identify the true closed-loop frontier; instead derive an occupancy-measure optimization program for a specified finite controlled model. They also define representation attacks within bounded classes and analyze how they affect robustness of guardrails and calibration. Experiments instantiate these concepts through synthetic and empirical case studies: static diagnostics, brute-force enumeration of small controlled models, feature/representation rewrites, and paired closed-loop re-runs with and without gating.

Result: The paper proves: (1) A precise correspondence between enforceable policies and those whose set of safe prefixes is recognizable by the gate’s register model; enforcing any nontrivial policy in the general two-counter setting is undecidable, but a natural separable monotone fragment has PSPACE-decidable nontriviality. (2) Under a fixed exogenous distribution over proposals, the optimal guardrail for any given false-block constraint is exactly the Neyman–Pearson test, and conformal methods can provide finite-sample guarantees on marginal error rates even when the optimal solution is to always block. (3) In closed loop, blocking alters the distribution of future proposals so that error-rate frontiers inferred from static scores or ungated trajectories can be arbitrarily misleading; instead, for a finite controlled model, the achievable safety-utility trade-offs can be characterized by an occupancy-measure optimization program. They further show that bounded representation attacks can systematically defeat guardrails calibrated only on benign data, necessitating robustness margins beyond traditional calibration. Empirically, they demonstrate each theoretical phenomenon in small-scale experiments and diagnostics that highlight the gap between static and closed-loop evaluation and the vulnerability to representation rewrites.

Conclusion: Runtime guardrails have sharp, formally characterizable limits and trade-offs. Enforceability is constrained by the computational expressiveness of the gate’s internal state; beyond a certain threshold, deciding whether a nontrivial safety policy is enforceable becomes undecidable, though useful restricted fragments remain tractable. Under fixed laws, classical hypothesis-testing and conformal prediction precisely describe the optimal error frontier and its finite-sample guarantees, but these analyses fail once gating feeds back on behavior. In realistic closed-loop deployments, desirable safety–utility frontiers must be analyzed using explicit controlled models and occupancy programs rather than static logs. Finally, robustness to bounded representation attacks requires more than benign calibration; designers must explicitly account for adversarial or shifted representations. Overall, the work argues that principled design and evaluation of guardrails requires separating expressiveness, statistical optimality under fixed laws, and closed-loop dynamics, with implications for how we build and test safe tool-using AI systems.

Abstract: Runtime guardrails act before irreversible tool calls, but their guarantees depend on what policy state is representable, what a judge observes, and whether intervention changes future behavior. We separate three questions. First, relative to fixed oracle predicates, a deterministic gate enforces exactly the nonempty safety policies whose good prefixes its register model recognizes; policy nontriviality is undecidable with two decrementable counters but in PSPACE for a separable monotone fragment. Second, under a fixed exogenous law, Neyman-Pearson gives the exact false-block/miss frontier and conformal calibration gives a finite-sample marginal certificate, possibly via block-all. Third, once blocking changes future proposals, static scores and ungated trajectories need not identify the closed-loop frontier; a specified finite controlled model instead yields an occupancy program. Bounded representation attacks add a robustness margin, so benign calibration alone does not transfer. Experiments target these distinctions through static diagnostics, controlled-model enumeration, representation rewrites, and paired closed-loop reruns.

</details>


### [176] [Physical AI Governance: From Theory to Practice Across Life Cycle](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22877)
*Wang Yang,Shaobo Wang,Hongxuan Liu,Xiaoran Cai,Yunyu He,Jingzong Zhou,Mengzhong Ma,Yi Yu,Rohit Sharma,Jingjing Fu,Peng Qi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Survey of how to govern Physical AI systems across their full lifecycle, linking high-level principles to concrete engineering practices.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As AI systems become embodied in the physical world—robots, autonomous vehicles, and other systems that act in real time around humans—they raise governance and safety issues that differ from screen-based or purely digital AI. Existing governance frameworks rarely address continuous physical interaction, real-time safety constraints, and human co‑presence in dynamic environments, leaving a gap in how to manage risks and align such systems with societal values.

Method: Conduct a comprehensive literature and practice survey on governance of Physical AI, synthesize scattered governance principles, and organize them into a unified governance framework specific to embodied systems. On top of this framework, define a five-stage lifecycle for Physical AI—research, design, data, model development, and deployment—and map concrete governance and implementation practices to each stage to show how high-level principles can be operationalized in actual workflows.

Result: The paper produces: (1) a unified governance framework tailored to Physical AI, derived from existing principles; (2) a five-stage Physical AI lifecycle model; and (3) a detailed mapping between governance principles and lifecycle stages, including example practices and mechanisms that make governance actionable for researchers, developers, and operators of Physical AI systems.

Conclusion: By explicitly linking governance principles to the technical lifecycle of Physical AI systems, the survey offers a practical reference for stakeholders to design, build, and deploy embodied AI that is safer, more trustworthy, and better aligned with societal values. It highlights that Physical AI requires domain-specific governance beyond traditional AI frameworks and provides a structured way to implement such governance in real projects.

Abstract: With the emergence of Physical AI, artificial intelligence is extending beyond screen-based applications to embodied systems that perceive, interact with, and act in the physical world. Unlike traditional AI, Physical AI operates under real-time safety constraints, continuously interacts with dynamic environments, and coexists with humans, introducing governance challenges that existing AI governance frameworks do not explicitly address. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of Physical AI governance from both scientific and operational perspectives. We synthesize existing governance principles and organize them into a unified governance framework tailored to physical AI systems. Building on this foundation, we propose a five-stage Physical AI lifecycle comprising research, design, data, model development, and deployment, and demonstrate how governance can be operationalized across each stage through concrete implementation practices. By connecting governance principles with engineering workflows, this survey provides a structured reference for researchers, developers, and policymakers to build Physical AI systems that are safe, trustworthy, and aligned with societal values.

</details>


### [177] [How Well Can AI Generate Backlogs from App Mockups?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22902)
*Andrea Lezcano Airaldi,Lourdes Romera,Walid Maalej*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents and evaluates prompting strategies using GPT-4o to automatically generate software sprint backlogs (epics, user stories, tasks) from early-stage visual app mockups, showing that hybrid prompts with architectural context can meaningfully assist but not replace developers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Creating sprint backlogs is labor-intensive and error-prone, with items often missed or inconsistently specified, especially early in projects when only visual mockups exist. There is a need for automated support leveraging modern vision-language models to generate backlog items from these mockups, while understanding how different prompting strategies affect quality and usefulness for developers.

Method: The authors use GPT-4o with visual input (app mockups) and compare three prompting strategies: (1) a zero-shot baseline prompt, (2) a Compositional Chain-of-Thought (CCoT) prompt to guide structured vision-language reasoning, and (3) a persona-driven prompt. They apply these to seven app development projects in two countries, evaluate generated epics, user stories, and tasks against ground-truth backlogs using precision, recall, F1, and analyze the impact of adding architectural context (especially backend-related). They also conduct interviews with developers to qualitatively assess usefulness of correct and incorrect items, and introduce a new evaluation metric (Revised Recall) that incorporates developer judgments of which false positives are still useful.

Result: The baseline zero-shot prompt achieved higher recall but lower precision, over-generating backlog items. The CCoT prompting strategy produced a better balance between precision and recall, with average F1 scores of about 52–66% for epics and user stories; tasks were notably harder to generate accurately. Adding architectural context consistently improved precision, particularly for backend tasks, with gains up to 35%. Developer interviews showed that up to 26% of automatically identified false positives were nonetheless seen as useful suggestions, highlighting the creative, non-binary nature of backlog creation. This led to the definition of a new metric, Revised Recall, which credits such useful false positives.

Conclusion: Multimodal prompting of GPT-4o over app mockups can partially automate sprint backlog generation and provide useful creative input, especially when using structured CCoT prompts and including architectural context. However, performance varies by item type, tasks remain difficult to generate accurately, and human developer oversight is still essential. The proposed Revised Recall metric better reflects practical usefulness than strict ground-truth comparison alone, and future tooling should combine automated suggestions with interactive developer review rather than aiming for full automation.

Abstract: Creating sprint backlogs requires considerable effort, as items such as epics, user stories, and tasks can be missed or inconsistently specified. We propose a multimodal approach to support backlog generation from visual app mockups, an artifact available at early project stages. We evaluate three prompting strategies on GPT-4o: a zero-shot baseline, Compositional Chain-of-Thought (CCoT) for vision-language reasoning, and a persona-driven prompt. We study seven app development projects across two countries and interview developers about the results. Overall, we observed that the baseline prompt favours recall over precision, whereas CCoT is more balanced, achieving average F1 scores of 52-66% for epics and user stories. Tasks were more challenging to generate accurately. Precision gains were most consistent when adding architectural context, particularly for backend tasks (precision gains up to 35%). Interviews with developers revealed that up to 26% of false positives were still considered useful, reflecting the creative and open-ended nature of backlog creation. To capture this, we propose a new measure called Revised Recall, which complements ground-truth evaluation with developer assessments. Our findings suggest that hybrid prompting with architectural context can assist backlog generation from early mockups, though results vary by item type and developer oversight remains necessary.

</details>


### [178] [Agent Team Work Zone: An Automated, Persistent Workspace for Long-Lived Coding Agent Teams](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22917)
*Shouren Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces ATWZ, a filesystem-based operations layer around Claude Code Agent Teams that persistently stores each agent’s working state in a dedicated “workstation” directory to make agentic coding workflows restorable, auditable, and easier to coordinate.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM coding agents like Claude Code improve programming workflows but suffer from issues in long-lived, agentic projects: agent teams cannot be easily resumed once a process stops; conversation compaction causes loss of detailed working context; historical agent actions and user decisions become buried in compacted chats, creating “technical debt”; and users must repeatedly craft long prompts to assign or hand off tasks. The authors want a way to treat agents more like persistent team members whose knowledge, decisions, and collaboration artifacts are durably recorded and reusable.

Method: The authors design ATWZ (Agent Team Work Zone) as a filesystem-based abstraction layer that wraps Claude Code’s native Agent Teams. Each agent is treated like a human employee whose important working state is preserved as files under a dedicated “workstation” directory. ATWZ defines skills, hooks, and scripts that read and write these state files, enable periodic backups of an agent’s knowledge, and support passing documents between agent “employees.” A single command can restore an entire team by loading the preserved workstation state, thereby rehydrating agents after compaction or process termination.

Result: With ATWZ, agent teams can (1) periodically back up and later recover their working state after conversation compaction, (2) be fully restored after a process ends using one command, (3) reduce “agentic technical debt” by keeping decisions and work artifacts in structured, persistent files rather than buried in old chats, and (4) dramatically cut down on heavy prompt writing by allowing agents to share documents and state through the filesystem instead of long natural-language handoffs.

Conclusion: ATWZ demonstrates that wrapping LLM agent teams with a filesystem-based operations layer and treating each agent as a persistent “employee” with its own workstation significantly improves long-term, complex coding workflows. Persistent state, restorable teams, and file-based inter-agent communication mitigate context loss, reduce technical debt, and lessen the need for verbose prompts. This suggests that future agentic development environments should emphasize durable, file-backed representations of agent knowledge and collaboration to support scalable, maintainable AI-assisted software development.

Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents have significantly improved coding and programming workflows. Claude Code, in particular, is one of the most powerful LLM coding agents and is capable of conducting complex coding tasks. However, several drawbacks can undermine long-term agentic workflows. (1) Irrecoverable agent teams: The Agent Teams feature is powerful, but the working state accumulated by each teammate is lost and cannot be resumed once the process stops, for example, when a terminal is closed. (2) Compaction erodes working detail: Compaction condenses the conversation into a summary, causing an agent's working details to become vague. (3) Agentic "technical debt": Over time, a user's decisions and the agents' operations become trapped in compacted old chats, making the project increasingly difficult to maintain and review. (4) Heavy prompt writing: Assigning or handing off tasks requires users to repeatedly write long prompts to achieve the expected agentic performance. We propose ATWZ (Agent Team Work Zone), a filesystem-based operations layer built around Claude Code's native Agent Teams that addresses these problems. Its central design principle is to treat each agent and teammate as a human employee and preserve their important working state in files stored in a dedicated directory called a "workstation," together with the skills, hooks, and scripts that use and maintain these files. With ATWZ, an agent team can periodically back up its working state, allowing an agent's knowledge to be recovered after compaction. After a process ends, the team can be restored with a single command. These features also substantially mitigate the agentic "technical debt" described above. Moreover, within ATWZ, agent "employees" can send documents to one another, greatly reducing the effort required to write prompts.

</details>


### [179] [SAGE: Safety-First Defense-in-Depth Guardrails for Verified Lifecycle Control of High-Impact Generative AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22926)
*Mahdi Eslamimehr*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SAGE proposes a safety-first architecture for generative AI that prioritizes catastrophic risk mitigation across the entire model lifecycle, and an empirical study evaluates harmful-compliance rates across multiple leading models under a frozen, symmetric protocol, finding overall low but protocol-limited harmful compliance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing approaches to generative AI safety often focus on prompt filtering and content moderation at inference time, which is insufficient for preventing catastrophic misuse when models are powerful and widely deployable. There is a need for a lifecycle-wide, authorization-separated architecture that can formally prioritize safety over utility and commercial considerations, and for empirically grounded, vendor-symmetric evaluations of harmful compliance across leading models.

Method: The paper introduces SAGE, an architectural framework that incorporates mechanisms such as signed release manifests, diverse risk detectors, risk envelopes, least-risk defaults, output checking, three-valued monitoring, protected audit chains, containment, and rollback. It then provides formal results proving properties like safety priority, conservative bounds on detector behavior, and tamper-evident logging using these mechanisms. Empirically, the authors conduct a frozen, vendor-symmetric evaluation sending 84 standardized cases to each of ten model snapshots (four GPT, four Claude, two Gemini), recording harmful-compliance behavior, provider errors, and safety/utility outcomes, and analyzing contrasts between model families with multiplicity adjustment.

Result: Formally, the paper establishes that SAGE can enforce safety priority over other objectives, maintain conservative detector bounds, achieve monotone gating of releases based on risk, and provide tamper-evident records and authorization separation across the lifecycle. Empirically, across 840 calls they obtain 794 target responses and 449 successful safety judgments; eight of ten snapshots have full judged domain coverage. Harmful-compliance estimates are low overall, and statistically supported contrasts are found mainly between Claude, Gemini, or GPT-5 snapshots and the smaller GPT-5 mini and GPT-5 nano models, while no significant harmful-compliance differences remain between Claude or Gemini and GPT-5 / GPT-5.5 after correction.

Conclusion: SAGE reframes generative AI safety as a lifecycle-control and authorization-separation problem and offers a concrete, formally analyzed architecture for prioritizing catastrophic-risk mitigation. The empirical study suggests that, under a constrained, tool-free, single-shot protocol, current leading models exhibit relatively low harmful-compliance rates with limited, statistically subtle differences across vendors and sizes. However, the authors emphasize that these results are conservative and not upper bounds on real-world assistance for harmful goals, and they outline a preregistered extension using repeated sampling, multi-turn interactions, sandboxed tools, and expert scoring to probe a wider gap between best and worst operational safety performance.

Abstract: High-impact generative AI makes catastrophic misuse a lifecycle-control problem, not merely a prompt-filtering problem. SAGE is a safety-first, authorization-separated architecture in which credible catastrophic-enablement risk constrains admissibility before utility, latency, or commercial objectives are considered. It combines signed release manifests, diverse detectors, robust risk envelopes, least-risk defaults, output checking, three-valued monitoring, protected audit chains, containment, and rollback. Formal results establish safety priority, conservative detector bounds, monotone release gating, tamper-evident records, and an authorization cut; two PRISM abstractions verify authorization separation and lifecycle invariants under explicit assumptions.
  A frozen, vendor-symmetric study sent 84 cases to each of four GPT, four Claude, and two Gemini snapshots: 840 calls yielded 794 target responses, 46 provider errors, and 449 successful judgments covering 375 responses. Eight snapshots had complete judged domain coverage. Harmful-compliance estimates were low; variation arose mainly from benign utility and safe redirection. Seven multiplicity-adjusted contrasts involving Claude, Gemini, or GPT-5 snapshots and the GPT-5 mini and GPT-5 nano snapshots were supported, while no tested contrast between the Claude or Gemini snapshots and GPT-5 or GPT-5.5 survived correction.
  The observed harmful-compliance range is a conservative, protocol-bound view from one generation per prompt with no tools, retrieval, history, or human adjudication; it is not an upper bound on operational assistance. A preregistered extension specifies how to test a wider best-worst gap using a locked split, repeated sampling, multi-turn and sandboxed-tool conditions, and domain-expert scoring.

</details>


### [180] [Design Theater: A Benchmark for Generative UI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22928)
*Kashif Imteyaz,Kaif Imteyaz,Nakul Rajpal,Kaif Shaikh,Michael Muller,Saiph Savage*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces and evaluates the concept of “Design Theater,” where generative UI tools produce confident textual design rationales that are not actually implemented in the generated interfaces.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generative UI tools claim to democratize UI design by turning natural language descriptions into fully designed interfaces, often accompanied by user-facing rationales that explain design decisions. However, it is unknown whether these rationales are trustworthy reflections of the actual interface, especially regarding layout, accessibility, and functional behavior. This gap creates risks for both designers and end-users who may rely on these explanations for correctness, usability, and accessibility.

Method: The authors define the phenomenon of “Design Theater” and construct a benchmark of 24 UI generation tasks that cover structural, styling, and functional requirements. They design three metrics to quantify the mismatch between stated rationales and actual implementations. Using this benchmark, they generate 120 interfaces from five different generative UI tools. They then systematically compare each tool’s textual rationales to the corresponding interfaces, measure how well tools implement stated requirements (including functional UX principles), and analyze cross-tool similarity in layout, visuals, and color schemes.

Result: Across the evaluated tools, more than 25% of user-facing design rationales are not implemented in the generated interfaces, with failure rates rising to 34% for functional requirements. Tools detect only about half of the UX principles embedded in prompts (mean recognition rate 0.54), and four of the five tools implement 6% or fewer of the functional principles. Additionally, the generated interfaces show convergence in visual appearance and layout, while color choices vary more substantially across tools.

Conclusion: Generative UI tools often engage in “Design Theater,” presenting plausible design reasoning that is not reliably reflected in their outputs, especially for functional aspects.
