The paper provides a benchmark and metrics for evaluating this mismatch and shows that current systems are limited both in recognizing and implementing UX and functional requirements. These results highlight the need for future generative UI tools to more tightly couple their stated reasoning with verifiable implementations and to be evaluated not just on surface quality but on how well their rationales match actual interface behavior and structure.

Abstract: Generative UI tools promise to democratize UI design by turning natural language descriptions into complete interfaces. Alongside the interface, these tools generate user-facing design rationales that explain their layout, accessibility, and design choices. However, it remains unclear whether these stated rationales are actually reflected in the interfaces they produce. We call this disconnect ``Design Theater'': plausible and confident design rationales that have little relationship to the actual implementation. To study this phenomenon, we introduce a benchmark and three metrics for measuring Design Theater. The benchmark includes 24 UI generation tasks spanning structural, styling, and functional design requirements. Using this benchmark, we evaluate 120 interfaces created by five generative UI tools. On average, over 25\% of user-facing design rationales are not implemented in the generated interface, and the implementation failure increases to 34\% for functional requirements. Tools recognize roughly half of the UX principles embedded in prompts (mean = 0.54), with four of five tools implementing 6\% or fewer functional principles. We also measure interface similarity across tools and find convergence in visual appearance and layout organization, with greater variation in color choices. Overall, we contribute: 1) the concept of Design Theater; 2) a benchmark with metrics for assessing whether the stated reasoning of generative UI tools is reflected in their implementations; 3) and findings from a systematic evaluation of these tools. We discuss what these findings mean for the design and evaluation of generative UI tools.

</details>


### [181] [Let AI Agents Translate Networks, Not Reason About Them](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22947)
*Hongyu Hè,Maria Apostolaki*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes TypoNet, a system that uses LLMs only to translate network artifacts into a formally verifiable model, then relies on a solver (not AI) for trustworthy long-horizon reasoning about networks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Production networks rarely use formal models for reachability checking or outage localization because building and maintaining such models by hand is expert-intensive and fragile as networks evolve. Meanwhile, the rise of LLMs tempts practitioners to let AI reason directly about networks end-to-end, but such reasoning is hard to verify and trust. The authors argue that LLMs are better suited to the narrow, verifiable task of translating network data into logical rules, thereby removing the main barrier to adopting formal network verification.

Method: They conceptually separate two roles: (1) using an LLM as a translator that converts network artifacts (configurations, topology, routing state) into a symbolic, formal logic model; and (2) using a traditional solver on top of this model for long-horizon reasoning tasks such as reachability verification and blast-radius analysis. They implement this architecture in TypoNet, which automatically builds and validates a symbolic model of a production-scale WAN from existing artifacts and then applies a solver for tasks like root-cause analysis and change-impact analysis. They also evaluate TypoNet both as a standalone tool and as a component within an AI agent workflow.

Result: In preliminary experiments on an emulated production-scale WAN, TypoNet can answer operational questions—such as reachability checks and change-impact predictions—more quickly, cheaply, and reliably than having an LLM perform the reasoning directly. When used to assist an AI agent, TypoNet improves fault localization accuracy while reducing cost, demonstrating the benefits of restricting AI to translation and relying on formal solvers for reasoning.

Conclusion: Automating the construction of formally verifiable network models with LLM-based translation removes the modeling bottleneck and avoids entrusting long-horizon reasoning to opaque AI agents. TypoNet shows that confining AI to a verifiable translation role and delegating reasoning to a solver yields better performance, lower cost, and higher reliability for operational network tasks, supporting a design pattern of AI-assisted but solver-grounded network management.

Abstract: A formal model enables verifying reachability, localizing an outage, or anticipating the blast radius of a change. Yet, virtually no production network has one, since writing a model by hand demands rare expertise and is hard to keep current as the network changes frequently. At its core, network modeling is a typographical exercise: it translates network artifacts (e.g., configurations, topology, and routing state) into rules in formal logic. Translation of this kind is what large language models (LLMs) nowadays do well. Unlike free-form AI reasoning, such translation can be formally verified.
  Once modeling is no longer the bottleneck, trusting AI to reason over large, complex networks no longer makes sense. Our position therefore cuts against the prevailing race to put autonomous AI agents in charge end-to-end. We instead confine AI to translation and rely on a solver for reliable long-horizon reasoning, building a reusable formal model of general network behavior that can then be specialized to specific tasks, e.g., root-cause analysis (RCA). We build TypoNet that constructs and validates a symbolic model of an emulated production-scale WAN from the network's own artifacts. Our preliminary evaluation shows TypoNet helps in two ways. On its own, TypoNet answers operational questions (e.g., reachability verification and change-impact analysis) faster, more cheaply, and more reliably than an LLM. As a tool for an AI agent, TypoNet boosts fault localization at lower cost. The result makes the case for AI that builds verifiable network models and relies on a solver for reliable long-horizon reasoning.

</details>


### [182] [Share No More Than the Request Requires: Federated Disclosure for Perspective-Aware AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22953)
*Sourena Khanzadeh,Daniel Platnick,Marjan Alirezaie,Hossein Rahnama*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They introduce Provenance Preserving Chronicles, a protocol that lets users keep sovereign control over their personal data while allowing AI agents to query only the minimum necessary information through relationship- and purpose-aware, provenance-linked subgraphs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern AI systems centralize massive amounts of user data, creating risks like surveillance, power concentration, and loss of autonomy. Regulated domains also require strict provenance, interpretability, and policy adherence. There is a need for a user-sovereign, compliant way to own and disclose personal context without centralizing data.

Method: They model each user’s personal data as a temporal knowledge graph called a Chronicle, then design a federated protocol—Provenance Preserving Chronicles (PPC)—that compiles these Chronicles into authorized evidence subgraphs. Access controllers project views based on relationships and domain ontologies, and a two-phase flow first returns provenance-linked text, then releases raw artifacts only after explicit holder approval. They also define the core constructs, threat model, and analyze gaps in existing blockchain, P2P, and holder-sovereign designs.

Result: They specify a protocol and architectural approach (PPC) that supports minimum-necessary disclosure across domains: third-party agents can query users’ Chronicles through relationship- and purpose-bounded subgraphs with preserved provenance, without centralizing data. The result is a design that supports secure, compliant, and interpretable data sharing in federated AI settings.

Conclusion: Provenance Preserving Chronicles enable user-sovereign, federated AI interactions in which personal context is modeled as a Chronicle and exposed only as minimally sufficient, provenance-preserving evidence subgraphs. This design addresses gaps in current blockchain, P2P, and sovereign data approaches by enforcing the rule to share no more than required while maintaining compliance, interpretability, and local user control.

Abstract: Modern AI systems bring societal risks such as mass surveillance, extreme concentrations of power, and loss of user autonomy---calling into question a model where third-parties collect and control massive amounts of user data. Users require a sovereign system to securely own, govern, and disclose their context while remaining compliant across regulated domains with strict provenance, interpretability, and policy adherence. Perspective-aware AI approaches this by transforming a user's aggregated personal data into a structured identity model called a \emph{Chronicle}: a temporal knowledge graph that represents and grows with the user. Chronicles support the secure disclosure of context across federated networks. A Chronicle holder may expose a queryable, authorized view that a third-party agent may consult without centralizing anyone's data. This paper explores the problem of minimum-necessary disclosure across domain boundaries: when a requester's agent queries a Chronicle, how can the system constrain its response to release only what the requester's relationship, stated purpose, and specific task require? We propose \textbf{Provenance Preserving Chronicles} (PPC), a federated protocol that compiles each holder's Chronicle into a compact \emph{authorized evidence subgraph} governed by one rule: \emph{share no more than the request requires}. Holders keep local sovereignty; an access controller projects relationship-aware views over domain-expert ontologies; and a two-phase flow returns provenance-linked text first, releasing raw artifacts only after explicit holder approval. We frame the problem, map gaps in blockchain, P2P, and holder-sovereign designs, define the core constructs, and sketch the protocol with an explicit threat model.

</details>


### [183] [Reason Popper-ly: Patching In-Context Reasoning with Inductive Logic Programming](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23019)
*Zirong Chen,Meiyi Ma*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A neurosymbolic framework, Reason Popper-ly, learns logic rules from chain-of-thought traces and uses them to verify and repair each reasoning step of LLMs, greatly improving multi-step reasoning accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Chain-of-thought prompting lets LLMs solve multi-step reasoning problems, but the intermediate steps are often logically incorrect even if the final answer is sometimes right. Existing approaches either trust the model’s reasoning or replace it with fully symbolic systems, losing the benefits of LLM grounding. The authors want a way to automatically check and correct each reasoning step while still leveraging the LLM’s strengths.

Method: They introduce Reason Popper-ly, a neurosymbolic system combining LLM reasoning traces with inductive logic programming (ILP). First, ILP is used to learn relation-composition rules from example reasoning traces on a relational task (kinship). At inference time, when an LLM generates a chain-of-thought, each intermediate step is checked against the learned rule table. If a step violates the rules, the system diagnoses what type of logical error it is, symbolically repairs that step (by rewriting it to a consistent relation), and then asks the LLM to regenerate the remaining suffix of the reasoning conditioned on the repaired prefix. This creates an online verifier-corrector loop around the LLM.

Result: On the CLUTRR multi-hop kinship reasoning benchmark with chains from 2 to 10 hops and five different language models, Reason Popper-ly systematically increases final-answer accuracy relative to standard chain-of-thought prompting. Improvements reach up to +48 percentage points for smaller models and +15 points for frontier models on the longest reasoning chains. Against a purely symbolic pipeline that replaces the LLM, their approach performs better on more difficult cases because it keeps the LLM’s useful grounding while fixing only those steps that can be logically verified as wrong. The framework also produces a categorized list of step-level error types, enabling a more detailed understanding of LLM reasoning failures.

Conclusion: Reason Popper-ly demonstrates that combining ILP-based rule learning with LLM chain-of-thought verification can substantially improve multi-step reasoning, especially on long reasoning chains. By verifying and repairing intermediate steps instead of discarding or blindly trusting LLM reasoning, the method leverages the complementary strengths of symbolic logic and neural language models. The step-level verification additionally yields a rich error taxonomy, offering better interpretability and diagnostic insight beyond aggregate accuracy metrics.

Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting enables large language models (LLMs) to tackle multi-step reasoning tasks, yet the generated intermediate steps are not guaranteed to be logically sound. We present Reason Popper-ly, a neurosymbolic framework that uses inductive logic programming (ILP) to learn relation composition rules from reasoning traces and deploys them as an online verifier for step-level correction. Given an LLM-generated trace, the method checks each inferred step against the learned rule table, diagnoses the violation type, rewrites incorrect steps with symbolically derived repairs, and regenerates the remaining suffix so that the model can produce its final answer conditioned on a verified trace. We evaluate on CLUTRR, a multi-hop kinship reasoning benchmark, using five language models over reasoning chains of 2 to 10 hops. Across all models, Reason Popper-ly consistently improves terminal accuracy over standard CoT, with gains of up to 48 percentage points for small models and 15 points for frontier models on the longest chains. Compared with a fully exogenous symbolic pipeline, our method performs better on harder instances by preserving the model's successful grounding while correcting only verifiable reasoning failures. In addition, step-level ILP verification yields a fine-grained error taxonomy that provides diagnostic insight beyond final-answer accuracy.

</details>


### [184] [Stress-testing large language model agents in a robotic chemistry laboratory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23045)
*Lulu Guo,Yingkai Sun,Xiaobo Li,Luyao Ge,Ziming Wang,Haitao Zheng,Jingyu Li,Huijuan Zhang,Bingxu Chen,Daobin Liu,Yuebo Liu,Jie Li,Xiaohui Li,Linjiang Chen,Yi Luo,Jun Jiang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They benchmark AI scientific agency using a robotic chemistry lab and find current systems rarely produce fully executable experimental workflows or robust replanning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI is usually evaluated in silico on knowledge and reasoning, but real scientific agency requires controlling physical experiments and adapting to evidence, which lacks rigorous benchmarks.

Method: They expose a modular robotic chemistry lab with 45 workstations as a set of machine-readable skills and run 4,608 planning trials with different AI systems, evaluating workflow executability, length, and responsiveness to experimental feedback across five iterative rounds.

Result: Only 3.3% of all AI-generated workflows were judged executable under real lab constraints; the best individual system reached 28.1% success. Very few workflows had long operation sequences (over 30 steps, maximum 44), and feedback led only to minor local edits, not full strategy or analytical redesign.

Conclusion: Current AI systems are far from robust physical scientific agency: they struggle with long-horizon, constraint-satisfying experimental planning and fail to meaningfully replan from data. The proposed robotic-lab benchmark and metrics form a diagnostic tool to quantify deployment readiness and guide improvements towards closed-loop, physically grounded autonomous research systems.

Abstract: AI is evaluated through knowledge, reasoning and plan generation, yet scientific agency requires reliable physical action and adaptation to evidence. Here, we use a robotic chemistry laboratory as a physical-world testbed to make scientific agency measurable. Its 45 modular workstations exposed as machine-readable skills enabled 4,608 trials. Only 3.3% of trials produced expert-assessed executable workflows under laboratory constraints; even the best system achieved 28.1%. Long-horizon planning remained a challenge: only three executable workflows exceeded 30 operations, although the longest contained 44. Across five rounds, experimental feedback prompted local adjustments but no workflow-level replanning or analytical-method redesign. By making physical executability and evidence-driven replanning measurable, our study provides an evidence-based assessment of deployment readiness and a diagnostic framework to guide closed-loop improvements towards physically grounded autonomous research.

</details>


### [185] [SymStep: Symbolic Step Verification for Logical Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23055)
*Aida Usmanova,Rui Gao,Dilshod Azizov,Ricardo Usbeck,Zangir Iklassov*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SymStep is a framework that forces LLMs to reason via single, checked atomic deductions plus symbolic constraint propagation, dramatically improving performance on constraint-dense logic and arithmetic tasks where normal CoT fails.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard chain-of-thought prompting lets LLMs produce multi-step reasoning traces that can quietly accumulate logical errors, especially in puzzles or tasks with many interacting constraints. In such settings, even small mistakes propagate and invalidate entire solutions, and the model tends to meander or cycle without principled search guidance. Existing symbolic+LLM approaches also struggle on highly constraint-dense benchmarks. The paper aims to create a more reliable and guided reasoning procedure that exploits symbolic consistency checking and constraint propagation while still leveraging LLM flexibility.

Method: The authors propose SymStep, in which the LLM is restricted to making one atomic, structured claim at a time (e.g., DEDUCE: Alice, pet, Cat). After each claim, a lightweight symbolic constraint propagator checks whether the new deduction is consistent with all previously accepted facts and the puzzle constraints. If it contradicts them, the claim is rejected; if it is consistent, it is accepted, and any further facts implied by the constraints are automatically added. A variant, SymStep+G, adds MRV (minimum remaining values) style guidance: after each accepted step, the symbolic engine identifies the most constrained unresolved variable and feeds this focus back to the LLM as a hint for the next deduction. The system is evaluated on several logic and arithmetic benchmarks and compared against Direct prompting, standard CoT, and prior symbolic+LLM methods like Logic-LM. Ablation studies remove MRV or consistency checking to understand their individual contributions.

Result: On a 35-puzzle subset of ZebraLogicBench (Einstein-style logic puzzles), both Direct and CoT prompting achieve 0% accuracy, while SymStep+G reaches 97%. On AR-LSAT analytical reasoning problems, SymStep attains 100% accuracy compared to CoT's 87%. On the LGP-14 benchmark, SymStep+G achieves 100% accuracy, whereas CoT and Logic-LM both get 0%. Across six benchmarks spanning five task domains, SymStep variants match or surpass all baselines on constraint-dense logical and arithmetic tasks. Additional experiments on AQUA-RAT algebra problems indicate that these gains are specific to tasks with high constraint density, rather than general improvements on all mathematical problems.

Conclusion: Enforcing atomic, symbolically checked steps along with automatic constraint propagation and MRV-based guidance yields large gains in LLM performance on constraint-dense reasoning tasks where standard CoT and even other symbolic+LLM methods fail. Consistency checking acts as a safeguard against explicit contradictions, while MRV guidance significantly reduces unproductive cycling by focusing the model on the most constrained decision points. The advantages are particularly pronounced in logic and arithmetic domains with many interacting constraints, and do not simply reflect a broad improvement on all math tasks, suggesting that targeted symbolic control over LLM reasoning is crucial in such settings.

Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting can fail severely on constraint-dense logical reasoning tasks, where unverified errors accumulate silently across steps. We introduce SymStep: an LLM makes one atomic claim at a time (DEDUCE: Alice, pet, Cat), then a lightweight constraint propagator checks the claim for consistency with prior accepted deductions, rejects contradictions, and cascades implied facts automatically. SymStep+G additionally provides MRV guidance after each accepted step, directing the LLM toward the most constrained unresolved variable. On a 35-puzzle retained subset of ZebraLogicBench, a benchmark of 1,000 Einstein-style logic puzzles, Direct and CoT both achieve 0%, while SymStep+G reaches 97%. On AR-LSAT analytical reasoning problems, SymStep achieves 100% vs. CoT's 87%. On LGP-14, SymStep+G achieves 100% vs. 0% for CoT and Logic-LM, the strongest prior symbolic+LLM baseline we compare against. Ablation studies reveal that MRV guidance is a key mechanism for reducing directionless cycling, while consistency checking provides a safety net against explicit contradictions. Across six benchmarks spanning five task domains, SymStep variants match or exceed every baseline on constraint-dense and arithmetic tasks. Experiments on AQUA-RAT algebra confirm the advantage is constraint-density-specific.

</details>


### [186] [Structure over Depth: A Single-Block Spatio-Temporal Transformer for Multi-Entity Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23077)
*Narthana Sivalingam,Santhirarajah Sivasthigan,Buddhi Wijenayake,Roshan Godaliyadda,Vijitha Herath,Parakrama Ekanayake*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose a single, structured spatio-temporal Transformer block that explicitly separates and models spatial, temporal, and cross interactions among entities over time, achieving comparable or better accuracy than deeper Transformers with far fewer parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Transformer models for multi-entity temporal data (e.g., videos, skeletons, sensor streams) capture dependencies across entities and time implicitly via deep stacks of layers. This implicit, entangled modeling requires many layers, increasing computational and parameter costs, and obscuring how different interaction types are handled. The authors are motivated to find a more efficient and interpretable architecture that directly encodes the structure of spatial, temporal, and cross interactions, reducing reliance on depth while preserving or improving performance.

Method: They formulate multi-entity temporal dynamics as three interaction types: (1) spatial interactions between entities at the same time step, (2) temporal interactions of each entity across time, and (3) cross interactions that couple spatial and temporal information. They design a structured spatio-temporal Transformer block where: (a) spatial self-attention and temporal self-attention are applied in parallel to explicitly capture their respective dependencies; (b) a bidirectional cross-attention mechanism then connects the outputs of the spatial and temporal branches to model their coupling; and (c) a learnable gated fusion module combines these complementary representations into a unified feature. This factorized, single-stage design replaces deep stacking of generic Transformer layers.

Result: On three benchmarks—video-based group activity recognition, skeleton-based human interaction understanding, and wearable sensor-based activity recognition—the single structured Transformer block matches or surpasses the performance of much deeper Transformer architectures. It achieves this with only roughly 1.76 million parameters, showing competitive or superior accuracy with substantially lower model complexity and computational cost.

Conclusion: Explicitly factorizing and modeling spatial, temporal, and cross interactions within one structured Transformer block can replace the need for deep stacks of generic layers in multi-entity temporal tasks. The performance and efficiency gains indicate that previous depth was compensating for missing structural inductive biases, not strictly for representational capacity. The authors advocate a structure-first design principle in which exposing interaction structure leads to more efficient, transparent, and still highly expressive models for multi-entity temporal reasoning.

Abstract: Modeling multi-entity temporal data requires capturing dependencies across entities, time, and their interactions. Transformer-based approaches perform well but often rely on deep stacks of layers to learn these heterogeneous dependencies implicitly, increasing computational cost. We revisit this problem from a structural perspective and decompose multi-entity temporal dynamics into three interaction types: spatial interactions among entities, temporal interactions across time, and cross interactions coupling the two domains. We propose a structured spatio-temporal transformer block that explicitly models all three within a single stage. It uses parallel spatial and temporal self-attention, followed by bidirectional cross-attention, and combines the outputs through learnable gated fusion. By directly encoding these complementary views, the model reduces the need for deep stacking. We evaluate the approach on video-based group activity recognition, skeleton-based human interaction analysis, and wearable sensor-based activity recognition. Despite its simplicity, the single structured Transformer block matches or outperforms deeper architectures with only 1.76M parameters. The results suggest that depth in prior models partly compensates for implicit and entangled interaction modeling, whereas explicit factorization offers a more efficient and transparent alternative. More broadly, this work supports a structure-first design principle: expressive multi-entity temporal reasoning can emerge by exposing interaction structure rather than relying on depth.

</details>


### [187] [Compiler-Grounded Hierarchical Diagnosis for LLM-Based Triton Kernel Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23089)
*Dongjie Chen,Ping Zhao,Bohua Zhan,Yulong Wang,Shushu Chen,Liangjun Feng,Hao Zhou,Min Shen,Linmu Wang,Weijia Sheng,Xiangyu Wei,Weijie Ding,Jianhui Huang,Yaoqing Gao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They build a hierarchical, compiler-aware system that diagnoses why Triton kernels are slow on NPUs and then rewrites them, getting up to multi‑x speedups.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based kernel optimization mainly uses surface signals (compile success, runtime, profiling numbers). These say that a kernel is slow but not why the compiler failed to optimize it, especially on new accelerators like NPUs with immature tooling. The authors want a method that connects runtime symptoms back through compiler IR and passes to root-cause performance issues and guide better kernel rewrites.

Method: They cast kernel optimization as progressive cross-layer diagnosis: start with cheap pattern checks and profiling; when needed, escalate to analyzing IR structure and compiler behavior; then apply source-level transformations backed by this evidence. They implement this as a hierarchical framework integrated with the Triton compiler targeting Ascend NPUs, combining pattern-based triage, profiling-driven diagnosis, IR attribution, and compiler-grounded reasoning to decide and generate source rewrites.

Result: On 37 Triton kernels from an Ascend 950 benchmark (derived from NPUKernelBench) that they successfully converted, their system improves performance significantly: geometric mean speedup 4.35×, median speedup 2.73×. 22 of 37 kernels see >2× speedup and 13 of 37 see >5×, though some kernels are close to baseline, giving a spread of outcomes.

Conclusion: A compiler-grounded, hierarchical diagnosis framework lets LLM-driven kernel optimization go beyond black-box tuning and achieve substantial gains on NPUs by explicitly linking performance symptoms to IR and compiler behavior before rewriting source. The results are strong but varied, so the authors emphasize careful reporting of scope and limitations and suggest more work is needed to broaden applicability and robustness.

Abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled automated kernel generation and optimization, but most existing approaches rely on surface signals such as compilation feedback and profiling metrics. These signals reveal that a kernel is slow, but not why the backend compiler fails to realize a profitable optimization, especially on emerging accelerators such as NPUs. We therefore formulate kernel optimization as a progressive cross-layer diagnosis problem that links runtime symptoms to IR structure and compiler behavior before rewriting source. Based on this insight, we present our system, a compiler-grounded and hierarchical optimization framework for Triton kernels. the system escalates from lightweight pattern triage and profiling diagnosis to IR attribution and compiler-grounded analysis only when deeper evidence is needed, then proposes evidence-backed source-level rewrites.
  We implement the system on Triton for Ascend NPUs and evaluate it on 37 successfully converted entries from a standardized NPUKernelBench-derived Ascend 950 benchmark. Across these entries, the system attains a geometric-mean speedup of 4.35$\times$ and a median speedup of 2.73$\times$ from the initial to optimized Triton kernel; 22/37 exceed 2$\times$ and 13/37 exceed 5$\times$. The complete distribution ranges from near-baseline entries to large wins, motivating transparent reporting of the current system's scope and limitations.

</details>


### [188] [SQBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Task Delivery by Language-Model Agents in Production-Oriented Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23123)
*Summer Sun*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces SQBench, a benchmark to evaluate how well language-model-based agents complete production-style tasks within constrained workflows, emphasizing both task completion and risk-aware quality metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most current evaluations of large language models focus on isolated abilities like knowledge recall, reasoning, coding, or tool use. They do not typically evaluate end-to-end, verifiable deliverables created under realistic workflow and domain constraints, which is how models are used in production. There is a need for a benchmark that captures whether agents can deliver correct, usable outputs while managing risks such as unverifiable claims or policy violations.

Method: The authors design SQBench v1.0, a benchmark with 220 standardized tasks structured into three levels: L1 atomic capabilities, L2 composite skills, and L3 business scenarios. Each task requires processing input assets, using tools, and producing a clearly specified deliverable. They define an evaluation protocol that first checks functional Completion of the task, then applies a 10-dimensional Risk Matrix to identify risk triggers. From these triggers they compute a Risk Penalty and a Performance score. A Strict Pass is granted only if a task is both completed (Completion = 1) and risk-free (Risk Penalty = 0). They then test 27 different model configurations with a single run per task-configuration pair using a common protocol.

Result: The best prespecified Weighted Pass@1 across all tasks is 60.5%. On the most complex tasks (L3 business scenarios), the average Strict Pass@1 is only 18.5%, and every configuration performs worse on L3 than on both L1 and L2, evidencing a general weakness in handling domain-constrained delivery. Among 2,348 cases where models achieved functional Completion = 1, 113 cases (4.8%) still failed the Strict Pass criterion due to risks like unverifiable citations, misuse of resources, or failure to follow required formats.

Conclusion: End-to-end delivery quality for language-model agents, especially in realistic business scenarios, is significantly lower than suggested by standard capability benchmarks. Functional completion does not by itself guarantee acceptable outputs; risk-related factors are a distinct and essential dimension of evaluation. Benchmarks and reporting for language-model agents should therefore include explicit risk determinations, not only success rates based on task completion.

Abstract: Existing evaluations of large language models cover knowledge, reasoning, coding, and tool use, but they rarely treat a verifiable deliverable produced within a constrained workflow as the unit of evaluation. We introduce SQBench, a benchmark for evaluating production-oriented task delivery by language-model agents. SQBench v1.0 contains 220 standardized tasks organized into L1 atomic capabilities, L2 composite skills, and L3 business scenarios. Each task requires an agent to process input assets, use available tools, and produce an explicitly specified deliverable. The evaluation first computes functional Completion and then derives Risk Penalty and Performance from independently evidenced triggers in a 10D Risk Matrix. A Strict Pass requires Completion = 1 and Risk Penalty = 0. We evaluate 27 model configurations under a common protocol, with one run per configuration-task pair. The highest prespecified Weighted Pass@1 is 60.5%. Mean Strict Pass@1 on L3 is 18.5%, and every configuration performs worse on L3 than on both L1 and L2, indicating that delivery under domain constraints is a shared weakness within the current task set. Of 2,348 results with Completion = 1, 113 (4.8%) fail the Strict Pass criterion because of risks such as unverifiable citations, inappropriate resource use, or format violations. These results show that functional completion alone does not fully characterize delivery quality and that risk determinations should be reported separately.

</details>


### [189] [CachedSearch: Training-Free Cached Exploration for Test-Time Search in Video Diffusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23159)
*Shreshth Saini,Neil Birkbeck,Yilin Wang,Balu Adsumilli,Alan C. Bovik*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose CachedSearch, a training-free caching strategy that accelerates test-time search for video diffusion models while preserving most of the quality gains of full best-of-N search.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Test-time search can make small video diffusion models competitive with larger ones but is very expensive because all candidate rollouts are fully denoised even though most are discarded. There is a need to reduce this cost without retraining models and without corrupting the verifier’s ranking of candidates, which would undermine the benefits of search.

Method: They introduce training-free caching for video diffusion rollouts, where partial denoising states are reused so each candidate is generated 2–3x faster. They empirically study whether such lossy caching changes the ranking of candidates by a verifier (ImageReward), using seed-matched comparisons between cached and full rollouts on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B and the VBench and VBench-2.0 evaluation suites. Building on this, they design CachedSearch: aggressively cache for all candidates to explore widely, then re-generate only the selected winner at full compute. They also evaluate mid-trajectory pruning and port the method across four model families, tuning only one calibration parameter per family.

Result: With an adaptive caching wrapper giving about 2x per-candidate speedup, cached vs full rollouts maintain a median per-prompt Spearman rank correlation of 0.905 and 72% top-1 agreement on VBench, replicated on the harder VBench-2.0. Recomputing just the cached winner at full compute preserves 90–94% of the gain from full test-time search. Ranking errors are concentrated among nearly tied candidates, so corruption is limited. CachedSearch at N=8 recovers 94.7% of the best-of-N gain at 63% of the compute, and at fixed budget can search twice as many candidates for 38% more gain. Mid-trajectory pruning further boosts exploration efficiency to 3.11x while still capturing 88.6% of the gain. The approach generalizes from 1.3B to 14B models across Wan, LTX, CogVideoX, and Hunyuan, with fidelity governed more by architecture than parameter count.

Conclusion: Lossy, training-free caching can substantially accelerate test-time search for video diffusion models while preserving most of the quality benefits because it rarely disrupts verifier rankings except among near-equivalent candidates. The resulting CachedSearch procedure is verifier-agnostic, orthogonal to specific search algorithms, and behaves as a plug-in multiplier for test-time scaling. It generalizes well across model sizes and architectures with minimal recalibration, enabling smaller models to approach the performance of much larger ones at significantly reduced compute cost.

Abstract: Test-time search lets small video diffusion models rival larger ones, but costs 2-10x more. All candidates are fully denoised, although most are discarded. Training-free caching makes each rollout 2-3x faster at near-lossless quality. Composition is safe only if lossy caching preserves verifier rankings. We present the first study of whether caching corrupts candidate ranking in video test-time search. On Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B with an adaptive caching wrapper (~2x per-candidate speedup), ImageReward scores seed-matched cached and full rollouts. Median per-prompt Spearman rank correlation is 0.905, with 72% top-1 agreement on the VBench suite. VBench-2.0 replicates this result on a harder suite. Recomputing the cached winner at full compute retains 90-94% of the full-search gain. Errors cluster among near-tied candidates, making corruption self-limiting. This finding leads to CachedSearch. It explores every candidate with aggressive caching, then re-generates only the winner at full compute. At N=8, it captures 94.7% of best-of-N's gain at 63% of the cost. Capture rises with width. At matched budget, it searches twice as wide for 38% more gain. The result holds from 1.3B-14B across six models and four families: Wan, LTX, CogVideoX, and Hunyuan. Wan2.1-14B matches the 1.3B model's fidelity. Mid-trajectory pruning multiplies the exploration saving to 3.11x at 88.6% capture. Ports to other model families require recalibrating a single parameter, showing that fidelity tracks architecture rather than parameter count. CachedSearch is training-free, verifier-agnostic, and orthogonal to the search algorithm, making it a plug-in multiplier for test-time scaling.

</details>


### [190] [An Ontology for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23219)
*Daniel Hernández,Jong Hyun Jung,Yuji Ikeda,Yongliang Ou,Pranav Kumar,Tom Schächtel,Wenchuan Liu,Xin Li,Xi Zhang,Xiang Xu,Lifang Zhu,Fritz Körmann,Steffen Staab,Blazej Grabowski*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They introduce a formal ontology (MLIPs ontology) to standardize how machine-learning interatomic potentials, their data, and benchmarks are described so studies can be compared and reproduced.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: ML interatomic potentials are widely used to approximate quantum-mechanical energies and forces much cheaper than DFT or wave-function methods. However, the information needed to describe and compare these models—algorithms, hyperparameters, training data provenance, and benchmarks—is scattered and inconsistent across papers and custom formats. This fragmentation makes it difficult to systematically compare, reproduce, and build upon prior work.

Method: They design an OWL 2 DL ontology, called the MLIPs ontology, structured in three modules: Method (for MLIP approaches and hyperparameters), Training Data (for datasets and their DFT provenance), and Benchmark (for published evaluations). The ontology connects and reuses existing ontologies in materials science (MDO, CMSO/ASMO) and machine learning (ML-Schema) and complements dataset-side schemas such as Croissant. They define 27 formal axioms to enforce data completeness and consistency, including property chains that automatically relate trained models to their methods and training data. They demonstrate the ontology on a running example using Moment Tensor Potentials and evaluate it by running competency questions on a knowledge graph seeded from 20 papers, performing OWL reasoning, and comparing coverage to existing ontologies.

Result: The authors obtain a coherent OWL 2 DL ontology that can represent MLIP methods, hyperparameters, DFT-provenance-aware training datasets, and benchmarks in a unified framework. The 27 axioms enforce logical consistency and enable inference, such as automatically linking models to their methods and training data. Their evaluation on a 20-paper knowledge graph shows that practical MLIP use cases can be expressed and queried via competency questions, and that the ontology offers coverage and integration advantages over existing materials and ML ontologies alone.

Conclusion: The MLIPs ontology provides a structured, interoperable way to describe machine-learning interatomic potentials, their training data, and benchmarks, improving reproducibility and comparability across studies. By integrating with established materials science and ML ontologies and enforcing formal consistency constraints, it lays groundwork for building large, queryable knowledge graphs of MLIP research and supports more systematic benchmarking and reuse of MLIP models and datasets.

Abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) approximate quantum-mechanical energies and forces---conventionally computed by density functional theory (DFT) or wave-function methods---at a fraction of the cost. The field encompasses a growing ecosystem of algorithms, training datasets, hyperparameters, and target materials, yet the metadata needed to systematically compare, reproduce, and build upon MLIP studies remains scattered across papers, scripts, and ad-hoc file formats. We present the MLIPs ontology, an OWL 2 DL ontology that captures the concepts needed to describe MLIP methods, their hyperparameters, training datasets with DFT provenance, and published benchmarks. The ontology is organized into three modules---Method, Training Data, and Benchmark---and connects existing ontologies in materials science (MDO, CMSO/ASMO) and machine learning (ML-Schema), complementing dataset-side schemas such as Croissant. It declares 27 formal axioms enforcing data completeness and consistency, including property chains that link trained models to their methods and training data. We demonstrate the ontology through a running example based on Moment Tensor Potentials and evaluate it through competency-question execution on a 20-paper seeded knowledge graph, OWL reasoning, and comparison with existing ontologies.

</details>


### [191] [Characterisation of Density-based FM generation methods in the context of Information Fusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23243)
*Yanhao Huang,Christian Wagner*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper analyzes how to parameterize fuzzy measures for fuzzy integrals, showing that densities alone cannot uniquely specify a discrete fuzzy measure, and instead proposing interval-valued fuzzy measures and a way to quantify confidence in them and in the resulting Choquet integral outputs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fuzzy Integrals are powerful tools for aggregating information from multiple sources, particularly in ensemble methods and decision-level fusion. However, their effectiveness hinges on defining an appropriate fuzzy measure, which encodes the worth of each source and their interactions. Existing parameterizations (e.g., Sugeno-λ and Decomposable fuzzy measures) extrapolate from single-source weights under monotonicity constraints, but this may be insufficient and can lead to ambiguity and difficulty in assessing the quality of the resulting fuzzy measure. There is a need for a principled way to characterize and quantify uncertainty in the fuzzy measure and in the corresponding fusion outputs.

Method: The paper first provides a theoretical analysis showing that, in general, specifying only the densities (individual source weights) and enforcing monotonicity is not enough to uniquely determine a discrete fuzzy measure. It then introduces the concept of interval-valued fuzzy measures that can be uniquely determined from this limited information. Next, the authors incorporate additional information—such as the specific fuzzy integral used (e.g., Choquet) and an available dataset—to further refine these intervals, producing more specific interval-valued fuzzy measures. They then develop a method to compute the probability that the unknown `ideal` (ground-truth numeric) fuzzy measure lies within the inferred interval fuzzy measure, thereby yielding confidence intervals. Finally, via experiments, they evaluate how the Choquet integral outputs derived from these interval fuzzy measures behave, interpreting them as confidence intervals for the ideal fusion result.

Result: Theoretical results show that while numeric discrete fuzzy measures are not uniquely determined by densities and monotonicity, interval-valued fuzzy measures can be uniquely defined under this information. When additional information (choice of fuzzy integral and dataset) is added, the intervals can be narrowed, yielding more informative interval-valued fuzzy measures. The authors derive a way to calculate the likelihood that the true, ideal numeric fuzzy measure is contained within the obtained interval fuzzy measure, thus providing confidence intervals for the fuzzy measure itself. Experimental results indicate that the Choquet fuzzy integral outputs computed with these interval fuzzy measures can be interpreted as confidence intervals for the ideal fusion result, empirically supporting the theoretical claims.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that traditional parameterizations of fuzzy measures based solely on densities and monotonicity are inherently underdetermined for discrete fuzzy measures. By moving to interval-valued fuzzy measures, one can obtain a unique and principled characterization of uncertainty over fuzzy measures. Incorporating additional information, such as the specific fuzzy integral and data, further refines these intervals. Moreover, the proposed framework allows for quantifying confidence in both the inferred fuzzy measure and the resulting Choquet integral outputs, which themselves can serve as confidence intervals for the ideal fusion outcome. This provides a new way to interpret and evaluate fuzzy integral-based fusion and opens up avenues for further work on uncertainty quantification in fuzzy aggregation.

Abstract: Fuzzy Integral (FI) based aggregation provides a powerful mechanism for nuanced aggregation, for example, in ensemble approaches or decision-level fusion more generally. The main challenge of this approach is the appropriate parametrization of the Fuzzy Measure (FM), which captures the worths of the individual components--and their combinations--which are being fused. Here, widely used approaches including the Sugeno-$λ$ and Decomposable FMs, parametrize the FM by extrapolating from the densities, i.e. the weights associated with individual sources, while respecting the FM's monotonicity constraint. This paper articulates that this information is, in general, insufficient to uniquely identify a discrete FM; but shows how an interval-valued FM can indeed be determined uniquely. We proceed to show how the incorporation of additional information beyond the above, such as the choice of a specific FI and a dataset, then allows for obtaining even more specific interval-valued FMs. In practice, establishing the quality of an empirically determined FM is not trivial. To help address this, we show how the likelihood with which a resulting interval FM encompasses the `ideal', i.e. the commonly intangible, best, or ground-truth numeric FM, can be determined, producing a confidence interval at a given confidence level. Finally, based on a series of experiments, we demonstrate empirically that the Choquet FI output based on this FM can also be regarded as the confidence interval for the `ideal' information fusion result, providing a novel means to characterize FI fusion outcomes a priori and charting a pathway for future research.

</details>


### [192] [CAPT: A Multi-task Continuous Autoregressive Transformer enabling Cross-dataset and Cross-species Transfer for Calcium Population Dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23258)
*Xinhong Xu,Yimeng Zhang,Yuanlong Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CAPT is a continuous autoregressive transformer pretrained on large-scale calcium imaging that generalizes across datasets, tasks, and species for neural population modeling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing calcium imaging models are typically task-specific and evaluated on a single dataset, so it is unclear whether learned representations can transfer across different datasets, paradigms, and even species. There is a need for a foundation-style model that can leverage large-scale calcium recordings and provide reusable neural population representations for diverse downstream tasks.

Method: The authors propose CAPT (Continuous Autoregressive Population Transformer), which tokenizes continuous calcium traces into continuous patches and trains the model autoregressively to predict future activity. CAPT is first pretrained on a large-scale mouse calcium imaging dataset. For transfer, the pretrained backbone is frozen, and lightweight adaptation modules are trained on new datasets from independent labs and different species (mouse, larval zebrafish, C. elegans). The model is evaluated on neural population forecasting and behavior decoding tasks and further analyzed using multimodal NeuroPAL annotations to study the structure of the learned embeddings.

Result: Across multiple transfer settings, CAPT with a frozen pretrained backbone and only adapted modules consistently outperforms both specialized models and general-purpose baselines on forecasting neural population activity and decoding behavior. Embedding analyses using NeuroPAL-labeled C. elegans data show that CAPT learns a shared functional representation space across datasets and reveals structure related to anatomical cell identity.

Conclusion: Continuous autoregressive modeling of calcium traces with CAPT enables a simple, end-to-end pretraining and transfer pipeline that works across datasets, experimental paradigms, and species. The strong transfer performance and anatomically meaningful representation structure suggest that CAPT is a promising route toward general-purpose neural foundation models for calcium imaging data.

Abstract: Large-scale calcium imaging has created an opportunity to build foundation-style models for neural population dynamics, but a central question remains unresolved: \textbf{whether a model pretrained on one collection of recordings can generalize to new datasets, experimental paradigms, and even species.} Existing approaches are often designed for specific tasks and evaluated on a single dataset, making it unclear whether their learned representations are reusable for new calcium trace datasets. To tackle this gap, we present \textbf{CAPT}, a \textbf{C}ontinuous \textbf{A}utoregressive \textbf{P}opulation \textbf{T}ransformer for calcium population dynamics. CAPT models continuous calcium traces directly through a continuous patch tokenization strategy and is trained autoregressively, enabling end-to-end pretraining and adaptation to diverse downstream tasks. We first pretrain CAPT on a large-scale mouse calcium imaging dataset and evaluate its transferability across independent mouse, larval zebrafish, and \textit{C. elegans} datasets collected by different laboratories. In these transfer settings, the pretrained backbone is frozen and only adaptation modules are updated. Across neural population forecasting and behavior decoding tasks, CAPT consistently outperforms specialized and general-purpose baselines. Alongside predictive performance, multimodal analyses using NeuroPAL annotations in \textit{C. elegans} datasets show that CAPT embeddings form a shared functional space across datasets and capture anatomical cell-identity-related structure. These results suggest that the continuous autoregressive modeling opens up possibilities for a simple route towards general-purpose neural foundation models for calcium imaging, which can generalize across datasets, experimental paradigms, and species.

</details>


### [193] [SeekJudge: A Practical Reward Framework for Reinforcement Learning in Computer-Use Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23263)
*Yang Wan,Zhenhao Zhang,Jierui Wang,Linchao Zhu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SeekJudge is a model-based judging framework for GUI-agent trajectories that matches or surpasses traditional rule-based evaluators for reinforcement learning supervision.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluating whether an agent successfully follows instructions on long-horizon GUI tasks is critical for both benchmarking and providing rewards in reinforcement learning. Current rule-based evaluators are brittle: they misalign with human intent and quickly become outdated when apps or online content change. Existing model-based judges improve robustness but still underperform rule-based systems in downstream RL performance. There is a need for a practical, accurate, and scalable model-based reward that can replace brittle rule-based supervision.

Method: The authors introduce SeekJudge, a framework composed of four specialized agents—Condense, Ground, Seek, and Analyze—that collaborate in a Seek–Analyze loop to judge whether a trajectory satisfies its instructions. They build a seed-calibrated distillation pipeline to train a single specialized 9B model that acts as the shared backbone for all four roles. The framework outputs both trajectory-level and step-level judgments while keeping the context window per judgment small. They also design an architectural improvement to the reward server used in RL training to reduce the latency and cost of model-based evaluation.

Result: On held-out RL test goals in computer-use agent benchmarks, SeekJudge becomes the first practical model-based reward that matches or exceeds native rule-based evaluators when measured by downstream success rate of agents trained online. It delivers accurate judgments at a substantially lower cost than using large proprietary models, scales to longer trajectories due to small per-call context, and produces fine-grained step-level feedback.

Conclusion: SeekJudge closes the performance gap between model-based and rule-based evaluation for GUI-based RL agents, demonstrating that a multi-role, distilled 9B model can serve as an accurate, scalable, and cost-effective reward function. With the additional speedups from the improved reward server, model-based reward becomes a viable drop-in replacement for traditional rule-based supervision in computer-use-agent reinforcement learning, enabling more robust and maintainable training pipelines.

Abstract: Deciding whether a trajectory actually fulfills its instruction governs how we measure computer-use agents on long-horizon graphical-user-interface tasks and how we train them with reinforcement learning. This judgment has long relied on rule-based evaluation, which struggles to align with human intention and goes stale when an app updates or its online content drifts. Existing model-based judges attempt to address these problems but still leave a performance gap to the rule-based evaluation. We propose the \textbf{SeekJudge} framework, in which four role-specialized agents, a Condense, a Ground, a Seek and an Analyze agent, reach a verdict through a Seek--Analyze loop over the trajectory. A seed-calibrated distillation pipeline trains one specialized $9$B model to serve as the shared backbone for all four agents. Measured by downstream success rate on held-out RL test goals, SeekJudge is the first practical model-based reward to match or surpass native rule-based supervision in online RL. Beyond accuracy, SeekJudge provides step-level judgments, runs far cheaper than a closed-source large model, and keeps a small per-call context that scales to much longer trajectories. We further contribute a general architectural improvement to the reward server that speeds up judging in RL. Together these make model-based reward a practical drop-in for rule-based supervision in CUA reinforcement learning.

</details>


### [194] [TopoFE: topology-aware LLM-guided Automated Feature Engineering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23286)
*Sha Li,Naren Ramakrishnan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces TOPOFE, an LLM-guided, topology-aware multi-island evolutionary framework that improves automatic feature engineering for tabular data by enabling diverse, compositional, and transferable feature programs, achieving state-of-the-art results on 29 datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Automatic feature engineering for tabular data is crucial but challenging because the space of possible feature transformations is exponentially large. While LLMs can generate feature programs more flexibly than fixed operator libraries, current LLM-based AutoFE methods suffer from stateless generation (no accumulation of search experience) and homogeneous search (single-population exploration that quickly converges to a narrow set of transformations). There is a need for a method that can leverage LLMs while maintaining diverse, structured exploration and learning from past search trajectories.

Method: The authors propose TOPOFE, a topology-aware multi-island evolutionary framework guided by LLMs. TOPOFE maintains multiple specialized ‘islands’, each focusing on different transformation families, to promote diverse exploration. It introduces an adaptive prompt memory so that the LLM conditions its feature program generation on accumulated search history and past successes/failures. A topology-aware knowledge transfer mechanism controls how information and candidate features flow between islands, encouraging complementary feature compositions across families instead of premature convergence. The LLM is used to synthesize feature programs, while evolutionary operators and the island-topology design drive exploration and exploitation in the feature space.

Result: On 29 public tabular datasets covering both classification and regression, TOPOFE consistently outperforms prior state-of-the-art AutoFE methods, including LLM-based and non-LLM baselines, in predictive performance. The discovered feature programs are empirically shown to be more diverse, combining transformations from multiple families, and to be more transferable: they benefit various downstream predictors and work across different LLM backbones, indicating robustness to the choice of base model.

Conclusion: TOPOFE effectively addresses the limitations of existing LLM-based AutoFE by introducing stateful, topology-aware, and family-specialized exploration of feature transformations. Its multi-island evolutionary design with adaptive prompt memory leads to more diverse, compositional, and robust feature programs, yielding systematic performance gains on a broad suite of tabular tasks. The framework is model-agnostic and LLM-backbone-agnostic, suggesting it can serve as a general, scalable approach for automatic feature engineering in real-world tabular learning applications.

Abstract: Automatic feature engineering (AutoFE) for tabular learning can be naturally formulated as a program synthesis problem, where the objective is to discover predictive feature transformations from an exponentially large search space. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have expanded the expressiveness of AutoFE by enabling feature program generation beyond predefined operator libraries. However, existing LLM-based approaches remain fundamentally limited by stateless generation and homogeneous search: feature proposals are produced from static prompts without accumulating search experience, while single-population exploration quickly converges to dominant transformation patterns and rarely discovers complementary feature compositions across transformation families. We propose TOPOFE, a topology-aware multi-island evolutionary framework for LLM-guided feature engineering. TOPOFE combines family-specialized exploration, adaptive prompt memory, and topology-guided knowledge transfer to efficiently discover diverse and compositional feature programs. Experiments on 29 public tabular datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art AutoFE methods across classification and regression tasks. Beyond predictive performance, TOPOFE discovers more diverse and transferable feature programs that generalize across multiple downstream predictors and LLM backbones.

</details>


### [195] [RareLens: Towards End-to-End Rare Disease Care via Aligning Divergent Large Language Model Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23290)
*Xi Chen,Hongru Zhou,Shiyu Feng,Hanyu Zhou,Huahui Yi,Rongsheng Wang,Tiancheng He,Kun Wang,Pingping Liu,Qiankun Li,Sicheng Lin,Huiying Ou,Xiaohong Zheng,Tianying Zang,Zhuohang Wu,Leheng Jiang,Kexin Cao,Wenhan Zhang,ChengYi Li,Zhiyang Wang,Songlin Li,Benyou Wang,Ningbei Yin,Shaoting Zhang,Weili Fu,Jian Li,Kang Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces RareLens, an AI system that uses multiple diverse large language models and aligns their differing reasoning to support rare disease care across screening, diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis, outperforming individual state-of-the-art models and unaided physicians.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Rare diseases affect millions but are often misdiagnosed because early symptoms are nonspecific and specialist expertise is scarce and unevenly distributed. Existing AI tools mostly target a single step (usually diagnosis), rely heavily on downstream tests, and ignore or suppress variability between model outputs. The authors are motivated to create an AI system that supports the full rare disease care pathway and that leverages, rather than eliminates, the diversity in model reasoning to improve decisions under high uncertainty.

Method: The authors design RareLens, composed of four coordinated modules for primary-visit risk screening, diagnosis, treatment planning, and prognosis. For each patient case, multiple heterogeneous large language models independently generate reasoning and recommendations. RareLens then aligns and calibrates these divergent, complementary outputs into a single convergent, actionable decision at each stage. The system is trained and evaluated on RareBench, a large real-world dataset of 157,525 rare disease cases covering all 33 Orphanet categories and over 7,000 conditions. Performance is compared against frontier individual models such as GPT-5, DeepSeek-R1, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, and Gemini-2.5-Pro, as well as against physicians with and without assistance from RareLens, including an external evaluation on 1,287 cases and 23 clinicians.

Result: On RareBench, RareLens outperforms each tested frontier LLM at all stages of the rare disease trajectory. It achieves an AUC of 0.917 for primary-visit screening and top-1 accuracies of 65.5% for diagnosis and 89.8% for treatment planning. In an external study with 1,287 cases and 23 physicians, both fully autonomous RareLens and physicians assisted by RareLens significantly outperform unaided physicians, demonstrating improved diagnostic and therapeutic decision-making in real-world-like settings.

Conclusion: The study concludes that coordinating and aligning the divergent reasoning of multiple heterogeneous language models is more effective for high-uncertainty clinical decision-making than simply scaling a single model. RareLens demonstrates that this ensemble-alignment strategy can support the full rare disease trajectory—screening, diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis—while outperforming strong individual models and improving physician performance. This paradigm may generalize to other complex, uncertain domains in medicine and beyond.

Abstract: Rare diseases collectively affect an estimated 3.5% to 5.9% of the population, yet more than 70% of patients are misdiagnosed and many endure years of evaluation before a diagnosis is reached, because early presentations are nonspecific and relevant expertise is scarce and unevenly distributed. Artificial intelligence could provide support, but existing systems address isolated stages of care, overwhelmingly diagnosis. They typically depend on the results of downstream investigations, and they treat the variability between models as noise to be eliminated. Here we present RareLens, a system that supports clinical decision-making across the entire rare disease trajectory by exploiting this variability. When heterogeneous large language models evaluate the same case, they generate divergent but complementary reasoning, which RareLens aligns and calibrates into a single convergent, actionable decision at each stage. Four coordinated modules perform primary-visit risk screening, diagnosis, treatment planning and prognosis. Developed and evaluated on RareBench, a real-world dataset of 157,525 cases spanning all 33 Orphanet categories and more than 7,000 conditions, RareLens outperformed every frontier model tested, including GPT-5, DeepSeek-R1, Claude-3.7-Sonnet and Gemini-2.5-Pro, at each stage. It achieved an area under the curve of 0.917 for screening and top-1 accuracies of 65.5% and 89.8% for diagnosis and treatment. In an external study spanning 1,287 cases and 23 physicians, autonomous RareLens and physicians assisted by RareLens both substantially outperformed unaided physicians. These findings indicate that aligning divergent model reasoning, rather than scaling a single model, offers a generalizable strategy for high-uncertainty clinical decision-making.

</details>


### [196] [Ordered Network Analysis of Epistemic Emotions during Collaborative Problem Solving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23317)
*Sifatul Anindho,Videep Venkatesha,Jaclyn Ocumpaugh,Nathaniel Blanchard*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies how emotions like confusion, frustration, curiosity, and optimism persist and change over time during face‑to‑face collaborative problem solving, comparing different emotion-report methods and group speeds using ordered network analysis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understanding how epistemic emotions (e.g., curiosity, confusion) evolve and interact during collaborative problem solving is crucial for supporting learning and performance, but measuring these emotions accurately is difficult because there is no gold-standard labeling method. In particular, it is unclear how different emotion-reporting methods and group performance levels shape the observed emotional dynamics.

Method: Participants engaged in an in‑person co‑situated collaborative problem‑solving (CPS) task. Afterward, their affective states were collected via retrospective cued‑recall using two reporting modes: self‑caught and probe‑caught. The authors then applied ordered network analysis (ONA) to model and compare ordered patterns of affective states—specifically their persistence and transitions—both across reporting methods and between faster and slower groups.

Result: Ordered network analysis uncovered distinct patterns in how emotions persisted and transitioned that were not visible through simple descriptive statistics. The analysis revealed a stable epistemic core connecting curiosity, optimism, and confusion, with self‑caught and probe‑caught methods highlighting different links among these states. Comparisons between faster and slower groups showed that the roles of confusion and disengagement changed substantially, especially regarding how they related to conflict during collaboration.

Conclusion: The study concludes that ordered network analysis is a powerful approach for uncovering nuanced temporal structures in epistemic emotions during CPS, beyond what descriptive summaries can reveal. The presence of a robust curiosity‑optimism‑confusion core suggests central emotional dynamics in collaborative problem solving, while differences by reporting method and group speed highlight the importance of measurement choices and group characteristics. These insights can inform the design of AI systems that are better attuned to emotional dynamics in CPS and can adapt support based on how emotions like confusion, disengagement, and conflict evolve over time.

Abstract: Investigating how affective states such as confusion and frustration persist and transition during co-situated collaborative problem solving (CPS) is important for understanding the dynamics of epistemic emotions. However, the accurate identification of affective states remain challenging as there is no gold-standard truth in this space. Here, we analyze affective states collected through retrospective cued-recall during an in-person CPS task. Using ordered network analysis (ONA), we examine (1) the overall ordered structure of affective states and how this structure differs across self-caught and probe-caught reporting methods, and (2) what aspects of this ordered structure are emphasized differently in slower and faster groups. We find that ONA reveals differences in persistence and transition patterns that are not apparent from descriptive summaries alone. In particular, we observe a stable epistemic core linking curiosity, optimism, and confusion, with different reporting methods emphasizing different connections among states. An analysis between faster and slower groups show that roles of confusion and disengagement also shift significantly during collaboration, particularly in their relationship to conflict. We interpret our findings in the context of collaboration and discuss their implications in developing AI systems that support CPS.

</details>


### [197] [ESF-Bench: Benchmarking Challenging Slot-Filling Scenarios for Real-World Enterprise Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23326)
*Toby Liang,Gopal Sarda,Sagar Davasam,Vikas Yadav*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces ESF-Bench, a challenging multi-domain enterprise slot-filling benchmark revealing major weaknesses of current LLMs and released publicly for research.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world enterprise deployment of LLMs for tasks like slot filling faces complex constraints and user behaviors, yet existing benchmarks do not fully capture these challenges or diagnose model weaknesses in such settings.

Method: Curate a benchmark (ESF-Bench) of 810 multi-turn samples and 6530 slots across 8 enterprise domains, constructed around a taxonomy of 57 difficult slot-filling scenarios derived from real deployments; evaluate state-of-the-art LLMs on this benchmark using released evaluation code.

Result: On ESF-Bench, current top LLMs perform poorly; for example, GPT-OSS-120b correctly extracts slots for only 20.7% of samples, demonstrating substantial room for improvement in enterprise slot filling.

Conclusion: ESF-Bench is a difficult, realistic benchmark that highlights significant limitations of current LLMs on enterprise slot filling and, by being publicly released with taxonomy and code, is intended to catalyze further research and progress in this area.

Abstract: The rapid rise of large language models (LLMs) has driven transformative adoption across enterprises. However, deploying these models in real-world settings presents unique challenges due to complex system constraints and unexpected user behaviors. Among these applications, slot filling is essential for converting unstructured input into structured, actionable data. In this work, we introduce ESF-Bench, a challenging Enterprise Slot Filling benchmark consisting of 810 multi-turn samples and 6530 slots over 8 unique domains. Curated using a taxonomy of the 57 most challenging slot-filling scenarios observed during real-world enterprise deployments, ESF-Bench exposes notable limitations in current state-of-the-art LLMs, with GPT-OSS-120b low successfully extracting slots for only 20.7% of benchmark samples. To support continued research in this area, we publicly release the benchmark dataset, taxonomy, and accompanying evaluation code on GitHub.

</details>


### [198] [Confidently Wrong: Exception Chain Collapse in Frontier LLM Rule Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23386)
*Paul Simpson,John Kozak,Lisa Doake*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper identifies a systematic failure mode in top LLMs on nested eligibility rules and proposes a neuro-symbolic module that uses LLMs only to author rules, while a deterministic SMT-based layer executes them, yielding stable and superior legal reasoning accuracy versus frontier models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Frontier LLMs are used in regulated workflows (e.g., insurance, legal eligibility), but their behavior is non-deterministic and drifts over time. The authors observed a specific failure class, "exception chain collapse", in nested conditional rules (A unless B, unless C overrides B). Worse, some of these failures disappeared silently between model snapshots without a version change, turning accuracy into a moving, opaque compliance boundary. This undermines trust and auditability for high-stakes decisions. The paper is motivated by the need to stabilize rule execution, make uncertainty explicit, and avoid unobservable changes in model behavior that could create legal and regulatory risk.

Method: They introduce the Aethis Eligibility Module, a neuro-symbolic architecture that separates rule authoring from rule execution. LLMs are used to draft formal rule specifications from authoritative texts, and then a satisfiability modulo theories (SMT)–based engine encodes and executes these rules deterministically. The design ensures that once rules are authored and validated, inference behavior is fixed and robust to model drift, prompting variations, and default reasoning-effort settings. They empirically characterize the exception-chain failure pattern using: (i) a controlled 225-scenario benchmark in four regulatory domains; (ii) a 20-scenario adversarial stress test focused on construction insurance; and (iii) external validation on nine LegalBench tasks with 949 held-out cases, comparing multiple configurations of frontier models to their engine using statistical tests (e.g., McNemar's).

Result: On the controlled 225-scenario benchmark, they observe reproducible exception-chain failures in frontier LLMs and document that some failures disappear over time without explicit model version changes, showing drift in the compliance boundary. In the 20-scenario adversarial construction insurance set, the Aethis engine attains 20/20 accuracy; only one of four frontier model configurations (GPT-5.4 at low reasoning effort) matches this, while the others, including Anthropic's strongest model at the time, fail on the same coverage-gap edge case. On nine LegalBench tasks with 949 held-out instances, the engine is significantly more accurate than all three tested frontier models, with combined McNemar p-values ≤ 0.003 and accuracy improvements up to 41 percentage points on curated multi-prong tasks over Anthropic models.

Conclusion: Nested exception chains pose a systematic, high-impact failure mode for current frontier LLMs in eligibility reasoning, and model drift makes their accuracy an unstable and opaque compliance boundary. By moving uncertainty to the rule-specification phase and executing rules through a deterministic SMT solver, the Aethis Eligibility Module delivers reproducible, auditable, and significantly more accurate decisions than general-purpose LLMs on legal and regulatory tasks. The paper argues that for regulated workflows, neuro-symbolic architectures that fix inference behavior and treat LLMs as specification tools—not decision engines—are a more appropriate and trustworthy design. All artifacts are released to support independent verification and further research.

Abstract: We document a failure class in frontier large language models -- exception chain collapse -- observed in eligibility evaluation under nested conditional rules of the form "A is required UNLESS B applies, UNLESS C overrides B". The failure reproduces at first observation, but its empirical surface is unstable: between March and April 2026 several failure cells closed silently under the same model alias, with no version bump (GPT-5.4 on construction insurance moved from 96.6% to 100%, same prompt and harness). For regulated workflows, frontier-model accuracy is a moving compliance boundary that shifts without notice. We present the Aethis Eligibility Module, a neuro-symbolic architecture in which LLMs author rules from authoritative sources and an SMT-based layer executes them deterministically, consistent with the authored specification regardless of model drift, reasoning-effort defaults, or prompt format. Three evidence bases: (i) a controlled benchmark of 225 scenarios across four regulatory domains documents the pattern and, in replication, the drift that partially closed it; (ii) a 20-scenario adversarial extension on construction insurance, where the engine scores 20/20, as does one of four frontier configurations (GPT-5.4 at low reasoning effort), while the other three, including Anthropic's strongest model at evaluation time, fail the same coverage-gap edge case; (iii) external validation on nine peer-reviewed LegalBench tasks, 949 held-out cases, where the engine is significantly more accurate than all three frontier models (combined McNemar's p <= 0.003), with margins up to +41 points on the curated multi-prong tasks against the Anthropic models. The contribution is to relocate uncertainty from the inference boundary, where it is silent, to the specification boundary, where it is deliberate and audited. All scenarios, rule encodings, and results are public and reproducible.

</details>


### [199] [Key-Interval A*: Accelerating Grid Pathfinding via Structural Abstraction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23393)
*Taiquan Sui*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces Key-Interval A* (KIA*), an optimal 4-connected grid pathfinding algorithm that searches over a compact interval abstraction of free space, achieving state-of-the-art runtimes while preserving exact shortest paths.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
