Motivation: Existing exact 4-connected grid pathfinding methods either keep fine-grained cell-level search states, which is computationally expensive online, or need heavy preprocessing, which is costly in memory and setup time. There is a need for an algorithm that reduces online search effort, maintains optimality, and uses only lightweight preprocessing with a more compact representation of free space.

Method: The paper proposes Key-Interval A* (KIA*), which first abstracts free grid space into intervals, defined as maximal contiguous runs of traversable cells. From these, it identifies key intervals that correspond to structural boundary changes in the map. It builds a key-interval graph by connecting these key intervals via contiguous non-key regions. The search is then performed using an A*-style algorithm over this compact interval graph. After finding an interval-path solution, KIA* reconstructs the corresponding cell-level path constructively from the chain of intervals, without additional local cell-level search. The authors also provide formal proofs of completeness and optimality on 4-connected grids.

Result: On standard grid pathfinding benchmarks, KIA* exactly preserves shortest-path distances while significantly reducing runtime. It is reported to be the fastest method on seven out of eight benchmark groups, with particularly large improvements on structured and game-like maps, demonstrating the effectiveness of the interval abstraction and lightweight preprocessing.

Conclusion: KIA* demonstrates that a compact, interval-based abstraction of grid free space, combined with lightweight preprocessing and A*-style search on a key-interval graph, can achieve optimal 4-connected grid pathfinding with state-of-the-art runtime performance. The method remains complete and optimal while substantially reducing online search cost, making it especially well-suited for structured and game maps.

Abstract: Existing exact methods for 4-connected grid pathfinding reduce online search, but often either retain fine-grained search states or require substantial preprocessing. This paper presents Key-Interval A* (KIA*), an optimal pathfinding algorithm that uses lightweight preprocessing to construct and search over a compact interval-level abstraction of free space. KIA* represents free space using intervals: maximal contiguous runs of traversable cells. It extracts key intervals that capture structural boundary changes and connects them through contiguous non-key regions. KIA* then performs A*-style search on the resulting key-interval graph and constructively reconstructs grid paths from interval chains, without cell-level local search. We prove the completeness and optimality of KIA* on 4-connected grids. Experiments on standard benchmarks show that KIA* preserves exact shortest-path lengths and achieves the fastest runtime on seven of eight benchmark groups, with the largest gains on structured and game maps.

</details>


### [200] [Inference-Time Consensus for Mitigating Hidden Behaviors from LLM Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23394)
*Adhyyan Narang,Artin Tajdini,Claire Zhang,Jamie Morgenstern*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose a decoding-time ensemble method (consensus decoding) over multiple separately fine-tuned models so that only behaviors agreed upon across data sources are expressed, thereby blocking source-specific poisoned behaviors while preserving shared capabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fine-tuning LMs on even small amounts of poisoned or subtly biased data can imprint targeted misbehavior or hidden preferences that evade typical defenses like data filtering or regularization. Existing strategies reduce but do not fully remove such backdoors or misalignments, especially when malicious data is mixed with benign data. There is a need for a defense that can robustly prevent source-specific malicious behavior, even when some training data sources are compromised, while still retaining useful, benign behaviors.

Method: Instead of aggregating all fine-tuning data into one training run, they collect multiple datasets from distinct sources and fine-tune a separate reference model on each source's data. At inference time, they aggregate the models’ next-token distributions using new ‘consensus decoding’ strategies. The first is a token-wise minimum rule, assigning each token the minimum probability any model gives it, which penalizes tokens not supported across sources. The second is a base-relative variant that compares models’ shifts from a shared base model and reverts to the base probability on tokens where sources move probabilities in opposing directions. They further extend these schemes to allow partial agreement (not necessarily unanimous) and to handle different surface forms that express the same intention.

Result: In experiments on controlled data-poisoning tasks, subliminal preference learning, and more realistic emergent-misalignment settings, consensus decoding largely eliminates behaviors that originate from only a subset of data sources while maintaining behaviors that are common across sources. It successfully blocks source-specific misbehavior in cases where standard methods like union training on all data or averaging fine-tuned weights still exhibit the undesirable behaviors.

Conclusion: Consensus decoding—ensemble-style aggregation of multiple fine-tuned models at inference—can provide robustness to data poisoning and source-specific misalignment by only expressing behaviors that different data sources agree upon. This approach outperforms common baselines such as mixed-data training and weight averaging in suppressing malicious behaviors while preserving shared, beneficial capabilities, suggesting redundancy across data sources and agreement-aware decoding as a promising direction for alignment and safety defenses.

Abstract: Recent work shows that fine-tuning language models on even a small amount of poisoned data can install targeted misbehavior, and ostensibly benign data can transmit hidden preferences that generalize broadly. Standard defenses, such as data filtering, mixing in harmless data, and regularization, attenuate these effects but do not eliminate them. We instead pursue robustness through redundancy: collecting multiple datasets from different sources and only learning what is common between them. Thus, if only a subset of sources are malicious, the misbehavior will be blocked. In order to implement this defense strategy, we fine-tune a separate reference model on each source's dataset and aggregate their next-token distributions at decoding time. We introduce two consensus decoders: a token-wise minimum, which caps each token at the lowest probability any source assigns, and a base-relative variant, which reverts to the base probability on any token the sources move in opposing directions. We further relax exact agreement to tolerate partial support across sources and different surface expressions of the same intention. Across controlled poisoning tasks, subliminal learning, and emergent misalignment, consensus decoding suppresses source-specific misbehavior while preserving shared desirable behavior, including cases where union training and weight averaging retain the unwanted behavior.

</details>


### [201] [NeurGO: Learning to Generate Elite Candidates for Meta-Black-Box Expensive Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23408)
*Jintao He,Huixiang Zhen,Wenyin Gong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: NeurGO is a generative meta black-box optimization framework that learns from historical populations to directly propose elite candidates, improving performance and convergence under tight evaluation budgets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Expensive black-box optimization problems limit the number of function evaluations, making it inefficient for traditional evolutionary algorithms and existing MetaBBO methods that spend many evaluations on screening large offspring pools. Surrogate and Bayesian methods try to reduce evaluations but struggle with building accurate global models from scarce data and may get stuck in local optima.

Method: NeurGO uses an attention-based encoder to model population-level search dynamics from historical population states, and a conditioned decoder to directly generate high-quality candidate solutions, bypassing the need to evaluate large numbers of offspring. It incorporates a quality-diversity loss to jointly encourage solution quality and maintain population diversity during the search.

Result: On standard benchmarks including CEC 2008 and the COCO BBOB test suites, NeurGO achieves superior optimization performance compared to baselines under the same evaluation budget and shows faster convergence.

Conclusion: Generative meta black-box optimization via NeurGO effectively exploits historical population information to synthesize elite candidates without heavy reliance on surrogate modeling, improving efficiency and robustness for expensive black-box optimization tasks.

Abstract: Expensive black-box optimization is ubiquitous in science and engineering, where function evaluations are costly and the evaluation budget is limited. Traditional evolutionary algorithms and Meta-BlackBox Optimization (MetaBBO) approaches typically consume most evaluations on candidate selection, often wasting precious budget on inferior solutions. Although surrogate-assisted evolution and Bayesian optimization aim to reduce evaluations through surrogate models, constructing an accurate global model from limited data remains challenging, and model bias can easily trap the search in local optima. To overcome these limitations, we propose NeurGO, a generative MetaBBO framework that directly synthesizes elite candidates from historical population states. Specifically, we employ an attention-based encoder to capture the population-level search trend and condition a decoder on this representation to generate high-quality candidates, avoiding the expensive evaluation of large offspring pools. We then design a quality-diversity loss to maintain solution quality and population diversity throughout the search. Through extensive benchmarking on CEC 2008 and the COCO BBOB test suites, our method achieves better optimization performance under the same evaluation budget and exhibits faster convergence.

</details>


### [202] [Separating Capability from Permission: A Governance Framework for Agentic AI Autonomy Levels](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23438)
*Haining Zheng,Qian Dong,Rodolfo K. Depena,Jonathan D. Bhatia,Feng Xiao,Peng Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a governance framework that distinguishes what AI agents can technically do from what they are allowed to do, and defines structured autonomy levels plus a risk-based process for assigning permissions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current discussions of AI autonomy often blur the line between an AI system’s technical capabilities and the level of autonomy it should be granted in real-world use. This conflation makes it difficult to govern increasingly agentic AI systems, manage risk, and ensure appropriate oversight and accountability. There is a need for a clear framework that separates capability from authorization and guides organizations in safely deploying powerful agentic AI.

Method: The authors define two distinct dimensions: Autonomous Capability Levels (ACL), describing the inherent technical abilities of an AI agent, and Allowed Autonomy Levels (AAL), describing the degree of autonomy the agent is authorized to exercise in practice. They construct a structured hierarchy of autonomy levels—from simple reactive execution up through delegated operational authority—and characterize how control, reversibility, oversight, and accountability vary across these levels. They then propose a risk-aware decision process for mapping capability to allowed autonomy, accounting for risk, reversibility, and organizational readiness. Finally, they illustrate and validate the framework through an applied case study of a deployed enterprise data engineering agent, showing how a high-capability system can be constrained to a lower allowed autonomy level.

Result: The paper produces: (1) a taxonomy of autonomy levels covering reactive execution, decision support, supervised action, goal-directed autonomy, and delegated operational authority; (2) a conceptual separation and formalization of Autonomous Capability Levels versus Allowed Autonomy Levels; (3) a risk-aware process for deciding allowed autonomy given risk, oversight, reversibility, and accountability considerations; and (4) an empirical demonstration via an enterprise data engineering agent where a technically capable system is intentionally restricted to a lower autonomy level based on governance concerns.

Conclusion: By clearly decoupling an AI system’s technical capabilities from the autonomy it is permitted to exercise, the proposed framework offers actionable guidance for governing agentic AI. Organizations can systematically assign allowed autonomy levels based on risk, reversibility, and accountability, rather than on raw capability alone. This separation supports safer design and deployment choices, enables more nuanced oversight, and helps align agentic AI systems with organizational readiness and risk tolerance.

Abstract: As AI systems increasingly exhibit agentic behavior, discussions of autonomy often conflate what systems are technically capable of doing with what they should be permitted to do in practice. This paper introduces a governance framework that explicitly separates Allowed Autonomy Levels (AAL), which define the degree of autonomy an AI agent is authorized to exercise given risk, oversight, and accountability considerations, from Autonomous Capability Levels (ACL), which characterize an agent's inherent technical abilities. We present a structured set of autonomy levels spanning reactive execution, decision support, supervised action, goal-directed autonomy, and delegated operational authority, and describe how control, reversibility, and accountability change as autonomy increases. To operationalize this framework, we propose a risk-aware decision process for assigning allowed autonomy, analyze how risk and accountability evolve across autonomy levels, and demonstrate its application through a deployed enterprise data engineering agent, illustrating how a system assessed at a high capability level can be deliberately constrained to a lower allowed autonomy based on risk, reversibility, and organizational readiness. By distinguishing authorization from capability, this work provides practical guidance for the design, deployment, and governance of Agentic AI systems.

</details>


### [203] [Do LLMs Know Their Vulnerable Scenarios?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23496)
*Ziheng Peng,Huiqi Deng,Haoran Jing,Xuankun Rong,Jiahui Han,Xiting Wang,Na Zou,Xia Hu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies why and how scenario-based prompts can bypass safety refusals in large language models and introduces a method, Concept2Scenario, that finds such vulnerable scenarios mechanistically rather than by trial-and-error red-teaming.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Safety-aligned LLMs are supposed to refuse harmful requests, but attackers can often succeed by wrapping the same request in a particular scenario (e.g., role-play, simulations). Current red-teaming mainly searches for such scenarios empirically and does not explain mechanistically why some scenarios reduce refusal. Prior interpretability work separately identified refusal-related directions and jailbreak features, but did not relate them or explain how scenario context alters refusal behavior. The authors want a mechanistic understanding of scenario-induced vulnerability and a systematic way to discover and compose such scenarios.

Method: The authors analyze internal activations and show that scenario-wrapped prompts reliably activate specific “scenario directions” whose causal manipulation changes refusal scores. They then propose Concept2Scenario, which builds a concept space using a sparse autoencoder over model activations, attributes changes in refusal behavior to individual latent concepts, and maps those concepts back into human-readable natural-language scenarios. They further compute interaction attributions to identify combinations of scenarios that synergistically suppress refusal. The resulting scenarios are used as reusable priors when constructing jailbreak prompts, and are evaluated across multiple models, datasets, and jailbreak strategies.

Result: On three open-source LLMs, two safety benchmarks, and six black-box jailbreak methods, Concept2Scenario discovers scenario prompts that, when reused, raise average attack success rates by up to 18.2 percentage points over baselines. These learned scenarios generalize beyond the models they were extracted from: they increase jailbreak effectiveness on closed-source models including GPT-5, Claude-Haiku-4.5, and Gemini-3-Flash. Scenario combinations found through interaction attribution outperform their individual component scenarios and allow iterative jailbreak attacks to reach success in fewer conversational turns.

Conclusion: Scenario context corresponds to distinct internal directions in LLM activations that causally suppress refusal, constituting a mechanistic link between safety behavior and jailbreak vulnerabilities. By learning a concept space and attributing refusal suppression to specific concepts, Concept2Scenario can automatically discover and linguistically realize vulnerable scenarios and their synergistic combinations. These scenarios are reusable, transfer across model families, and materially strengthen jailbreak attacks, implying that scenario-level refusal vulnerabilities are structured and partially shared across LLMs. The work highlights the need for safety methods that account for and robustly defend against scenario-induced shifts in internal representations, not just surface-level prompt patterns.

Abstract: Safety-aligned large language models are trained to refuse harmful requests, yet embedding the same requests in particular scenarios can bypass their safeguards. Existing red-teaming methods empirically identify effective scenarios through observed attack outcomes, but why particular scenarios weaken refusal remains mechanistically unclear. Meanwhile, mechanistic interpretability studies have characterized both refusal directions and jailbreak-associated features, without explaining the relationship between the two representations. In this work, we show that scenario-wrapped prompts activate internal scenario directions whose causal steering consistently reduces refusal scores. Building on this finding, we propose \textsc{Concept2Scenario}, a concept-based attribution framework for vulnerable scenario discovery. It instantiates a broad concept space with a sparse autoencoder, attributes refusal suppression to individual concepts, translates the identified concepts into interpretable natural-language scenarios, and identifies synergistic scenario combinations through interaction attribution. Across three open-source models, two safety benchmarks, and six black-box jailbreak methods, the discovered scenarios serve as reusable priors that improve average attack success rates by up to $18.2$ percentage points. They also transfer to GPT-5, Claude-Haiku-4.5, and Gemini-3-Flash, suggesting that some scenario-level refusal vulnerabilities are shared across model families. Moreover, the identified combinations outperform their individual constituents and enable iterative attacks to succeed in fewer turns.

</details>


### [204] [Delegation Intelligence in Deep Search: A Controllable Framework for Disentangled Capability Diagnosis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23524)
*Xinhao Yao,Yuanzhuo Liu,Changhao Wang,Yunfei Yu,Haoran Tan,Yuyao Zhang,Ruifeng Ren,Minlong Peng,Yong Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces a framework and benchmark to evaluate how well AI agents decide when and how to use deep search, beyond just measuring final answer accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluations of deep-search agents focus mainly on end-to-end answer accuracy, which conflates retrieval, long-context reasoning, evidence verification, and tool-use decisions. This makes it hard to know whether models truly understand when information is missing and how to delegate information seeking to search tools. The authors want a more precise, decomposed, and reproducible way to measure this meta-capability.

Method: They (1) define a new concept called Delegation Intelligence in deep search, split into two dimensions: Search Decision-Making and Information Synthesis and Verification; (2) build a controllable, document-grounded synthetic data pipeline via reverse engineering, enabling construction of controlled deep-search evaluations; (3) instantiate this as DelegSearchBench, a benchmark plus protocol that can independently test each capability dimension by manipulating document composition and tool access; and (4) run experiments with representative models on this benchmark.

Result: Using DelegSearchBench and the disentangled protocol, the authors show empirically that current models’ deep-search abilities are not captured by final-answer accuracy alone: models can get answers right for the wrong reasons or fail at specific sub-capabilities like search timing, evidence aggregation, or robustness to noisy/adversarial sources, even when overall accuracy looks similar.

Conclusion: Delegation Intelligence in deep search is a distinct, measurable meta-capability that requires decomposed evaluation. The proposed synthesis pipeline and DelegSearchBench provide a general recipe and concrete tools to separately assess search decisions and information synthesis/verification, revealing nuanced strengths and weaknesses in modern models that traditional accuracy metrics miss.

Abstract: Deep search is becoming a core capability of modern agent systems, yet it is typically evaluated solely based on end-to-end answer accuracy. This coupled evaluation paradigm entangles retrieval quality, long-context comprehension, evidence verification, and tool-use decisions, making it difficult to determine whether a model truly knows when and how to delegate information seeking to search. To this end: (1) We formalize this meta-capability as Delegation Intelligence in deep search and decompose it into complementary dimensions-Search Decision-Making (recognizing information insufficiency and deciding whether, when, and how to search) and Information Synthesis and Verification (aggregating evidence from multiple sources, judging source reliability, and synthesizing information under noisy, potentially adversarial conditions). (2) To enable disentangled and reproducible measurement, we develop a controllable synthesis pipeline built on document-grounded reverse engineering. This yields a general recipe for constructing controlled deep-search evaluations rather than a single fixed dataset. (3) As a concrete instantiation, we construct DelegSearchBench, together with a disentangled evaluation protocol that isolates each capability dimension by varying document composition and tool access. (4) Across representative models, we demonstrate that deep-search competence cannot be adequately characterized by final-answer accuracy alone...

</details>


### [205] [ObsDriveBench: Benchmarking Multimodal Understanding under Adverse Weather with Observability Awareness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23537)
*Qiao Yan,Yihan Wang,Zhenghao Xing,Jiaqi Xu,Pheng-Ann Heng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces ObsDriveBench, a real-world multi-modal benchmark to evaluate and improve vision-language models for autonomous driving under adverse weather, along three capability dimensions: observability awareness, spatial reliability, and risk-aware decision-making.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing vision-language benchmarks for autonomous driving mostly cover standard conditions, synthetic corruptions, or single-modality settings, leaving a gap in understanding how models behave under real-world adverse weather with multi-modal inputs where observations are degraded and cross-modally inconsistent.

Method: Construct a real-world dataset and benchmark, ObsDriveBench, with synchronized camera, LiDAR, and radar data collected in adverse weather (fog, rain, snow, low illumination). Add observability meta-annotations, scene descriptions, and capability-oriented multiple-choice questions to evaluate three dimensions: observability awareness, spatial reliability, and risk-aware decision-making, resulting in over 14k training and 13k test QA pairs. Evaluate existing vision-language models on this benchmark and develop the ObsDrive model, trained via normal-weather supervised fine-tuning followed by adverse-weather reinforcement learning.

Result: Experiments show that current vision-language models suffer consistent performance degradation under the adverse-weather, multi-modal conditions specified in ObsDriveBench. The proposed ObsDrive model, trained with the stated scheme, improves robustness and scores better across all three capability dimensions compared to baseline models.

Conclusion: Degraded environmental observability in adverse weather significantly challenges multi-modal vision-language models for autonomous driving, leading to performance drops in perception and decision-making. The ObsDriveBench benchmark enables fine-grained diagnosis of these weaknesses, and the ObsDrive training approach demonstrates that targeted fine-tuning and reinforcement learning under adverse-weather conditions can substantially enhance model robustness. The dataset and code are made publicly available for further research.

Abstract: Autonomous driving under adverse weather remains a critical challenge, yet existing vision-language benchmarks mainly evaluate under standard conditions, synthetic corruptions, or single modality. As a result, it remains unclear how vision-language models behave under real-world adverse weather with multi-modal inputs. We argue that a key difficulty lies in degraded environmental observability: under fog, rain, snow, and low illumination, multi-modal observations become unreliable and cross-modally inconsistent, posing challenges to scene understanding, and subsequent decision-making. To study this, we introduce \textbf{ObsDriveBench}, a real-world multi-modal benchmark for adverse-weather autonomous driving. Our benchmark is designed with three capability dimensions: \textbf{observability awareness}, \textbf{spatial reliability}, and \textbf{risk-aware decision-making}, enabling fine-grained diagnosis of model behavior under degraded observations. We construct the benchmark through observability meta-annotation, scene description, and capability oriented multiple-choice tasks over synchronized camera, LiDAR, and radar inputs, forming a benchmark with over 14k training and 13k test questions. Experiments reveal consistent performance degradation of existing vision-language models. We further introduce \textbf{ObsDrive} model with normal-weather supervised fine-tuning and adverse-weather reinforcement learning, improving robustness across all three capabilities. The dataset and evaluation code will be released at \href{https://github.com/russellyq/ObsDriveBench}{\texttt{ObsDriveBench}}.

</details>


### [206] [Verification-Notebook Learning for Source-Aware Multimodal Misinformation Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23581)
*Junyuan Tan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces Verification-Notebook Learning (VNL), a non-parametric framework that builds an external, interpretable notebook of verification heuristics for frozen LVLMs, improving multimodal misinformation verification without further model training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multimodal misinformation posts can be misleading in text, image, or their interaction, and verifying them requires different types of external evidence. Large vision-language models (LVLMs) are promising verifiers but their performance is highly sensitive to the chosen inference procedure for each instance. Existing approaches focus on better prompts, retrieval, or multi-step reasoning, yet they do not effectively accumulate and reuse verification knowledge from prior examples. There is a need for a method that can systematically capture, store, and reuse verification patterns without retraining the LVLM.

Method: The authors propose Verification-Notebook Learning (VNL), a non-parametric framework that operates on top of a frozen LVLM. During a pre-inference learning phase, VNL processes previous verification instances and distills them into a compact “verification notebook” that encodes decision principles, evidence cues, and common pitfalls. This notebook is an external, fixed artifact used at inference time: given a new instance, VNL consults the notebook to guide the LVLM’s verification process, rather than altering model parameters or relying solely on prompted demonstrations. The notebook is designed to be small, interpretable, and directly inspectable.

Result: Experiments across multimodal misinformation verification benchmarks show that VNL consistently outperforms strong baselines that rely on prompt engineering, retrieval, or deliberative reasoning alone. Quantitative analyses indicate that the notebook particularly enhances fine-grained source attribution, helping the model identify which components of a post are misleading. Despite being compact, the notebook captures sufficient verification knowledge to yield sizable performance gains over competing methods.

Conclusion: Verification-Notebook Learning offers an effective way to accumulate and reuse verification knowledge for multimodal misinformation detection without additional model training. By using an external, interpretable notebook of verification strategies to guide a frozen LVLM, VNL improves verification accuracy and source attribution while remaining compact and transparent. This demonstrates that non-parametric, artifact-based learning can substantially enhance LVLM-based verification beyond conventional prompting and retrieval approaches.

Abstract: Multimodal misinformation verification is challenging because misleading signals may come from different parts of a post and require different forms of evidence. LVLMs are well suited to this task, but their verification performance often depends on the inference procedure applied to each instance. Existing methods improve this procedure through stronger prompting, retrieval, or deliberation, but rarely retain the verification patterns learned from previous examples. We propose Verification-Notebook Learning (VNL), a non-parametric framework that learns an external verification procedure for a frozen LVLM before inference. VNL builds a compact notebook of decision principles, evidence cues, and recurring pitfalls from prior verification experience. The notebook remains fixed during inference and guides the verification of new examples. Rather than updating model parameters or storing demonstrations, VNL records learned knowledge in an artifact that can be inspected directly. Experiments show that VNL consistently outperforms a range of competitive baselines. Further analyses show that the Verification Notebook improves fine-grained source attribution while remaining compact and interpretable, providing an effective way to accumulate verification knowledge without model training.

</details>


### [207] [Are You Still the Agent I Authorized? Earned Authority under a Fixed Ceiling for Evolving Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23586)
*Zhaoxi Zhang,Xiaomei Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper defines and analyzes a security model for maintaining safe and valid user authorization as long-lived AI agents evolve, particularly when they use tools that can affect the external world.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As AI agents become long-lived, self-modifying, and heavily tool-using, they can change substantially after a user grants them authority. This evolution can turn small model errors or prompt injections into serious real-world actions, and existing tool-use policies do not say when previously granted permissions are still valid after an agent mutates. There is a need for a principled framework to reason about when an existing grant remains appropriate, and how to ensure that agent evolution does not silently expand the scope of user-granted authority.

Method: The authors introduce the concept of authorization continuity and formalize a “state-bound” model. At grant time, they define two key constructs: (1) a transition envelope that captures which types of agent mutations are allowed without invalidating the grant, and (2) an immutable effect ceiling that bounds the maximum protected effects the agent can have. They distinguish between requested effects (what the agent tries to do) and realized effects (what actually happens). Under assumptions like complete mediation of actions, sound abstraction of effects, attenuating delegation, and integrity of the monitoring mechanism, they prove that agent mutation cannot cause protected effects to exceed the preset ceiling. They also classify common mutation types and link each to its authorization impact within the model.

Result: They obtain formal guarantees that, under their conditions, evolution of an AI agent cannot increase its externally visible protected effects beyond an immutable ceiling defined at grant time, even though authority below that ceiling can be reallocated dynamically using agent-produced evidence. They also provide a mapping from six classes of agent mutations (such as learning from experience, acquiring tools, workflow revisions, etc.) to precise consequences for authorization continuity, clarifying when a grant persists, contracts, or must be revoked.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that safe, long-lived AI agents require explicit treatment of authorization continuity, not just static tool-use policies. By fixing a transition envelope and effect ceiling at the time of granting authority, and enforcing mediation and monitoring conditions, one can allow agents to evolve and reconfigure themselves while ensuring they never exceed the user-approved scope of power. This framework offers a principled way to constrain the security consequences of agent evolution and to reason about how different kinds of mutations affect ongoing authorization.

Abstract: Long-lived AI agents increasingly evolve after deployment by retaining experience, acquiring skills and tools, revising workflows, delegating work, and moving across task phases. This improves adaptation but creates a distinct authorization problem. Tool-enabled agents can turn model errors and prompt injections into consequential external actions; when evolution occurs under a live grant, the subject exercising that authority or the context in which it acts may no longer match what the user evaluated. Evolution can change both the effects reachable under an old grant and the authority required by the task, which may rise, fall, or become incomparable. Existing tool policies constrain actions but do not determine when a grant survives this change.
  We formulate authorization continuity: when does an existing grant remain valid, how may active authority change, and what boundary must never move? Our state-bound model fixes a transition envelope and an immutable effect ceiling at grant time. The envelope determines whether the grant survives a mutation; below the ceiling, authority may contract freely and expand only under specified evidence conditions. We distinguish requested from realized effects and prove that, under complete mediation, sound effect abstraction, attenuating delegation, and monitor integrity, mutation cannot amplify protected effects beyond the user-issued ceiling. Agent-produced evidence may allocate authority below the ceiling but cannot raise it. Finally, we map six mutation classes to their authorization consequences.

</details>


### [208] [Hybrid Advantage Estimation with Unified Critic for VLM Agentic Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23605)
*Wenxuan Zhang,Yuhui Wang,Donggang Jia,Xiaoqian Shen,Jian Ding,Ivan Viola,Jürgen Schmidhuber,Mohamed Elhoseiny*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HyGAE is an actor-critic training framework for large vision-language agents that jointly optimizes both token-level and turn-level decisions using a theoretically derived hybrid advantage and a unified critic, leading to significantly better multi-turn performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing training methods for VLM-based agents in interactive, multi-turn environments either optimize at the token level by treating an entire interaction as a long sequence, or at the turn level by assigning uniform credit within a turn. Both are suboptimal for complex, multi-step decision-making, as they fail to accurately assign credit across both fine-grained token actions and coarser turn outcomes. There is a need for a principled way to combine these two optimization granularities so that agents can reason and act coherently over multiple turns.

Method: The paper provides a theoretical formulation of token-wise and turn-wise optimization in multi-turn decision-making, and derives a hybrid advantage function that is compatible with both granularities. It further shows that, with a suitable discount factor and learning target, a single critic network can be used to estimate values that are valid for both token-level and turn-level optimization. Building on this, the authors propose HyGAE, an actor-critic framework for training VLM agents, where the actor is updated using the hybrid advantage and the critic is the unified value estimator, enabling joint optimization across token and turn levels.

Result: HyGAE is evaluated on five different multi-turn decision-making environments. It achieves an average success rate of 91%, representing about a 10% absolute improvement over competing methods that use only token-wise or only turn-wise optimization strategies. Ablation and analytical studies show that using the exact analytic form of the hybrid advantage and return is essential; approximate or heuristic variants degrade performance.

Conclusion: Jointly optimizing token- and turn-level objectives via a theoretically grounded hybrid advantage and a unified critic leads to substantially better training of multi-turn VLM agents than using either level alone. The work suggests that carefully designed multi-granularity credit assignment is key to improving reasoning and decision-making in interactive, multi-turn environments, and that accurate analytic formulations of advantages and returns are crucial for effective learning.

Abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) now act as agents in interactive environments, where success requires coherent reasoning and decision-making across turns. Although end-to-end training in agentic environments can improve such multi-turn decision-making abilities, current methods mainly rely on either token-wise optimization over concatenated token trajectories or turn-wise optimization with uniform within-turn credit. In this work, we establish theoretical formulations for the two levels of optimization and derive a hybrid advantage that serves both objectives. Furthermore, with an appropriate choice of discount factor and learning target, we prove that a unified critic model can estimate values for both turn-wise and token-wise. As such, we propose HyGAE, an actor-critic framework that jointly optimizes token- and turn-level objectives with the hybrid advantage and unified critic. We conduct extensive evaluations of HyGAE across five multi-turn decision-making environments, where it achieves an average success rate of 91% and a significant improvement of 10% over other methods. Furthermore, we provide an in-depth analysis showing that the exact analytic form of the hybrid advantage and return is crucial for optimization. Project Page: https://wx-zhang.github.io/hygae-web/.

</details>


### [209] [SpecAHD: Localize to Specialize for Automated Heuristic Design in Large-Scale Routing Problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23676)
*Kezhao Lai,Yutao Lai,Hai-Lin Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They present SpecAHD, a bilevel framework that uses LLMs to design specialized heuristics within a single routing instance by co-optimizing where to repair and how to repair, with theoretical guarantees and strong empirical gains over existing automated heuristic design methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based automated heuristic design typically designs a single construction rule per instance or solver component, evaluated on full instances or fixed solver parts. In large-scale routing with localized reconstruction, different repair regions inside the same solution can have very different structures, making one shared heuristic inherently compromising and suboptimal. The authors want a method that can specialize heuristic behavior to different local contexts within the same instance, while being principled and scalable.

Method: They propose SpecAHD, a coupled bilevel optimization framework. The upper level searches over programs that define where and how to carve a current routing solution into bounded repair regions, effectively defining a distribution of localized repair tasks. The lower level maintains and evolves a repertoire (pool) of executable heuristics, likely LLM-generated or LLM-shaped, that act as repair operators for those tasks. The interaction is coupled: the upper level shapes the repair tasks that the lower level sees; in turn, the actual repair performance feeds back to evaluate and guide the upper-level search. The lower-level objective is constructed so that it values heuristics that perform well on average and especially those that cover tasks currently underserved by the repertoire. For any fixed upper-level program and candidate pool, they prove that this repertoire-selection objective is monotone submodular, so a greedy selection procedure yields a (1-1/e)-approximate optimal repertoire. They instantiate this framework on large routing benchmarks with multiple LLM backbones as the heuristic generator/evaluator.

Result: On four different routing problems, across several LLM backbones, SpecAHD substantially improves solution quality compared to state-of-the-art AHD baselines. Specifically, it reduces held-out objective cost by up to 57.7% versus the strongest competing automated heuristic design method and, on most public benchmark instances, even beats the envelope formed by per-instance baseline methods. This indicates both strong generalization and real performance gains from within-instance specialization.

Conclusion: Within-instance specialization of heuristics via a bilevel framework can significantly outperform traditional LLM-based automated heuristic design that relies on a single construction rule. By letting an upper-level program choose repair regions and a lower-level search learn a diversified heuristic repertoire, SpecAHD exploits structural variation inside individual routing instances. The submodularity of the lower-level objective provides a theoretical foundation for efficient repertoire selection, and experiments show that this principled specialization leads to large performance improvements across several routing problems and model backbones.

Abstract: LLM-based automated heuristic design (AHD) typically scores executable programs on complete instances or within fixed solver components. In large-scale routing problems, localized reconstruction reduces the size of each optimization task, but repair regions within the same incumbent can exhibit substantially different structures. One construction rule must therefore compromise across them. In this paper, we propose SpecAHD, a coupled bilevel framework for within-instance specialization. An upper-level search learns where to expose bounded repair regions, while a lower-level search evolves a complementary repertoire of executable heuristics for the induced repair tasks. The upper-level program determines the repair tasks seen by the lower level, while checked repair outcomes determine how upper-level programs are evaluated. The lower-level objective favors heuristics that perform well on average or solve tasks that the current repertoire handles poorly. For the repair tasks induced by a fixed upper-level program and a fixed lower-level candidate pool, this objective is monotone submodular, allowing greedy repertoire selection with a (1-1/e) approximation guarantee. Across four routing problems and multiple LLM backbones, SpecAHD reduces held-out objective cost by up to 57.7% against the strongest competing AHD baseline and outperforms the per-instance baseline envelope on most public instances.

</details>


### [210] [Focus Is All You Need: Adaptive Goal-aware Attention Orchestration for Multi-Agent Graph Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23678)
*Mingzhou Fan,Siyuan Xu,Mingxuan Yuan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces Attention Orchestration for multi-agent LLM systems, using attention-style mechanisms to dynamically decide which agents in a graph to run, improving effectiveness and efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Graph-based multi-agent LLM systems can break down complex tasks into specialized nodes, but current orchestration usually treats all nodes similarly, leading to wasted computation on low-relevance or low-impact agents as workflows scale. There is a need for a principled way to selectively focus computation on the most goal-relevant parts of the agent graph, under resource constraints.

Method: Proposes Adaptive Goal-aware Attention Orchestration (AGAO), which lifts Transformer attention ideas from token sequences to graphs of agents. AGAO assigns dynamic importance weights to agents using three attention components: (1) goal-aware attention, computing semantic similarity between user goals and agent capabilities; (2) topology-aware attention, capturing structural and dependency relations in the agent graph; and (3) resource-aware attention, incorporating computation budgets and priorities. These attention scores guide which agents to execute and how much computation to allocate, turning a static execution graph into an adaptive one.

Result: Across multiple multi-agent workloads, applying AGAO yields better task performance while consuming fewer computational resources. Specifically, it reduces unnecessary agent executions, lowers latency, and cuts token usage compared to baseline graph-execution strategies that lack such adaptive attention mechanisms.

Conclusion: Attention Orchestration, instantiated as AGAO, is an effective framework for coordinating multi-agent LLM systems at the workflow level. By focusing computation on goal-critical reasoning paths through goal-, topology-, and resource-aware attention, it makes graph-based agent systems more scalable and efficient, and opens a broader research direction termed Attention Engineering for multi-agent orchestration.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) enable autonomous agents for reasoning, planning, and tool use. Recent systems increasingly organize these agents as graphs of specialized, interconnected nodes. Although graph-based orchestration supports flexible decomposition and coordination, it creates a key challenge: \textbf{attention allocation}. As workflows grow, existing approaches often execute graph components uniformly, wasting resources on irrelevant or low-impact tasks. We introduce \textbf{Attention Orchestration}, a paradigm that extends Transformer-style attention from token representations to workflow-level agent coordination. Our framework, \textbf{Adaptive Goal-aware Attention Orchestration (AGAO)}, dynamically estimates agent importance based on user objectives, graph dependencies, and computational constraints. AGAO combines three components: (1) goal-aware attention, measuring semantic relevance between user goals and agent capabilities; (2) topology-aware attention, modeling structural dependencies in agent graphs; and (3) resource-aware attention, allocating budgets and execution priorities across heterogeneous agents. Together, these mechanisms transform static agent graphs into adaptive systems that focus computation on goal-critical reasoning paths. Experiments across diverse multi-agent workloads show that AGAO improves task effectiveness while reducing unnecessary computation, latency, and token consumption compared with existing graph-based execution strategies. Our work establishes \textbf{Attention Engineering} as a direction for scalable, intelligent multi-agent systems. Code: https://github.com/MingzhouFan97/AGAO.

</details>


### [211] [Compute Globally, Materialize Locally: The Memory Contract of Sparse Event-KV](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23693)
*Zefeng Cai,Zerui Cai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies how information from earlier observations can still be recovered from later KV-cache entries in long-context language models, even after the original tokens are dropped, and formulates a practical “memory contract” for KV-based episodic memory systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Many long-horizon or tool-using LLM agents reuse KV caches as a form of memory but must evict most entries for efficiency. Existing eviction and memory-design strategies implicitly assume that if you keep a later event that depended on an earlier observation, you still preserve the useful information from that earlier observation, even after its tokens are gone. This premise has not been directly tested, yet it is critical to designing reliable sparse KV serving, memory compression, and episodic-memory schemes.

Method: The authors systematically ablate single earlier observations from otherwise identical histories served to an LLM, and then examine downstream items whose correct answer depends on the omitted observation. By comparing predictions when the source observation is present vs. removed (while keeping later, dependent events in the KV cache), they test whether the model’s answer follows the omitted value. They also design special “answer-free” but deliberately phrased events intended to write information into KV rows without explicitly stating the answer, and compare them to naturally occurring mentions in long dialogs. They vary payload size and phrasing to characterize what kinds of information survive in these semantic traces.

Result: When an earlier observation is omitted from the served context but later events that depended on it are kept, the model’s answers overwhelmingly follow the omitted value—even though no remaining tokens explicitly encode which value is correct. This phenomenon is termed “semantic materialization”: later cached rows embody a view of the prior computation whose explicit inputs are gone. Purposefully crafted, answer-free events can strongly encode donor-aligned information in KV (e.g., boosting recovery from 6% to 51% on Qwen3-8B) without naming the value, whereas simply reusing natural dialog snippets gives no measurable gain. The information encoded is limited: compact state survives well, larger payloads deteriorate toward chance, and whether information is written depends sensitively on surface phrasing, not just on semantic meaning. Different phrasings that the model understands equally well can diverge greatly in how much they write into KV.

Conclusion: KV-cache entries for downstream events can implicitly store and later expose information about upstream observations, even after those source tokens are evicted. This defines a concrete “memory contract” for sparse event-based KV serving: which types of information can be reliably written into later events, where in the KV they reside, and how robustly they survive source removal. For practitioners, not seeing an accuracy drop after evicting a source event does not prove the event was unnecessary; its influence may persist via semantic materialization in surviving rows. Memory and eviction policies therefore must be designed with this indirect persistence in mind.

Abstract: Long-horizon agents increasingly reuse their KV cache as memory: a serving system keeps a subset of cached entries and drops the rest. Eviction and episodic-memory schemes therefore rest on a premise rarely tested directly, that a retained event is still informative once the observations that produced it are gone. We test it by omitting one earlier observation from what is served, across otherwise identical agent histories. Among items sensitive to that observation, the answer overwhelmingly follows the omitted value, though no served span says which value is correct. We call this semantic materialization: a downstream event's cached rows act as an independently servable view of computation whose inputs are gone. It can also be written on purpose. A deliberately phrased, answer-free event raises donor-aligned recovery from 6% to 51% on Qwen3-8B without ever naming the value, whereas passively harvesting natural mentions from long-term dialog yields no detected advantage. What such a row carries is specific and bounded. Compact state survives, larger payloads decay toward chance, and whether a construction writes at all turns on phrasing rather than on meaning alone, so two phrasings the model comprehends equally well can diverge sharply. The result is a memory contract for sparse event-KV serving: what to write, where it lands, and what survives once the source is gone. For anyone who evicts the corollary is that dropping a source event and observing no accuracy loss does not show the source was unnecessary.

</details>


### [212] [Offline-to-Online Creative Optimization with Generative Models and Adaptive Testing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23696)
*Kevin Lee,Benjamin Letham,Zhiyuan Jerry Lin,Elodie Samson,Eric Onofrey,Poppy Zhang,Shawndra Hill,Eytan Bakshy*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose and deploy an offline-to-online workflow where a predictive model, trained on past A/B tests, guides a generative model to produce ad creatives, and a small slate of top candidates is then evaluated in online adaptive experiments, yielding much higher best-arm performance than human creatives.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ad creative optimization is bottlenecked by evaluation capacity, not by the ability to generate many variants. Online A/B tests can only test a limited number of creatives, while modern generative models can create huge numbers of plausible ads. The authors want a principled way to use historical A/B data to decide which machine-generated creatives should be tested online so that scarce experiment traffic is focused on high-potential candidates.

Method: They build a performance-driven workflow combining (1) a generative model that proposes many ad creative variants and (2) a predictive model, trained on historical online experiments, that serves as an inference-time critic. Offline, they generate variants and use the predictive model to rank and iteratively refine them, selecting a final slate of promising candidates. Online, they deploy this slate in adaptive experiments (e.g., multi-armed bandit-style) that allocate traffic to arms while learning, thereby identifying the best creatives with limited performance loss to poor variants.

Result: In a 50-arm real-world field experiment, the best model-generated creative outperformed the best human-authored creative by 45.1% in engagement. Two additional experiments showed similar improvements in the upper tail, with gains of 46.7% and 36.2%. Although the predictive model alone was too noisy to perfectly pick the single best creative offline, it consistently steered generation toward a set of strong candidates that contained very high performers.

Conclusion: A noisy but informative predictive model trained on past A/B tests can be effectively used as a critic to guide generative models in creating a compact slate of ad creatives for online testing. Success should be judged not by offline rank accuracy, but by whether the generated slate includes high-performing candidates at a feasible test size. Combined with adaptive online experiments to efficiently select among candidates and limit exposure to weak creatives, this offline-to-online design forms a practical principle for optimizing ad creatives with generative models.

Abstract: Ad creative optimization is increasingly constrained by evaluation rather than generation. Generative models can produce many plausible creatives, but reliable evaluation requires online experiments, in which only a limited slate can be tested. We study how to use data from historical A/B tests to generate and select the candidates in that slate. We developed and deployed a performance-driven offline-to-online workflow that guides creative generation with a predictive model as an inference-time critic. In the offline phase, we use a predictive model trained on historical experiments to rank and refine variants created by a generative model. A final test slate is then deployed in an online adaptive experiment. In a 50-arm field experiment, we found that the best creative generated with this method yielded 45.1% higher engagement than the best human-authored creative. Two additional experiments showed the same upper-tail pattern, with lifts of 46.7% and 36.2%. We found that despite the predictive model being too noisy to directly identify the best creative offline, it effectively guides the generative model toward creating strong candidates that can be efficiently evaluated in an adaptive experiment. The results suggest a design principle for creative optimization with generative models: use predictive models to guide generation of a slate to test, judge the slate by whether it contains high-performing candidates at a feasible test size, and use adaptive experiments to select among candidates while limiting traffic lost to weak arms.

</details>


### [213] [Offline-Online Curriculum RL for Multimodal Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23700)
*Wendi Deng,Hang Du,Guoshun Nan,Haokun Tian,Jiaqi Yu,Xinlei Cao,Jaile Li,Jingfeng Chen,Ling Deng,Ting Li,Hao Yang,Jun Liu,Xudong Jiang,Sicong Leng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose O^2-CritiCuRL, a curriculum reinforcement learning framework to teach multimodal large language models to focus on truly critical reasoning steps rather than redundant ones, improving both performance and efficiency on multimodal reasoning benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multimodal large language models can often get the final answer correct but with incorrect or unreliable intermediate reasoning steps, which hurts interpretability and suggests shortcut-based reasoning. Existing step-level supervision methods struggle to identify which steps are actually decisive versus redundant. The authors want a way to make models explicitly aware of which reasoning steps are critical and train them accordingly.

Method: They introduce O^2-CritiCuRL, which has an offline and an online stage. Offline, the method performs multi-rollout analysis over trajectories that have step annotations to estimate the importance of each reasoning step, then distills and keeps only critical steps while filtering out redundant ones. Online, they apply a progressive step-level reinforcement learning scheme: they create truncated chains (partial reasoning traces) and train the model via RL to infer the missing steps and refine its reasoning process, pushing the model to concentrate on the critical steps and avoiding the rigidity of purely static supervision.

Result: On multimodal reasoning benchmarks, O^2-CritiCuRL attains state-of-the-art performance while also improving training and inference efficiency compared with prior approaches.

Conclusion: Focusing training on automatically identified critical reasoning steps via a combined offline importance estimation and online curriculum RL framework leads to more effective and efficient multimodal reasoning. The proposed O^2-CritiCuRL improves both accuracy and efficiency, and offers a more faithful reasoning process than methods that do not differentiate between critical and redundant steps.

Abstract: Multimodal large language models exhibit capabilities on reasoning tasks, yet often produce flawed intermediate steps while yielding correct final answers. This behavior undermines interpretability and reliability, suggesting reliance on spurious shortcuts rather than faithful reasoning. Although efforts have explored step-level supervision, distinguishing decisive steps from redundant ones remains challenging. We propose $O^2$-CritiCuRL, a novel curriculum reinforcement learning framework that introduces critical-step awareness through an iterative offline-online paradigm. In the offline stage, $O^2$-CritiCuRL conducts multi-rollout analysis over step-annotated trajectories to estimate step-level importance, allowing the framework to distill critical reasoning steps and filter out redundant ones. In the online stage, we employ a progressive step-level reinforcement learning strategy, where truncated chains guide the model to infer missing steps and refine its reasoning, thereby sharpening its focus on critical steps and overcoming the limitations of static supervision. Extensive experiments on multimodal reasoning benchmarks show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance while delivering superior training and inference efficiency. Code is available at https://github.com/kk0013/CritiCuRL.

</details>


### [214] [E-Bench: Benchmarking Multi-Step Tool-Use Agents in Real-World Product Scenarios](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23722)
*Weihuang Zheng,Tianyuan Zou,Eileen Ye,Alphet Liu,Youyong Kong,Ya-Qin Zhang,Duran Zheng,Maxm Pan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: E-Bench is a synthetic benchmark to evaluate LLM agents’ multi-step tool use in realistic, stateful product environments, showing that even top models still struggle with reliable multi-step tool use.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing tool-use benchmarks mostly test single or short tool calls and are hard to scale or control, so they do not adequately evaluate LLM agents that must operate over many steps in complex, stateful environments. The authors want a benchmark that isolates and rigorously tests the capability of multi-step tool use—discovering hidden information, planning, and safely changing state—under controlled but realistic product-like settings.

Method: They build E-Bench, a fully synthetic benchmark with 323 state-changing tasks across three product domains (Honor of Kings, QQ Music, Tencent Meeting). They decouple environment and task synthesis: (1) graph-guided database filling constructs coherent, reusable product environments with no orphaned entities; (2) generator-solver asymmetry creates tasks that embed both an information gap (requiring exploration to uncover hidden data) and a tool gap (requiring composition of multiple tools) before any state change. Task success is graded deterministically via database state differences before and after an agent acts. They also add E-Bench-Code, an extension allowing code execution during tool use. They then evaluate 11 strong LLMs as tool-use agents on these tasks.

Result: Across 323 tasks and 11 state-of-the-art LLMs, multi-step tool use performance remains modest: even the strongest models achieve under 60% Pass^3 (succeeding within three attempts) on the core benchmark. In the E-Bench-Code extension, where models can execute code, Pass^3 improves but still stays below 70%, indicating persistent reliability gaps. The benchmark remains scalable and controllable due to its synthetic design, and grading is fully deterministic via database diffs.

Conclusion: E-Bench provides a scalable, controllable, fully synthetic benchmark for multi-step tool use in realistic, stateful product-like environments. Despite rapid progress in LLMs, current models still struggle with reliably discovering hidden information, planning multi-step tool sequences, and safely changing persistent states, as shown by sub-70% Pass^3 rates even with code execution. This highlights multi-step tool use as an open challenge and positions E-Bench as a useful testbed for future agent and tool-use method development.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as agents that interact with stateful environments over multiple steps: gathering hidden information, composing tool calls, and committing state changes. We refer to this capability as multi-step tool use. Existing benchmarks have advanced tool-use agent evaluation, but often focus on isolated API calls, short trajectories, or settings that are difficult to scale or control. We introduce E-Bench, a fully synthetic benchmark with 323 state-changing tasks across three product domains: Honor of Kings, QQ Music, and Tencent Meeting. E-Bench decouples environment synthesis from task synthesis: graph-guided database filling builds reusable, orphan-free product environments, while generator-solver asymmetry creates tasks with both an information gap and a tool gap, requiring agents to discover hidden data and compose multiple tool calls before changing state. Outcomes are graded deterministically by database-state diffs. Since both environments and tasks are synthetic, E-Bench is controllable at the environment level and scalable at the task level. Benchmarking 11 cutting-edge LLMs shows that multi-step tool use remains challenging: Pass^3 stays below 60% for the strongest models, and even with code execution in the E-Bench-Code extension, reliability (Pass^3) remains below 70%.

</details>


### [215] [Training Language Models to Cooperate with Inference-Time Controllers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23771)
*Moumita Choudhury,Vanshaj Khattar,Jing Liu,Toshiaki Koike-Akino,Ankush Chakrabarty,Shlomo Zilberstein,Ye Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose CALM, a post-training framework that trains language models jointly over many different reasoning controllers, so models generalize better to varied inference-time workflows rather than being optimized for just one pattern like chain-of-thought.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM post-training usually assumes a single fixed reasoning interaction pattern (e.g., plain chain-of-thought). In practice, however, real systems use many different inference-time controllers such as self-consistency, debate, planning, and verification pipelines. This leads to a mismatch between how models are trained and how they are used, which can hurt performance and generalization when switching controllers or composing them in new ways.

Method: They introduce CALM (Controller-Aware Language Models), a post-training framework that brings inference-time controllers into the training loop. They formalize controller-aware post-training as a multi-task reinforcement learning problem over interaction protocols induced by different controllers. Controllers are expressed as compositions of reusable local reasoning modules. This modular structure allows them to decompose training at the module level under a turn-level GRPO objective, and to explore strategies that are aware of both controllers and their constituent modules when mixing training over multiple controllers.

Result: Empirically, they evaluate CALM on unseen controller compositions and on broader shifts in which the inference-time controller used at test differs from those used during training. The experiments show that CALM yields better generalization to these new or shifted controllers compared with standard post-training that optimizes for a single controller, indicating improved robustness across diverse inference workflows.

Conclusion: Explicitly modeling and training on multiple controllers during post-training helps close the gap between training and deployment for LLMs. By framing controller-aware post-training as multi-task RL over modular controllers and using a turn-level GRPO objective, CALM improves cross-controller generalization and performance on workflows different from those seen during training, suggesting that controller-aware training is a promising direction for making LLMs more adaptable to real-world usage patterns.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) performance increasingly depends not only on the base model, but also on the inference-time controller used to organize reasoning. Existing post-training methods, however, typically optimize for a single fixed interaction pattern, despite real deployments relying on diverse controllers such as Chain-of-Thought, self-consistency, debate, planning, and verification pipelines. This creates a training--deployment mismatch and limits transfer to new workflows. We introduce CALM (Controller-Aware Language Models), a post-training framework that explicitly places controllers in the training loop. We formulate controller-aware post-training as multi-task reinforcement learning over controller-induced interaction protocols, where controllers are compositions of reusable local reasoning modules. This structure also induces a module-level decomposition of mixed-controller training under a turn-level GRPO objective, enabling a systematic study of controller and module-aware training strategies. We evaluate CALM on held-out controller compositions and broader controller shifts, showing that controller-aware post-training improves generalization across inference-time workflows beyond single-controller optimization.

</details>


### [216] [From RLVR to RLSVR: Task Transformation Induces Self-Verifiable Rewards for Open-Ended LLM Self-Improvement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23802)
*Qinsi Wang,Jing Shi,Huazheng Wang,Kun Wan,Yiran Wu,Bo Liu,Qingyun Wu,Hai Helen Li,Yiran Chen,Handong Zhao,Wentian Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They introduce RLSVR, a framework that converts open-ended language tasks into self-verifiable proxy games so reinforcement learning can be applied with automatically computed, verifiable rewards.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RL with verifiable rewards has worked well for math and code because correctness is clear, but most real-world language tasks (summarization, creative writing, open reasoning) lack deterministic correctness signals and instead depend on noisy, biased, and costly human or model-based judgments. The authors want a scalable way to do RL-based self-improvement on such open-ended tasks without relying on external judges.

Method: They propose Reinforcement Learning with Self-Verifiable Rewards (RLSVR), a task-transformation paradigm. Instead of directly optimizing on the open-ended task, they map it into a proxy multi-agent environment whose rules make outcomes automatically verifiable. Their concrete instantiation, SpyRL, is a self-play game inspired by "Who Is the Spy?": multiple agents receive asymmetric information, each must perform the same target task (e.g., write a summary), and then they vote on who is the designated spy whose information differs. Because the spy identity is known in advance, voting accuracy yields exact, deterministic reward signals. The idea is that better task performance and reasoning should correlate with better spy detection or deception, thus providing a training signal for the original open-ended tasks.

Result: On benchmarks including text summarization, creative writing, and math reasoning, models trained with SpyRL-based RLSVR improve more than with prior self-improvement methods that rely on preference learning or LLM judges. They also observe consistent performance gains even on already verifiable reasoning tasks, indicating the approach does not just match but can exceed existing RLVR strategies.

Conclusion: Transforming open-ended language tasks into self-verifiable multi-agent games allows reinforcement learning with clean, automatically computed rewards, removing dependence on external judges. SpyRL demonstrates that this task-transformation strategy scales RLVR-style self-improvement beyond inherently verifiable domains and can yield broad performance gains. The released models and code make the approach reproducible and extendable.

Abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has driven recent progress in reasoning-oriented large language models (LLMs) by enabling large-scale optimization. However, its applicability remains largely limited to domains such as mathematics and coding, where correctness can be deterministically verified. Open-ended tasks instead often rely on human preferences, reward models, or LLM-based judges, introducing evaluation bias, judge capability bottlenecks, and additional inference costs.Drawing on the principle of self-supervised learning, which constructs pretext tasks to derive supervision from the data itself, we propose Reinforcement Learning with Self-Verifiable Rewards (RLSVR), a task-transformation-based training paradigm for extending RLVR to open-ended tasks. RLSVR transforms open-ended tasks into verifiable proxy environments whose internal rules and interaction outcomes automatically generate reward signals. We instantiate RLSVR with SpyRL, a multi-agent self-play environment inspired by Who Is the Spy?. Agents receive asymmetric information, complete the same target task, and vote to identify a designated spy. Because the spy identity is predetermined, voting outcomes provide fully verifiable rewards, while successful identification remains closely related to output quality. Experiments on text summarization, creative writing, and mathematical reasoning show that SpyRL outperforms existing self-improvement methods on non-verifiable tasks and yields consistent gains on verifiable reasoning tasks. These results demonstrate that task transformation can extend scalable RLVR-based self-improvement beyond inherently verifiable domains. Models and code have been released at https://github.com/wangqinsi1/SpyRL.

</details>


### [217] [ACM: Agentic Context Management for Long Horizon Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23809)
*Xiaochuan Li,Ryan Ming,Meng Chu,Shuai Shao,Rong Jin,Chenyan Xiong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces Agentic Context Management (ACM), a lossless, agent-driven framework for managing long-horizon context using external memory and post-training to improve agentic search and coding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon, multi-turn agentic tasks accumulate large context, leading to token limits and the need for compression. Existing context compression methods lose information and rely on rigid, heuristic triggers, which misalign with what the agent actually needs to reason well. The paper aims to create a context management approach that avoids information loss and dynamically adapts to the agent’s evolving focus.

Method: Proposes ACM, which gives agents explicit context editing tools inspired by human short-term and long-term memory. The agent autonomously decides when to compress its active context, offloads discarded or compressed content to an external memory store, and retrieves it later via on-demand queries. On top of this, the authors design a post-training pipeline that generates high-quality demonstrations of good context management behavior and uses them to further train models. They evaluate ACM on agentic search and coding tasks.

Result: With ACM, agents manage context without losing information, lowering peak token usage, enabling longer explorations, and improving consistency of solutions across independent runs. The post-training with context management demonstrations improves performance on both agentic search and coding benchmarks compared to baselines that use traditional context compression.

Conclusion: Agentic Context Management offers a lossless, agent-driven mechanism for handling long-horizon context via external memory and learned editing policies. This approach alleviates token pressure, supports extended reasoning, and yields more stable performance, suggesting that integrating structured memory management into agents is a promising direction for complex, multi-turn tasks.

Abstract: Agentic tasks are inherently long-horizon and multi-turn, constantly accumulating context through interactions with the environment. Existing context compression methods inevitably incur information loss and are triggered by rigid heuristic rules, leaving them misaligned with the agent's evolving reasoning focus. We propose Agentic Context Management (ACM), a framework that equips agents with purpose-built context editing tools for lossless context management. Inspired by the interaction between short-term and long-term human memory, the agent autonomously decides when to compress its context, offloads discarded content to an external memory system, and queries it on demand for later retrieval. Building on this framework, we further develop a post-training pipeline that constructs high-quality demonstrations of context management and improves model performance on both agentic search and coding tasks. Further analysis reveals that effective context management reduces peak token pressure, enables extended explorations, and yields more consistent solutions across independent trials. Code, data, and model checkpoints are available at https://github.com/lixiaochuan2020/agentic-context-management.

</details>


### [218] [Do Visual Features Improve Other-Initiated Repair Detection? A Dyadic Multimodal Approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23845)
*Anh Ngo,Nicolas Rollet,Catherine Pelachaud,Chloé Clavel*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes and evaluates a multimodal model that detects and classifies other-initiated repair (OIR) in conversation by leveraging visual, textual, and audio features, showing that visual cues significantly boost performance over text/audio-only systems across two language/setting-diverse corpora.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Other-initiated repair is crucial for resolving misunderstandings in human conversation, and conversational agents must recognize when interlocutors signal trouble in speaking, hearing, or understanding. Conversation analysis has shown that humans use rich non-verbal behaviors (gaze, facial expression, posture, gestures) when initiating repair, but computational OIR detection methods have so far relied mostly on text and audio, missing key signals and limiting robustness. There is thus a need for models that systematically incorporate visual cues grounded in conversation-analytic findings.

Method: The authors design a multimodal OIR detection and classification model that integrates text, audio, and a curated set of visual features inspired by conversation analysis (e.g., gaze shifts, facial expressions, body posture changes, hand movements). They extract these features from video of interactions and fuse them with linguistic and acoustic representations to identify when a turn is an OIR and to classify the type of repair initiation. The approach is evaluated on two conversational corpora that differ in language and interaction setting to test generality and cross-modal contributions.
