Result: Across both corpora, models that include the visual feature set outperform baselines that rely only on text and audio for detecting and classifying OIR. The improvements are consistent, showing that visual information adds complementary signal beyond speech and language. Analysis of feature contributions reveals how specific visual cues contribute in different ways across the two datasets, offering insight into how non-verbal behavior supports OIR recognition in varied interaction contexts.

Conclusion: Incorporating conversation-analysis-inspired visual features into multimodal models significantly enhances automatic detection and classification of other-initiated repair in conversation, compared with text- and audio-only approaches. The findings underscore the importance of visual non-verbal cues for recognizing communication problems and suggest that effective conversational agents should integrate such cues to handle misunderstandings more accurately across diverse languages and settings.

Abstract: Other-initiated Self-repair, or in short Other-initiated Repair (OIR), is an essential mechanism in conversational interaction, whereby a recipient signals a problem in speaking, hearing, or understanding, prompting the previous speaker to resolve it. In the case of conversational agents, it is essential to accurately identify these repair initiation strategies to address communication breakdowns efficiently. While conversational analysis studies have shown that OIR initiation is accompanied by both verbal and non-verbal signals such as gaze shifts, facial expressions, body postures, and hand gestures, existing computational approaches rely mainly on text and audio. This paper introduces a novel multimodal model for OIR detection and classification, incorporating a set of visual features drawn from conversation analysis. We evaluate our approach on two corpora with distinct languages and interaction settings. Results demonstrate that visual information consistently improves performance over text and audio baselines, and provide insights into cross-modal feature contributions across two corpora.

</details>


### [219] [Understanding Human-like Solutions in Combinatorial Optimization via Learning and Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23854)
*Haijiang Yan,Jian-Qiao Zhu,Liqiang Huang,Ming Meng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper investigates why humans are so good at quickly finding near-optimal solutions to Euclidean Traveling Salesman Problems (TSP) and models this ability with neural networks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Although TSP is computationally hard, humans can rapidly construct routes that are close to optimal. The authors want to understand what makes a tour “human-like,” how human solutions differ from optimal ones, and how such human-like strategies could be captured or learned by machine learning models.

Method: They generate a wide variety of Euclidean TSP instances and collect human solution tours. They then train Pointer Network–based neural policies under several regimes: (1) reinforcement learning directly on TSP performance, (2) supervised learning from optimal tours, (3) supervised learning from human tours, and (4) a hybrid where networks are first pretrained on optimal tours then fine-tuned with RL. At test time, they also use Best-of-N sampling to select high-quality tours from multiple sampled outputs. They compare the resulting neural tours to human tours in terms of geometric and structural properties and optimality gaps.

Result: Human tours are consistently near-optimal but not exactly optimal; they form a “near-optimal geometric basin” that shares many structural properties with optimal tours while showing systematic, human-specific deviations. Among the neural models, the best match to human behavior is achieved not by directly imitating optimal tours, but by a model that is first trained on optimal solutions, then fine-tuned with RL, and evaluated with Best-of-N sampling. This configuration most closely reproduces the patterns seen in human tours.

Conclusion: Human-like solutions to Euclidean TSP appear to arise from a blend of structured learning of good solution patterns (from optimal examples), subsequent refinement via reinforcement learning, and a limited test-time search over candidate solutions. This combination mirrors principles found in modern AI systems and provides a computational account of how humans can quickly generate high-quality, but not perfectly optimal, solutions to complex combinatorial problems.

Abstract: Humans often find good solutions to combinatorial optimization problems that are computationally hard even for advanced computer algorithms. In the Euclidean traveling salesman problems (TSP), people rapidly produce tours that are near-optimal, despite severe limits on time and computation. What makes a tour human-like, and how might such solutions be learned? Here we address these questions through a large-scale behavioral and computational investigation of human performance in Euclidean TSP. We sampled a broad space of TSP instances, collected human solutions, and compared them with neural policies based on Pointer Networks, which are recurrent neural networks with an attention-based pointing mechanism that define probability distributions over valid tours. We trained these networks under multiple objectives, including reinforcement learning (RL), supervised learning from optimal tours, supervised learning from human tours, and RL fine-tuning after optimal-supervised pretraining. Human tours were not identical to optimal tours, but occupied a near-optimal geometric basin: they shared many structural properties with optimal solutions while preserving systematic human-specific deviations. The best account of human tours was not direct imitation of optimal tours, but a model pretrained on optimal tours, fine-tuned by RL, and decoded through $\text{Best-of-}N$ sampling. These findings suggest that human-like solutions may emerge from a combination of structured supervised learning, RL, and test-time search, echoing computational principles underlying many modern artificial intelligence systems.

</details>


### [220] [Cost-Aware Recovery-Pathway Identification and Bayesian Optimization for Autonomous Materials Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23896)
*Debajyoti Ray,Niranjan Srinivas*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces a coactive learning framework for autonomous labs that jointly decides which experimental recovery pathway to pursue and how to optimize within that pathway, under varying experimental costs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous laboratories can run experiments automatically but still need high-level decision-making on which recovery or synthesis pathway to optimize, especially when committing to a wrong pathway can be expensive. Existing methods either assume the correct pathway is known (oracle) or separate pathway discrimination and optimization in suboptimal ways, and they often ignore heterogeneous experimental costs.

Method: The authors cast pathway selection and optimization as a sequential decision problem with two stages: (1) a discrete pathway-identification stage and (2) a continuous within-pathway optimization stage under heterogeneous costs. They propose a coactive learning algorithm combining a cost-sensitive Bayesian hypothesis-discrimination policy inspired by EC2 with Gaussian-process-based Bayesian optimization (GP-UCB-style) for the within-pathway optimization. They provide an analysis bounding expected spending of a fixed-budget campaign as the sum of expected pathway-identification cost and a capped optimization budget. The approach assumes a given hypothesis space over pathways and a diagnostic likelihood model.

Result: On synthetic benchmarks calibrated using results from PNNL's CICERO selective-precipitation study, the proposed method achieves performance close to an oracle-pathway Bayesian optimization method and a strong split-plate baseline that uses its first experimental plate to discriminate pathways but has oracle knowledge of the correct pathway. The coactive method, without oracle labels, matches these baselines and, on an NdFeB-inspired problem, avoids penalties that arise when a simpler commit-first baseline locks into a plausible but suboptimal hydroxide pathway.

Conclusion: The coactive learning framework effectively integrates pathway identification and within-pathway optimization for autonomous labs under heterogeneous experimental costs. It can approach oracle-level performance and avoid costly early commitment to inferior pathways, though results depend on the assumed cost model. The authors release open-source code and benchmarks, and analyze how sensitive their conclusions are to variations in the cost assumptions.

Abstract: Autonomous laboratories automate experimental execution, but a campaign must also decide which recovery pathway merits optimization. We formulate this as a sequential decision problem with a discrete pathway-identification stage and a continuous within-pathway optimization stage under heterogeneous experimental costs. Our implementation, Coactive learning, combines a cost-sensitive Bayesian hypothesis-discrimination policy motivated by EC2 (Golovin et al., 2010) with Gaussian-process Bayesian optimization (Srinivas et al., 2010). Under explicitly stated assumptions, the expected spend of one fixed-budget campaign attempt is bounded by the expected pathway-identification cost plus the capped within-pathway optimization budget. We evaluate the method on synthetic benchmarks constrained by selected results reported for PNNL's CICERO selective-precipitation study (Ritchhart et al., 2026). The method performs comparably to an oracle-pathway Bayesian-optimization reference and to a strong split-plate baseline that discriminates pathways with its first plate, without receiving an oracle label for the correct pathway. It is given a candidate hypothesis space and a diagnostic likelihood model. On an NdFeB-inspired instance, it avoids the simulated penalty of a commit-first baseline that initially selects a plausible but inferior hydroxide pathway. This hypothetical wrong-first-commitment scenario is motivated by the hydroxide-oxalate performance contrast reported by CICERO. We characterize the sensitivity of these conclusions to the assumed cost model. The code and benchmark are open source.

</details>


### [221] [GOTS: Greedy Orthogonal Token Selection for High-Resolution Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23913)
*Jun Ling,Tao Huang,Junzhuo Liu,Bowen Tang,Peng Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a new, training-free method (GOTS) to aggressively reduce visual tokens in vision-language models while preserving performance and cutting inference time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern vision-language models use dynamic or very high-resolution visual encoders that output thousands of visual tokens. These many tokens make downstream language model inference slow and expensive. Existing token-reduction approaches decide which tokens to keep using notions like per-token importance, relevance to a query, coverage, or diversity, but they don’t directly reason about how much new information each token adds beyond what’s already selected.

Method: The authors reconceptualize token pruning as selecting tokens whose features are complementary (orthogonal) to those already chosen. They introduce Greedy Orthogonal Token Selection (GOTS), a training-free, query-agnostic algorithm. Iteratively, GOTS computes each candidate token’s residual component that lies orthogonal to the span of the currently retained tokens and chooses the token with the largest residual energy. This selection rule is equivalent to greedily maximizing the one-step increase in the Gram determinant of the selected set, providing a clear geometric optimality guarantee at each step.

Result: Applied to five high-resolution VLM backbones from the Qwen-VL and InternVL families and evaluated on eleven benchmarks, GOTS preserves task performance better on average than the strongest existing token-reduction baselines at comparable token budgets. A controlled study on OCRBench further shows that, even after including the overhead of the selection procedure itself, GOTS decreases the model-side time-to-first-token, meaning overall faster inference.

Conclusion: Viewing token selection through the lens of span complementarity and orthogonality leads to a simple yet effective greedy algorithm for visual token reduction. GOTS offers a principled geometric criterion, works without retraining or query dependence, and empirically outperforms prior methods in both performance retention and end-to-end efficiency on multiple VLM architectures and benchmarks.

Abstract: Modern vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly rely on dynamic or high-resolution visual encoding, producing thousands of visual tokens that substantially increase downstream language-model inference cost. Existing token-reduction methods assess token utility through token-wise importance, query relevance, coverage, pairwise diversity, or subset-level objectives. Our key insight is to view visual token reduction through selected-span complementarity: instead of scoring a token in isolation or through pairwise relations, we assess how much of its feature is orthogonal to the span of the already retained subset. Based on this perspective, we propose Greedy Orthogonal Token Selection (GOTS), a training-free and query-agnostic method. At each step, GOTS selects the token with the largest residual energy orthogonal to the current retained span. This rule exactly maximizes the one-step augmented Gram determinant among candidate additions, giving each greedy step a precise local geometric guarantee for subset expansion. Across five high-resolution VLM backbones from the Qwen-VL and InternVL families and eleven diverse benchmarks, GOTS achieves higher average performance retention than the strongest evaluated baselines, and a controlled OCRBench study shows that it reduces model-side time-to-first-token after accounting for selection overhead. Code is available at https://github.com/newLLing/GOTS.

</details>


### [222] [MemTX: Transactional Belief Commit for Stateful Agent Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23929)
*Xiaoyang Li,Yiqi Wang,Haohui Lu,Zhi Chen,Mo Li,Pingan Song,Taotao Cai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MemTX is a transactional belief-commit protocol for LLM agent shared memory that prevents unsafe actions from unreliable writes and repairs downstream effects when beliefs are retracted.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM agent memory systems treat every accepted memory write as ground truth, so errors, stale data, or partial notes can trigger irreversible, harmful tool calls. There is a need for a principled mechanism that distinguishes tentative information from committed beliefs and provides safety and repair guarantees for multi-agent, tool-using systems.

Method: MemTX introduces a transactional protocol for belief commits in agent memory. Memory records are enriched with evidence, permissions, provenance, and validity metadata. Writes are first staged in snapshot-isolated transactions and must pass a validate-and-commit pipeline before being admitted. Irreversible tool calls are gated on the current in-flight belief state, and when a belief is retracted, the system performs typed cascading repair of dependent records and tool side effects. The protocol's key invariants (action-safety gating and cascade-repair completeness) are verified via property-based testing and bounded exhaustive enumeration over 5.5 million protocol states.

Result: MemTX is evaluated on five LLM backbones from three model families and compared to eight baseline methods. It achieves statistically significant improvements (via paired McNemar tests) on four backbones and ties the best baseline on the fifth and strongest backbone, while uniquely achieving zero downstream harm on every backbone. No violations of the safety invariants are found across 5.5 million enumerated protocol states.

Conclusion: Treating memory writes as tentative beliefs rather than immediate ground truth, and enforcing a transactional commit protocol with validated gating and cascading repair, improves both safety and performance of LLM agent systems. Stronger backbones alone cannot replace disciplined commit management; structural safeguards like MemTX are necessary to prevent harmful side effects in tool-using, multi-agent configurations.

Abstract: LLM agents increasingly coordinate through persistent shared memory: one agent's write becomes another agent's premise, and eventually a tool call with real side effects. Current agent memory systems treat every accepted write as immediately actionable truth, so a polluted tool result, a stale update, or a teammate's half-finished note can silently drive an irreversible action. We argue that a memory write is not a belief commit. We present MemTX, a transactional belief-commit protocol. Each record carries evidence, permissions, provenance, and validity. Writes are staged inside snapshot-isolated transactions and admitted by a validate-and-commit pipeline, irreversible tool calls are gated on in-flight belief state, and retracting a belief triggers typed cascading repair of its derived records and tool side effects. Two invariants, action-safety gating and cascade-repair completeness, are machine-checked by property-based testing and bounded exhaustive enumeration of 5.5 million protocol states, with zero violations. Across five backbones from three model families, MemTX leads all eight baselines with paired-McNemar significance on four backbones and statistically ties the best baseline on the fifth and strongest, while remaining the only method with zero downstream harm on every backbone. Backbone capability does not substitute for commit discipline.

</details>


### [223] [From Cognitive Architectures to Language Agents: A Mechanism-Level Review of Lineage, Convergence, and Migration Gaps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23942)
*Haodi Fan,Zucong Lan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper surveys and systematizes how cognitive architectures and modern language-based agents implement core control mechanisms like memory, planning, reflection, and tool use, and proposes testable bundles of mechanisms as future research directions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current discussions of agents often reduce rich control concepts like memory or planning to simplistic feature checklists, making it hard to compare systems or see what mechanisms really drive behavior. There are many historical cognitive architectures and many new LLM-based agent runtimes, but no unified, mechanism-level view of how they relate or what remains missing. The authors want to disentangle labels from underlying control semantics, map the true mechanism landscape, and identify gaps where coupling between mechanisms is still underexplored.

Method: The authors review ten classic cognitive architectures, eight families of modern language-agent runtimes, and forty-two mechanism-focused systems. For each, they reconstruct the agent’s control structure along several dimensions: state representation, control and transitions, persistence, failure handling, learning, and resource governance. They then code each mechanism’s empirical maturity using an evidence scale (E1–E4) and its architectural migration depth using a deployment scale (D0–D4). Using this coding, they synthesize a landscape of which mechanisms are operationalized, how, and where coupling is missing.

Result: They find that many advanced capabilities are already instantiated in modern agents—adaptive memory, failure recovery, dynamic team composition, workflow search, skill induction, resource scheduling, and uncertainty-aware action selection—but they tend to arise through independent convergence rather than explicit inheritance from cognitive architectures. They also show that some supposed gaps are already filled; for example, the GraSP system integrates multiple advanced mechanisms (calibrated multi-skill selection, typed compilation, verification, bounded repair, and replanning/ReAct fallback). However, they identify persistent gaps in how mechanisms are coupled and coordinated, revealing several underexplored bundles of jointly necessary capabilities.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that the frontier for agent research lies less in inventing isolated mechanisms and more in composing them into robust, reusable runtime patterns. It offers three main contributions: (1) a catalog of distinctive mechanisms spanning memory, planning, reflection, and tool use; (2) an evidence-depth framework that separates empirical support from deployment maturity; and (3) a set of five hypothesized bundles of coupled mechanisms (e.g., activation with latency and utility; persistent intentions with reconsideration) proposed as composable runtime invariants. These bundles form a falsifiable agenda: they can be operationalized, implemented, and empirically tested in future agent systems.

Abstract: Memory, planning, reflection, and tool use are often compared as feature labels, obscuring the control semantics that determine how an agent actually runs. This review connects ten historical cognitive architectures, eight language-agent runtime families, and forty-two mechanism-focused modern systems. We reconstruct each mechanism through state, control, transition, persistence, failure, learning, and resource governance, then code evidence relation (E1-E4) separately from migration depth (D0-D4). The resulting landscape is uneven. Modern agents have operationalized substantial parts of adaptive memory, failure recovery, dynamic team selection, workflow search, skill induction, resource scheduling, and uncertainty-conditioned action, although often through independent convergence rather than documented inheritance. The strongest remaining opportunities lie in couplings among mechanisms. Closest-baseline screening closes one proposed gap: GraSP already combines calibrated multi-skill selection, typed compilation, verification, bounded repair, and replanning or ReAct fallback. Five residual bundles remain: activation with latency and action utility; typed impasse with isolated substates and resolution compilation; bounded content competition with broadcast and admission learning; persistent intention with reconsideration and live method authority; and uncertainty with resource allocation, interruption, and stopping. We contribute a distinctive-mechanism catalog, an auditable evidence-depth framework, and a falsifiable agenda for testing these bundles as composable runtime invariants.

</details>


### [224] [DICA: Dual-Indicator Guided Contrastive Alignment in Multimodal Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23944)
*Hao Yang,Jin Wang,Xuejie Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose DICA, a dual-indicator guided contrastive alignment method that monitors attention entropy and image-text dependence during inference to dynamically correct hallucinations in multimodal LLMs, improving visual grounding and benchmark performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multimodal large language models often hallucinate because their visual attention drifts away from relevant regions and they underuse visual evidence, breaking the natural coarse-to-fine human-like visual reasoning process. There is a need for mechanisms that can detect and correct these failures during inference, rather than only relying on static training-time improvements.

Method: They introduce DICA (Dual-Indicator Guided Contrastive Alignment), which tracks two information-theoretic indicators at inference time: (1) Visual Attention Entropy (VAE), quantifying how concentrated or diffuse the model’s visual attention is over the image; and (2) Output Image Correlation (OIC), measuring how strongly the model’s generated outputs depend on the actual visual input. When these indicators deviate from normal patterns—e.g., VAE abnormally increases (overly diffuse attention) or OIC drops (text decouples from the image)—DICA triggers targeted contrastive alignment operations designed to push the model back toward better visual grounding and tighter image-text coupling.

Result: Across multiple multimodal benchmarks, DICA yields consistent performance gains compared to existing hallucination-mitigation techniques, with substantial reductions in hallucinated content and improved alignment between generated answers and visual evidence.

Conclusion: Monitoring internal indicators of attention concentration and image-text dependence during inference, and using them to trigger contrastive alignment, is an effective strategy for reducing hallucinations and improving the reliability of multimodal large language models. DICA validates this indicator-driven intervention paradigm and offers a practical way to enhance visual grounding in deployed systems.

Abstract: Human visual reasoning typically follows a coarse-to-fine attention process, starting from global scene understanding and gradually focusing on question-relevant regions. However, multimodal large language models may deviate from this pattern due to attention drift and the underutilization of visual evidence, which can lead to hallucinations. To mitigate these issues, this study proposes a Dual-Indicator Guided Contrastive Alignment (DICA), which tracks two information-theoretic indicators during inference: Visual Attention Entropy (VAE), which reflects the concentration of visual attention, and Output Image Correlation (OIC), which measures the dependence of generated outputs on the visual input. An abnormal increase in VAE or a decrease in OIC corresponds to different failure modes, which trigger targeted contrastive alignment to restore visual grounding. Experimental results across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that DICA consistently outperforms existing approaches and substantially reduces hallucinations, highlighting the effectiveness of indicator-driven intervention in improving multimodal inference reliability. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/BGWH123/DICA/.

</details>


### [225] [EviBack: Search-Agent Reinforcement Learning via Evidence-Constrained Teacher Backoff](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23955)
*Xiao Ma,Zhiquan Hu,Yi Wei,Chenchen Zhao,Yijun Chen,Jicheng Zhao,Yuming Li Chuang Dai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces EviBack, a method that improves reinforcement-learning-based Agentic RAG systems by adding evidence-aware teacher supervision for cases where all rollouts fail, leading to better QA performance and more efficient search.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In RL-trained Agentic RAG systems for open-domain QA, many training groups end up with all-zero rewards, providing no learning signal even though some trajectories may contain useful search patterns. Moreover, existing teacher or reference-based supervision can inadvertently override correct judgments about insufficient evidence. The authors aim to extract more learning signal from such failed groups while keeping rewards verifiable and avoiding bias from reference answers.

Method: They propose EviBack, an evidence-constrained teacher backoff mechanism. When a rollout group has all-zero rewards, EviBack supplies auxiliary supervision that focuses on evidence assessment separately from answer refinement, ensuring that the teacher cannot force an answer when evidence is lacking. They build a fully automated APE (Automatic Prompt Engineering) pipeline, assisted by GPT-5.5, starting from a single manually written dual-task teacher prompt. This pipeline automatically partitions and labels rollout data, runs ablations and task decompositions, evaluates variants, and selects a gated two-stage teacher: one stage for evidence sufficiency judgment and one for answer refinement, gated to preserve evidence-based decisions.

Result: The learned two-stage teacher outperforms the original manually designed teacher, yielding higher downstream F1 and valid-answer rates, while also lowering search cost, reducing duplicate queries, and minimizing forced terminations in the search process. Empirically, across seven open-domain QA benchmarks and three different scales of Qwen3 models, EviBack improves F1 compared with Search-R1 baselines and increases both single-hop and multi-hop macro F1 scores.

Conclusion: EviBack effectively recovers useful supervision from otherwise uninformative all-zero rollout groups in RL-trained Agentic RAG systems by decoupling evidence assessment from answer refinement and by using an automated teacher-construction pipeline. This leads to more efficient search behavior and consistently stronger QA performance across tasks and model sizes, and the authors plan to release the implementation publicly.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning enables Agentic RAG systems to learn multi-turn search from verifiable outcome rewards, but all- zero rollout groups provide no comparative signal and may hide useful search behavior. We present EviBack, an evidence- constrained Teacher backoff that supplies auxiliary super- vision to such groups while preserving verifiable Actor re- wards. It separates evidence assessment from answer refine- ment, preventing reference answers from overriding evidence- insufficiency judgments. A fully automated, end-to-end GPT- 5.5-assisted APE pipeline starts from a manually authored single-prompt dual-task Teacher, automatically partitions and labels rollout data, and performs ablation, task decomposition, evaluation, and selection to produce a gated two-stage Teacher. Compared with the manual design, the resulting Teacher im- proves downstream F1 and valid-answer rate while reduc- ing search, duplicate queries, and forced termination. Across seven open-domain QA benchmarks and three Qwen3 scales, EviBack improves F1 over Search-R1 and raises both single- and multi-hop macro F1. We guarantee that the code will be made publicly available at a later stage.

</details>


### [226] [Grokking on the Weight-Decay Clock: A Rate Hierarchy from Softly Broken Symmetries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23967)
*Taeyoung Kim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper provides an exact, analytically solvable description of late-time grokking dynamics in certain models, identifying a specific “grokking subspace” that controls delayed generalization and deriving precise scaling laws for grokking time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Grokking—where a model memorizes training data long before it suddenly generalizes—has been widely observed but is theoretically poorly understood, especially in terms of what controls the long delay before generalization and how optimization and regularization shape this behavior. The authors aim to give a precise, mechanistic account of grokking dynamics that can explain timing, optimizer effects, and the role of weight decay, rather than relying only on empirical observation.

Method: They analytically study linear models trained with full-batch heavy-ball optimization (momentum) and weight decay, and extend the analysis locally to nonlinear neural networks via a quadratic approximation around a solution. By decomposing parameter space into subspaces, they isolate a special “population-active component of the empirical null space”—the grokking subspace—along which training predictions don’t change. This makes weight decay the only force driving motion in that subspace. They then derive exact discrete-time and continuous-time relaxation laws, compute how each subspace contributes to population risk decay, and obtain explicit iteration-scale formulas for grokking time under different regularization and optimizer setups. They test these predictions in a fully analyzable synthetic model and in modular addition tasks.

Result: They identify the grokking subspace as the only subspace responsible for slow late-time decay of population risk. Along this subspace, dynamics are governed purely by weight decay, leading to slow, dissipative relaxation whose rate they compute exactly. They derive a closed-form scaling for grokking time, showing it behaves like (1-β)/(ηλ) in the weak-regularization regime, where β is momentum, η is learning rate, and λ is weight decay strength. Their theory separates the effects of coupled L2 regularization and decoupled weight decay, predicts how changing the optimizer or directly intervening on the grokking component affects generalization timing, and matches all predictions without fitting parameters in a synthetic setup. In modular addition tasks, they observe real grokking dynamics whose delay and late-time relaxation closely follow the theoretical predictions.

Conclusion: Late-time grokking dynamics in certain optimized neural models can be understood as motion within a specific grokking subspace where training predictions are frozen and only weight decay acts, producing slow but predictable relaxation of population risk. This mechanism yields exact laws and scaling relations for grokking time, clarifies the distinct roles of different regularization and optimizer choices, and explains delayed generalization as a consequence of the dynamics within this subspace. The theory is validated both in fully analytic synthetic models and in modular addition tasks, suggesting it captures a real and practically relevant mechanism behind grokking.

Abstract: Delayed generalization, or grokking, remains poorly understood despite extensive empirical study. We identify an exactly solvable late-time relaxation mechanism for grokking in linear models trained with full-batch heavy-ball optimization and weight decay, together with a locally quadratic extension to nonlinear neural networks. Our analysis reveals a distinguished population-active component of the empirical null space, which we call the grokking subspace. Along this subspace, the training predictions remain unchanged, leaving weight decay as the sole restoring force and giving rise to a slow dissipative relaxation governed by an exact discrete-time and continuous-time law. We show that only this subspace contributes to the slow asymptotic decay of the population risk and derive explicit iteration-scale predictions for the grokking time, recovering the familiar $(1-β)/(ηλ)$ scaling in the weak-regularization regime. The theory further predicts distinct effects of optimizer choice, distinguishing coupled $L_2$ regularization from decoupled weight decay, and yields causal predictions for interventions that modify the grokking component. We verify all theoretical identities without fitted parameters in a synthetic model where every subspace and relaxation rate is computable in closed form. We further observe genuine delayed generalization in modular addition, where the measured delay follows the predicted scaling and the late-time relaxation agrees closely with the theoretical clock.

</details>


### [227] [Plato-Bio: verification-first biological novelty screening with temporal rediscovery and structural benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23975)
*Stefan G. Creadore*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Plato-Bio is a workflow-focused LLM research agent framework for biology that emphasizes provenance, auditing, and rigorous evaluation instead of relying on coherent but potentially invalid AI-generated output.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM-based research agents can draft literature reviews and analyses, but their fluent output can mask serious scientific invalidity, weak provenance, and unverifiable claims. There is a need for an agent architecture that embeds scientific rigor: explicit workflow states, traceable evidence, reproducibility, and clear boundaries between hypothesis generation and validated findings, particularly in complex domains like biology and genomics.

Method: The authors extend the open Plato/Denario architecture to create Plato-Bio, adding biology-oriented routing and several safeguards: explicit workflow states, detailed provenance records, citation checks, links between claims and supporting evidence, controlled/scoped file writing, and publication gates to limit what can be output as a “result.” They perform a source code audit to fix defects that might bias evaluation, then run a large Python test suite and focused domain-specific suites (biology, genomics, evidence/citation, adversarial safety). They also demonstrate Plato-Bio on two narrow tasks: (1) a historical literature rediscovery task about fish oil and Raynaud phenomenon, comparing ranking methods; and (2) comparing AlphaFold models to experimental protein structures for 15 human proteins, analyzing structural discrepancies and masking low-confidence regions.

Result: After the code audit, they identify and repair three issues: loss of task domain in a default factory, missing method signals in scoring, and evidence sidecars that lacked normalization to the number of drafted claims. With these fixes, the full Python test suite passes (931 passes, 6 skips, 0 failures/errors), and targeted domain-specific test suites also pass. In the rediscovery task, independent pre-1986 literature-based bridges rank the fish oil–Raynaud link first, with TF-IDF ranking it second and corpus frequency third, showing reasonable retrospective ranking but not true discovery. In the AlphaFold comparison, 11/15 proteins have high-confidence core Cα RMSD <1 Å (median 0.501 Å), while 4 proteins show >2 Å deviations; confidence masking notably reduces a large discrepancy for SUMO1 from 16.61 to 2.58 Å over 74 residues. The workflow outputs 27 traceable structural discrepancy regions, explicitly marked as unvalidated hypotheses.

Conclusion: Plato-Bio offers a reproducible, auditable framework for using LLM-based agents in biological research workflows, emphasizing software contracts, provenance, and cautious interpretation. The system is suitable for building screening pipelines and hypothesis lists but does not, by itself, establish biological novelty or agent “intelligence.” The authors stress that stronger claims about agent performance or new biology require preregistered study designs, independent evaluation, and prospective experimental validation.

Abstract: Large language model research agents can connect literature retrieval, analysis code, and manuscript preparation, but coherent output does not establish scientific validity. We developed Plato-Bio, a biology-routed extension of the open Plato/Denario architecture that couples explicit workflow states with provenance records, citation checks, claim-to-evidence links, scoped file writes, and publication gates. A source audit identified and repaired three defects that could distort evaluation: loss of task domain in the default factory, omission of declared method signals from scoring, and evidence sidecars that lacked the drafted-claim denominator. On the current clean revision, the full Python suite completed with 931 passes, six skips, and no failures or errors; targeted biology, genomics, evidence/citation, and adversarial-safety suites likewise completed without failure. We evaluated two narrow use cases. In a frozen historical rediscovery task, independent pre-1986 literature bridges ranked the later-studied relation between fish oil and Raynaud phenomenon first; TF-IDF ranked it second and corpus frequency third. This single curated task measures retrospective ranking, not prospective discovery. In a separate comparison of AlphaFold models with experimental structures for 15 human proteins, 11 targets had high-confidence-core C-alpha RMSD below 1 Angstrom (median 0.501 Angstrom). Four targets exceeded 2 Angstrom, and confidence masking reduced the SUMO1 discrepancy from 16.61 to 2.58 Angstrom over 74 residues. The workflow emitted 27 traceable discrepancy regions, all retained as unvalidated hypotheses. Plato-Bio therefore provides reproducible software contracts and auditable screening baselines; broader claims of agent efficacy or biological novelty require preregistered evaluation, independent review, and prospective validation.

</details>


### [228] [Exploring Budgeted Image Classification with Content-Sensitive Resource Allocation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23997)
*Athanasios G. Papadopoulos*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Paper studies how to dynamically allocate computational budget across multiple early/late-exit points of a deep image classifier so as to maximize accuracy under a per-batch compute constraint, formulating it as a budgeted image classification problem.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI models, especially deep neural networks, are increasingly deployed in environments where available computation (e.g., CPU/GPU time, energy, latency) fluctuates. Fixed-complexity models are inefficient: sometimes they waste resources; other times they cannot meet tight budgets. There is thus a need for principled ways to adapt the inference complexity of a classifier to current computational constraints while maintaining as much accuracy as possible.

Method: Formulate Budgeted Image Classification as a resource allocation integer program: given a classifier with multiple decision points (early exits), a batch of images, and a total compute budget, decide for each image at which decision point to stop so as to maximize overall accuracy. Because the integer program is NP-hard, introduce a continuous relaxation that yields a simple, content-agnostic allocation rule (images treated symmetrically). To overcome its limitations, design a content-sensitive allocation strategy that leverages information about individual images’ difficulty or confidence to choose appropriate decision points. Provide theoretical analysis that derives conditions decision points must satisfy to be useful in budgeted settings and examine failure cases.

Result: The content-agnostic strategy is computationally tractable but suboptimal because it ignores per-image characteristics. The proposed content-sensitive strategy empirically outperforms the content-agnostic baseline, achieving higher accuracy under the same budget across tested settings. Theoretical results characterize when decision points are beneficial for budgeted classification and identify structural issues that can lead to poor performance. An analysis of failure cases highlights situations where the methods struggle, suggesting how architectures or decision points might be redesigned.

Conclusion: Adapting inference complexity across images within a batch under a global compute budget can be framed as an optimization problem, but exact solutions are NP-hard. Relaxations lead to simple budget allocation policies, and incorporating content sensitivity substantially improves performance. The paper clarifies design requirements for decision points (e.g., early exits) to be effective in budgeted settings and identifies common failure modes, providing guidance for future work on dynamic, resource-aware deployment of deep classifiers.

Abstract: The ever-growing adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) creates the need to deploy Deep Neural Networks in a variety of computational environments. We consider dynamic environments, where computational requirements are subject to change, and we pose the following question: How do we adjust the complexity of an AI classification system, in order to maximize its accuracy, while meeting changing computational constraints? We call this problem Budgeted Image Classification, and we formally formulate it as a resource allocation integer program. Given a computational budget, a batch of images, and a classification system that can make decisions with varying complexity (it has multiple decision points), we explore strategies to allocate images to decision points, in order to maximize accuracy within the available budget. The original integer program is NP-Hard, so, we propose a continuous relaxation, leading to a content-agnostic allocation strategy which assigns images to decision points without considering their particular content. We address this issue by proposing a content-sensitive strategy, that we experimentally show it leads to superior performance. We theoretically study the behavior of our strategies, deriving conditions that must be satisfied by decision points to be suitable for budgeted classification. We analyze fails cases, offering insights for future research directions.

</details>


### [229] [Self-Supervised Consistency Enhanced Disentangled Learning for Neural Decoding Generalization in Brain-Machine Interface](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24023)
*Jiyu Wei,Di Hong,Zhanjie Zhang,Dazhong Rong,Qinming He,Yueming Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes SSCDL, a self-supervised, consistency-based, disentangled neural decoding framework that combats neural drift in invasive BMIs and achieves state-of-the-art, cross-day-robust decoding of motor parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Brain-Machine Interfaces degrade over time due to neural drift, which limits their long-term usability, especially for invasive systems. Existing decoders struggle to learn neural representations that remain stable over days and typically treat all motor parameters uniformly, ignoring that drift may affect velocity, direction, and speed differently. There is a need for a decoding framework that both learns drift-invariant representations and explicitly accounts for the distinct neural preferences underlying different motor components, to ensure robust, long-term control of assistive and robotic devices.

Method: The authors introduce a Self-Supervised Consistency enhanced Disentangled Learning (SSCDL) framework. First, they design a Consistency enhanced Neural Decoder (CND) that uses a teacher–student paradigm with self-supervised consistency constraints: artificial perturbations are applied to neural signals, and the student is trained to match the teacher’s outputs, enforcing drift-invariant representations. Second, they instantiate three specialized CNDs within a Complementary-Disentangled Generalization (CDG) mechanism, where decoding is factorized into separate sub-models for velocity, direction, and speed, inspired by neural preference theory. This disentangled architecture aims to capture complementary, stable neural features for each motor parameter and then integrate them for improved generalization across days.

Result: Experiments show that SSCDL achieves state-of-the-art performance on cross-day neural decoding tasks relative to existing BMI decoders. The method exhibits strong robustness to neural drift, maintaining high decoding accuracy and stability across multiple recording days. Quantitative evaluations demonstrate significant gains in cross-day generalization, indicating that both the consistency-based training and the disentangled multi-parameter design contribute to improved long-term decoding performance.

Conclusion: SSCDL effectively addresses neural drift in invasive BMIs by combining self-supervised teacher–student consistency with disentangled decoding of distinct motor parameters. By learning invariant neural representations from multiple neural preference perspectives, it substantially improves cross-day generalization and robustness. These properties make SSCDL a promising foundation for stable, long-term control in human-centered robotics and fine-grained assistive technologies, advancing the practical viability of BMIs in real-world, extended-use scenarios.

Abstract: Brain-Machine Interfaces (BMIs) provide a direct communication pathway between the brain and external devices, enabling humans to control assistive and robotic technologies, with potential applications in rehabilitation, human motor augmentation, and human-centered robotics. However, due to neural drift, the performance of BMIs decreases over time, posing challenges for long-term viability, particularly for invasive BMIs (iBMIs). Existing solutions suffer from two main drawbacks: (i) difficulty in learning robust neural representations, and (ii) neglecting that neural drift varies across motor parameters (e.g., velocity, direction, and speed). To overcome these limitations, we propose Self-Supervised Consistency enhanced Disentangled Learning (SSCDL), a neural decoding generalization framework built on two key innovations. We first design a backbone model named Consistency enhanced Neural Decoder (CND), using a novel teacher-student consistency constraint with simulated neural signal perturbations to learn robust representations invariant to neural drift. Then, we employ three dedicated CNDs under the Complementary-Disentangled Generalization (CDG) mechanism, which disentangles motor signals into velocity, direction, and speed with inspiration from neural preference theory. This disentangled learning enables SSCDL to capture invariant neural representations from diverse neural preference perspectives, significantly enhancing cross-day generalization. Extensive experimental results show that SSCDL delivers state-of-the-art decoding performance, exhibiting high robustness and cross-day stability. These capabilities underscore its strong potential for long-term interaction in human-centric robotic and fine-grained assistive applications.

</details>


### [230] [A Cyclic Adaptation-Generalization Framework with Uncertainty-Guided Self-Paced Learning for Long-Term Brain-Machine Interfaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24031)
*Jiyu Wei,Di Hong,Zhanjie Zhang,Dazhong Rong,Qinming He,Yueming Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes UnSPC, a new framework that combines domain adaptation and domain generalization with uncertainty-guided self-paced pseudo-labeling to combat long-term neural drift in invasive brain-machine interfaces.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Invasive brain-machine interfaces suffer from neural drift over time, which changes the neural signal distributions and causes decoding performance to deteriorate, requiring frequent and costly recalibration. Existing approaches typically use either domain adaptation or domain generalization in isolation and fail to handle fine-grained, subdomain-level distribution shifts, limiting their effectiveness for long-term, stable BMI control.

Method: The authors introduce Uncertainty-guided Self-paced Cycling (UnSPC), which centers on an Uncertainty-guided Self-paced Pseudo-labeling (UnSPL) mechanism and a Cycling Adaptation and Generalization (CycAG) strategy. UnSPL iteratively selects reliable pseudo-labeled target samples using a noise-robust ranking strategy based on prediction uncertainty, progressively expanding the training set from easy to harder samples. CycAG then alternates between domain adaptation (aligning source and target distributions) and domain generalization (learning target-agnostic, robust representations) using these high-quality pseudo-labeled samples, thus jointly addressing global and subdomain neural drift in a cyclical, iterative manner.

Result: Through extensive experiments on several neural decoding datasets, the proposed UnSPC framework demonstrates improved robustness and effectiveness in mitigating performance degradation due to long-term neural drift compared to state-of-the-art methods that only employ domain adaptation or domain generalization. The results show better alignment to evolving target distributions and more stable decoding performance over time.

Conclusion: UnSPC, by cyclically integrating domain adaptation and domain generalization under an uncertainty-guided, self-paced pseudo-labeling scheme, provides a more robust solution to long-term neural drift in invasive BMIs. The framework effectively captures both global and subdomain distribution shifts, maintains transferable neural representations, and improves long-term decoding stability, representing a novel direction for stable, long-term BMI control systems.

Abstract: Brain-Machine Interfaces (BMIs), which link the brain to external devices, hold great potential in rehabilitation, human performance augmentation, and human-centered robotics. However, invasive BMIs face a critical challenge for long-term deployment due to neural drift, which degrades decoding performance over time and necessitates frequent recalibration. Existing methods designed to mitigate neural drift typically rely on either domain adaptation (DA) or domain generalization (DG) alone and often fail to capture fine-grained distribution shifts across neural subdomains, resulting in limited performance. To overcome these limitations, we propose Uncertainty-guided Self-paced Cycling (UnSPC), a robust framework that synergizes DA and DG for target domain refining under an Uncertainty-guided Self-paced Pseudo-labeling (UnSPL) mechanism. To handle subdomain neural drift across domains, UNSPL is proposed to iteratively mine reliable pseudo-labeled samples with a noise-robust ranking strategy for further fine-tuning. Leveraging these high-quality samples, we introduce a novel Cycling Adaptation and Generalization (CycAG) strategy, which integrates DA and DG within an iterative cycle to progressively mitigate both global and subdomain drift. This cyclic process enables effective alignment to evolving target distributions while preserving robust and transferable representations, thereby mitigating performance degradation under long-term neural drifts. Extensive experiments on multiple neural decoding datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of UnSPC. To our knowledge, our proposed UnSPC is the first to cyclically integrate DA and DG with pseudo-labeling, paving the way toward stable long-term BMI controls.

</details>


### [231] [The Half-Lives of Generative-AI Evidence: A 40-Record Audit, a Claim-Currency Framework, and a Reflexive Case of Frontier-Model-Assisted Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24032)
*Carlo Iacono*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper audits how quickly evaluations of generative AI models become outdated, analyzes 40 recent empirical studies for model age and reporting practices, and reflects on its own rapid, AI-assisted production, proposing better reporting standards for model use and currency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Because generative AI models and their capabilities change rapidly, empirical studies that test them can be partly obsolete by the time they are published. This temporal instability threatens the interpretability, reproducibility, and policy relevance of research on generative AI. The authors aim to understand how old the models in recent studies actually are at the time of publication, how well this is reported, and how to make AI-assisted research more transparent and auditable.

Method: The authors construct a maximum-variation purposive sample of 40 empirical records on generative AI published between 18 July 2025 and 17 July 2026, including journal articles, preprints, and one lab report. They code each record for publication route, execution timing, model identity, age of the newest named generation or immutable snapshot at appearance, whether newer same-family models had superseded it, and whether the study refreshed model evidence. They also analyze their own paper as a reflexive case, documenting a two-day, frontier-model-assisted workflow (using GPT-5.6 Sol Pro in ChatGPT) and applying a structured "Model Facts" and model-currency statement.

Result: Across the 40 studies, the newest named model at appearance was a median of 281 days old, with an interquartile range of 75–478 days and extremes from 11 to 939 days. Journal articles had notably older models (median 395 days) than preprints (56 days) and the single lab report (49 days. Thirty-five records used a model family that had already been superseded; only seven studies provided precise dated identifiers for the models used; three clearly refreshed their model evidence, and one added a late sensitivity analysis. All 40 records included at least one OpenAI model, reflecting corpus construction rather than overall ecosystem prevalence.

Conclusion: The paper argues that model age and claim currency are distinct: an older model does not automatically invalidate a study, but lack of precise temporal and version reporting undermines interpretability. To address this, the authors propose six reporting practices, including clear model identification, dating, and statements on model currency and supersession. Their reflexive case shows that rapid, AI-assisted research is possible while keeping model contributions inspectable and avoiding treating AI output as independent validation. The "half-lives" metaphor is used to highlight temporal decay of relevance, not to claim a universal decay rate for generative-AI evaluations.

Abstract: Generative-AI evaluations can become historical before publication, yet calendar age does not affect every conclusion equally. This paper has two linked purposes. First, it audits a maximum-variation purposive corpus of 40 empirical records appearing between 18 July 2025 and 17 July 2026. The audit coded publication route, execution timing, model identity, age of the newest named generation or immutable snapshot, same-family supersession and refresh behaviour. At appearance, the newest named model was a median 281 days old (middle 50%: 75-478; range: 11-939). Median age was 395 days for 25 journal articles, 56 days for 14 preprints and 49 days for one laboratory report. Thirty-five records included a superseded family, seven supplied a precise dated identifier, three clearly refreshed model evidence, and one added a late sensitivity test. All 40 included an OpenAI system, a feature of this corpus rather than a prevalence estimate. The paper distinguishes model age from claim currency and proposes six reporting practices. Second, it treats its own two-day production process as a reflexive case of frontier-model-assisted research creation. GPT-5.6 Sol Pro in ChatGPT supported candidate discovery, source reconciliation, calculations, drafting and critique; the author checked sources, made all substantive decisions and accepts responsibility. This is a proof-of-practice, not a controlled estimate of productivity or quality. By applying its own Model Facts and model-currency statement, the paper shows how rapid AI-assisted research can be made inspectable without treating model output as independent validation. The title uses half-lives metaphorically; no universal decay rate is estimated.

</details>


### [232] [Quantum-Inspired Evolutionary Neighborhood Search for Arrival-Departure Track Utilization Adjustment under Short-Term Disturbances](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24049)
*Xiaobin Li,Wuming Lei,Yanbin Gao,Weiguang Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose a joint rescheduling model and a quantum-inspired evolutionary algorithm to reassign tracks and station resources after short disturbances, reducing total delay versus CP-SAT but needing faster computation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Short-term disruptions at busy stations cause knock-on delays because arrivals, departures, and platform/resource usage are tightly coupled. Existing approaches often treat timing and resource allocation separately or are too slow for real-time use. The authors want a method that jointly adjusts track allocation and train times while respecting detailed station resource constraints, and that performs better than a standard exact solver under realistic data.

Method: Model station operations (arrival, track occupancy, departure) as zone-level resource-occupation intervals and formulate an optimization model for adjusting arrival-departure track allocations under a disturbance. Enforce resource compatibility constraints and use an objective combining train delays and costs of reassigning resources. To solve it, design a hybrid metaheuristic: a quantum-inspired evolutionary algorithm enhanced with neighborhood search (QEA-NS). Build test perturbation scenarios using GTFS timetable data for Frankfurt Hauptbahnhof and compare QEA-NS to a CP-SAT solver under identical resource sets and feasibility rules.

Result: On a main test instance, both QEA-NS and CP-SAT find feasible plans satisfying all modeled resource constraints. QEA-NS delivers a total delay of 388 minutes versus 519 minutes for CP-SAT, a 25.2% reduction; mean delay per delayed train drops from 4.99 to 3.73 minutes, though QEA-NS takes longer to compute. Over 10 random perturbation instances, QEA-NS outperforms CP-SAT in every case, with mean total delay 390.5±35.9 minutes compared to 673.8±105.7 minutes for CP-SAT.

Conclusion: Representing station operations via zone-level resource intervals and solving the resulting adjustment problem with QEA-NS can substantially improve delay outcomes in recovery planning relative to CP-SAT, under the tested assumptions. The approach reliably finds feasible, lower-delay solutions across multiple disturbance scenarios, but its runtime is still relatively high, so further work is needed to improve computational efficiency for practical deployment.

Abstract: Short-term disturbances at major passenger railway stations alter train arrival and departure times as well as the release sequence of station resources. Effective recovery therefore requires coordinated adjustment of arrival-departure track allocation, station resource occupation, and train retiming. This study represents the station resources involved in train arrival, track occupancy, and departure operations as zone-level resource-occupation intervals. An arrival-departure track allocation adjustment model is formulated. Resource compatibility is imposed as the feasibility condition, while train delays and resource reassignment costs are jointly considered. A quantum-inspired evolutionary algorithm combined with neighborhood search (QEA-NS) is proposed to solve the model. Perturbation instances are constructed using GTFS timetable data from Frankfurt Hauptbahnhof, Germany. QEA-NS is compared with CP-SAT under the same candidate resource set and feasibility criteria. Both methods generate solutions satisfying the modeled resource compatibility constraints. QEA-NS yields a total delay of 388 min, compared with 519 min for CP-SAT, representing a reduction of 25.2\%. The mean delay of delayed trains decreases from 4.99 to 3.73 min, although QEA-NS requires a longer solution time. Across 10 random perturbation instances, QEA-NS achieves lower total delay in every case. Its mean total delay and standard deviation are 390.5 min and 35.945 min, respectively, compared with 673.8 min and 105.739 min for CP-SAT. The results indicate that, under the adopted resource representation and constraints, QEA-NS improves the delay performance of recovery plans. Its computational efficiency, however, requires further improvement.

</details>


### [233] [Success Is Not Self-Explanatory: Auditing Success Provenance in Agent Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24054)
*Jingkun Luo,Da-Tian Peng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose AcquaBench, a benchmark to measure whether an AI system’s correct answers actually depend on having the right internal information, not just on producing the correct output.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluations focus on whether an agent’s final answer is correct, but that can hide how the agent got there. Once an agent’s internal information state changes during evaluation, correctness alone cannot distinguish genuine intended reasoning from mere answer lookup or spurious correlations. Current methods like outcome measurements and exposure detection also fail to reveal whether success truly depended on the correct underlying information (the “target”). The authors call this missing piece of evaluation “success provenance” and aim to provide a way to audit it.

Method: They introduce AcquaBench, which evaluates “success provenance” using controlled value substitutions on standardized input surfaces. For each question, they construct three conditions: CLEAN (only benchmark-authorized information is present), GOLD (the correct target value is injected and made available), and SHAM (a structurally matched but incorrect value is injected, preserving exposure opportunity without giving the right answer). They then analyze performance differences between these conditions, clustered by question IDs, to see how scores change when correct vs. incorrect values are available while keeping exposure structure constant. The key contrasts are GOLD minus CLEAN (effect of having correct target available) and GOLD minus SHAM (whether performance gains are specifically due to target correctness rather than just exposure).

Result: In the D0 setting, models perform 19.1–25.9 percentage points better in GOLD than in SHAM, indicating that success closely follows access to the correct value rather than merely any injected value. In the more distributed D2 setting, GOLD still outperforms SHAM, showing continued dependence on correct targets, but a previously useful marker—colocation (coloc)—no longer reliably indicates high scores (AUROC falls to 0.376 and 0.142). This suggests that behavioral dependence on correct internal information can extend beyond the probe’s assumed observation unit. In model comparison, an initial 5.0-point score difference under CLEAN shrinks to only -0.6 points under GOLD, which is not enough to conclusively reverse the ranking between models.

Conclusion: AcquaBench shows that merely checking whether an agent’s answers are correct is insufficient; evaluations should also assess whether the internal information state that the benchmark exposes actually supports those successes. Their GOLD/SHAM contrast provides an operational way to audit success provenance, revealing when models’ performance truly depends on having the correct target information. They argue that agent benchmarks should routinely report both outcome success and whether the evaluated information state underwrites that success.

Abstract: A correct answer can conceal why an agent succeeded. Once agents change their information state during evaluation, correctness no longer distinguishes intended reasoning from answer acquisition. Outcome evidence and exposure detection do not establish whether success depended on an acquired target; we call this missing evaluation object success provenance. AcquaBench audits it through matched CLEAN, GOLD, and SHAM value substitution on four standardized surfaces with joint qid-clustered analysis. CLEAN retains benchmark-authorized information. GOLD makes the correct target available. SHAM preserves source structure and exposure opportunity but substitutes a matched incorrect value. GOLD minus CLEAN measures the total score response to correct-target availability; GOLD minus SHAM tests whether that response tracks target correctness beyond matched source exposure. In D0, GOLD exceeds SHAM by 19.1 to 25.9 percentage points, showing that success follows the correct value. In D2, GOLD still exceeds SHAM under distributed sufficiency while coloc no longer transfers as a high-score marker, with AUROC 0.376 and 0.142. Behavioral dependence can thus persist beyond this probe's intended observation unit. In model comparison, a supported 5.0-point CLEAN score gap compresses to a raw GOLD difference of -0.6 points without establishing rank inversion. Agent benchmarks should report success together with whether the evaluated information state supported it.

</details>


### [234] [The Cost of Knowing: A Resource-Aware Protocol for Benchmarking Hallucination Beyond Static Leaderboards](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24063)
*Keyu Li,Jin Gao,Dequan Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces MAS-HQ, a resource-aware benchmark that evaluates factuality jointly with computational cost, showing that systems that look best on standard factuality leaderboards can be worse once token and latency costs are accounted for.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing factuality benchmarks treat compute as free, so models that use brute-force strategies (e.g., Best-of-N decoding, many calls, long chains) can top leaderboards simply by spending more tokens and latency. As frontier models’ factuality saturates near the ceiling, it becomes hard to distinguish genuinely better systems from more expensive ones, and static leaderboards offer no guidance about which system is preferable to deploy in practice.

Method: They propose MAS-HQ (Multi-Agent System Hallucination Quest), a resource-aware evaluation framework that can wrap any factuality detector. Instead of scoring systems in isolation, MAS-HQ pits systems against each other in competitive matches. It introduces Q-Score, which equals a model’s factuality score minus a normalized cost term (based on tokens and latency), with a tunable cost weight. They analyze scenarios like a brute-force Best-of-4 agent versus a more efficient baseline, and run experiments across summarization and open-domain QA, sweeping cost weights and running many trials (100) to test stability.

Result: They show a concrete ranking reversal: a Best-of-4 agent that appears superior on standard factuality (H-Score 0.9169 vs 0.9103) becomes worse once cost is considered (Q-Score 0.5169 vs 0.5217), while also using about four times the tokens and latency. Across tasks, single-agent baselines naturally drift toward resource-heavy over-optimization under static metrics, whereas the competitive MAS-HQ setup encourages more resource-efficient strategies. The improvements from cost-aware competition are modest but consistent and robust, and the Q-Score axis remains discriminative even among very strong, ceiling-level models such as Gemini-2.5-Pro and a simulated GPT-5 preview.

Conclusion: Static factuality leaderboards can be misleading for deployment decisions, since they ignore computation cost and reward brute-force resource use. MAS-HQ and its Q-Score provide a principled, reproducible way to evaluate factual systems under a cost-factuality trade-off, revealing ranking reversals and encouraging more resource-efficient policies. This makes it possible to compare frontier systems not just by how factual they are, but by how much factuality they deliver per unit of compute.

Abstract: On standard factuality tasks, frontier models now cluster near the top of the scale. The question is therefore shifting from how factual a system is toward how much compute that factuality costs. Static leaderboards score factuality in isolation and treat compute as free, so they cannot tell a genuinely better system apart from one that simply spends more. Consider a ranking reversal. A brute-force Best-of-4 agent posts the higher raw factuality score (H-Score 0.9169 vs 0.9103) and would top a static leaderboard, but once cost is counted it is the worse system, losing on Q-Score (0.5169 vs 0.5217) at roughly four times the tokens and latency, under a reported cost weight whose sensitivity we sweep. So the system that tops a static leaderboard can be the worse one to deploy. To make this trade-off visible, we introduce MAS-HQ (Multi-Agent System Hallucination Quest), a resource-aware evaluation protocol. It wraps any factuality detector and normalizes for cost, and it pits systems against each other rather than scoring them in isolation. The Q-Score measures factuality minus normalized cost under a competitive match. Across summarization and open-domain QA, single-agent baselines drift into resource-heavy over-optimization, while competition elicits more resource-efficient policies. These gains are small but consistent, and stable across 100 trials. The axis stays discriminative for frontier systems (Gemini-2.5-Pro, and GPT-5 in simulated preview) whose raw factuality scores are already bunched near the ceiling. MAS-HQ provides a reproducible way to measure how much a factual answer costs.

</details>


### [235] [MiSS: A Logic-Driven Explanation of Minimal Sufficient Coalitions for Point Cloud Classifiers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24074)
*Mengda Xing,Jean-Marie Lagniez*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MiSS is a black-box framework that explains 3D point cloud classifiers by finding minimal sets of geometric regions (superpoints) that are sufficient to preserve the model’s prediction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing explainers for 3D point cloud models often require white-box access, Boolean feature spaces, or logical encodings, and they struggle to provide statistically certified, minimal sufficient explanations under realistic perturbations. There is a need for a practical, black-box method that can identify which regions of a 3D object are truly sufficient for a classifier’s decision, with guarantees on minimality and statistical validity.

Method: MiSS partitions a 3D point cloud into superpoints that serve as interpretable units. It then formulates the search for sufficient coalitions of these regions as a weighted MaxSAT problem. The framework separates proposal and verification: (1) a MaxSAT-based search proposes region coalitions using strategies such as heuristic adaptive cardinality floors, exact-size fallback, tightened upper bounds, blocking clauses, and a surrogate acquisition heuristic trained on previous oracle calls; (2) a black-box statistical oracle evaluates whether a candidate coalition is sufficient by querying the underlying classifier under a specified perturbation distribution. When the search completes, MiSS outputs a coalition with provably minimal cardinality that is statistically certified as sufficient.

Result: On ModelNet40 and ShapeNet benchmarks using PointNet and PointMLP classifiers, MiSS achieves higher precision and coverage of explanations than rule-based baseline explainers in most experimental configurations, while also reducing explanation time compared to exhaustive search methods.

Conclusion: MiSS provides a practical, black-box, query-based explanation framework for 3D point cloud classifiers, capable of finding statistically verified, minimally sufficient sets of geometric regions that account for a model’s prediction. Its MaxSAT-driven search with learned heuristics yields more precise and broadly applicable explanations than rule-based baselines, at lower computational cost than exhaustive approaches.

Abstract: We present MiSS, a black-box, query-based framework for explaining 3D point cloud classifiers through perturbation-relative sufficiency reasoning. MiSS treats a superpoint partition as an interpretable abstraction layer and asks whether the original prediction can be certified from a minimal coalition of geometric regions under a specified perturbation distribution. Unlike abductive explainers that require Boolean feature spaces or white-box logical encodings of the predictor, MiSS separates candidate proposal from verification: a weighted MaxSAT procedure proposes coalitions using a heuristic adaptive cardinality floor, certified exact-size fallback, a safely tightened upper bound, blocking clauses, and a surrogate acquisition heuristic learned from previous oracle evaluations, while a blackbox statistical oracle decides sufficiency from prediction queries. The system returns a statistically verified sufficient coalition as a binary attribution, with minimum cardinality guaranteed when certified search completes. Experiments on ModelNet40 and ShapeNet with PointNet and PointMLP classifiers show higher precision and coverage than rule-based baselines in most settings, with lower explanation time than exhaustive search.

</details>


### [236] [Towards High-Level Semantic Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24082)
*Xiujie Song,Gefei Yang,Yining You,Jiahui Gan,Qi Jia,Shota Watanabe,Tianxi Wan,Mengyue Wu,Kai Yu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Survey of AI’s progression from basic semantics to high-level semantic intelligence across multiple modalities and tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI has moved from handling simple, literal semantics to tasks requiring complex, high-level semantic understanding (e.g., humor, metaphor, empathy). However, there is no systematic, comprehensive review of this shift from basic-level semantic intelligence (BLSI) to high-level semantic intelligence (HLSI), especially framed in terms of semantic complexity. This gap motivates a dedicated survey.

Method: The paper conducts a structured survey of research on high-level semantic (HLS) tasks—such as humor, sarcasm, metaphor, empathy, persuasion, narrative, and other HLS phenomena—across text, speech, vision, and multimodal settings. It reviews and organizes: (1) data construction practices, (2) modeling and optimization strategies, and (3) evaluation methodologies, for both understanding and generation tasks related to HLS.

Result: The survey organizes and synthesizes a broad body of work on HLS tasks into a coherent framework centered on semantic complexity and the progression from BLSI to HLSI. It identifies representative datasets, modeling approaches, optimization techniques, and evaluation protocols across modalities, and clarifies common patterns and distinctions among different HLS phenomena.

Conclusion: High-Level Semantics (HLS) is crucial for moving AI toward more human-like intelligence. By framing prior work through the lens of semantic intelligence and systematically summarizing methods, resources, and evaluations for HLS tasks, the survey provides a conceptual roadmap and practical reference to guide future research toward achieving High-Level Semantic Intelligence (HLSI).

Abstract: Recent advances in AI have substantially expanded its cognitive and reasoning capabilities. From the perspective of semantic complexity, the development of AI reveals a clear trajectory from simple to complex semantic processing. While early AI systems mainly addressed tasks involving direct and literal semantic perception or expression, contemporary systems are increasingly expected to perform more sophisticated cognitive reasoning, enabling the understanding and generation of High-Level Semantics (HLS). A similar trajectory can also be observed in human cognitive development. We define this transition as the shift from Basic-Level Semantic Intelligence (BLSI) to High-Level Semantic Intelligence (HLSI). However, this issue has not yet been systematically and comprehensively examined in prior work. Motivated by this gap, this survey reviews the development of AI semantic intelligence from the perspective of semantic complexity. We systematically survey existing research on HLS tasks, including humor, sarcasm, metaphor, empathy, persuasion, narrative, and other general HLS phenomena, across text, speech, vision, and multimodal scenarios. Specifically, we summarize data construction methods, modeling and optimization strategies, and evaluation methodologies for both understanding and generation. HLS is essential for advancing AI toward genuinely human-like intelligence. By synthesizing existing methods and insights from the perspective of semantic intelligence, this survey aims to support the continued development of AI toward HLSI.

</details>


### [237] [MemChain: Learning Interpretable Memory Traces for Memory-Augmented LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24097)
*Yiwen Ma,Songjun Tu,Qichao Zhang,Dong Li,Linjing Li,Dongbin Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI
