TL;DR: MemChain introduces a learned ‘memory mediator’ between retrieval and answering, turning many noisy retrieved items into a compact, structured evidence context that improves long-term reasoning and reduces context length.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing memory-augmented LLM agents simply stuff retrieved memories into the answer model’s context. This makes the model handle redundancy, conflicts, and loosely relevant items, which is inefficient and harms performance on long-term memory tasks. There is a need for an explicit, trainable component that can organize, filter, and ground retrieved memories into a reasoning-ready form before passing them to the answer model.

Method: MemChain is a post-retrieval memory policy. Given a query and retrieved memory candidates, it: (1) generates a question-conditioned evidence plan; (2) builds an ordered, grounded evidence trace that assigns semantic roles and dependencies to memories; and (3) executes explicit memory actions to form a concise evidence context fed to the answer model. Training uses a two-stage framework: (a) supervised trace learning to teach the policy to output valid plans, traces, actions, and evidence contexts; and (b) Trace-Guided Memory Policy Optimization (TMPO), a reinforcement-learning objective that optimizes the policy for downstream answer quality while incentivizing grounding, support, structural validity, and answer stability across rollouts.

Result: On long-context benchmarks LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S, MemChain reaches state-of-the-art performance with both closed-source and open-weight frozen answer models, while significantly shrinking the size of the memory context that must be passed to the answer model.

Conclusion: A learned, structured memory policy between retrieval and answering can substantially improve long-term reasoning in memory-augmented LLM agents. By converting raw retrievals into a compact, grounded evidence trace and optimizing it directly for downstream QA performance, MemChain outperforms prior methods and reduces context overhead, showing that memory organization is as important as retrieval quality.

Abstract: Memory-augmented LLM agents typically answer queries by retrieving relevant memories and feeding them directly to an answer model. This retrieval-as-evidence paradigm assumes retrieved memories are already suitable for reasoning, leaving the answer model to resolve redundancy, conflicts, and weak relevance while incurring substantial context overhead in long-term memory tasks. We propose MemChain, a trainable post-retrieval memory policy that transforms retrieved candidates into answer-facing active memory, represented as a compact and grounded evidence context. Given a user query and retrieved candidates, MemChain first generates a question-conditioned evidence plan, then constructs an ordered grounded evidence trace that organizes retrieved memories according to their semantic roles and dependencies, and finally executes explicit memory actions to produce a concise evidence context for answer generation. To train the mediator, we introduce a two-stage learning framework. Supervised trace learning first teaches the policy to generate structurally valid plans, traces, actions, and evidence contexts. We then propose Trace-Guided Memory Policy Optimization (TMPO), a reinforcement learning objective that optimizes the memory policy using downstream answer quality while jointly encouraging trace grounding, evidence support, structural validity, and answer stability across multiple rollouts. Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S demonstrate that MemChain consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance across both closed-source and open-weight frozen answer models while substantially reducing the memory context passed to the answer model.

</details>


### [238] [Scaling GUI Agents with Visual State Transitions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24112)
*Xiangyan Liu,Kaixin Li,Haonan Wang,Biao Wu,Meng Fang,Longxu Dou,Chao Du,Michael Qizhe Shieh,Tianyu Pang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: State Transition Pretraining (STP) improves GUI agents by pretraining on visual state transitions, learning both inverse and forward dynamics before instruction-tuned trajectory fine-tuning, leading to better performance and scaling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing GUI agents rely mostly on direct fine-tuning on instruction-labeled trajectories, which can be data-hungry and may not fully capture underlying GUI dynamics. The authors seek a more scalable, data-efficient way to endow agents with action-grounded visual understanding and an internal model of how GUIs evolve over time, across both desktop and mobile environments.

Method: They propose State Transition Pretraining (STP), a continual pretraining stage for a unified multimodal model using large-scale visual state transition data. The model is trained jointly on inverse dynamics (predicting the action given consecutive GUI states) and forward dynamics (predicting the next GUI state given the current state and action). This joint optimization is used to learn richer representations and an internal world model of GUI behavior, after which the model is fine-tuned on instruction-conditioned trajectories for specific tasks.

Result: STP-pretrained models, when later fine-tuned with task instructions, consistently outperform models trained only with direct trajectory fine-tuning on several benchmarks: AgentNetBench, AndroidControl, and GUIOdyssey, covering both desktop and mobile GUI tasks. Empirical analysis shows that combining both forward and inverse dynamics losses yields more stable and stronger gains than using either alone, and that downstream performance improves smoothly as more transition data is used.

Conclusion: Pretraining on state transitions with joint forward and inverse dynamics provides a powerful new scaling axis for GUI agents. It leads to better action-grounded visual representations, an internal world model of GUI dynamics, and systematically improved performance across multiple benchmarks, with clear benefits from scaling up transition data volume and using joint dynamics objectives.

Abstract: We introduce State Transition Pretraining (STP) as a new scaling axis for GUI agents. During the STP stage, we continually pretrain a unified multimodal model on visual state transitions by jointly optimizing inverse dynamics (predicting actions from state changes) and forward dynamics (predicting next states from current states and actions). This optimization equips the model with better action-grounded visual representations and an internal world model of GUI dynamics. When subsequently fine-tuned on trajectories with task instructions, our STP-trained models consistently outperform baselines trained solely via direct trajectory fine-tuning across agent benchmarks in both desktop and mobile GUI scenarios (AgentNetBench, AndroidControl, and GUIOdyssey). Further empirical studies show that joint dynamics optimization yields stable improvements over single-objective training, and downstream performance scales steadily with the volume of transition data.

</details>


### [239] [Grading the Narrators: An Isnad-Rijal Framework for Claim-Level Provenance in Multi-Agent Knowledge Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24117)
*Ali Zahid Raja*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper adapts classical hadith science’s chain-of-transmission methodology to modern multi-agent AI knowledge pipelines, providing a formal framework, schema, and decision process for grading and routing claims based on transmitter reliability and content criticism, and evaluates it on physics-textbook-derived claims.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern multi-agent systems generate knowledge through multi-step transformation chains (tool calls, agents, models), where traditional provenance and source-reliability tools capture events and coarse reliability but lack an operational way to attach fine-grained, per-claim, per-domain reliability to entire transmission chains. The authors note a structurally analogous historical problem in hadith science—assessing reliability of narrated reports—and aim to transfer its mature, rigorous methodology to AI pipeline design to better manage trust, completeness, and routing of claims.

Method: 1) The authors formally map concepts from classical hadith methodology (isnad, rijal, weakest-link evaluation, corroboration via multiple chains, matn/content criticism) onto components of multi-agent AI pipelines. 2) They design a relational schema that encodes claim-level transmission chains and a graded registry of “narrators” (agents/tools/transforms) with per-domain reliability scores. 3) They define a decision matrix that combines chain grade (via weakest-link and corroboration logic) with independent content criticism to route claims into accepted, served-with-caveats, reviewed, or quarantined states. 4) They empirically evaluate the framework using 20,000 claims drawn from real physics textbooks, testing behaviors such as weakest-link quarantine, corroboration by independent chains, and the ability to recover unreliable narrators via feedback from errors.

Result: The evaluation shows that: (a) weakest-link-based chain grading effectively routes low-quality chains into quarantine, (b) corroboration from independent transmission chains meaningfully boosts confidence in claims, and (c) the proposed framework can be implemented at scale over 20,000 textbook-derived claims. However, the grade-recovery feedback loop only partially succeeds, failing to identify the single worst narrator (highest-fault transmitter). Two analyses are inconclusive: one matched-coverage comparison where their framework and a reference content critic cannot be brought to comparable coverage, and another unspecified analysis where evidence is insufficient for a strong conclusion. Throughout, the authors document where their evidence is strong, weak, or missing.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that hadith-science-inspired mechanics—explicit claim-level chains, per-transmitter grading, weakest-link evaluation, and independent content criticism—can be fruitfully operationalized for modern multi-agent AI systems. This yields a more structured and transparent way to manage reliability and routing of derived claims than existing provenance alone. Nonetheless, limitations in the narrator-grade recovery loop and inconclusive evaluations show that the framework is not yet complete; further work is needed on better learning of transmitter grades, improved alignment with strong content critics, and extending the methodology beyond the physics domain.

Abstract: Modern multi-agent knowledge systems increasingly accumulate knowledge through chains of autonomous transformations rather than direct retrieval. Existing provenance work records what happened - execution traces, tool calls, evidence links - and source-reliability estimation is long established (truth discovery, reputation systems). What is missing is an operational framework that attaches graded, per-domain transmitter reliability to claim-level transmission chains, with completeness semantics, transformation-typed aggregation, decoupled content criticism, and serve/review/quarantine routing.
  Classical Islamic hadith science confronted a structurally similar problem: deciding whether knowledge transmitted through chains of human narrators should be accepted. Over centuries it developed a rigorous methodology - isnad (a complete transmission chain attached to every claim), rijal (systematic grading of each narrator's integrity and precision), weakest-link chain evaluation, corroboration through independent chains, and matn criticism (content evaluated independently of chain quality). This paper transfers that methodology to AI system design.
  We contribute a formal mapping from hadith-science concepts to multi-agent pipelines, a relational schema implementing claim chains and a graded narrator registry, a decision matrix combining chain grade with content criticism, and an evaluation on 20,000 claims from real physics textbooks. The evaluation validates weakest-link quarantine and independent-chain corroboration; reports a partial failure of the grade-recovery loop, which missed the highest-fault narrator; and reports two analyses as inconclusive, including a matched-coverage comparison the framework could not reach with the reference content critic. The paper is explicit throughout about which claims the evidence does and does not yet support.

</details>


### [240] [A Motion-Aware Vector Quantization Framework with Centroid Reuse for Efficient VLA Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24148)
*Zhuoran Song,Haozhe Jiang,Chunyu Qi,Minnan Pei,Gang Li,Xiaoyao Liang,Haibing Guan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: VQVLA is an algorithm–hardware co-design that accelerates vision-language-action model inference by motion-aware vector quantization and a centroid-reuse GEMM paradigm, achieving multi-x speedups over GPUs and prior accelerators with minimal accuracy loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision-language-action models are powerful for embodied AI but incur high inference latency and are treated as full-precision workloads by existing accelerators, leaving redundancy in memory and computation unused. There is a need for specialized compression and compute schemes tailored to VLA dynamics to enable real-time deployment on robots.

Method: The paper proposes VQVLA, combining: (1) MotionVQ, a motion-aware vector quantization that adjusts quantization precision based on the robot’s execution state to reduce memory access while preserving task success; and (2) a merged-centroid vectorized GEMM that operates directly on codebook-index representations, aggregating spatially and reusing centroids temporally to remove redundant multiplications. A custom accelerator is designed to support dynamic precision selection and efficient centroid-reuse computation.

Result: On benchmark VLA workloads, VQVLA attains speedups of 6.5x over NVIDIA A100 GPU and 2.8x, 1.9x, 3.3x, and 4.3x over Dadu-Corki, LUT-DLA, CodeGEMM, and ShiftAddLLM, respectively, while maintaining nearly the same accuracy (negligible degradation).

Conclusion: By exploiting weight similarity and execution dynamics through motion-aware quantization and centroid-reuse GEMM, coupled with a tailored accelerator, VQVLA significantly reduces memory and compute costs for VLA models and enables much faster inference without sacrificing task performance.

Abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong potential for embodied AI, yet their high inference latency on GPUs limits real-time deployment. Existing accelerators, such as Dadu-Corki, improve efficiency but treat VLA models as full-precision workloads, leaving substantial redundancy in both memory and computation underexploited.
  In this paper, we propose VQVLA, an algorithm-hardware co-design framework that accelerates VLA inference by exploiting weight similarity and execution dynamics. We first introduce MotionVQ, a motion-aware vector quantization scheme that dynamically adjusts quantization precision based on the robot's execution state, reducing memory access while preserving task success rate. We then propose a merged-centroid vectorized GEMM paradigm that operates on the codebook-index representation, eliminating redundant multiplications through spatial aggregation and temporal reuse of centroids. To realize these optimizations, we design an accelerator that efficiently supports dynamic precision selection and centroid-reuse computation. Experimental results show that VQVLA achieves 6.5x, 2.8x, 1.9x, 3.3x, and 4.3x speedup over the A100 GPU, Dadu-Corki, LUT-DLA, CodeGEMM, and ShiftAddLLM, respectively, with negligible accuracy degradation.

</details>


### [241] [Agent-UCT: Upper Confidence Bounds Applied to Trees for Agentic Workflow Optimization with Cost-Awareness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24162)
*Yang Li,Hai Liu,Dian Shao,Yu Wang,Xiyu Chen,Sergey Volkov,Bozhi Wang,Ziyu Sun,Sihang Liu,Ye Luo,Xiaowei Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose Agent-UCT and a supporting framework to efficiently search and optimize RAG/agentic workflows by reusing shared prefixes of configurations, achieving large cost reductions while matching or beating existing presets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Optimizing agentic/RAG workflows involves choosing among many discrete components (retrievers, rerankers, generators, controllers, etc.) under a limited evaluation budget. Existing search and optimization methods treat each configuration independently and ignore that many configurations share long common prefixes of components, causing redundant runs and poor use of compute. The authors want a principled, budget-aware way to explore this combinatorial space that explicitly exploits shared structure and ensures reproducible, efficient experimentation across different RAG frameworks.

Method: They design Agent-UCT, a variant of the UCT tree search algorithm augmented with a cost-aware, reuse-aware regularization term. They model workflow configurations as paths in a tree and construct a bipartite prefix reuse graph that tracks which configuration prefixes have already been materialized and can be reused. Agent-UCT’s selection policy is biased toward branches that reuse these prefixes, reducing redundant computation while preserving exploration. Around this, they build RAGSpace, which defines a unified five-dimensional configuration space that harmonizes components from LongRAG, LightRAG, and Self-RAG so they can be recombined systematically. They also implement WTB (Workflow Test Bench), which offers deterministic replay, content-addressable caching, and transactional consistency so that intermediate states are computed once and then reused reliably throughout the search. They evaluate on QA benchmarks, comparing against fixed framework presets and different evaluation regimes (full-pool vs sampling-based).

Result: On HotpotQA and UltraDomain, Agent-UCT discovers RAG configurations whose out-of-sample performance is at least as good as, and often better than, the best fixed presets from the included frameworks. When they evaluate all configurations (full-pool), explicitly modeling bipartite prefix reuse cuts the logical search cost by 73.6% versus a baseline that ignores prefix sharing. Moving from full-pool to sampling-based evaluation yields an additional 4.2× wall-clock speedup, showing that their cost-aware, reuse-focused design makes exploration much more efficient without sacrificing solution quality.

Conclusion: Explicitly leveraging compositional structure and prefix reuse is highly beneficial for optimizing complex agentic/RAG workflows under budget constraints. Agent-UCT, together with the unified RAGSpace configuration space and the WTB infrastructure, offers a practical and reproducible framework that: (1) reuses intermediate computations across related configurations, (2) intelligently allocates evaluation budget through a cost-aware UCT variant, and (3) enables systematic cross-framework recombination of RAG components. Overall, their approach significantly reduces search cost and evaluation time while achieving top-tier performance among compared workflows.

Abstract: Optimizing agentic workflows, such as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines, requires navigating a combinatorial space of discrete component choices under tight evaluation budgets. Existing approaches - heuristic search, black-box optimization, and standard tree search methods - do not explicitly exploit the compositional structure of these workflows, leading to redundant computation and inefficient budget allocation. We introduce Agent-UCT (Agent-based Cost-Aware Upper Confidence Bounds Applied to Trees), a tree search algorithm that extends UCT with a reuse-aware regularization term derived from a bipartite prefix reuse graph. Agent-UCT biases selection toward branches that leverage previously materialized configuration prefixes, reducing redundant execution while maintaining effective exploration. Our framework, RAGSpace, unifies heterogeneous RAG components from LongRAG, LightRAG, and Self-RAG into a five-dimensional configuration space, enabling systematic cross-framework recombination. WTB (Workflow Test Bench) provides deterministic replay, content-addressable caching, and transactional consistency, ensuring that intermediate states are materialized once and reused across the search. Experiments on HotpotQA and UltraDomain demonstrate that Agent-UCT identifies configurations with the highest out-of-sample performance among the evaluated fixed framework presets. Under full-pool evaluation, bipartite prefix reuse reduces logical search cost by 73.6% relative to the no-prefix-sharing cost upper bound. Compared with full-pool evaluation, sampling-based evaluation further achieves a 4.2x wall-clock speedup. Agent-UCT, RAGSpace, and WTB together provide a unified framework for cost-aware, reproducible, and compositionally efficient agentic workflow optimization.

</details>


### [242] [Falsifiable Commitment Planning for Self-Correcting Web Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24167)
*Guangyi Liu,Huan Zhao,Quanming Yao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces FCPAgent, a web agent framework that makes each plan step explicitly testable and repairable via falsifiable commitments, improving long-horizon task success.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon web agents tend to drift off the correct course while still producing locally plausible actions, because their plans do not specify under what evidence a step should continue to be trusted or should be abandoned. Existing approaches can plan and reflect but lack explicit, checkable assumptions for each action, leading to brittle behavior on long tasks.

Method: The paper proposes FCPAgent, which structures plans into Falsifiable Commitment Units (FCUs). Each FCU is a subgoal tied to a reusable skill and is annotated with confirming evidence, falsifying evidence, and a confidence score. Execution uses a plan-test-repair loop: before acting, a hybrid commitment testing module checks whether the planned action is still warranted using lightweight evidence matching and, when needed, LLM-based diagnostic verification. After actions, observations are also checked. If a commitment is falsified, a scope-aware repair mechanism identifies whether the problem lies in the current execution, the underlying skill, or the higher-level plan and then revises the smallest necessary component.

Result: On the WebArena benchmark, FCPAgent outperforms the strongest baseline agent by 13.8% in average success rate, with particularly strong improvements on tasks that require long sequences of actions (long-horizon tasks).

Conclusion: Making each plan step an explicit, falsifiable commitment—paired with hybrid evidence testing and scoped repair—yields more robust web agents that stay on track in long-horizon tasks and can efficiently recover when assumptions fail.

Abstract: Long-horizon web agents often go off track before final failure: a trajectory can remain locally plausible even after the current state, reused skill, or plan assumption no longer supports the user instruction. Existing agents can plan, reflect, or reuse experience, but their plans rarely specify the evidence under which an active step should still be trusted. We propose FCPAgent, a falsifiable commitment planning framework for robust long-horizon web agents. FCPAgent represents each plan step as a Falsifiable Commitment Unit (FCU): a subgoal grounded in a reusable skill, together with confirming evidence, falsifying evidence, and a confidence score. Execution is organized as a plan-test-repair loop. The hybrid commitment testing module checks candidate actions before they modify the browser and checks observations after execution; for efficiency, it combines lightweight evidence matching with LLM-based diagnostic verification. When evidence falsifies a commitment, scope-aware repair localizes the contradiction to the execution, skill, or planning level and revises the smallest adequate part. On WebArena, FCPAgent achieves a 13.8% relative improvement in average success over the strongest baseline, with especially large gains on long-horizon tasks.

</details>


### [243] [Myopia Prevention and Control 3.0: Artificial Intelligence--Driven Risk Stratification, Proactive Monitoring, and Personalized Intervention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24187)
*Tieniu Wang,Cangzhu Huang,Qianhui Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a next-generation framework, "Myopia Prevention and Control 3.0," that uses AI, digital sensing, and ubiquitous computing to shift myopia prevention from broad, reactive programs to proactive, personalized, closed-loop management.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing myopia prevention strategies—school-based screening and generic risk-factor management—are inadequate in the face of a projected global epidemic, with half the world’s population expected to be myopic by 2050. There is a need for more precise, individualized, and continuously adaptive prevention and control methods that can leverage recent technological advances.

Method: This is a review and conceptual framework paper. The authors synthesize current evidence on AI applications in myopia and organize it into a three-part closed-loop pipeline: (1) AI-driven risk stratification using multimodal data and machine learning; (2) AI-enabled proactive monitoring through wearables, smartphones, and school screening networks; and (3) AI-powered personalized interventions with continuous feedback. They then critically appraise existing work in each domain and discuss technical and ethical challenges.

Result: The review identifies substantial progress in AI models that can predict myopia risk, early onset, and progression, as well as emerging digital tools for continuous monitoring of visual behavior and environment. However, it finds gaps in data quality, external validation, real-world implementation, integration of multimodal data, and rigorous assessment of AI-driven personalized interventions. It also surfaces concerns about bias, equity, and ethics in deploying such systems at scale.

Conclusion: The authors conclude that "Myopia Prevention and Control 3.0"—a closed-loop, AI-centered paradigm—is both feasible and promising but not yet fully realized. They argue that future work should focus on building robust multimodal foundation models, developing digital twins of ocular and behavioral states, and applying causal machine learning to move from correlation-based risk prediction to truly individualized, effective intervention strategies, while addressing data, validation, ethical, and equity challenges.

Abstract: The convergence of artificial intelligence (AI), digital sensing, and ubiquitous computing has created an unprecedented opportunity to transform myopia prevention from a reactive, population-based model into a proactive, precision-driven one. Despite evidence that half the world's population will be myopic by 2050, conventional approaches---school-based vision screening (Phase 1.0) and evidence-based risk factor management (Phase 2.0)---have proven insufficient. We review the emergence of Myopia Prevention and Control 3.0, defined by AI integration across three interconnected domains forming a closed-loop pipeline: (1) AI-driven risk stratification predicting individual-level risk through machine learning on multimodal data; (2) AI-enabled proactive monitoring via wearables, smartphones, and school screening networks; and (3) AI-powered personalized intervention with closed-loop feedback. We critically evaluate evidence across each stage, discuss challenges in data quality, model validation, ethics, and equity, and outline future directions including multimodal foundation models, digital twins, and causal machine learning.

</details>


### [244] [Integrating Factual and Normative Industrial Knowledge via Constraint-Aware Graph Attention for Process Plan Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24213)
*Yuntong Chen,Yingqi Li,Yingying Xiao,Ziang Wang,Zewei Liu,Jiahao Liu,Xitian Tian,Lijiang Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces PCA-GAT, a knowledge-graph–enhanced collaborative filtering model with Bayesian Personalized Ranking and constraint-aware attention to recommend machining process plans, achieving high accuracy and robustness, and providing a standardized evaluation protocol.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Industrial process planning must integrate heterogeneous knowledge such as materials, geometric features, and quality constraints. Existing machining plan recommendation methods lack a unified ranking objective, do not exploit structured domain constraints systematically, and lack standardized evaluation protocols, which limits their reliability and generalization.

Method: The authors formulate process plan recommendation as a collaborative filtering problem enhanced by a knowledge graph that encodes industrial entities and relations. They use Bayesian Personalized Ranking as the training objective and Recall@K / NDCG@K as evaluation metrics. A graph attention network propagates information over the knowledge graph, while four domain constraints—material compatibility, precision requirements, feature applicability, and operation sequencing—are injected as attention biases. Type-specific weights are learned to assess the importance of each constraint type, and an adaptive gating mechanism adjusts the contribution of constraints based on local graph context. The approach is compared with seven baseline methods from three categories on multiple datasets, with ablation studies to isolate contributions of each component.

Result: On a real aerospace machining dataset (115 parts, 507 plans), PCA-GAT achieves Recall@1 of 0.9087, outperforms all baselines, and exhibits strong robustness in cold-start and sparse-data regimes, with only about half the performance degradation of the best baseline. Ablation experiments show that the knowledge graph component is crucial, constraint-aware attention further improves performance, and naive (ungated) constraint injection can reduce accuracy. Learned constraint weights highlight material–operation compatibility as the most influential factor, aligned with expert knowledge. On three public recommendation benchmarks without explicit constraints, PCA-GAT performs competitively without degradation, demonstrating that the architecture generalizes beyond manufacturing domains.

Conclusion: PCA-GAT effectively integrates heterogeneous industrial knowledge and domain constraints into a unified recommendation framework for machining process planning, substantially improving accuracy and robustness over existing methods. The study establishes a standardized ranking-based protocol and metrics for engineering process plan recommendation, benchmarks seven representative approaches, and shows that the primary limitation in this domain is knowledge representation rather than model capacity. The proposed constraint-aware, knowledge-graph–based design generalizes to non-industrial recommendation tasks when explicit constraints are absent.

Abstract: Integrating heterogeneous industrial knowledge, including factual relations and decision constraints, remains a core challenge in industrial information systems. Machining process planning exemplifies this problem because engineers must select operations by combining material properties, feature characteristics, and quality requirements. Existing methods rely mainly on similarity retrieval or classification, without a unified ranking objective or standardized evaluation. We propose PCA-GAT, which formulates machining process plan recommendation as a knowledge graph enhanced collaborative filtering problem. Bayesian Personalized Ranking provides the learning objective, while Recall@K and NDCG@K define evaluation. The knowledge graph supplies semantic structure when collaborative signals are sparse. Four domain constraints, material compatibility, precision requirements, feature applicability, and operation sequencing, are introduced as attention biases during graph propagation. Type-specific weights learn their importance, and an adaptive gate adjusts their influence using local context. On a real aerospace dataset with 115 parts and 507 plans, PCA-GAT achieves Recall@1 = 0.9087 and strong cold-start robustness, with about half the degradation of the strongest baseline under severe sparsity. Ablation studies show that knowledge graph enrichment is essential, constraints add value, and ungated constraint injection can hurt performance. The learned weights identify material-operation compatibility as the dominant factor, consistent with domain expertise. Results on three public benchmarks show no degradation when constraints are absent, supporting generalization beyond manufacturing. This study establishes a standardized recommendation protocol for engineering process planning and benchmarks seven methods across three categories, showing that knowledge representation is the main bottleneck.

</details>


### [245] [Epistemic Norms for AI Safety and Alignment Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24243)
*Keivan Navaie*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper argues that AI safety and alignment need a distinct, stricter epistemic code from mainstream AI research and proposes a concrete framework (ECAISA) to improve how safety claims are generated, checked, disclosed, and audited.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mainstream AI research optimises for average-case performance and accepts some failure rates, which is unsuitable for AI safety where even rare catastrophic failures are unacceptable. Current epistemic practices and institutions are not designed to handle sparse evidence, adversaries, and fat-tailed risks inherent in powerful AI systems. The authors see gaps such as lack of independent verification and want to create a more robust epistemic foundation for safety and alignment work.

Method: The authors perform a structured synthesis of the AI safety and alignment literature, grounded in a preregistered bibliometric baseline, to map current epistemic practices and identify weaknesses. From this analysis they distill five major gap dimensions and then design a comprehensive epistemic code (ECAISA) with explicit principles, rubrics, disclosure mechanisms, applicability tiers, and anti-gaming provisions tailored to AI safety needs.

Result: They identify five cross-cutting gaps in current alignment research, notably the scarcity of institutionalised independent verification of safety claims. They then develop ECAISA: eight epistemic principles, a three-level scoring rubric for how well work adheres to them, a four-level disclosure ladder balancing transparency with information hazards and commercial secrecy, a tiered scheme indicating when and how the code applies, an information-hazard assessment and adjudication process, and seven mechanisms intended to reduce strategic gaming of the code.

Conclusion: AI safety and alignment require different epistemic standards than mainstream capability-focused AI research, focusing on demonstrated absence of hazardous behaviours and bounding worst-case risks. Existing practices are insufficient, so the authors propose ECAISA as a governance tool targeting auditability of safety-relevant claims rather than certification of system safety. If adopted, it could structure how safety evidence is generated, reported, scrutinised, and trusted, while managing information hazards and strategic manipulation.

Abstract: Mainstream AI research emphasises capability growth and tolerates low failure rates when average-case performance is high. AI safety and alignment research has a different mission: to ensure that catastrophic failures never occur, under sparse evidence, adversarial dynamics, and fat-tailed risk. We argue that the two domains differ along two analytically independent axes---{\it capability profile}, demonstrating the absence of hazardous behaviours rather than the presence of positive capabilities, and {\it risk profile}, bounding worst-case outcomes under fat-tailed uncertainty rather than optimising average-case performance---and that mainstream epistemic practices are inadequate on both. Building on a structured synthesis grounded in a preregistered bibliometric baseline, we identify five cross-cutting gap dimensions in current alignment research, including the near-absence of institutionalised independent verification. To address these gaps, we propose {\sc ECAISA}, an Epistemic Code for AI Safety and Alignment comprising eight principles, a three-level scoring rubric, a four-level disclosure ladder that reconciles transparency with information-hazard and commercial-confidentiality constraints, a tiered applicability scheme, an information-hazard adjudication procedure, and seven anti-gaming mechanisms. {\sc ECAISA} does not certify that any AI system is safe; it constrains how safety-relevant research claims are documented, checked, and relied upon, with auditability rather than certification as its governance target.

</details>


### [246] [Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) to convert images of queuing networks into verifiable simulation models: an open-weight LLM workflow approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24259)
*Thomas Monks,Alison Harper,Amy Heather,Navonil Mustafee*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Sketch2DES is a workflow that turns queuing-network diagrams into verifiable discrete‑event simulations using open-weight LLMs, improving transparency and reproducibility over direct code generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Directly generating simulation code from natural language with LLMs makes verification and reproducibility hard, especially for non-programmers. There is a need for a more transparent, inspectable process that bridges visual models and executable simulations while ensuring correctness.

Method: The authors design Sketch2DES, a three-stage workflow: (1) use a multimodal LLM to convert a queuing-network diagram into a semi-structured textual description; (2) use a text LLM plus a reflection-based verification loop to convert this description into schema-validated JSON; (3) deterministically transform the JSON into an executable discrete-event simulation via a software adapter. They test the workflow on eight queuing-network diagrams of varying complexity and compare outcomes to human-coded and analytical benchmarks, and to direct code generation baselines.

Result: Across eight queuing-network diagrams, all workflow stages show high reliability. The simulations produced by Sketch2DES yield performance results that are statistically indistinguishable from human-coded implementations and analytical solutions. Relative to direct LLM code generation, the approach offers better reproducibility, transparency, and verifiability while reducing dependence on users’ programming skills.

Conclusion: Structured, multi-stage, artefact-based workflows can make LLM-assisted simulation modelling more robust than direct code generation. Sketch2DES demonstrates that queuing-network diagrams can be automatically converted into trustworthy discrete-event simulation models using open-weight LLMs, though the current scope is limited to certain model classes and relies on accurate visual interpretation.

Abstract: Recent work has explored the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) to automate simulation model building, typically by generating executable code directly from natural language descriptions. However, this raises challenges for verification and reproducibility particularly for users without programming expertise. We propose Sketch2DES, a sketch-to-simulation workflow that converts diagrammatic representations of queuing networks into verifiable discrete-event simulation models using open-weight LLMs. The workflow has three stages: (1) translation of a diagram into a semi-structured textual description using a multimodal LLM; (2) conversion into schema-validated structured data (JSON) via an LLM with a reflection-based verification loop; and (3) deterministic transformation into an executable simulation model using a software adapter. Intermediate artefacts can therefore be inspected and automatically validated before execution. We evaluate the approach on eight queuing-network diagrams of varying complexity. The workflow achieved high reliability for all stages, and results were statistically indistinguishable from human-coded and analytical benchmarks. Compared to direct code generation, the workflow improves reproducibility, transparency, and verifiability, while reducing the need for programming expertise. Limitations include restricted model scope and dependence on accurate visual interpretation. The results demonstrate the feasibility of structured, workflow-based model generation as a robust foundation for LLM-assisted simulation modelling.

</details>


### [247] [From Proprietary to Open-Source: Bridging the Distribution Gap via Multi-Agent Protocol Distillation in Agentic Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24280)
*Junlin Liu,Jiangwang Chen,Zixin Song,Shuaiyu Zhou,Chunji Lv,Hank Wu,Kailin Jiang,Jinyang Wu,Bohan Yu,Chenxi Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces MAPD, a framework that combines structured distillation from proprietary LLMs with reinforcement learning to improve agentic search for knowledge-intensive tasks, overcoming issues of sparse RL signals and style imitation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agentic search improves LLM performance on knowledge-intensive tasks via multi-step reasoning and retrieval, but optimizing such behavior with outcome-based RL yields sparse, inefficient supervision. Distilling from stronger proprietary models could provide denser guidance, but standard logit matching is impossible due to hidden logits and tokenizer mismatch, and naive trajectory imitation mainly copies superficial style instead of true reasoning ability. There is a need for a method that can leverage heterogeneous proprietary teachers to transfer core reasoning competence while avoiding style drift and verbosity issues.

Method: The authors propose Multi-Agent Protocol Distillation (MAPD), which uses a structured, style-normalized intermediate representation (a JSON protocol) to bridge student and proprietary teacher models. An offline multi-agent system decomposes each query, performs retrieval, repairs failed searches, and logs an exploration trace as a protocol describing task type, reasoning plan, and extractive grounding facts. During training, this protocol is only visible to a privileged branch of the student policy; the token distributions from this branch are then distilled into the main policy, providing dense supervision in combination with sparse RL on task success.

Result: Across seven question-answering benchmarks, MAPD is shown to consistently outperform strong baselines in both distillation-only and RL-only settings. On Qwen3-1.7B, it achieves an average success rate of 39.4%, and on Qwen3-4B, 44.4%. The approach works robustly with different proprietary teacher models and reduces issues such as style drift and verbosity degeneration in the student policy.

Conclusion: MAPD demonstrates that using a structured, style-normalized protocol as an intermediate representation enables effective heterogeneous distillation from proprietary LLMs while combining the benefits of dense distillation and sparse RL. The framework reliably boosts agentic search performance on knowledge-intensive QA tasks, generalizes across different teacher models, and mitigates undesirable stylistic artifacts, suggesting a promising direction for training smaller open models with guidance from stronger proprietary systems.

Abstract: Agentic search enables large language models to solve knowledge-intensive tasks by interleaving multi-step reasoning with retrieval, yet optimizing this with outcome-based reinforcement learning (RL) provides only sparse supervision. Knowledge distillation can supply denser guidance, and advanced proprietary models with their strong reasoning capabilities are promising teachers. While distilling from proprietary models can densify this supervisory signal, conventional logit-matching is precluded by hidden logits and mismatched tokenizers, whereas raw natural language trajectory imitation transfers superficial stylistic artifacts rather than core reasoning competence. To address the heterogeneous distillation problem and bridge the distribution gap, we propose Multi-Agent Protocol Distillation (MAPD), a joint distillation and RL framework uses a structured, style-normalized protocol as an intermediate representation. An offline multi-agent system (MAS) decomposes each query, retrieves supporting evidence, repairs failed searches, and converts the resulting exploration trace into a JSON protocol containing the task type, reasoning plan, and extractive grounding facts. During training, the protocol is provided only to a privileged branch of the student policy, whose token distributions furnish a dense distillation signal alongside the sparse RL objective. Extensive evaluations across seven QA benchmarks demonstrate that MAPD consistently outperforms competitive distillation and RL, achieving average success rates of 39.4\% on Qwen3-1.7B and 44.4\% on Qwen3-4B. Crucially, the framework generalizes robustly across diverse proprietary teachers while effectively mitigating the student policy from style drift and verbosity degeneration.

</details>


### [248] [Unequal Trips, Unequal Places: Diagnosing and Mitigating Delay Inequity in Autonomous Vehicle Fleet Coordination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24336)
*Nicole Hu,Mingtao Zhang,Haoyang LI,Chen Jason Zhang,Li Qing*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper audits how delays are distributed in city-scale autonomous vehicle fleets and proposes a rerouting framework (SPARE) that improves both efficiency and fairness without full-fleet replanning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing fleet coordinators optimize for average travel time, which can hide inequities in how delays are distributed across trips, regions, and origins versus destinations in real cities. There is a need to understand and mitigate these inequities while maintaining scalability.

Method: The authors perform a distributional audit of trip delays on three real-world datasets (Manhattan, Chicago, San Francisco) under several coordinators, examining inequity by trip length and spatial grouping (origin vs. destination). Based on the audit, they design SPARE, a budgeted online coordination framework that selectively assigns limited replanning capacity to delayed vehicles and reroutes them using recent data on waiting pressure, with guarantees on the number and impact of online route updates.

Result: The audit uncovers pervasive but city- and coordinator-dependent inequities, with spatial inequity worsening under higher demand and being stronger when grouping trips by origin. Experimental evaluation on all three datasets against six baseline methods shows that SPARE achieves the best combined performance on efficiency (e.g., travel/wait time) and fairness metrics while remaining scalable to city-sized fleets.

Conclusion: Delay in autonomous fleet coordination is distributed inequitably across trips and regions, and these inequities intensify with demand and are more tied to where trips originate. A targeted, congestion-responsive rerouting approach with bounded replanning, as implemented in SPARE, can significantly improve both overall performance and equity without the cost and complexity of full-fleet replanning.

Abstract: City-scale autonomous vehicle fleet coordinators are typically optimized for aggregate travel time, yet fleet averages conceal how delay is distributed across trips and regions. We conduct a distributional audit on three real-city road-network and taxi-demand datasets from Manhattan, Chicago, and San Francisco. The audit reveals pervasive trip-length inequity whose direction depends on the city and coordinator. After accounting for trip length, spatial inequity becomes more pronounced as demand grows and is consistently stronger when trips are grouped by origin rather than destination. These findings motivate SPatially Aware RErouting (SPARE), a budgeted online coordination framework that assigns limited replanning capacity to delayed vehicles and redirects them using recently observed waiting pressure. SPARE provides a per-review decision guarantee and explicitly bounds online route updates. Experiments on all three datasets against six representative baselines show that SPARE delivers the strongest joint efficiency-fairness performance while retaining city-scale scalability. The results demonstrate that bounded congestion-responsive rerouting improves performance and equity without full-fleet replanning.

</details>


### [249] [Simulating Tenant Responses to Energy Policy Interventions with Transaction-Cost-Aware LLM Age](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24341)
*Weijie Xia,Stefanie Horian,Hanyue Huang,Queena K. Qian,Jie Yang,Pedro P. Vergara Barrios*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces a friction-aware persona modeling framework for LLM simulations of policy responses, showing that encoding perceived transaction costs (PTC) into personas improves prediction of people’s reactions to energy-efficient renovation policies across multiple models and training setups.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based simulations of human opinions rely mostly on static demographic or high-level persona prompts and ignore practical frictions—like effort, uncertainty, and coordination—that strongly influence real-world policy responses. The authors aim to close this gap by grounding LLM personas in perceived transaction costs from policy theory, to make simulations more realistic, interpretable, and useful for policy design.

Method: They adopt perceived transaction cost (PTC) theory to define friction-aware personas that encode individuals’ perceived costs, benefits, barriers, and uncertainties about energy-efficient renovation (EER). Using a Dutch survey of 1,068 citizens (≈40k QA pairs), they condition LLMs on these personas and compare (1) standard demographic/persona prompts vs PTC-based personas and reasoning, and (2) prompt-only vs fine-tuned models. They test GPT-3.5-turbo and open models (Ministral-8B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), and for local models they apply supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), then evaluate predictive performance on survey responses.

Result: Across all tested models and settings, adding PTC-based personas and explicit reasoning improves the models’ ability to simulate survey respondents’ opinions and choices regarding EER compared with baseline demographic/persona approaches. Both prompt-only and fine-tuned configurations benefit, and open-weight models improved further with SFT and GRPO when using PTC-based representations.

Conclusion: Modeling perceived transaction costs within LLM personas yields more accurate and interpretable simulations of policy responses than relying on demographics alone. This friction-aware persona design operationalizes institutional policy theory in LLMs and appears robust across architectures and training regimes, suggesting a promising direction for policy analysis and agent-based simulation. The authors release code to support replication and extension.

Abstract: Recent studies use Large language models (LLMs) to simulate human opinions and decisions by prompting models with demographic, attitudinal, or persona-based descriptions. Yet such simulations rarely model the practical, cognitive, or social frictions that shape how people respond to policy interventions. Perceived transaction cost (PTC) provides a useful lens for modeling the practical frictions that shape policy responses, such as information burden, administrative effort, coordination demands, and perceived uncertainty. We use this lens to develop a friction-aware persona modeling approach for LLM-based simulation. In the context of energy-efficient renovation (EER), tenants are represented not only by who they are demographically, but by how they perceive the costs, benefits, barriers, and uncertainties associated with proposed renovation plans. Using survey data collected from 1,068 citizens in the Netherlands, comprising approximately 40,548 survey question and answer pairs, we compare prompt-only and fine-tuned settings across GPT-3.5-turbo, Ministral-8B-Instruct, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and evaluate supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) for local open-weight models. Results show that incorporating PTC-based personas and reasoning consistently improves model performance across both prompt-only and fine-tuned settings, suggesting that PTC-based persona design provides a useful bridge between institutional policy theory and interpretable LLM-based policy simulation. Code is available at https://github.com/xiaweijie1996/socialagent.

</details>


### [250] [Are Prompt Optimizers Blind? Cross-Modal Visual Feedback for Automatic Prompt Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24354)
*Haoyue Liu,Xiaoyu Ma,Ye Chen,Yuexian Zou,Xiaoying Tang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes Cross-Modal Visual Feedback (CMVF), a method that uses visual inspection of failed examples to improve automatic prompt optimization for vision-language models while keeping deployment cost identical to text-only prompts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing automatic prompt optimization (APO) methods for vision-language models only use textual feedback—questions, predictions, and gold answers—without ever looking at the underlying images. This blind feedback channel prevents APO from identifying and correcting visually grounded errors, which are central to multimodal tasks like visual question answering. There is a need for an approach that can leverage visual information during optimization without increasing inference-time costs.

Method: CMVF adds a cross-modal feedback loop to APO with two key stages: (1) a failure-conditioned visual diagnosis stage, where a stronger optimizer VLM examines each image corresponding to failed predictions, but without seeing the model’s prediction or the ground-truth label; it produces descriptions of what might be visually problematic or overlooked. (2) an error-aware aggregation stage, which compresses these per-example diagnoses into higher-level, task-level patterns describing recurring visual blind spots. These patterns are then used to rewrite or refine the text prompt for the target VLM. Importantly, images are only used during the optimization phase; at deployment time, the system uses only the optimized text prompt.

Result: Across 12 visual question answering datasets and 4 different target vision-language models, CMVF consistently outperforms existing APO baselines. It improves over the strongest baseline by an average of 2.4 accuracy points and achieves up to 6.5 points improvement on specific benchmarks. Additionally, the optimizer’s outputs naturally organize into expert-like visual checklists that capture common failure modes and can be transferred to other models without re-running the optimization process.

Conclusion: Incorporating cross-modal visual feedback into automatic prompt optimization allows vision-language models to better address visually grounded errors while preserving the low inference cost of text-only prompts. CMVF yields consistent and often substantial gains across diverse VQA benchmarks and models, and the learned visual checklists generalize across models, highlighting the potential of visual-error-aware prompt design for multimodal systems.

Abstract: Automatic prompt optimization (APO) has been widely adopted to adapt vision-language models (VLMs) to downstream tasks without weight updates, yielding promising results. However, on multimodal tasks, the effectiveness of APO is fundamentally bottlenecked by a blind feedback channel: the optimizer reads the question, the prediction, and the gold answer, but never the input image on which the model failed, and therefore cannot diagnose visually grounded errors. As a remedy, we introduce Cross-Modal Visual Feedback (CMVF). CMVF incorporates (1) a failure-conditioned visual diagnosis stage, in which a stronger optimizer VLM inspects each failed image without access to predictions or labels, and (2) an error-aware aggregation stage that compresses these observations into reusable, task-level visual blind-spot patterns that drive the prompt rewrite. Crucially, the image is consumed only during optimization; the deployed artifact is an ordinary text prompt that runs at the same inference cost as any text-only baseline. Extensive results across 12 VQA datasets and 4 target VLMs demonstrate that CMVF consistently ranks first, improving over the strongest baseline on every target by 2.4 points on average, with gains of up to 6.5 points on individual benchmarks. Moreover, the optimizer self-organizes into expert-style visual checklists that transfer across models without re-optimization.

</details>


### [251] [Failures Reveal What Metrics Miss: An Evidence-Driven Agent for Recursive Refinement of ECG Classifiers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24419)
*Jinliang Deng,Yiming Niu,Yibo Pan,Zhiqi Shao,Qin Luo,Yongxin Tong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RecursiveECG is an LLM-as-Designer framework that automatically refines ECG classifiers using evidence from concrete model failures and deterministic ECG measurements, yielding better performance without using LLMs at deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep models for 12-lead ECG classification are strong but still depend on manual expert inspection of failure cases to improve models. LLM-based automated design methods exist but usually rely only on aggregate metrics and lack case-level, evidence-based understanding of failures. There is a need for a systematic, auditable, and automated way to refine ECG classifiers grounded in objective ECG evidence rather than just performance summaries.

Method: The authors propose RecursiveECG, an offline LLM-as-Designer framework. First, they introduce Criteria-to-Measurement Compilation, which translates curated clinical ECG criteria into deterministic, validated functions that compute standardized measurements on individual ECGs. Then, using these measurements plus raw waveforms and model outputs, an Evidence-Grounded Failure Review process lets the LLM analyze failure and comparator cases, diagnose model limitations, and suggest classifier revisions. These candidate revisions are implemented and evaluated under a fixed problem contract; only revisions supported by improved evidence are retained. The refined predictor is then frozen for deployment, eliminating any LLM inference at test time, and an audit trail records each accepted change and its supporting evidence.

Result: On three ECG datasets (PTB-XL, Georgia, CPSC2018), RecursiveECG consistently surpasses strong baseline classifiers, achieving an average relative performance gain of 10.0%. Ablation studies show that removing key components (evidence grounding, criteria-based measurements, etc.) degrades performance, and transfer studies demonstrate that the refinement process generalizes across datasets and settings.

Conclusion: Evidence-grounded LLM-as-Designer workflows can effectively and autonomously refine ECG classifiers by leveraging deterministic ECG measurements and systematic failure analysis. RecursiveECG not only improves accuracy over baselines but also yields a fixed, deployable predictor with an interpretable audit trail linking each model change to objective ECG evidence, suggesting a promising direction for trustworthy, data-driven model refinement in clinical time-series tasks.

Abstract: Deep models have substantially advanced 12-lead ECG classification, yet their refinement still relies heavily on human experts to inspect failures and iteratively revise classifier designs. Recent LLM-based agents have demonstrated the potential for automated model design, but when guided only by aggregate performance metrics, they lack insight into why individual cases fail and how the classifier should be revised. We present RecursiveECG, an evidence-driven LLM-as-Designer framework in which an LLM serves as an offline model designer that refines ECG classifiers based on concrete failures and objective ECG evidence. To ground failure diagnosis in executable evidence, Criteria-to-Measurement Compilation converts curated ECG criteria into validated deterministic functions that produce reproducible, reference-backed measurements for individual ECGs. Building on these measurements, Evidence-Grounded Failure Review analyzes failed and comparator cases by jointly considering raw waveforms, measurements, and model outputs, enabling the LLM to diagnose classifier limitations and formulate targeted revisions. Candidate revisions are executed and re-evaluated under a fixed problem contract, and only evidence-supported updates are retained. The resulting predictor is frozen after refinement and requires no LLM inference during deployment, while an audit trail links each accepted revision to its supporting evidence. Across PTB-XL, Georgia, and CPSC2018, RecursiveECG consistently outperforms strong baselines, achieving an average relative improvement of 10.0%. Extensive ablation and transfer studies further validate the effectiveness of its evidence-grounded refinement process.

</details>


### [252] [From Execution to Capability: Scientific Experience Consolidation via Procedural Knowledge Synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24459)
*Liwei Dong,Jiahao Zhao,Nan Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes SciConsolidate, a framework that turns verified runtime experience from scientific-computing tasks into generalizable procedures that improve language models’ future performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large language models can solve many scientific-computing problems, but what they learn while solving one problem usually does not become persistent, reusable capability on later tasks. Existing approaches lack a robust way to consolidate execution-time experience into durable, cross-task procedural knowledge, and weaker models often fail to apply high-level procedures even when these are available (the abstraction-execution gap).

Method: The authors introduce SciConsolidate, which: (1) collects and contrasts verified successful and failed trajectories to induce candidate cross-task computational procedures; (2) filters these procedures with a development-validation gate; (3) performs failure-informed, answer-free query synthesis to expand consolidation data without needing ground-truth answers; and (4) uses a stronger teacher model to concretize abstract procedures into executable code traces for standard supervised fine-tuning of a weaker student. A matched teacher branch without procedures serves as a control to isolate the effect of procedural guidance.

Result: When procedures are injected at runtime on the SciCode benchmark, a stronger model (Qwen3.6-27B) gains +3.85 sub-step and +6.26 main-problem points, while a weaker model (Qwen3.5-9B) shows almost no net main-problem improvement, empirically demonstrating the abstraction-execution gap. After procedure-guided concretization and procedure-free deployment, the 9B model improves by +3.89 sub-step and +6.25 main-problem points over a no-procedure SFT control, and by +5.62 and +11.25 points, respectively, over the original 9B baseline.

Conclusion: The study shows that verified execution experience from scientific-computing tasks can be converted into reusable procedural knowledge that measurably improves downstream performance, even for weaker models when procedures are concretized into executable supervision. This establishes a practical pipeline for experience-to-capability transformation and suggests a scalable path toward self-improving scientific assistants.

Abstract: Large language models increasingly solve scientific-computing tasks, but executable feedback from one problem rarely becomes durable capability on subsequent problems. We study scientific-computing experience consolidation: converting verified runtime experience into transferable procedural knowledge and persistent model improvement. This setting presents two challenges: trajectory-derived artifacts may encode source-specific repairs rather than cross-task computational mechanisms; and a weaker target model may be unable to operationalize an otherwise valid abstract procedure - an abstraction-execution gap. We introduce SciConsolidate, which contrasts verified successes and failures to induce cross-task procedures, selects them through a development-validation gate, and uses failure-informed, answer-free query synthesis to expand the consolidation data without requiring pre-existing reference answers. Because the target model may not directly execute these abstractions, a stronger model concretizes them into executable code supervision for standard, procedure-free SFT; a matched no-procedure teacher branch isolates the value of procedural guidance. On SciCode, runtime procedure injection improves Qwen3.6-27B by +3.85/+6.26 sub-step/main-problem points, but yields almost no aggregate main-problem gain for Qwen3.5-9B, providing operational evidence of the abstraction-execution gap. After procedure-guided concretization, the 9B student improves under procedure-free deployment by +3.89/+6.25 points over the no-procedure SFT control and by +5.62/+11.25 over the original 9B model. These results establish an experience-to-capability pathway for scientific computing and provide a practical starting point for scaling self-improving scientific assistance.

</details>


### [253] [Making Mathematical Knowledge Explainable, Accessible and Interoperable Through Large Language Model Integration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24512)
*Jan Range,Björn Schembera,Dominik Göddeke*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents an architecture that links a curated mathematical model knowledge base (MathModDB) with Large Language Models via the Model Context Protocol to enable natural-language, epistemically grounded access and integration with external research data repositories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mathematical model descriptions are crucial but are often poorly documented and not compliant with FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) principles. While MathModDB offers a semantically rich, curated knowledge graph of mathematical models, its usage is hindered by the need to understand complex web interfaces or master SPARQL/Wikibase APIs. Furthermore, integrating this curated knowledge with external research data repositories such as Dataverse is technically challenging, limiting broader adoption and automated reasoning over both models and data.

Method: The authors build an integration layer between Large Language Models and MathModDB using the Model Context Protocol (MCP). This layer exposes a vector-indexed schema retrieval mechanism so that natural-language queries can be mapped to relevant parts of the MathModDB schema, and a Steiner-tree-based join planner to automatically determine how to connect different entities in the knowledge graph to answer complex queries. The system uses Semantic Web technologies underneath and is instantiated on a Wikibase-backed knowledge graph but is designed to be transferable to other Wikibase-based repositories. The LLM acts as a dialogue interface, while the MCP server mediates structured, epistemically grounded access to the curated knowledge base and external tools/databases such as Dataverse.

Result: The integrated system allows users to query and explore mathematical models in MathModDB using natural language, without needing SPARQL or detailed knowledge of the Wikibase interface. The combination of vector-based schema retrieval and graph-based join planning enables complex, semantically accurate queries and better explainability of retrieved models. The architecture also simplifies interoperability between MathModDB and external repositories (e.g. Dataverse), demonstrating practical workflows where model descriptions and associated datasets can be jointly accessed. These capabilities are showcased through use cases in continuum mechanics and enzyme kinetics, highlighting improvements in model accessibility and interpretability compared to the baseline Wikibase interface.

Conclusion: Integrating LLMs with Wikibase-based mathematical model knowledge graphs via MCP offers a promising solution to improve FAIR-compliant access to model metadata and to bridge curated knowledge with heterogeneous research data repositories. The approach maintains epistemic grounding by relying on a curated knowledge base while leveraging the usability and flexibility of LLM-driven natural language interaction. The architecture is generalizable beyond MathModDB to other Wikibase installations and paves the way for more explainable and interoperable computational research workflows involving mathematical models and their associated data.

Abstract: Mathematical models are central to formalizing research problems, yet their documentation often falls short of FAIR principles. Knowledge bases such as the Mathematical Model Database (MathModDB) address this gap by providing curated, semantically rich representations of mathematical models. Built on Wikibase, the same open-source infrastructure underlying Wikidata, MathModDB utilizes Semantic Web technologies to support Linked Open Data, collaborative editing, and the storage of semantically enriched metadata, making it a domain-specific knowledge graph within the broader Wikidata ecosystem. However, access to MathModDB currently requires either navigating a complex web interface or proficiency in SPARQL and Wikibase APIs, posing significant barriers for potential users. In addition, the combination of such curated knowledge bases with actual research data stored, e.g., in Dataverse repository instances, remains a challenge. To overcome these limitations, we propose integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) with MathModDB via a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that exposes a vector-indexed schema retrieval and Steiner-tree-based join planner, combining dialogue-based natural language interaction with curated, epistemically grounded knowledge. Although instantiated on MathModDB, the architecture can be applied to other Wikibase-based systems. We demonstrate that this approach enables epistemically grounded LLM usage, improves model explainability and accessibility beyond what the standard Wikibase interface offers, and simplifies interoperability with external databases and tools, such as Dataverse data repositories. We illustrate the benefits of combining the accessibility of an LLM with the epistemic safety of a curated knowledge base through the adaptability of the MCP protocol by two use cases involving mathematical models in the fields of continuum mechanics and enzyme kinetics.

</details>


### [254] [Task-Conditional Faithfulness Auditing of Multimodal LLMs for Grid Diagnosis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24539)
*Tianqiao Zhao,Meng Yue,Jianhui Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces a framework to check whether multimodal LLMs use the correct task-specific evidence when diagnosing power grids, and to correct them when they do not.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multimodal LLMs can accurately answer grid diagnosis questions by combining topology, measurements, and incident text, but accuracy alone does not ensure that the models relied on the right evidence or modalities. This lack of faithfulness can be dangerous in safety-critical power system applications, so there is a need for a systematic way to audit whether models base their answers on task-appropriate information.

Method: The authors propose a task-conditional faithfulness audit framework that: (1) preregisters task-specific evidence requirements (engineering importance); (2) compares those requirements with the model’s self-reported reliance on different modalities and with behavioral reliance measured via controlled ablations of modalities; and (3) when discrepancies are found, applies an evidence-gated correction mechanism that regenerates answers under explicit evidence constraints and re-audits them with independent ablations to verify improved grounding without degrading performance.

Result: Through case studies on IEEE 39-bus and 118-bus power system scenarios and three multimodal LLMs of different scales, the framework successfully identifies mismatches between required evidence and model behavior, diagnoses where faithfulness fails, and shows that evidence-gated regeneration can improve grounding while maintaining answer quality.

Conclusion: The proposed framework is effective for detecting, diagnosing, and correcting task-conditional faithfulness issues in multimodal LLMs used for grid diagnosis, providing a principled way to ensure that models not only answer correctly but do so based on the appropriate, engineering-relevant evidence.

Abstract: Multimodal large language models (LLMs) can combine topology, measurements, and incident text for grid diagnosis, yet answer accuracy does not establish that task-appropriate evidence was used. This letter proposes a general framework in order to conduct task-conditional faithfulness audit. It compares self-reported reliance, intervention-derived behavioral reliance, and preregistered engineering importance. The framework first registers task-specific evidence requirements and compares them with self-reported reliance and behavioral changes under controlled modality ablations. To resolve detected discrepancies, we design an evidence-gated correction and re-audit mechanism that regenerates failed responses under evidence constraints and independently re-ablates them to verify improved grounding without performance loss. Case studies evaluate three differently scaled LLMs on IEEE 39- and 118-bus scenarios. These results validate the framework ability to detect, diagnose, and correct task-conditional faithfulness failures.

</details>


### [255] [LLM-Assisted Ontology Engineering and Construction of a French Legal Knowledge Graph](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24551)
*G{é}nesis Montenegro,Mokhtar Boumedyen Billami,Catherine Faron,Fabien Gandon,Pierre Monnin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They build a two-stage, LLM-assisted workflow to turn complex French maintenance regulations into an ontology and a legal knowledge graph, showing that modern LLMs can produce robust, structured legal data with manageable post-processing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Maintenance regulations are hard to use in concrete cases and difficult to integrate into operational systems because they are long, complex legal texts; there is a need for automated, structured representations like ontologies and knowledge graphs to make this content computationally exploitable.

Method: They propose a two-stage workflow. Stage 1: start from a SEMLEG-based core ontology, use LLMs to openly extract typed entities and triples from a stratified sample of the corpus, normalize labels via embedding-based clustering/fusion, and induce candidate object properties together with their domain and range (signatures). Stage 2: use the resulting ontology as a schema to constrain a closed, ontology-guided extraction of triples across the full corpus to construct an RDF legal knowledge graph. They test this with GPT-4.1 and mistral-large-2512 on French maintenance regulations.

Result: LLMs produce stable structured outputs; nearly all extracted classes align with the ontology; embedding-based fusion strongly reduces duplicates in entities and predicates; fewer than 20% of extracted triples use properties not seen in the ontology-learning phase; however, many triples reuse known predicates with new domain–range combinations, indicating partial mismatch with learned signatures.

Conclusion: Their approach makes it feasible to transform complex French maintenance regulations into an ontology-grounded legal knowledge graph using LLMs, but it highlights that additional work on predicate normalization and systematic validation of new domain–range signatures is crucial before deployment in industrial maintenance workflows.

Abstract: Maintenance regulations are complex legal texts that are difficult to exploit when addressing a specific case and challenging to integrate into operational systems. This paper presents a two-stage LLM-assisted workflow for French maintenance regulations: ontology engineering from a SEMLEG-based core ontology, followed by construction of an ontology-grounded French legal knowledge graph. The first stage consists in the open extraction of typed entities and triples from a stratified corpus sample, the normalization of labels through embedding-based fusion, and the induction of candidate object properties with their signature (domain and range). The second stage uses the resulting ontology to guide the closed extraction of triples and RDF graph construction over the full corpus. Experiments with GPT-4.1 and mistral-large-2512 show robust structured outputs, near-complete class alignment, and a substantial reduction of duplicated entities and predicates after fusion. Fewer than 20% of triples introduce unseen properties, while lower exact signature compliance reveals new domain-range combinations for existing predicates. These results point to predicate normalization and the validation of newly observed relation signatures as key refinement steps for industrial maintenance settings.

</details>


### [256] [Hierarchical Group-Conditional Conformal Risk Control for Selective Prediction in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24562)
*Murilo Salem,Luísa Böhm,Daniel Pontes,Anderson Ferrugem*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces HG-CRC, a hierarchical post-hoc calibration method that extends conformal risk control to provide simultaneous error-rate guarantees across groups arranged in a user-defined hierarchy, improving fairness across heterogeneous user subpopulations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard conformal risk control (CRC) gives only marginal (population-level) risk guarantees for selective prediction with abstention. This allows systematic over-exposure of certain subgroups to errors, especially under shifts in group composition, leading to violations of risk budgets despite overall guarantees. The authors aim to provide stronger, per-group style guarantees that remain robust under heterogeneity and distribution shift, particularly for large language model applications with diverse users and tasks.

Method: They propose HG-CRC (Hierarchical Group-Conditional CRC), a post-hoc calibration scheme that operates over a user-defined hierarchy of groups (e.g., domain, difficulty, style).
