They perform a Bonferroni correction across all hierarchy nodes to obtain simultaneous coverage guarantees and use a leaf-first decision policy: for each example, they first try the most specific (leaf) group threshold; if its guarantee is uncertified or it abstains, they back off to increasingly coarser ancestor nodes. The method uses only a held-out calibration set and does not require retraining the underlying model.

Result: Across three LLMs (Qwen3-4B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Gemma-3-4B) and two benchmarks (ARC Challenge, MMLU-Pro) under eight stress-test configurations (including heterogeneity, distribution shifts, label noise, and quantization), HG-CRC achieves very low empirical violation rates of group risk budgets. On ARC Challenge for the stronger models (Qwen3-4B, Llama-3.1-8B), the observed violation rate is 0% and worst-group error rate (WGER) is 0; with 500 bootstrap trials, these are empirical upper bounds (true violation rate could be up to ~0.6%). On MMLU-Pro, the same models either abstain heavily or (for Llama) retain a small WGER of 0.014, while Gemma-3-4B, which is poorly calibrated, tends to abstain rather than violate budgets. Participation cost relative to standard global CRC is a 22–37 point decrease in non-abstained coverage. Ablation shows that including difficulty as a hierarchy dimension is critical: removing it brings violations back to ~11%. Bonferroni correction is required for the formal simultaneous guarantee and mainly affects setups with many hierarchy nodes.

Conclusion: HG-CRC provides a practical, training-free way to extend conformal risk control from population-level to hierarchical group-conditional guarantees, reducing worst-group risk and empirical violations across heterogeneous settings. While this comes at a coverage/participation cost and benchmark-specific behavior (sometimes heavy abstention), the method appears robust under diverse shifts and demonstrates that appropriate hierarchy design and multiple-testing correction can substantially improve fairness and reliability of LLM predictions across user subgroups.

Abstract: Large language models serve heterogeneous populations structured by domain, topic difficulty, and linguistic style. Conformal risk control (CRC) gives rigorous marginal risk guarantees for selective prediction with abstention, but marginal guarantees do not imply per-group ones: a model can meet the population budget while systematically over-exposing subgroups to errors. Under mild shift in group composition, standard CRC violates the budget in up to 47% of trials.
  We propose HG-CRC (Hierarchical Group-Conditional CRC), a post-hoc calibration framework enforcing simultaneous risk guarantees across all nodes of a user-defined group hierarchy. It applies a Bonferroni correction over nodes and a leaf-first policy that uses the most specific applicable threshold, falling back to coarser nodes when a finer one is uncertified or rejects the example. It needs only a held-out calibration set, with no retraining.
  We evaluate on three models (Qwen3-4B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Gemma-3-4B) and two benchmarks (ARC Challenge, MMLU-Pro) across eight configurations probing IID generalization, heterogeneity, mixture/domain/prompt/difficulty shift, label noise, and quantization. Main result: HG-CRC reaches an empirical 0% violation rate and WGER=0 on ARC Challenge for high-accuracy models (Qwen3-4B, Llama-3.1-8B). At 500 bootstrap trials these zeros are empirical upper bounds (true rate up to 0.6%), not certified. Results are benchmark-specific: on MMLU-Pro these models abstain entirely or (Llama) retain WGER=0.014. Gemma-3-4B, poorly calibrated here, degrades gracefully by abstaining. Participation cost vs. global CRC is 22 to 37 points. Ablations show hierarchical depth clears the budget: removing difficulty level returns violations to about 11%. Bonferroni is needed for the theoretical guarantee, though its empirical effect matters only with many nodes.

</details>


### [257] [TRACE-CTI: Auditable Post-Extraction Governance of TTP Claims with Knowledge Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24563)
*Federico Valletta,Giacomo Longo,Enrico Russo,Alessio Merlo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TRACE-CTI is a governance framework that manages, validates, and tracks trust in automated mappings from CTI reports to MITRE ATT&CK, using graph-based assertions, provenance, and consensus to improve precision at the cost of recall.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Automated extractors that map Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) reports to MITRE ATT&CK are error-prone, yet their outputs are often stored and consumed without adequate evidence, provenance, or validation history. This makes it hard for Security Operations Centers to know which extracted mappings can be trusted, to audit decisions, or to revoke trust safely over time. The paper is motivated by the need for explicit, auditable governance over extracted TTP (tactics, techniques, and procedures) claims, rather than opaque flat outputs.

Method: The authors propose TRACE-CTI, a post-extraction governance framework that operates on the outputs of different retriever–generator setups. It: (1) preserves run-level Predictions from individual extraction runs; (2) aggregates them into configuration-level GraphAssertions; (3) deduplicates and aggregates corroborating evidence across setups into ConsensusAssertions; and (4) exposes only those GraphAssertions that have validation grounds satisfying explicit policies. The framework encodes full provenance paths, versioned trust decisions, and revocation history across multiple GraphVersions. They evaluate it on two public CTI corpora (65 reports, 5,303 sentences) using a 2×3 matrix of retrieval and generator configurations, incrementally added across six graph versions.

Result: TRACE-CTI can ingest all experimental setups without changing schema, while keeping provenance complete and scopes disjoint. In the final graph, requiring more setup-level corroboration sharply increases precision but reduces recall: with at least one supporting setup, gold-aligned precision and recall are 25.3% and 88.2%; with unanimity across all six setups, precision rises to 90.6% while recall falls to 16.3%. The resulting graph can directly answer seven governance-related questions (on provenance, trust, versioning, dependency, disagreement, review queues, etc.) that a minimal flat output cannot fully answer without extra processing. Cross-family model pairs yield higher output diversity than same-family pairs, but the paper does not claim causal effects or independence.

Conclusion: TRACE-CTI demonstrates that governing extracted CTI-to-ATT&CK mappings as auditable graph assertions—with explicit provenance, validation grounds, and versioned trust states—enables fine-grained control over precision–recall trade-offs and supports complex governance queries that flat extractor outputs cannot. The work argues for treating TTP mappings as governed claims rather than static annotations, while noting that observed corroboration patterns are descriptive and do not establish strong statistical or causal conclusions.

Abstract: Security Operations Centers increasingly rely on automated mapping of Cyber Threat Intelligence reports to MITRE ATT&CK, yet extractor outputs remain fallible and are often stored without the evidence, provenance, and validation history needed to decide whether an individual mapping should be trusted. We present TRACE- CTI, a post-extraction claim-governance framework that preserves run-level Predictions, aggregates them into configuration-level GraphAssertions, materializes setup-deduplicated corroboration as ConsensusAssertions, and exposes only GraphAssertions backed by policy-compliant validation grounds. The framework retains native evidence granularity, complete extraction provenance, versioned trust decisions, and non-destructive revocation history. We evaluate TRACE-CTI on two public CTI corpora comprising 65 reports and 5,303 sentences, using a controlled 2 x 3 matrix of retrievers and generator families, incrementally ingested across six GraphVersions. All setups are incorporated without schema modification; provenance paths remain complete, operational scopes remain disjoint, and every trusted GraphAssertion has an active qualifying validation ground. Cross-generator-family setup pairs exhibit greater output diversity than same-family pairs. At the final graph state, increasing setup support from k >= 1 to six-setup unanimity raises gold-aligned precision from 25.3% to 90.6%, while recall decreases from 88.2% to 16.3%. The graph also directly answers seven questions about provenance, trust, versioning, dependency, disagreement, and review-queue that the evaluated minimal flat output cannot fully answer without enrichment or reprocessing. These results support explicit, auditable governance of extracted TTP claims; the observed corroboration trajectory is descriptive and does not establish statistical independence or a causal model-family effect.

</details>


### [258] [DSCH-Loss: A Dynamic Semantic Channel Objective for Deep Semantic Hashing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24567)
*Tobias J. Bauer,Christian Riess,Daniel Loebenberger,Christian Bergler*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes Dynamic Semantic Channel Hashing (DSCH), a new loss function for deep semantic hashing that removes loss discontinuities and improves retrieval performance, measured with tie-aware mAP, over state-of-the-art methods across datasets, modalities, architectures, and hash lengths.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing deep semantic hashing methods rely on fixed, predefined semantic channels in Hamming space and loss functions based on label-derived Hamming distances. This causes discontinuities in the loss landscape, making optimization harder and potentially limiting retrieval performance. Moreover, evaluation with standard mAP does not properly handle ties induced by discrete Hamming distances, leading to ambiguous performance assessments.

Method: The authors redesign the semantic-channel-based loss by introducing Dynamic Semantic Channel Hashing (DSCH), where the semantic channels in Hamming space are dynamically sized and positioned instead of being fixed a priori. This is intended to smooth the loss landscape and provide better gradients for training deep hashing networks. They also advocate and adopt tie-aware mAP as the evaluation metric to correctly deal with tied distances in Hamming space. Experiments are conducted on two popular datasets, using two different deep model architectures and multiple hash code lengths, for both intra-modal and cross-modal retrieval tasks.

Result: Across 40 different retrieval tasks (cross-modal and intra-modal) and four hash code lengths, models trained with DSCH outperform those trained with other state-of-the-art loss functions in 35 tasks. The gains are consistent, with tie-aware mAP improvements up to 1.75 percentage points over the second-best method, and are robust across datasets and architectures.

Conclusion: Dynamic Semantic Channel Hashing produces a smoother, more optimizable loss landscape for deep semantic hashing and, when combined with tie-aware mAP for evaluation, leads to consistently better retrieval performance than prior loss formulations. The approach generalizes well across modalities, architectures, datasets, and hash lengths, making it a strong candidate for semantic hashing tasks that require efficient approximate nearest neighbor search in high-dimensional spaces.

Abstract: Semantic hashing methods for generating short binary hash codes that allow efficient approximate nearest neighbor search in high-dimensional data spaces have gained extensive consideration in recent years. Deep learning-based methods offer better semantic capturing capabilities than traditional approaches relying on manual feature engineering. Moreover, they enable a data-driven approach to semantic hashing across diverse data modalities, yielding high-quality cross-modal hash codes within a shared Hamming space. Previous work investigated the properties of this Hamming space and introduced a loss function based on predefined so-called semantic channels with fixed width and Hamming distances derived from label similarities. However, this formulation also introduced discontinuities into the loss landscape, complicating optimization. Based on these observations, we propose a newly designed loss function, Dynamic Semantic Channel Hashing (DSCH), using dynamically sized and positioned semantic channels in order to avoid loss landscape discontinuities. Furthermore, we endorse the use of tie-aware Mean Average Precision (mAP) as evaluation metric as it addresses the ambiguity in sample retrieval ordering, which emerges from the discreteness of hash code distances. Finally, multiple experimental settings conducted on two popular datasets and incorporating two different model architectures provide strong evidence that training using the DSCH objective outperforms training using other state-of-the-art loss functions. In a total of 35 out of 40 cross-modal and intra-modal retrieval tasks, models trained with DSCH achieve significantly higher tie-aware mAP scores across all four tested hash code lengths, showing compelling results across model architecture and used dataset. The mAP score uplifts are consistent and amount up to 1.75 percentage points compared to the respective second best.

</details>


### [259] [LLM-SoccerArena: Benchmarking LLMs on Real-World Predictions in Sports](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24573)
*Jonas Schröder,Jonas Schweisthal,Oliver Müller,Markus Weinmann,Stefan Feuerriegel*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They propose LLM-SoccerArena, a live, prospective benchmark and platform to evaluate how well large language models forecast real-world sports outcomes, demonstrated on the 2026 FIFA World Cup.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluating LLMs’ forecasting ability on real-world uncertain events is hard because existing benchmarks are static, retrospective, and cannot test how models synthesize current information to predict unknown future outcomes. The authors want a systematic, prospective way to measure forecasting performance in realistic settings.

Method: They design LLM-SoccerArena, an open-source, prospective benchmark platform focused on real-world soccer tournaments. It logs timestamped, schema-validated probabilistic forecasts for unresolved events along with prompts, model versions, tool traces, and costs. The benchmark uses a factorial experimental design varying four factors: (1) LLM model version, (2) level of information access (e.g., web vs no web), (3) prompting strategy, and (4) forecast horizon (how far before kickoff the prediction is made). They test the setup via a large-scale evaluation of the 2026 FIFA World Cup, having seven LLMs forecast all 104 matches plus 15 tournament-level questions.

Result: The platform successfully collects structured, prospective forecasts and supports detailed performance analysis. In the World Cup case study, they produce quantitative comparisons across models and experimental conditions. One concrete finding: LLMs with web access perform better than those without, but only slightly, with a 0.023 improvement in Brier score. They also analyze how performance changes with forecast horizon, information access, and prompting strategy, though details are not in the abstract.

Conclusion: LLM-SoccerArena is a practical, extensible framework for live evaluation of LLM forecasting on unresolved sports events. It shows that current state-of-the-art LLMs can be systematically compared on real-world prediction tasks and that additional web access yields only modest forecasting gains. The authors position the platform as a continuously updated, open-source benchmark that can generalize to future tournaments and league competitions, offering a foundation for ongoing, prospective evaluation of LLMs’ predictive capabilities.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly support decisions about uncertain future events, yet evaluating their ability to forecast real-world outcomes remains difficult. In particular, existing benchmarks are typically static and retrospective, and therefore cannot test how information is synthesized by LLMs to predict future events under uncertainty. We introduce LLM-SoccerArena (https://llm-soccerarena.com), a prospective live benchmark that evaluates how well LLMs forecast real-world sports events before the outcomes are known. LLM-SoccerArena provides (1) a prospective live benchmark protocol, (2) a public open-source platform, and (3) a factorial benchmark design together with tournament-related questions (e.g., which team will win). LLM-SoccerArena automatically records timestamped, schema-validated forecasts of unresolved events, together with prompts, model versions, tool traces, and costs. The factorial design varies along four dimensions: (1) model version (e.g., GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.8); (2) information access; (3) prompting strategy, and (4) forecast horizon. We demonstrate LLM-SoccerArena through a large-scale evaluation of the 2026 FIFA World Cup, in which seven LLMs generated forecasts for all 104 matches and 15 tournament-related questions. We provide a detailed analysis of model performance across information access, prompting strategy, and forecast horizon. As a result, LLM-SoccerArena provides new evidence about the forecasting performance of state-of-the-art LLMs. For example, LLMs with web access outperform those without, but only by a small margin (i.e., a 0.023 improvement in Brier score). Overall, LLM-SoccerArena provides a flexible, open-source platform for prospective benchmarking of unresolved events. LLM-SoccerArena will be continuously updated, and can be directly applied to future national and international tournaments and league competitions.

</details>


### [260] [SIREN: Towards End-to-End Extreme-Weather Early Warning with Experience-Grounded LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24588)
*Hang Ni,Weijia Zhang,Fan Liu,Mengqian Lu,Hao Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They build a benchmark and an LLM-agent framework (SIREN) for fully automated extreme-weather early warning, and show it beats prior weather agents on many tasks and full warning chains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Extreme-weather early warning is crucial but current systems rely heavily on human experts, making them costly, slow, and hard to scale. Existing LLM-based weather tools only handle narrow, isolated tasks and do not model the full, interdependent workflow from data analysis to actionable warnings. The authors want to automate this full chain to improve efficiency, scalability, and potentially timeliness and quality of warnings.

Method: 1) Design SIREN-Bench, a benchmark with 600 QA instances covering 19 tasks mapped to four core warning procedures plus a full end-to-end warning chain. 2) Use this benchmark to systematically evaluate current weather-agent frameworks and identify capability gaps. 3) Propose SIREN, an experience-grounded LLM-agent framework that: (a) provides an agentic execution environment able to integrate heterogeneous weather evidence and tools; and (b) introduces a family of agent harnesses that leverage historical cases via retrieval, skill distillation, and predictive modeling. 4) Experimentally compare SIREN to baseline weather agents across both individual tasks and complete warning chains.

Result: Benchmarking on SIREN-Bench shows that existing weather-agent systems perform poorly on many tasks and particularly struggle with end-to-end warning workflows, highlighting substantial capability gaps. In extensive experiments, SIREN consistently achieves higher performance than baseline agents on individual early-warning procedures as well as on full, chained early-warning scenarios, demonstrating the benefits of its experience-grounded design and case-based harnesses.

Conclusion: Automated, end-to-end extreme-weather early warning with LLM agents is feasible but requires frameworks explicitly designed around operational workflows and historical-case grounding. SIREN-Bench exposes the limitations of current systems, while SIREN’s experience-grounded architecture significantly improves both component tasks and full warning chains. This establishes a new benchmark and a stronger baseline for future research on AI-assisted operational weather warning systems.

Abstract: Early warning of extreme weather is essential for mitigating the societal, economic, and environmental risks posed by hazardous weather events. However, expert-centered warning workflows are costly, labor-intensive, and difficult to scale throughout the warning-to-action process. Although recent advances in Large Language Model (LLM) agents have enabled the automation of weather-related tasks, existing studies remain centered on isolated scientific tasks and overlook the chain of interdependent processes required for operational extreme-weather early warning. To bridge this gap, this study investigates automated end-to-end extreme-weather early warning through LLM agents. We first develop SIREN-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark comprising 600 question-answer instances across 19 tasks, and covering four individual warning procedures and an end-to-end warning chain. Evaluation on SIREN-Bench reveals substantial capability gaps in existing weather agent frameworks. This motivates us to develop SIREN, an experience-grounded agent framework inspired by experts' use of historical cases, which combines an agentic execution environment integrating heterogeneous weather evidence and tools with a family of agent harnesses that exploit historical cases through retrieval, skill distillation, and predictive modeling. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SIREN outperforms weather-agent baselines on both individual warning procedures and end-to-end warning chains.

</details>


### [261] [Artificial Intelligence and Innovation Ecosystem: Evolutionary Developments, Challenges, and Future Directions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24589)
*Zhimin Zhang,Chengzhen Ma,Jia Chai,Rongxin Zhan,Huansheng Ning,Lingfeng Mao,Dan Zhang,Suiping Jiang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper conceptualizes an Artificial Intelligence Innovative Ecosystem (AIIE), analyzes how AI shapes its evolution across stages, and discusses opportunities and future challenges.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing work on Innovative Ecosystems (IE) lacks a systematic account of how AI, as a general-purpose digital technology, reconfigures innovation spaces and dynamics. As AI becomes deeply embedded in economic and social systems, there is a need to clarify its specific roles, contributions, and risks within IEs to guide theory building and practice.

Method: The authors: (1) review and synthesize conceptual frameworks of IEs and decompose them into physical, social, and thinking spaces; (2) define the concept of an Artificial Intelligence Innovative Ecosystem (AIIE) from a spatial perspective and characterize AI’s contributions; (3) adopt an evolutionary perspective to describe AI’s roles at different development stages of AIIE; (4) use enterprise development cases to validate the feasibility, effectiveness, and rationality of the AIIE concept and its evolutionary description; and (5) conduct a forward-looking analysis of challenges AIIE may face, structured around four perspectives.

Result: They obtain a structured definition and conceptual model of AIIE anchored in three spaces, identify stage-specific roles AI plays in the evolution of innovation ecosystems, and provide case-based support that this framework is applicable in real enterprise contexts. They also categorize key future challenges for AIIE into four dimensions (not fully detailed in the abstract) that could hinder its development.

Conclusion: AI not only accelerates digitization and intelligence within existing Innovative Ecosystems but also reshapes the ecosystem itself, forming a distinct Artificial Intelligence Innovative Ecosystem with specific spatial characteristics and evolutionary patterns. The proposed AIIE framework is conceptually and empirically plausible, and recognizing AI’s limitations and the outlined challenges is essential to unlocking new research directions and guiding the sustainable evolution of AIIE.

Abstract: The development of the Innovative Ecosystem (IE) presents a new paradigm for economic integration, collaborative advancement, and shared achievements. The rise of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has significantly accelerated the global processes of digitization, informatization, and intelligence. Exploring how AI can leverage inherent characteristics to influence the development trajectory of IE is a topic that warrants further investigation. Given AI's increasing prominence and role within IE, the paper analyzes this new form, examining both AI's unique contributions to IE and its potential challenges. Firstly, the paper synthesizes the conceptual frameworks surrounding IE, decomposing them into manifestations in physical, social, and thinking spaces. Furthermore, the concept of Artificial Intelligence IE (AIIE) is introduced from a spatial perspective, with an exploration of the characteristics AI contributes to IE. Subsequently, the paper employs an evolutionary perspective to analyze the roles provided by AI during different development periods of AIIE. The paper then verifies the feasibility, effectiveness, and rationality of the AIIE's definition and analyzes AIIE development from an evolutionary perspective using enterprise development examples. Finally, acknowledging AI's inherent limitations, the paper examines potential challenges facing AIIE in the future from four perspectives, aiming to identify new research avenues for the further development of AIIE.

</details>


### [262] [Efficiency Matters in Autonomous Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24647)
*Haiqian Yang,Yuan Cao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper argues that AI-driven autonomous research systems should be evaluated not only on final solution quality but also on how efficiently they search, proposes AUC of the Pareto frontier as a metric for search efficiency, shows that no single search algorithm dominates across tasks, and introduces a fluid search method that adaptively combines multiple search strategies to achieve near-oracle efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluations of AI-driven autonomous research systems largely focus on the final outcome quality (e.g., best-found solution), ignoring how much evaluation budget is spent to get there. As AR moves into domains where evaluating candidate solutions is costly (e.g., physical experiments in science), efficiency of the search process becomes crucial. There is a need for metrics and methods that explicitly consider this efficiency dimension and for search strategies that perform well when the best search structure is not known in advance.

Method: The authors propose a new evaluation dimension: search efficiency, quantified by the area under the curve (AUC) of the Pareto frontier that trades off solution quality against evaluation cost. They empirically compare several families of search algorithms—hill climbing, beam search, tree search, and evolutionary search—on twelve systems-optimization tasks, analyzing both efficiency and final outcome quality. Recognizing that no single search structure is uniformly best, they introduce "fluid search," an adaptive procedure that uses a portfolio bandit to dynamically allocate a fixed evaluation budget over a forest of heterogeneous search processes, effectively learning which structures work best on a given task as the search proceeds.

Result: Experiments on twelve systems-optimization tasks show that: (1) no single search structure (hill climbing, beam search, tree search, evolutionary search) is consistently the most efficient across tasks; (2) methods that ultimately find the best final result can nonetheless be inefficient, consuming much more evaluation budget before reaching that result; and (3) the proposed fluid search procedure yields the highest overall search efficiency, with performance that closely approaches that of an oracle that is pre-informed of the best search structure for each task.

Conclusion: Search efficiency is a critical but distinct performance dimension for evaluating AI-driven autonomous research systems, especially in settings where evaluations are costly. Final outcome quality alone is insufficient to characterize system performance. The proposed AUC-based efficiency metric and empirical analysis demonstrate the variability and trade-offs among common search structures. Fluid search, by adaptively allocating budget across multiple search strategies, provides a practical, generally strong approach that achieves near-oracle efficiency without prior knowledge of which search structure is best for a given task.

Abstract: AI-driven autonomous research (AR) systems are becoming increasingly effective across a broad range of tasks. Their performance, however, is still evaluated primarily by the quality of the final outcome. In this paper, we argue that the efficiency of the solution-search process is an equally important but often overlooked dimension of performance. A strong AR system should not only produce high-quality results, but also reach them with as small a budget as possible. Search efficiency will become increasingly important as AR expands from domains with inexpensive verification, such as mathematics and coding, to real-world scientific settings in which solution evaluation may require costly physical experiments. To capture this dimension, we propose evaluating AR systems using the area under the curve (AUC) of the Pareto frontier, alongside final outcome quality. We compare several families of search algorithms, including hill climbing, beam search, tree search, and evolutionary search, across twelve systems-optimization tasks. We find that no single search structure is consistently the most efficient. We also show that search efficiency and final outcome quality are distinct performance dimensions: a method that eventually achieves the best result may nevertheless improve slowly and consume substantially more evaluation budget before reaching that result. Because the most effective search policy is generally unknown in advance, we introduce an adaptive procedure called fluid search, which uses a portfolio bandit to dynamically allocate a fixed evaluation budget across a forest of search processes. Across the evaluated tasks, fluid search achieves the highest overall search efficiency, closely matching the performance of a per-task oracle that is given the best search structure for each task in advance.

</details>


### [263] [Reason-Mediated Behavioral Models for Auditing LLM Social Simulators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24649)
*Atharva Pandey,Gautam Jajoo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper evaluates whether large language models used as social simulators not only match human survey answers but also match the underlying reasons, using a sunscreen product test as a case study.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluations of LLM social simulators mostly check if model-generated outcomes resemble human outcomes, ignoring whether the underlying rationales align with humans. This is problematic because models can give the right final answers for the wrong reasons, undermining their use in research and decision-making. The authors want a stronger evaluation that tests alignment of intermediate reasoning, not just outcomes.

Method: They run a 94-person sunscreen concept test where each participant evaluates three product concepts and provides open-ended rationales. They convert these rationales into structured, signed "reason states" Z (positive reasons supporting adoption, negative reasons blocking it). Holding fixed respondent descriptors D, category context K, and treatment X, they test (1) whether human rationale-derived Z improves prediction of purchase intent Y, and (2) whether an LLM, without access to human rationales or outcomes, can simulate comparable Z. They then compare predictive power and qualitative alignment of human vs LLM reason states.

Result: Human rationale-derived reason states significantly enhance held-out prediction of purchase intent, demonstrating that the extracted reasons are behaviorally informative. LLM-generated reasons, while often linguistically plausible, are brittle: they tend to mirror the wording and framing of the concept board rather than capturing the respondent’s true acceptance or rejection path. Consequently, LLM-simulated reasons are less predictive and less aligned with actual human reasoning patterns.

Conclusion: The paper introduces an evaluation framework for LLM-based social simulators centered on "reason states"—structured representations of rationale-derived reasons. While these states do not themselves identify causal effects, they offer a practical, interpretable audit of whether a simulator’s stated reasons track the evidence used by humans. The findings show that current LLMs can produce plausible-sounding justifications that fail to match human reasoning, implying that evaluations must go beyond outcome similarity to scrutinize intermediate reasoning alignment.

Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as social simulators, including as synthetic survey respondents. Most evaluations ask whether simulated outcomes resemble human outcomes. We argue that this is necessary but too weak: a simulator can match the final answer while using the wrong rationale-derived reason pattern. We study this problem through a 94-person sunscreen concept test in which each respondent evaluated three product concepts and wrote open-ended rationales. We map those rationales into signed reason states $Z$, where positive signs support adoption and negative signs block it. This gives a practical audit: holding respondent descriptors $D$, category context $K$, and concept treatment $X$ fixed, do human rationale-derived reasons help predict behavior $Y$, and can an LLM simulate the same reason state without seeing the human rationale or outcome? Human rationale-derived reasons substantially improve held-out prediction of purchase intent. LLM-simulated reasons are more brittle: they often sound plausible, but frequently echo the concept board rather than recover the respondent's acceptance or rejection path. The paper contributes an evaluation framework for social simulators. Reason states do not identify natural causal effects by themselves, but they provide an interpretable test of whether a simulator's stated reasons align with human evidence.

</details>


### [264] [Eviction as Estimation: A Fixed-Lag Smoothing View of Test-Time Memory, and When Measuring Beats Accumulating](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24667)
*Maruthi Vemula,Neeraj Praneeth Gajula*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper studies how language models with limited memory should decide which past tokens to retain, framing it as estimating whether each item will be reused and exploring a middle ground between online policies and ideal offline optimal caching.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing KV-caching and memory management methods for language models (e.g., StreamingLLM, H2O, SnapKV) must irrevocably decide what to keep or discard immediately when a token arrives, either based only on the past or on a prediction of the future. This is suboptimal compared to Belady’s offline optimum, which assumes full knowledge of future use, but that is unrealizable in practice. There is an unexplored middle regime where one can look slightly into the near future via the model’s own behavior before committing memory decisions. The authors want to formalize this space, understand when more sophisticated measurement helps over simple attention accumulation, and honestly characterize the limits of such approaches on realistic benchmarks.

Method: They recast memory retention as a hidden-signal estimation problem: for each stored item, predict whether it will be reused. They introduce a single axis, the commit lag H, to unify methods: H=0 corresponds to online filters and learned predictors that decide immediately; infinite H corresponds to Belady’s offline optimum with full future knowledge. They then propose using fixed-lag smoothing: wait a bounded number of steps, observe which items near-future correct predictions actually attend to, and only then commit the keep/drop decision. This yields a training-free policy called RMM, a strict generalization of H2O that reduces to H2O when the measurement over items is uniform. They evaluate RMM in controlled synthetic settings where reuse patterns are endogenous and separated in time and in realistic settings using NVIDIA’s KVPress harness to compare against SnapKV, H2O, and StreamingLLM on question answering and streaming multi-turn tasks.

Result: In controlled experiments where token reuse is clearly separated and driven by the model’s own behavior, the proposed demonstrated-utility signal (attention weighted by correctness) is much better at identifying which memory slots will be reused than simple accumulated attention. In these settings, a model with small bounded memory under RMM can behave similarly to one with much larger memory. However, on independent third-party benchmarks using natural text, RMM provides little or no advantage: it is roughly comparable to H2O for single-turn question answering and actually underperforms both H2O and SnapKV in streaming multi-turn scenarios.

Conclusion: Measuring demonstrated utility via fixed-lag smoothing provides a principled framework that interpolates between purely online heuristics and the offline optimal policy, and can substantially improve memory use in synthetic regimes with sharp, endogenous reuse. Yet on standard natural-text benchmarks, where the model is mostly correct and attention already aligns well with reuse, demonstrated utility degenerates to accumulated attention and yields no clear gains. The main contribution is thus a conceptual and empirical mapping of when and why measurement-based memory management can beat simple attention accumulation, rather than a new state-of-the-art compression method.

Abstract: A language model with a bounded working memory must repeatedly decide which stored items to keep. Every deployed method decides the moment an item arrives, from the past (StreamingLLM, H2O) or from a guess about the future (SnapKV). We recast the choice as an estimation problem on a hidden signal, whether an item will be reused, placing existing methods on one axis, the commit lag $H$: online filters and learned predictors commit at $H=0$, while Belady's offline optimum sits where the whole future is known. The missing regime in between, fixed-lag smoothing, waits a bounded number of steps, observes which items a correct near-future prediction attended to, and only then commits. This measurement, demonstrated utility, turns Belady's unobservable future request into something we read off the model itself. We instantiate it as a training-free policy, RMM, a strict generalization of H2O that reduces to it exactly when the measurement is uniform. In controlled settings where reuse is endogenous and separated in time, demonstrated utility identifies used memory far better than accumulated attention, and a small bounded memory behaves like a much larger one. But on independent third-party benchmarks, run inside NVIDIA's KVPress harness against its own SnapKV, H2O, and StreamingLLM implementations, the advantage mostly disappears: RMM is on par with H2O for single-turn question answering and loses to both H2O and SnapKV in a streaming multi-turn setting. The cause is simple: on natural text the model is correct about most tokens, so weighting attention by correctness barely changes it, and demonstrated utility collapses onto accumulated attention unless reuse is sharp and endogenous, which standard benchmarks do not exercise. Our contribution is the framework and an honest map of when measuring beats accumulating, not a new state of the art.

</details>


### [265] [ERUnderstand: Evaluating Vision-Language Models on Structured ER Diagrams](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24707)
*Ali Ansari,Yasmin Mohammadi,Farnoush Nili,Parsa Esmaeilkhani,Longin Jan Latecki,Eduard Dragut*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: They build and release ERUnderstand, a large-scale benchmark and dataset for converting ER diagrams in images into structured, machine-readable schemas, and evaluate current vision-language models on it.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: ER diagrams are crucial for conceptual database design, but they are usually only available as images, not structured schemas. This makes it hard to use AI systems to understand, transform, or generate databases from existing ERDs, and there is no standardized, large-scale benchmark to measure progress on this task.

Method: The authors collect 2,960 ER diagrams from three sources: curated educational material, real-world schemas, and synthetically generated diagrams. These span various domains, notations, complexities, and include extended ER (EER) constructs. For each diagram, they create a standardized, machine-readable representation of the schema elements. They then design an evaluation protocol for fine-grained measurement and benchmark state-of-the-art vision-language models, including reasoning-augmented variants, on the task of extracting schema structures from ERD images.

Result: On this benchmark, current vision-language models can reliably recover common ERD elements (achieving F1 scores above 0.74) but perform poorly on more complex or less frequent constructs such as weak entities (down to 0.28 F1), multivalued attributes (0.14 F1), and N-ary relationships (0.07 F1). Models that incorporate explicit reasoning improve overall scores by 15–25%, yet they still degrade significantly with more complex diagrams and are influenced by linguistic priors rather than purely visual evidence.

Conclusion: ERUnderstand fills a key gap by providing the first standardized, large-scale benchmark for structured understanding of ER diagrams, enabling systematic evaluation of multimodal models on conceptual database schema understanding. Current models are far from solving the task, particularly for advanced EER constructs and complex diagrams, so the benchmark highlights substantial headroom for future research. The dataset, toolkit, and generation code are openly released to foster progress.

Abstract: Entity-Relationship Diagrams (ERDs) are central to conceptual database design, yet they are typically available only as rendered images rather than machine-readable schemas, limiting AI-assisted database engineering. We introduce ERUnderstand, the first large-scale benchmark for structured understanding of ER diagrams, comprising 2,960 diagrams collected from curated educational sources, real-world schemas, and synthetically generated examples spanning diverse domains, notations, complexity levels, and Extended Entity-Relationship (EER) constructs. Each diagram is paired with a standardized machine-readable representation for fine-grained evaluation of schema elements. Evaluating state-of-the-art Vision-Language Models (VLMs), we find that while common ERD elements are recovered reliably (F1 > 0.74), performance drops sharply on weak entities (as low as 0.28 F1), multivalued attributes (0.14 F1), and N-ary relationships (0.07 F1). Reasoning-augmented models improve overall performance by 15-25% but remain sensitive to linguistic priors and increasing diagram complexity. ERUnderstand provides a standardized benchmark for evaluating multimodal understanding of conceptual database schemas. The benchmark, dataset, evaluation toolkit, and generation code are publicly available at https://github.com/salinaria/ERUnderstand.

</details>
